## Khuddaka Nikāya
## Udāna-aṭṭhakathā
## Namo Tassa Bhagavato Arahato Sammāsambuddhassa
## Introduction (Ganthārambhakathā)

I pay homage to the Buddha, the true refuge, who is the Great Compassionate One, who has crossed to the further shore of the ocean of the fivefold knowable things (ñeyyadhamma) [through his omniscient knowledge], who teaches the Dhamma that is subtle, profound, and beautiful through various methods, and who desires the welfare and happiness of those to be led (veneyya) through the power of loving-kindness.

I pay homage to that supreme ten-fold Dhamma, which is constantly honored [through practice and realization] by the Buddhas, and by which [the Buddha], being endowed with the three knowledges, the eight knowledges, and the fifteen modes of conduct (caraṇa), leads his kinsmen to be converted out of the world of saṃsāra.

I pay homage to that Noble Saṅgha (Ariya Saṅgha) of eight individuals, who are endowed with virtues such as morality (sīla), concentration (samādhi), wisdom (paññā), and liberation (vimutti), and who are established in the paths and fruits; they are like an unsurpassed field for sowing the seeds of merit.

I have gained this merit through the intention of paying homage to the Triple Gem; by the power of that merit, may all obstacles be removed in every way [as I compose this commentary].

The Great Sage (Mahesi), who greatly desires the welfare of beings and who sought the noble Dhamma such as the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha), preached those inspired utterances (udānas) through various pure origins.

The teachers who performed the communal recitations (saṅgīti) of the Dhamma, while collecting all those inspired utterances together, included the text named 'Udāna' in the collection.

[This Udāna text] illustrates the joy arising from the Buddha's spiritual urgency (dhamma-saṃvega) and is adorned with verses originating from the mind associated with joy (somanassa).

Because the meaning of that Udāna text is to be penetrated only by profound knowledge, although it is difficult for me to compose a commentary (aṭṭhakathā) explaining its meaning, [I shall do so].
2:
Because the Dispensation (Sāsana) of the Teacher together with the commentaries still exists, and the decisions of the former great teachers also remain, therefore, relying on that Dispensation, penetrating the five Nikāyas with knowledge, and depending on the method of the ancient commentaries, I shall compose the commentary explaining the meaning of the Udāna according to my ability. It will be very pure, unconfused with the views of those not belonging to the Mahāvihāra, containing subtle decisions on the meaning, and not contradicting the tradition of the noble dwellers of the Mahāvihāra, while carefully avoiding meanings that have appeared repeatedly. Let the virtuous ones properly receive this explanation of the meaning from me, who desires the long-lasting of the True Dhamma and is analyzing its meaning.

In that word 'Udāna', for what reason is it called 'Udāna'? It is called Udāna because it is 'uttered forth' (udānanatṭhena). What is this called Udāna? It is an utterance (udāhāra) inspired by the force of rapture (pīti). For example, just as a substance to be measured, such as oil, which cannot be contained in the measuring vessel and overflows, is called 'avaseka' (overflow); and just as water that cannot be contained in a tank and flows over is called 'ogha' (flood); even so, when a particular utterance, accompanied by the expansion of thought (vitakka) inspired by the force of rapture, cannot be contained within the heart, it becomes excessive and, unable to remain inside, comes out through the vocal door (vacīdvāra). Such a special utterance, made without regard for a recipient, is called an 'Udāna'. This kind of occurrence is also found through the power of spiritual urgency (dhamma-saṃvega).

This Udāna occurs in some places in the form of verses (gāthā) and in some places in the form of prose (vākya). As for the characteristic of Udāna mentioned in the commentaries as 'associated with verses consisting of joy and knowledge', that is said according to the majority. This is because, for the most part, Udānas are preached in the form of verses and are inspired by rapture and joy (pīti-somanassa). However, the characteristics of Udāna are also found in prose passages such as, 'Monks, there is that sphere where there is neither earth nor water...' and in verses such as, 'Whoever harms with a stick beings who desire happiness...' and in passages such as, 'If you fear suffering, if suffering is unpleasant to you...'

Thus, this Udāna is of three types: spoken by the Omniscient Buddha (Sabbaññu-buddha-bhāsita), spoken by Paccekabuddhas (Paccekabuddha-bhāsita), and spoken by disciples (Sāvaka-bhāsita). Among them, the Udāna spoken by Paccekabuddhas includes those found in the Khaggavisāṇa Sutta, such as, 'Having laid aside the stick against all beings, not harming any one of them...' Udānas spoken by disciples include those such as, 'All my lust is exhausted, all hatred is uprooted, all delusion is destroyed...'
3:
"Laying aside the stick toward all beings, and not harming even a single one among them," and so forth, this appears in the Khaggavisāṇa Sutta (Sutta Nipāta, Cūḷaniddesa, Khaggavisāṇa Sutta Niddesa). There are also inspired utterances (udānas) spoken by the disciples—

"All passion has been abandoned by me, all hatred has been uprooted, all delusion has been specially destroyed by me; I have become cooled and attained Nibbāna," and so forth, as found in the Theragāthā—

"I was restrained in body, in speech, and also in mind; having uprooted craving along with its root, I have become cooled and attained Nibbāna," and so forth, as found in the Therīgāthā. These inspired utterances of those Elders and Sisters are not only inspired utterances (udānas) but are indeed also lion's roars (sīhanāda). Although there are inspired utterances spoken by deities such as Sakka, like "O, the gift, the supreme gift, is well-established in Kassapa," and those spoken by humans such as the Brahmin Ārāmadanda, like "Namo tassa bhagavato," which were included in the three Councils, those inspired utterances are not intended here. Indeed, only those inspired utterances which were spoken by the Blessed One himself through the impact of the vocal organs, which are the words of the Conqueror (Jinavacana), and which the Blessed One referred to as 'Udāna' when pointing out the ninefold division of the scriptural Dhamma (pariyatti-dhamma)—only those were chanted as 'Udāna' by the Great Elders who were the Reciters of the Dhamma (dhamma-saṅgāhaka). Only those are taken here as the subject to be commented upon.

However, the inspired verse shown by the stanza "Anekajātisaṃsāraṃ," etc., which was uttered by the Blessed One at the foot of the Bodhi tree by way of an inspired utterance, and which is an inspired verse not abandoned by many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas—because it was spoken by the Blessed One to the Treasurer of the Dhamma (Venerable Ānanda) at a later time, the teachers who were the Reciters of the Dhamma did not include it in the Udāna Pāḷi but chanted it in the Dhammapada. Also, the inspired utterance, "Kondañña has indeed understood, Kondañña has indeed understood," which was spoken by the Blessed One with a resonance capable of informing the deities and humans in the ten-thousandfold world system—that speech, uttered by the Blessed One at the conclusion of the teaching of the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta...
4:
...seeing that the Elder Kondañña was the very first among all disciples to attain the Noble Path (Ariya Magga), which is a portion of the Dhamma realized by Himself as it was taught, and having as its cause the reflection on the fruitfulness of His own exertion; and at the first Enlightenment (paṭhama-bodhi), having as its cause the proper reflection on all inspired utterances—it was merely an exclamation produced by joy and gladness (pīti-somanassa), like the words "Evaṃ me sutaṃ..." etc. It should be understood that because it does not manifest the process of arising or ceasing like the words "Yadā have pātubhavanti dhammā," etc., it was not chanted by the Reciters of the Dhamma in the Udāna Pāḷi.

This Udāna teaching is included in the Suttanta Piṭaka among the three Piṭakas: Vinaya Piṭaka, Suttanta Piṭaka, and Abhidhamma Piṭaka. Among the five Nikāyas: Dīgha Nikāya, Majjhima Nikāya, Saṃyutta Nikāya, Aṅguttara Nikāya, and Khuddaka Nikāya, it is included in the Khuddaka Nikāya. Among the nine factors of the Teacher's Dispensation (navaṅga-satthusāsana): Sutta, Geyya, Veyyākaraṇa, Gāthā, Udāna, Itivuttaka, Jātaka, Abbhutadhamma, and Vedalla, it is categorized under the Udāna factor.

"I received eighty-two thousand from the Buddha, and two thousand from the monks; these eighty-four thousand Dhammas are current in me." Among the eighty-four thousand units of Dhamma (dhammakkhandha) thus acknowledged by the Treasurer of the Dhamma, Venerable Ānanda, it is counted as consisting of several units of Dhamma. By way of chapters (vagga), there are eight chapters: Bodhivagga, Mucalindavagga, Nandavagga, Meghiyavagga, Soṇavagga, Jaccandhavagga, Cūḷavagga, and Pāṭaligāmiyavagga. By way of discourses (sutta), it is counted as eighty suttas. By way of verses (gāthā), it is counted as ninety-five inspired verses. By way of recitation sections (bhāṇavāra), there are about eight and a half recitation sections.

By way of connections (anusandhi), there is one connection by way of the connection of inquiry (pucchā-nusandhi) in the Bodhi Sutta. In the Suppavāsā Sutta, there are two connections by way of the connection of inquiry and the natural connection (yathā-nusandhi). In the remaining suttas, there is one connection each by way of the natural connection. There is no connection by way of inclination (ajjhāsayā-nusandhi) here. Thus, in every way, it is counted as eighty-one connections. By way of words (pada), there are twenty-one thousand and one hundred words. By way of verse-feet (gāthā-pāda), there are eight thousand four hundred and twenty-three feet. By way of syllables (akkhara), there are sixty-seven thousand three hundred and eighty-two syllables. Therefore, the teachers of the Council said this:

"The discourses of the Udāna text are exactly eighty,
The chapters are eight in brief,
And the verses are shown to be ninety-five."
5:
"In measure, there are eight and a half recitation sections (bhāṇavāra), and likewise, the connections (anusandhi) of the Udāna are eighty-one. The wise one should point out the words (pada) of this Udāna by counting them as twenty-one thousand and one hundred." By way of verse-feet (gāthā-pāda)—"One should point out the feet of this Udāna as eight thousand four hundred and twenty-three. The syllables (akkhara) of the Udāna are known to be sixty-seven thousand three hundred and eighty-two."

Among the eight chapters of that Udāna, the Bodhivagga is the first. Among the discourses, the first Bodhi Sutta is the beginning. Of that Bodhi Sutta also, the prologue (nidāna) beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ," spoken by the Venerable Ānanda at the time of the First Great Council, is the beginning. That First Great Council is indeed established in the order of the Pāḷi in the Vinaya Piṭaka (Cūḷavagga). The sequence of the narrative that should be spoken for the sake of proficiency in the prologue here has already been stated in the Sumangalavilāsinī, the Commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya; therefore, it should be understood in the same manner as stated in that commentary.

## 1. Bodhivagga
## 1. Commentary on the First Bodhi Sutta

In this Udāna scripture, there is the prologue beginning with "Eva၁ me suta၁" (Thus have I heard). In that prologue, "eva၁" is an indeclinable particle (nipāta). "Me" and so forth are nouns (nāma). In the phrase "Uruvelāya၁ viharati," "vi" is a prefix (upasagga) and "harati" is a verb (ākhyāta). In this same manner, the grammatical analysis of words should be understood in all places.

As for the meaning, the word "eva၁" has many different meanings, such as simile, instruction, approval, reproach, acceptance of words, manner, indication, emphasis (restriction), questioning, this meaning, measure, and so forth.

Indeed, the word "eva၁" occurs in the sense of a simile in such passages as: "Thus should a mortal, once born, perform many good deeds." It occurs in the sense of instruction (upadesa) in such passages as: "Thus you should advance, thus you should retreat." It occurs in the sense of approval (sampaha၁sana) in such passages as: "So it is, Blessed One; so it is, Sugata." It occurs in the sense of reproach (garaha၁a) in such passages as: "This low woman speaks thus of the shaven-headed ascetic, no matter who he may be." It occurs in the sense of acceptance of words (vacanasampaၱiggaha) in such passages as: "'Yes, Bhante,' those monks replied to the Blessed One." It occurs in the sense of manner (ākāra) in such passages as: "Bhante, I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One in this manner."

It occurs in the sense of indication (nidassana) in such passages as: "Young man, come, go to the Venerable Ānanda and, in my name, ask if the Venerable Ānanda is free from illness, free from suffering, active, strong, and living in comfort. Say, 'The youth Subha, son of Todeyya, asks if the Venerable Ānanda is free from illness, free from suffering, active, strong, and living in comfort.' And also say this: 'It would be good if the Venerable Ānanda would come to the house of the youth Subha, son of Todeyya, out of compassion.'"

It occurs in the sense of emphasis or ascertainment (avadhāra၁a) in such passages as: "'Kālāmas, what do you think? Are these things wholesome or unwholesome?' 'Unwholesome, Bhante.' 'Are they blameworthy or blameless?' 'Blameworthy, Bhante.' 'Are they censured by the wise or praised by the wise?' 'Censured by the wise, Bhante.' 'When undertaken and followed, do they lead to harm and suffering, or not? What is your view on this?' 'Bhante, when undertaken and followed, they lead to harm and suffering; such is our view (ascertainment) on this.'" It occurs in the sense of questioning in such passages as: "Do these people bathe well thus, anoint themselves well thus, trim their hair and beards thus..."

## Various Meanings of the Word 'Eva၁'

In the scriptures (Dĩ. Ni. 1.286) such as "Do they wear jeweled earrings thus?", the word "eva၁" occurs in the sense of questioning (pucchā). In passages such as "Many arts of this kind are thus; they have this manner," the word "eva၁" occurs in the sense of "this" (ida၁). Indeed, just as the word "gata" is a synonym for "pakāra" (kind/manner), so too the words "vidha" and "ākāra" are synonyms for "pakāra." Therefore, secular grammarians speak of the word "gata" combined with "vidha" in the sense of "pakāra." In the scriptures (A. Ni. 1.48) such as "Thus it revolves quickly; thus is the limit of life," the word "eva၁" occurs in the sense of measure (parimā၁a).

If one were to object: "In this passage, 'Did you think thus? Thus is the limit of life,' since the manner of questioning and the manner of comparison are expressed by the word 'eva၁,' is not 'eva၁' only in the sense of manner (ākāra)?" No, it is not, because there are specific distinctions. Here, the word "eva၁" is intended in the sense of manner (ākāra) when it denotes manner alone. However, in passages such as "Eva၁ byā kho," the word "eva၁" denotes a specific manner. These instances of "eva၁" denote a specific manner because they express the manner of questioning or the manner of measure. Thus, being used to denote a specific manner, similes and examples such as "Thus should a mortal..." are appropriate.

In that example:
"Just as from a heap of flowers one might make many garlands, so should a mortal, once born, perform many meritorious deeds."

In this context, the mortal who is subject to death should perform many meritorious deeds which are like garlands, because of the collection of causes for meritorious actions such as obtaining a human existence (which is like the base of the flower heap), associating with the virtuous, hearing the True Dhamma, wise reflection, and the possession of wealth, and because of being endowed with specific qualities such as beauty and fragrance. Since there is no difference in nature, the flower heap and the garlands are called similes. The manner of the simile for those meritorious actions is expressed indefinitely by the word "yathā" (as). Then it is expressed definitely by the word "eva၁" (so/thus). Since that manner of simile is made definite and is essentially a simile in meaning, it is said to "occur in the sense of a simile."

Furthermore, in the fulfillment of the appearance befitting a monk, which is indicated by "Thus, in this manner, one should advance," etc., whatever manner of indication exists there is essentially an instruction. Therefore, it is said to be "in the sense of instruction (upadesa) in such passages as: 'Thus you should advance, thus you should retreat.'"

In the passage "So it is, Blessed One; so it is, Sugata," those who understand the meaning as spoken by the Blessed One without distortion express a certain rejoicing and a certain manner of joy through the various qualities manifest therein...
8:
Gladdening and delighting by various means is called sampahaṃsana. In pointing out the meaning of that sampahaṃsana, that aspect of gladdening should be understood by applying it according to the method already stated.

In the passage "Evamevaṃ panāyaṃ," it should be understood by applying it according to the method already stated as an aspect of reproach. That aspect of reproach is understood to be manifested by the word "evaṃ" here because of its proximity to words of contempt such as "vasalī" (outcast/wretch). Just as reproach is shown here, it should be understood that aspects of similes and so forth are also stated because of their proximity to words such as "puppharāsi" (a heap of flowers) which are spoken by way of similes and so forth.

In the passages such as "Evaṃ no," in order to produce a decision by way of accepting a view that those aforementioned dhammas lead to harm and suffering, when the question "No vā kathaṃ vo ettha hoti" (Or how does it appear to you here?) is asked, it is said "Evaṃ no ettha hoti" (Thus it appears to us here); therefore, the determination of that aspect is clearly manifested by the word "evaṃ." However, when the aspect of those dhammas leading to harm and suffering is specifically marked, the word "evaṃ" has the sense of avadhāraṇa (ascertainment/emphasis); thus, it is said that in passages such as "Evaṃ no ettha hoti," it occurs in the sense of avadhāraṇa.

"Evañca vadehi" means "Speak to the monk Ānanda just as I speak." Since the aspect of what is to be spoken now is indicated by the word "evaṃ," it is said that here the word "evaṃ" has the sense of nidassana (indication).

These words "evaṃ," though expressing specific aspects, are said to have the meanings of similes and so forth because they occur in those specific senses such as similes. In the phrase "Evaṃ, bhante," however, because it is spoken by monks who are devoted to properly hearing and attending to the Dhamma, by way of acknowledging their established state in that taught Dhamma, the word "evaṃ" there has the sense of vacanasampaṭiggaha (acceptance of words). By that word "evaṃ" in the sense of vacanasampaṭiggaha, it means "It is well, Venerable Sir; it is excellent, Venerable Sir." That word "evaṃ" should be understood here in the senses of aspect (ākāra), indication (nidassana), and ascertainment (avadhāraṇa).

Among those three meanings, the word "evaṃ" in the sense of aspect (ākāra) shows this meaning: Who would be able to understand in every way the word of that Blessed One, which is subtle through various methods, which arises from many dispositions, which is endowed with meaning and phrasing, which possesses various miracles, which is profound in terms of Dhamma, meaning, teaching, and penetration, and which reaches the ears of all beings in accordance with their respective languages? Indeed, having generated the desire to hear with all one's might, it shows this meaning: "In such an aspect I have heard, remembered, and mastered it; I too have heard, remembered, and mastered it in one particular aspect."
9:
In this Dispensation, there are various methods by way of the divisions of gratification (assāda) and so forth, and by way of the divisions of objects and so forth, which possess the nature of unity (ekatta), diversity (nānatta), non-effort (abyāpāra), and suchness (evaṃdhammatā), known as the Nandiyāvaṭṭa method, the Pukkhalasīhavikkīḷita method (the method of the designation of persons), the Sīhavikkīḷita method, the Disālocana method, and the Aṅkusa method. Because it possesses such various methods, it is called nānānaya. Alternatively, the methods are the sequences of the Pali texts, which are of various kinds by way of designation (paññatti) and secondary designation (anupaññatti); by way of the partaking of defilement (saṃkilesa), purification (vodāna), the mundane (lokiya), the supramundane (lokuttara), and the mixture of both; by way of wholesome states (kusala) and so forth; by way of aggregates (khandha) and so forth; by way of summary (saṅgaha) and so forth; by way of the occasionally liberated (samayavimutta) and so forth; by way of establishment (ṭhapanā) and so forth; by way of wholesome roots (kusalamūla) and so forth; and by way of the Triplets of the Paṭṭhāna (tikapaṭṭhāna) and so forth. Therefore, they are called nānānaya. Because it is very subtle and fine through those various methods, it is called nānānayanipuṇa.

Inclination or desire itself is called ajjhāsaya (disposition). That disposition is of many kinds by way of the divisions of eternalism (sassata) and so forth, and by way of the divisions of having little dust in the eyes (apparajakkhata) and so forth. Alternatively, one's own disposition (attajjhāsaya) and so forth are themselves the many dispositions (anekajjhāsaya). Because that disposition is the source and cause for the arising of this Dhamma teaching, it is called anekajjhāsayasamuṭṭhāna.

It is called atthabyañjanasampanna (endowed with meaning and phrasing) because it is endowed with the fulfillment of meaning such as virtue (sīla) and so forth, and with the fulfillment of phrasing that clarifies that meaning; and because it is endowed with the six terms of meaning (atthapada): showing in brief (saṅkāsana), showing first (pakāsana), opening up (vivaraṇa), analyzing (vibhajana), making plain (uttānīkaraṇa), and designating (paññatti); and with the six terms of phrasing (byañjanapada): syllable (akkhara), word (pada), phrasing (byañjana), aspect (ākāra), language (nirutti), and description (niddesa).

It is called vividhapāṭihāriya (various miracles) because it has various or manifold miracles by way of the divisions of psychic power (iddhi), mind-reading (ādesanā), and instruction (anusāsanī), and by way of the divisions of the objects (visaya) and so forth of each of those three. In that word vividhapāṭihāriya, although there is a meaning that it is called pāṭihāriya because it removes opposites or because it clears away defilements such as lust (rāga), for the Blessed One there are no opposites such as lust that need to be removed. Even for worldlings (puthujjana), when the mind is free from upakkilesa, endowed with the eight qualities, and has struck down opposites, the various kinds of psychic power (iddhividha) can occur. Therefore, it cannot be called pāṭihāriya here by the common usage applied to those worldlings. However, if it is said that for the Great Compassionate Blessed One, the defilements in the continuities of beings to be tamed (veneyya) are the opposites, and it is called pāṭihāriya because it removes those defilements, then this statement is quite appropriate. Alternatively, it is called pāṭihāriya because it subdues the heretics (titthiya) who are the opposites of the Blessed One and the Dispensation. Those heretics are removed and cleared away by iddhi, ādesanā, and anusāsanī, both by way of removing their wrong views and by way of their inability to manifest their own views. Alternatively, this word "paṭi" makes known the meaning of "pacchā" (afterwards), as in the Pali passages such as "After he had entered, another brahmin came." Therefore, it is that which is made to occur afterwards by the task performed when the mind is concentrated and free from defilements; thus it is called pāṭihāriya. Alternatively, that which is made to occur after having killed one's own defilements by the path of the fourth jhāna is called pāṭihāriya. Iddhi, ādesanā, and anusāsanī are made to occur again for the benefit of beings after one is free from defilements and has completed the task.
10:
It is called *pāṭihāriya* (miracle/wonder) because it is brought forth later when the mind is concentrated, free from defilements, and the task to be done is completed. Alternatively, it is called *pāṭihāriya* because it arises after the defilements of one's own mind have been destroyed by the fourth *jhāna* and the Path (*magga*). The display of psychic power (*iddhi*), the teaching by reading minds (*ādesanā*), and the instruction (*anusāsanī*) are brought forth again for the benefit of beings by one whose defilements are cleared and whose task is done. Even though one's own defilements have been destroyed, they are called *pāṭihāriya* because they are capable of removing the defilements of others. *Paṭihāriya* itself is *pāṭihāriya*. Alternatively, each individual element in the collection of psychic power, mind-reading, and instruction that can remove defilements is called *pāṭihāriya*. Or, the fourth *jhāna* and the Path are called *pāṭihāriya* because they remove opposing defilements. The meaning of *pāṭihāriya* should be understood as that which arises in those states, or as the cause, or as that which proceeds from those states.

The four factors known as *dhamma* (the text), *attha* (the meaning), *desanā* (the teaching), and *paṭivedha* (the penetration) are profound. Just as the great ocean provides no footing and is difficult to enter for small animals like hares, so too the word of the Blessed One, endowed with these four kinds of profundity, provides no footing and is difficult to enter for those who have not accumulated a store of merit; thus it is called the profundity of *dhamma*, *attha*, *desanā*, and *paṭivedha* (*dhammatthadesanāpaṭivedhagambhīra*).

Although the sound of the Blessed One's Dhamma teaching is one, when it is being uttered in a single moment, it is capable of being understood by beings of various languages according to their own respective tongues, simultaneously. It should be understood that the power of the Buddhas is inconceivable, and thus the teaching reaches the ears of all beings in accordance with their own languages.

By way of introduction, [the Elder Ānanda] releases himself from the claim of being self-enlightened, saying, 'I am not the Self-Existent One (Svayambhū), I did not realize this by myself,' and instead points to the entire Sutta to be spoken now by saying, 'Thus have I heard; I too have heard it in this way.'

By way of affirmation, the Blessed One said, 'Monks, among my monk disciples who are of great learning (*bahussuta*), Ānanda is the foremost; among those who possess good memory, those who possess mindfulness, those who possess fortitude, and those who are attendants, Ānanda is the foremost.' And as the General of the Dhamma (Venerable Sāriputta) also praised him, saying, 'Venerable Ānanda is skilled in the meaning (*attha*), skilled in the Dhamma, skilled in the phrasing (*byañjana*), skilled in the linguistics (*nirutti*), and skilled in the sequence of what precedes and follows.' In accordance with such praise, Ānanda shows his own power of retention to arouse the desire to listen in beings. He conveys this meaning: 'Thus have I heard, noted, and retained; this Dhamma which was heard should be understood exactly as it is, without deficiency or excess, whether in meaning or in phrasing; it should not be understood in any other way than how it was recited at the Council.' Alternatively, it means it should not be understood in any other way than how it was heard in the presence of the Blessed One and how it was taught. Because the Blessed One's teaching has inconceivable power, this meaning implies that it is not possible to know that teaching in all its aspects.
11:
It arouses the desire to listen in beings. It conveys the meaning: "Thus have I heard, and that which was heard is exactly so, without deficiency or excess, whether in meaning or in phrasing; it should be regarded in this very way and not otherwise." "Not otherwise" means not in a manner different from how it was heard in the presence of the Blessed One; it does not mean in a manner different from how it was taught by the Blessed One. For the teaching of the Blessed One has inconceivable power, and it is said that it is not possible to understand it in all its aspects. The power of retention (*dhāraṇabala*) is simply the non-contradiction of the manner in which it was heard.

The word "me" is seen in three senses. Indeed, in passages such as "Food over which verses have been chanted is not to be eaten by me (*me*)," it has the sense of "by me" (*mayā*). In passages such as "It would be good for me (*me*), Bhante, if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief," it has the sense of "to me" (*mayhaṃ*). In passages such as "Monks, be heirs of my (*me*) Dhamma," it has the sense of "of me" (*mama*). In this context, however, it is suitable in both senses: "it was heard by me" and "my hearing."

In this regard, although the word "me" is seen in all three senses because it refers to one's own internal continuity (*sasantāna*) known as the self (*atta*) which is not another, it should be understood that the distinction in meaning is recognized through the specific roles of the instrumental (*karaṇa*), dative (*sampadāna*), and so on; thus it is said, "The word 'me' is seen in three senses."

The word "sutaṃ" (heard), whether with a prefix (*upasagga*) or without, has many different meanings such as going, being famous, being wet, accumulating, devotion/application, being cognizable by the ear, and being understood through the ear-door. Although a prefix modifies the action, because of its indicative nature (*jotakabhāva*), the word *suta* itself expresses those various meanings even when the prefix is present. Therefore, in extracting the meaning of the word *suta* without a prefix, it is not contradictory to include terms that have a prefix.

Among those meanings, in passages such as "*senāya pasuto*," it means "one who goes." In passages such as "*sutadhammassa passato*," it means "one who has a famous Dhamma." In passages such as "*avassutā avassutassa*," it means "a woman wet with lust for a man wet with lust." In passages such as "*tumhehi puññaṃ pasutaṃ anappakaṃ*," it means "accumulated." In passages such as "*ye jhānappasutā dhīrā*," it means "those wise ones devoted to *jhāna*." In passages such as "*diṭṭhaṃ sutaṃ mutaṃ*," it means "cognizable by the ear." "*Sutadharo*..."
12:
In terms such as "sutasannicaya" (Majjhima Nikāya, 1, 339), it means one who bears the Dhamma known by following the ear-door. In this sutta, however, the meaning of the word *suta* is "that which is borne by following the ear-door" (passive sense/kammasādhana) or "the act of bearing" (abstract sense/bhāvasādhana). If the word *me* is in the instrumental sense of "by me" (*mayā*), it is appropriate to say, "Thus by me it was heard and noted by following the ear-door." If it is in the possessive sense of "of me" (*mama*), it is appropriate to say, "Thus my hearing was the act of bearing by following the ear-door."

Thus, among these three words, the word *evaṃ*, used in conjunction with the word *suta*, indicates the function of the mind-door consciousness that arises immediately after the ear-door consciousnesses such as ear-consciousness and receiving consciousness, because it illuminates the act of hearing. The word *me* indicates the person endowed with the aforementioned consciousness. All sentences are accompanied by the meaning of the word *eva* because they have the benefit of emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*). The word *sutaṃ* indicates a grasping that is not deficient, not excessive, and not distorted, by way of rejecting non-hearing. Just as a Dhamma that is heard deserves to be called "only that which is heard," so too, such good hearing is a grasping that is not deficient, not excessive, and not distorted. Alternatively, in the view that a word expresses a meaning by way of excluding other meanings, since this word *sutaṃ* means "it is not unheard," it indicates a grasping that is not deficient, not excessive, and not distorted, by rejecting non-hearing. This is what is meant: "Thus have I heard; I did not see this with my own eyes, nor did I realize it through self-enlightened knowledge, nor did I obtain it by any other means. Indeed, it was only heard, and that hearing was a good grasping without deficiency, excess, or distortion." Or, if the word *evaṃ* is in the sense of emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*), the meaning should be construed thus: since the fixed (*niyama*) meaning of the word *suta* which depends on that emphasis is possible, the word *suta* depending on that emphasis should be understood as rejecting non-hearing and indicating a grasping that is not deficient, not excessive, and not distorted. Thus, it should be noted that the meaning of the word *suta* is also construed by way of the cause of hearing and the distinction of hearing.

Furthermore, the word *evaṃ* is taken to have the meaning of "manner" (*ākāra*), showing the occurrence in various ways upon the object because of grasping various meanings and syllables through the cognitive process (*vīthi*) occurring by following the ear-door. The word *me* shows oneself. The word *sutaṃ* shows the Dhamma, because the aforementioned cognitive process has the scriptural Dhamma (*pariyattidhamma*) as its object. The summary here is: "By the cognitive process, which is the instrument occurring in various ways upon the object, I have done nothing else; I have only done this act of listening to the Dhamma; this Dhamma has been heard."
13:
Furthermore, the word "evaṃ" is an indication of the Dhamma to be shown. Considering the word "evaṃ" as having the sense of indication (nidassana), it is so because the Dhamma to be shown has the nature of being indicated. Therefore, it should be understood that by the word "evaṃ", the entire sutta is encompassed and reflected upon. The word "me" shows the person. The word "sutaṃ" shows the function of the person. This is because the act of hearing mentioned in the word "suta" is connected with the stream of hearing-consciousness. In that stream of consciousness, the conventional designation "person" occurs. The act of hearing cannot be found in a mere stream of phenomena (dhamma) devoid of the conventional designation "person". The summary of this sentence is: "The sutta which I shall indicate, that sutta was thus heard by me."

Furthermore, the word "evaṃ" indicates the various modes of the stream of consciousness which grasps various meanings and sounds due to its occurrence on various objects. This is because the word "evaṃ" has the sense of "manner" (ākāra). This designation "evaṃ" is a designation of manner, because it has the nature of being designated based on the various modes of occurrence of phenomena. The word "me" is the indication of the agent (kattar). The word "sutaṃ" is the indication of the object (visaya). This is because the Dhamma to be heard is the place of occurrence for the person who is the agent of the act of hearing, by way of the act of hearing. By these words, the decision in grasping the object by the agent endowed with that stream of consciousness, which occurs in various ways, is shown.

Alternatively, the word "evaṃ" indicates the function of the person. This is because, by the word "evaṃ" which has the nature of showing the manner grasped or the emphasis of the heard Dhamma, the bearing of that manner etc. is the activity of the phenomena based on the conventional designation of a person; thus it is called the indication of the person's function. The word "sutaṃ" indicates the function of consciousness. This is because even for one who holds the view that a person exists, the act of hearing cannot occur without depending on consciousness. The word "me" indicates the person endowed with both functions. The occurrence of the word "me" certainly has a specific being as its objective basis, and the function of consciousness must be combined right there. The summary here is: "By me, the person endowed with the consciousness of the function of hearing, and who has the conventional designation of the act of hearing obtained by the power of consciousness, it was heard."

Furthermore, the designations "evaṃ" and "me" are "concepts of the non-existent" (avijjamānapaññatti) by way of the true ultimate reality (paramattha). This is because all meanings to be understood through sound must be approached through the medium of designation, and all designations are included within the six types of designations, such as the concept of the existent (vijjamānapaññatti). Therefore, just as a false meaning like a magic trick or a mirage is grasped through hearsay etc...
14:
It is not that the meaning is non-existent. Those ultimate realities (paramattha), such as form (rūpa) and sound (sadda), which are characterized by being affected (ruppana) and experiencing (anubhavana), etc., exist by way of ultimate reality in the true sense (saccikaṭṭha-paramattha). The meaning of the aspect (ākāra) expressed as 'evam' (thus) and 'me' (by me) is not an ultimate reality; therefore, it is called a concept of the non-existent (avijjamāna-paññatti), as it is not found by way of ultimate reality in the true sense. Therefore, in this context, how could that which is designated as 'evam' or 'me' exist in the ultimate sense? The concept 'suta' (heard) is a concept of the existent (vijjamāna-paññatti). This is because the sound-object (saddārammaṇa) perceived here by the ear-sensitivity (sotapasāda) exists in the ultimate sense.

Furthermore, 'evam' occurs by way of repeatedly reflecting on the aspects (ākāra) etc. to be considered, based on the phenomena (dhamma) that have come into the ear-door. 'Me' is called a derivative concept (upādā-paññatti) because it is spoken based on the aggregates (khandha) included in one's own continuity, which are distinguished by specific features such as the instruments of action (karaṇa), etc. 'Suta' is called a comparative concept (upanidhā-paññatti) because it is spoken in comparison to seeing (diṭṭha), etc. Although it occurs in the sound-base (saddāyatana) which is devoid of the nature of seeing, etc., the conventional term 'suta' is spoken in comparison to seeing, etc. This is because it is known as 'heard' (suta) in relation to what is seen (diṭṭha), sensed (muta), and cognized (viññāta), just as the concepts 'second', 'third', etc., occur in dependence on 'first', etc. This meaning is expressed as 'suta' because it is not unheard.

Here, by the word 'evam', non-delusion (asammoha) is shown. This is because the Venerable Ānanda reflects on the various aspects of the teachings he heard as 'evam' (thus), thereby demonstrating his non-delusion. A deluded person is unable to penetrate various meanings; [here] the discourses (suttas) are indicated, which are diverse and difficult to penetrate by way of the mode of conditions (paccayākāra). By the word 'suta', non-forgetfulness (asammosa) regarding what was heard is shown. This is because it can show the aspect of what was heard exactly as it was. One who forgets the teaching heard cannot later claim, "I have heard [this]."

Thus, through non-delusion, wisdom (paññā) is perfected. Due to the absence of delusion, it is perfected by the wisdom arising at the time of listening as well as by the wisdom of subsequent times. Likewise, through non-forgetfulness, mindfulness (sati) is perfected. Between that wisdom and mindfulness, by means of mindfulness preceded by wisdom, one is able to retain the sounds and syllables (byanjāna). The aspect of sounds to be penetrated is not very deep; since it is only necessary to retain them as heard, the function of mindfulness is greater. Wisdom is merely an auxiliary there. By means of wisdom preceded by mindfulness, one is able to penetrate the meaning (attha). Since the aspect of the meaning to be penetrated is very deep, the function of wisdom is greater. Mindfulness is merely an auxiliary there, and of mindfulness...
15:
Through mindfulness preceded by wisdom, one is able to bear only the words. In truth, the aspect of penetrating the words is not very deep; since it is merely bearing what has been heard, the function of mindfulness is more predominant there. Wisdom exists there only as an accompaniment. Because of this precedence of wisdom, and because of the ability to penetrate the meaning through wisdom preceded by mindfulness, by being endowed with the power of both, he is able to constantly guard the treasury of the Dhamma, which is complete in meaning and phrasing; thus, his status as the Treasurer of the Dhamma (Dhammabhaṇḍāgārika) is established.

Alternatively, by the word 'Evaṃ' (Thus), wise attention (yoniso manasikāra) is shown. Through that wise attention, the unerring accomplishment of the words to be mentioned hereafter—which have the meanings of manner (ākāra), illustration (nidassana), and emphasis (avadhāraṇa), and which illuminate various kinds of penetration—is established because it is grounded in the nature of the Dhamma. For one who does not attend wisely, various kinds of penetration are not possible. By the word 'Sutaṃ' (Heard), non-distraction (avikkhepa) is shown. Hearing the Sutta that has come down in the sequence of the text through the power of questioning such as 'Where was the Paṭhamabodhi Sutta spoken?', etc., is possible only when there is concentration (samādhi). For one with a distracted mind, there is no hearing. This is true; even when a person with a distracted mind is addressed with words complete in all meaning and phrasing, he says, 'I did not hear; please say it again.'

In this context, through wise attention, he fulfills the two wheels: right self-direction (attasammāpaṇidhi) and having done merit in the past (pubbe ca katapuññatā). For one who has not directed himself rightly or has not done merit in the past, such hearing of the Dhamma is not possible. Through non-distraction, he also fulfills the [other] two wheels: hearing the True Dhamma (saddhammassavana) and associating with good people (sappurisūpanissaya). For one who does not hear and is devoid of association with good people, such hearing is not possible. A distracted person is unable to hear, and for one who does not associate with good people, there is no hearing.

Alternatively: 'For whichever mental continuum there is the grasping of various meanings and phrasings due to various occurrences, for that person there is the pointing out of various aspects.' Such a good manner—which is the cause for fulfilling the welfare of others without remainder by penetrating the entire Dispensation through the distinction of the meaning and phrasing of the Buddha's words—is not possible for one who has not directed himself rightly or has not done merit in the past. Therefore, by this good manner 'Evaṃ', the Venerable Ānanda shows his endowment with the latter two wheels. By the word 'Sutaṃ', which is associated with hearing, he shows his endowment with the former two wheels. For one living in an unsuitable locality or devoid of association with good people, there is no hearing of the Dhamma.

Thus, through endowment with the latter two wheels, the purity of inclination (āsayasuddhi) is accomplished for the Venerable Ānanda. One who has directed himself rightly and has done merit in the past is one of pure inclination, because the defilements (kilesa) that are the causes of impurity of inclination are far removed. This is true; for it was said: 'A rightly directed mind can do for him what is even better than that' (Dhp. 43), and 'Ānanda, you have done merit; strive in exertion, and you will soon be free from taints (anāsava)' (DN. 2.207).

Through endowment with the former two wheels, there is purity of effort (payogasuddhi). Through living in a suitable locality, associating with good people, and following the example of the virtuous, the effort is exceedingly pure. Through that purity of inclination, endowment with practice (paṭipatti) is accomplished, because defilements such as craving (taṇhā) have been cleansed beforehand. Through purity of effort, endowment with learning (pariyatti) is accomplished. One who has exceedingly pure bodily and verbal effort is not distracted in learning but is courageous and clear, because there is no mental dissatisfaction. Thus, for the words of the Buddha, for which the Venerable Ānanda—who is pure in effort and inclination and endowed with both learning and practice—is like the dawn that precedes the rising sun, or like wise attention that precedes wholesome states...
16:
By following the example of the virtuous, a very pure application (payoga) arises. Through that purity of inclination (āsaya), the accomplishment of attainment (adhigama) is achieved. Since the defilements such as craving (taṇhā) and wrong view (diṭṭhi) have been cleansed from the very beginning, the accomplishment of learning (pariyatti) is achieved through the purity of application. One who possesses very pure bodily and verbal application, being free from remorse (vippaṭisāra), has an undistracted mind and becomes bold and proficient in the scriptures (pariyatti). Therefore, the words of Venerable Ānanda, who is pure in application and inclination and endowed with learning and attainment, are worthy to be the precursor to the words of the Blessed One, just as the dawn is the precursor to the rising of the sun, and as wise reflection (yoniso manasikāra) is the precursor to wholesome actions. Thus, wishing to establish the introduction (nidāna) in its proper place, he said "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" and so forth.

In another way—by this word "Evaṃ" (Thus), as mentioned before, by showing the penetration of various aspects, he shows his possession of the analytical insight of meaning (attha-paṭisambhidā) and the analytical insight of perspicuity (paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā). By this word "sutaṃ" (heard), either because of its proximity to the word "Evaṃ" or by showing the penetration of the various aspects to be heard with regard to the teachings to be spoken, he shows his possession of the analytical insight of Dhamma (dhamma-paṭisambhidā) and the analytical insight of language (nirutti-paṭisambhidā). And by speaking the word "Evaṃ" which shows wise reflection, he shows: "These dhammas have been reflected upon by me with the mind and well-penetrated by wisdom." Indeed, when the scriptural Dhamma (pariyatti-dhamma) is reflected upon by the mind in such a way as, "Here virtue is spoken of, here concentration, here wisdom; there are this many sequences (anusandhi)," and when the material and immaterial dhammas taught in those various discourses are well-defined and penetrated by wisdom—known as the acceptance of the Dhamma through reflection (dhamma-nijjhānakkhanti) or the full understanding of the known (ñāta-pariññā) accompanied by successive hearing and thought—in such a way as, "This is matter, this much is matter," then one becomes a bringer of welfare and happiness to oneself and others. By speaking the word "sutaṃ" which shows the engagement of hearing, he shows: "Many dhammas have been heard by me, retained, and practiced verbally." For the hearing, retention, and practice of the scriptural Dhamma are connected to the application of the ear. By both of these, showing the completeness of the meaning and the phrasing due to the Dhamma being well-proclaimed, he generates respect in hearing. For a person who does not respectfully listen to the Dhamma that is complete in meaning and phrasing is excluded from great welfare; therefore, having generated respect, the Dhamma should be heard attentively.

By this entire phrase "Evaṃ me sutaṃ," Venerable Ānanda, not claiming the Dhamma proclaimed by the Tathāgata as his own, transcends the ground of the unvirtuous and, by professing his status as a disciple, enters the ground of the virtuous. Likewise, from the false Dhamma...
17:
Venerable Ānanda raises the mind (from the false Dhamma) and establishes the mind in the true Dhamma. By showing, "This is merely what I have heard; indeed, it is the word of that Blessed One," he frees himself (from blame), points to the Teacher, entrusts the word of the Victor, and establishes the guide of the Dhamma (dhamma-netti).

Furthermore, by saying "Evaṃ me sutaṃ," not claiming it as his own creation and revealing his prior hearing, he says: "I personally received this from the Blessed One, who is bold due to the four grounds of self-confidence (vesārajja), who possesses the ten powers (dasabala), who stands in the place of the pre-eminent, who roars like a lion, who is the most excellent of all beings, the Lord of Dhamma, the King of Dhamma, the Master of Dhamma, who has the Dhamma as a lamp, who has the Dhamma as a refuge, the Turner of the excellent Wheel of Dhamma, the Perfectly Enlightened One. In this Dhamma, no doubt or uncertainty should be made regarding the meaning, the text, the word, or the phrasing." Thus, he destroys the lack of faith in this Dhamma among all gods and humans and generates the fulfillment of faith. Therefore, it is said:

"The disciple of Gotama, speaking thus, 'Evaṃ me sutaṃ,' destroys lack of faith and increases faith in the Dispensation."

"Ekaṃ" (One) is a designation for the limit of counting. This word "eka" is seen in the senses of "other," "excellent," "solitary," "number," and so forth. For instance, it is seen in the sense of "other" in such passages as: "Some say, 'The self and the world are eternal; this alone is true, any other is empty.'" It is seen in the sense of "excellent" in such passages as: "Unification of mind (ekodibhāva)." It is seen in the sense of "solitary" in such passages as: "One who has withdrawn alone." It is seen in the sense of "number" in such passages as: "Monks, there is only one (eka) moment and occasion for living the holy life." Here also, it should be understood in the sense of number. Therefore, it is said: "Ekaṃ is a designation for the limit of counting."

"Samayaṃ" (Occasion) is a designation for a defined time. "Ekaṃ samayaṃ" is an indefinite indication. In that context, the word "samaya" is seen in:
"Concordance, moment, time, group, cause, view, acquisition, abandonment, and penetration."

For instance, in such passages as: "Perhaps we might approach tomorrow, depending on the time and the occasion (samaya)," the meaning is "concordance" (samavāya); the intention is "having obtained the suitable time and the assembly of conditions." Therefore, it should be known as the concordance of conditions. "Monks, the moment for living the holy life..."
18:
It should be understood. In the words such as "Monks, there is only one moment (khaṇa) and one occasion (samaya) for living the holy life" (from the Aṅguttara Nikāya), it should be understood that "moment" (khaṇa) means "opportunity" (okāsa). Indeed, the arising of the Tathāgata and so forth is the opportunity for the holy life of the Path. Because of obtaining the cause which is the arising of the Buddha, the moment itself is the occasion. Whatever is called "moment" and "occasion" refers to the same single thing; this is the meaning. In the words such as "the hot occasion, the feverish occasion" (from the Vinaya Pācittiya), "occasion" (samaya) means "time" (kāla). In the words such as "the great assembly (mahasamaya) in the forest" (from the Dīgha Nikāya), "occasion" (samaya) means "group" or "assembly" (samūha). "Mahāsamaya" means the great gathering of monks and deities. In the words such as "Bhaddali, you did not penetrate the occasion... Bhaddali, you also did not penetrate this occasion" (from the Majjhima Nikāya), "occasion" (samaya) means "cause" (hetu). Here, "occasion" refers to the reason for the promulgation of the training rule. In the words such as "At that time, the wanderer Uggāhamana... was staying in Queen Mallikā’s park" (from the Majjhima Nikāya), "occasion" (samaya) means "view" (diṭṭhi). Because the sectarians residing in that park expressed their own "samaya"—meaning their own views—that park of the wanderers is called "Samayappavādaka" (the park where views are propounded).

"Whatever welfare there is in the present life,
And whatever welfare there is in the life to come,
Because of the attainment of welfare (atthābhisamaya), the steadfast one
Is called a wise man (paṇḍita)."

In these words (from the Saṃyutta Nikāya), "abhisamaya" means "attainment" (paṭilābha). "Atthābhisamaya" means the attainment of welfare. In the words such as "By the right abandonment of conceit, he has made an end of suffering" (from the Majjhima Nikāya), "abhisamaya" means "abandonment" (pahāna). Peace, abandonment, and disappearance are called "abhisamaya" (pahāna). In the words such as "the sense of oppression of the truth of suffering, the sense of being conditioned, the sense of burning, the sense of change, the sense of penetration" (from the Paṭisambhidāmagga), "abhisamaya" means "penetration" (paṭivedha). Because it is to be thoroughly known (penetrated), "paṭivedha" is called "abhisamaya". Since "abhisamaya" itself is the meaning, it is called "abhisamayaṭṭha". The characteristics such as oppression are spoken of collectively by way of being thoroughly known. Or, the object of "abhisamaya" or "paṭivedha" is called "abhisamayaṭṭha". These characteristics are spoken of in that way with certainty. Among those meanings, "oppression" (pīḷana) means the harming of one who possesses the truth of suffering, making them unable to expand. "Burning" (santāpa) means the burning or scorching by way of the suffering of suffering (dukkha-dukkhata) and so forth.
19:
In this context, it is called "samaya" in the sense of "concordance" (samavāya) because it brings about the meeting of cooperating causes. In this moment of the Buddha's arising, the holy life of the Path arrives well together with the individuals who are the support for that Path; thus, it is called "samaya" in the sense of "moment" (khaṇa/opportunity). At this time, or by this time, a being or a natural phenomenon arises together with [factors like] arising (uppāda) or co-nascent (sahajāta) conditions; thus, it is called "samaya" in the sense of "time" (kāla). In reality, "time" is merely the occurrence of phenomena and does not exist as a distinct entity, yet it is expressed in accordance with conventional usage as if it were the locus (adhikaraṇa) or the instrument (karaṇa) for the occurrence of phenomena. Because of the harmony or the simultaneous occurrence and existence of parts, it is called "samaya" in the sense of "group" (samūha), like the word "samudāya" (aggregation). Indeed, the simultaneous existence of parts is what is called a group. When the remaining conditions meet, the result arises or proceeds from this [meeting]; thus, it is called "samaya" in the sense of "cause" (hetu), like the word "samudaya" (origin). Because it is well-connected in the form of a fetter and occurs in its own objective field, or because beings, having firmly grasped it with this net of views, occur according to their inclinations, it is called "samaya" in the sense of "view" (diṭṭhi). Indeed, beings are bound excessively by the fetter of views. Because of meeting or combining, it is called "samaya" in the sense of "attainment" (paṭilābha). Because of peace or cessation, it is called "samaya" in the sense of "abandonment" (pahāna). Because it is the abandonment by cutting off (samuccheda-pahāna), the superior "samaya" is called "abhisamaya", like the word "Abhidhamma". It is called "abhisamaya" because it should be rightly reached and known face-to-face by knowledge; it is the undistorted nature of phenomena. It is called "abhisamaya" because one rightly goes to or understands [the truth] by being face-to-face with it; it is the penetration of the nature of phenomena as they really are. Thus, the occurrence of the word "samaya" in various meanings should be understood.

The reason for including the word "abhisamaya" when extracting the meanings of the word "samaya" should be understood in the same way as previously mentioned. In this particular context, however, the meaning of the word "samaya" should be noted as "time" (kāla), since concordance (samavāya) and other meanings are not applicable. Indeed, just like the location, the teacher (desaka), and the audience, only "time" is desired as the origin (nidāna) of the teaching. Since "samaya" here is intended as "time", among the various divisions of time such as year, season, month, half-month, night, day, morning, noon, evening, the first watch, the middle watch, the last watch, and the moment (muhutta), it is shown as "one occasion" (ekaṃ samayaṃ).

If it is asked: Why is time indicated here in an indefinite manner, and not specified by season, year, or day? Even though, among these occasions of years and so forth, whichever sutta [was taught] in whichever year...
20:
The Venerable Ānanda Thera knew well with his wisdom and had well-ascertained all that was spoken in terms of season, month, fortnight, part of the night, or part of the day. However, if one were to say, "Thus I heard: in such a year, in such a season, in such a month, in such a fortnight, in such a part of the night, or in such a part of the day," it would not be easy to remember, to teach, or to have others learn it; moreover, there would be much to be said. Therefore, having summarized all that meaning into a single phrase, he said "Ekaṃ samayaṃ" (At one time).

In another way... among the many various times (samaya) of the Blessed One that are very well-known among devas and humans—such as the time of conception, the time of birth, the time of spiritual urgency (saṃvega), the time of the Great Renunciation, the time of practicing austerities, the time of victory over the five Māras, the time of attaining Buddhahood, the time of dwelling in happiness in the present life, the time of teaching the Dhamma, and the time of Parinibbāna—among these times, he points to the "Ekaṃ samayaṃ" (one time) known as the time of teaching. Or else, among the times of the function of wisdom and the function of compassion, he refers to the time of the function of compassion; among the times of practicing for one's own benefit and the benefit of others, he refers to the time of practicing for the benefit of others; among the two duties of the assembled audience, he refers to the time of the Dhamma talk; among the times of teaching (desanā) and practice (paṭipatti), he refers to the time of teaching. Referring to one of these times, he said "Ekaṃ samayaṃ."

But why is it that here, unlike in the Abhidhamma where it is indicated by the locative case (sattamī-vibhatti) as "At which time (Yasmiṃ samaye) a wholesome consciousness of the sense sphere has arisen," and in other Sutta passages as "Monks, at which time (Yasmiṃ samaye) a monk, secluded from sensual pleasures...," and in the Vinaya where it is indicated by the instrumental case (karaṇa-vacana) as "At that time (Tena samayena) the Buddha, the Blessed One...," it is instead indicated by the accusative case (upayoga-vacana) in the sense of continuous duration (accanta-saṃyoga) as "Ekaṃ samayaṃ"? This is because a different meaning is possible in those [texts] and a different one here. For in that Abhidhamma and in other Suttas, the sense of the locative (adhikaraṇa) known as the basis (ādhāra-visaya) and the sense of the characteristic of an action by another action (bhāvena-bhāva-lakkhaṇa) are possible. Indeed, the term "samaya" in the sense of time or in the sense of a collection (samūha) is the basis (ādhāra) for the states such as contact (phassa) mentioned in that Abhidhamma. Likewise, although time does not exist in the ultimate sense (paramattha) as it is merely the occurrence of natural phenomena, it is designated as a basis for the phenomena occurring at that moment.
21:
Because it does not exist as a basis before or after that moment, it is like in the expressions "born in the morning" or "born in the evening." A group (samūha), too, though not existing in the ultimate sense apart from its members, is designated as the basis of its members through a form established merely by conceptualization, as in "a branch on a tree" or "barley grown in a heap of barley." The meaning in that Abhidhamma is: at whichever time and in whichever collection of states a wholesome consciousness of the sense sphere arises, at that very time and in that collection of states, contact and so forth also occur. Furthermore, by the occurrence of the samaya known as the coincidence of the moment and cause (khaṇa-samavāya-hetu), the occurrence of the states such as contact mentioned therein is marked. Just as in the example, "He goes while the cows are being milked; he comes when they have been milked," where the action of going is marked by the action of milking the cows, so too here, although it is said "Yasmiṃ samaye," since it is not devoid of the presence of ultimate phenomena, the meaning "when there is" is understood. Therefore, by the action of the presence of the samaya, the action of the arising of consciousness and the action of the occurrence of contact and so forth are marked. Likewise, when there is a certain time, a certain ninth moment, a certain cause such as wise attention (yoniso manasikāra), or a coincidence of conditions, a wholesome consciousness of the sense sphere arises; at that time, moment, cause, and coincidence of conditions, contact and so forth also occur. Therefore, to illustrate that meaning, it is indicated by the locative case.

In the Vinaya Piṭaka, the sense of cause (hetu) as in "he lives by means of food" or "he lives by means of study," and the sense of instrument (karaṇa) as in "he cuts with an axe" or "he digs with a spade," are appropriate. The time of the prescription of a training rule (sikkhāpada) is difficult to know even for the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta) and others. Taking that time of prescription as the cause or instrument, having heard of a transgression, having caused the Saṅgha of monks to assemble, having questioned and rebuked the person involved in the incident, and without letting the time known as the occasion of the incident pass, the Blessed One, while prescribing the training rules and considering the cause for the prescription of the training rule as in the case of the third Pārājika and others, dwelt in various places. Therefore, to illustrate that meaning, it is indicated by the instrumental case in the Vinaya.

However, in this Udāna text and others of this nature, the sense of continuous duration (accanta-saṃyoga) is appropriate. At whichever time this Udāna teaching arose along with its cause of origin, throughout that time the Blessed One dwelt continuously reflecting on the Dhamma, preceded by the Noble Dwelling (ariya-vihāra). Therefore, to illustrate the meaning of the accusative case as in "he recites for a whole month," it is indicated here by the accusative case. Because it should be so, this verse is stated: "Regarding those various meanings, the word 'samaya' is spoken in other places (Abhidhamma, Vinaya) with the locative and instrumental cases; but in this (Udāna), it is spoken with the accusative case." Ancient teachers, however, say that the indications as "Yasmiṃ samaye," "Tena samayena," and "Ekaṃ samayaṃ" differ only in usage; in all cases, only the sense of the locative case exists, and even when it is spoken as "Ekaṃ samayaṃ," the meaning is only "Ekasmim samaye" (At one time).
23:
The meaning of the word "Bhagavā" should also be understood by virtue of this verse. That meaning is explained in every aspect in the Visuddhimagga (Vism. 1.142); therefore, it should be expanded upon according to the method stated in that text. Alternatively, He is called "Bhagavā" because He associated with (*vani*) fortunes or because He vomited (*vamī*) fortunes. Indeed, the Tathāgata associated with, resorted to, cultivated, and practiced extensively the perfections (*pāramī*) such as giving (*dāna*) and virtue (*sīla*), as well as superhuman states (*uttari-manussadhamma*) such as the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and liberations (*vimokkha*); therefore, He is called "Bhagavā." Or else, He is called "Bhagavā" because He desired (*vani*) those very superhuman states, thinking, "How might they arise in the continuities of beings to be tamed?" Or else, He is called "Bhagavā" because He vomited (*vamī*) and discarded without lingering concern, like a glob of spit, the sovereignty (*issariya*) and retinue (*yasa*) known as "bhaga." This is true: the Tathāgata, regarding the glory of a Universal Monarch already in His hand—sovereignty over the four continents similar to the lordship of the deva realms—and the retinue of a Universal Monarch shining with the seven jewels, as not even worth a blade of grass, renounced them without attachment and went forth, and then penetrated and realized Perfect Enlightenment (*Sammāsambodhi*). Therefore, because He vomited these fortunes (*bhaga*) such as glory, He is called "Bhagavā." Or else, "bhāni" refers to the stars (constellations); they are called "bhaga" because they move and revolve together with them. The beauty depending on the distinctions of the physical world (*okāsaloka*) such as Mount Sineru, Mount Yugandhara, the continent of Uttarakuru, and the Himavantā mountains, exists for the duration of an aeon; He also vomited those worlds called "bhaga." This is because He transcended the abodes (*āvāsa*) of the beings living in those worlds, and because He abandoned the desire and lust (*chandarāga*) bound to those worlds, thus "vomiting" the *bhagas*. In such ways, the meaning of the word "Bhagavā" should be understood.

By this much, through the words "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" (Thus have I heard), by speaking the Dhamma as it was heard through the act of listening, the speaker makes the Dhamma-body (*dhamma-sarīra*) of the Blessed One manifest. By doing so, he consoles the people who are distressed at not seeing the Teacher, saying, "This Dispensation is not one whose Teacher has passed away; this Dhamma is your Teacher." For this was said by the Blessed One: "Ānanda, the Dhamma and Vinaya I have taught and laid down shall be your Teacher after my passing." By the words "Ekaṃ samayaṃ Bhagavā" (At one time the Blessed One...), he shows that the Blessed One was no longer present at that time, thereby establishing His Final Passing (*Parinibbāna*) with respect to the form-body (*rūpakāya*). By showing this, he strikes terror into those people intoxicated with the pride of life, saying, "Even that Blessed One, the teacher of such a Dhamma, the possessor of the ten powers, whose body was as solid as a diamond, has attained Parinibbāna; who else besides the Buddha should produce a longing for life?" Thus, he inspires them to strive with diligence in the True Dhamma.
24:
By saying the word "Evaṃ" (Thus), the perfection of the teaching (desanāsampatti) is indicated, as "Evaṃ" points to the entire discourse that is about to be spoken. By the words "Me sutaṃ" (I have heard), the perfection of the disciple (sāvakasampatti) and the perfection of hearing (savanasampatti) are indicated. This is because it shows the state of hearing of the Venerable Ānanda, the Treasurer of the Dhamma, who attained the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā) and was placed in the foremost position (etadagga) in five categories by the Blessed One. It also clarifies this meaning: "This Dhamma was heard by me personally; it is not something heard by hearsay, nor is it a tradition handed down through a succession of teachers." By the words "Ekaṃ samayaṃ" (At one time), the perfection of time (kālasampatti) is indicated, showing the occasion adorned by the appearance of a Buddha, as it was the time when the Blessed One was dwelling in the Uruvelā forest. Indeed, the time of a Buddha's appearance is the supreme perfection of time. By the word "Bhagavā" (The Blessed One), the perfection of the teacher (desakasampatti) is indicated, showing the state of the Teacher who is distinguished by His attributes, supreme among beings, and worthy of respect and honor.

"Uruvelāyaṃ" means in a place with a great heap of sand, or in a large mound of sand. Alternatively, "Uru" means sand, and "Velā" means limit or boundary. It should be understood here that "Uruvelā" refers to sand that has been brought and has exceeded its boundary.

In the past, before the appearance of a Buddha, ten thousand ascetics were living in that region. They made a pact: "Physical and verbal actions are evident to others, but mental actions are not. Therefore, if any ascetic thinks an unwholesome thought (micchāvitakka), let him accuse himself and, carrying sand in a leaf-cup or bowl, pour it in this spot; let this be his punishment (daṇḍakamma)." From that day on, whenever an ascetic thought such a thought, he would carry sand in a leaf-cup and pour it there. In this way, a great heap of sand gradually formed in that place. Later, people surrounded that great sand heap and made it a place for a shrine (cetiya). With reference to that sand-heap shrine, it is said: "Uruvelāyaṃ means in a place with a great heap of sand, or in a large mound of sand."

The word "viharati" (dwells), without specification, indicates being endowed with one of the dwellings: the dwelling of postures (iriyāpatha-vihāra), the divine dwelling (dibba-vihāra), the Brahma-dwelling (brahma-vihāra), or the noble dwelling (ariya-vihāra). In this context, however, it should be understood as indicating the engagement with the posture of sitting (āsana) among the postures of standing, sitting, walking, and lying down, as well as being endowed with the noble dwelling. Among those four postures, the Blessed One carries and maintains the physical body without it falling, by interrupting the discomfort of one posture with another. Therefore, the meaning of the word "viharati" should be understood here through the power of the dwelling in postures. Furthermore, since the Blessed One brings, offers, conveys, and produces various benefits for beings through the divine dwelling and others, the meaning should also be understood as "He dwells" in the sense of bringing various benefits through those dwellings.
25:
It is called "nadī" (river) because it sounds (nadati) and flows (sandati). "Tassā najjā" means of that flowing river (ninnagā). Regarding "Nerañjarāya," it should have been said "Nelañjalā" because it has pure water (nelaṃ jalaṃ), but by changing the letter 'l' to 'r', it is called "Nerañjarā." It means a river with water free from defects such as mud, moss, and weeds. Some teachers say that "Nerañjarā" is said where it should have been "Nīlajalā" (river with blue water). Alternatively, it should be understood as simply the name of that river. To show the place where the Blessed One dwelt on the bank of that river, it is said "Bodhirukkhamūle" (at the foot of the Bodhi tree).

In the phrase "Bodhirukkhamūle," the word "Bodhi" refers to the knowledge (ñāṇa) occurring in the four paths (magga); in this context, path-knowledge is called Bodhi. In the passage "The Great One of noble and vast wisdom reached Bodhi," Bodhi refers to omniscient knowledge (sabbaññutañāṇa). Since the Blessed One attained both types of Bodhi knowledge at this tree, the tree also received the name "Bodhi tree." Alternatively, the Blessed One is called "Bodhi" because He realized the seven factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga); because that tree was the support for the Buddha who was thus realizing them, the tree also received the name "Bodhi tree." "Mūle" means near that Bodhi tree. This word "mūla" is seen in the sense of "root" in passages such as "one should uproot the roots, even down to the roots of the usīra grass." It is seen in the sense of "extraordinary cause" (asādhāraṇa-hetu) in passages such as "Greed is the root (mūla) of the unwholesome." It is seen in the sense of "proximity" in passages such as "The area as far as the shadow spreads at noon, or where leaves fall when the wind is still, is called the foot of the tree (rukkhamūla)." In this context as well, the sense of proximity is intended. Therefore, "Bodhirukkhamūle" should be understood as "near the Bodhi tree."

"Paṭhamābhisambuddho" means having first become a Buddha by realizing the Four Noble Truths by Himself without a teacher, meaning the very first of all. By this much, the Venerable Ānanda, the Treasurer of the Dhamma, while establishing the introduction (nidāna) of the Udāna teaching, has clearly shown the time, the place, and the teacher, along with their specific qualities.

Here, an objector asks: "Why is the introductory statement (nidāna-vacana) spoken when the Dhamma and Vinaya are being compiled? Should not only the words spoken by the Blessed One be compiled?" The answer is given: It is for the purpose of ensuring the long endurance of the teaching, its non-confusion, and its credibility. Indeed, a teaching that is established by being linked with the time, place, teacher, and subject matter lasts for a long time, is not confused, and is credible. It is like a legal decision (vohāra-vinicchaya) that is bound by the place, time, actor, cause, and sign. For that very reason, when the Venerable Mahākassapa asked about the place and so on, saying, "Friend Ānanda, where was the first Udāna spoken?" the Venerable Ānanda, the Treasurer of the Dhamma, wishing to provide the answer...
26:
Venerable Ānanda, the Treasurer of the Dhamma, wishing to provide an answer, spoke the introduction to the Udāna teaching, starting with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" and so forth.

Furthermore, the introductory words are spoken to demonstrate the perfection (sampatti) of the Buddha. For the Blessed One, who is endowed with the six glories, the state of a Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha) is established because of the absence of prior composition, inference, tradition, or speculation. For the Perfectly Enlightened One, there is no use for prior composition and so forth, because his knowledge ranges over all things without obstruction, being the sole measure in all knowable things (ñeyya-dhamma). Likewise, the state of an Arahant (khīṇāsava) is established because of the absence of the teacher's fist (ācariya-muṭṭhi), stinginess regarding the Dhamma (dhamma-macchariya), and affection for the disciples of the Teaching. For an Arahant whose taints are entirely exhausted, there is no possibility of a teacher's fist and so forth in any matter; therefore, the teaching of the perfectly pure Arahant is for the sake of favoring others.

In this way, the first two kinds of intrepidity (vesārajja) are established by the Buddha's pure states, which indicate the absolute absence of ignorance and craving—the faults of a speaker that corrupt the perfection of view and virtue—and which manifest the perfection of knowledge (ñāṇa-sampadā) and the perfection of abandonment (pahāna-sampadā). From that, the latter two kinds of intrepidity are established because of the absence of confusion regarding things that are obstructive and things that lead out [of suffering]. Thus, the Blessed One's possession of the fourfold intrepidity and his practice for the benefit of himself and others are demonstrated by the introductory words, because he teaches the Dhamma with ready wit (paṭibhāna) arising on the spot, in accordance with the inclinations of the assembly gathered in various places. In this sutta, however, it should be connected by demonstrating the experiencing of the bliss of liberation (vimutti-sukha) and the contemplation of dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda). Therefore, it is said: "The introductory words are spoken to demonstrate the perfection of the Buddha."

Furthermore, the introductory words are spoken to demonstrate the perfection of the Teaching (Sāsana). For the Blessed One, whose every action is embraced by knowledge and compassion, there is no practice that is useless, nor is there a practice that is solely for his own benefit. Therefore, for the Perfectly Enlightened One, whose every action is for the benefit of others, his entire bodily, verbal, and mental action is called "Sāsana" (Teaching) because it repeatedly instructs beings according to their needs with the present benefit, the future benefit, and the ultimate benefit; it is not a poetic composition (kabba-racanā). That conduct of the Teacher, together with the time, place, speaker, assembly, and occasion, is demonstrated in various texts by the introductory words as appropriate. In this Udāna text, however, it should be connected by the attainment of supreme omniscience, the experiencing of the bliss of liberation, and the contemplation of dependent origination. Therefore, it is said: "The introductory words are spoken to demonstrate the perfection of the Teaching."

Furthermore, the introductory words are spoken to show the authority of the Teaching by demonstrating the authority of the Teacher. That demonstration of his authority should be understood according to the method mentioned below. By this word "Bhagavā" (the Blessed One), the Buddha's...
27:
...this meaning is clearly shown in every way by demonstrating the abandonment of all stains of defilements (kilesa-mala) such as greed, hatred, and delusion, and faults such as misconduct; by demonstrating his state as the most excellent of all beings; and by demonstrating his possession of special qualities such as omniscience and compassion which are not shared with others. This is a brief demonstration of the purpose of speaking the introductory words in this context.

That introduction should be understood as the prologue of this Udāna, starting from "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" up to the word "imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi" (uttered this inspired utterance). This is because it is the word spoken by the Reciters (Saṅgītikāras) at the time of the Council to demonstrate the Teacher's bodily and mental conduct from the beginning, showing how the Blessed One practiced and uttered this inspired utterance.

(An objection might be raised:) "Is it not that the words such as 'When this exists, this comes to be' should only be the words of the Blessed One? For apart from the Teacher, no one else is able to teach dependent origination." This is true. However, just as the Blessed One contemplated dependent origination at the foot of the Bodhi tree by way of reflecting on the nature of things (dhamma-sabhāva), so too, the Great Elders who were the Reciters of the Dhamma (Dhamma-saṅgāhaka) chanted the introduction to this Udāna uttered by the Blessed One, having made the contemplation of dependent origination the occasion (atthuppatti), by way of imitating the manner of teaching and the words taught in the Paṭiccasamuppāda-sīhanāda Sutta and others for the sake of enlightening those who are capable of being enlightened. Thus, a conclusion should be reached here that the aforementioned words are indeed the words of the Reciters. This same method applies to the suttas that follow.
