In this context, it should be understood that there are four ways of delivering a Sutta (sutta-nikkhepa): by one's own inclination (attajjhāsaya), by the inclination of others (parajjhāsaya), by way of a question (pucchāvasika), and by way of an occasion (atthuppattika). Just as suttas, though they are many hundreds and thousands in variety, do not exceed the sixteenfold division according to the method of the Paṭṭhāna such as the partaking of defilement (saṃkilesabhāgiya) and so forth, so too, all those suttas do not exceed the fourfold state by way of the delivery of a sutta such as by one's own inclination and so forth. Although in this context, the division of mixing one's own inclination and the occasion with the inclination of others and the way of a question is certainly possible, because the sequence of inclination and the sequence of questions can occur, yet because there is no mutual mixing of one's own inclination and the occasion, the absolute method of the Paṭṭhāna is not possible. Or, because the remaining deliveries that occur are included within them, it is said that there are four ways of delivering a sutta by way of the original delivery.
28:
Regarding these four types of Sutta-nikkhepa (occasions for the delivery of a Sutta), the following is the etymological definition (vacanattha): The setting down of a Sutta is 'nikkhepa'; the setting down of a Sutta is 'sutta-nikkhepa', which means the preaching of a Sutta. Alternatively, it is called 'nikkhepa' because it is set down; since the Sutta itself is the thing set down, it is called 'sutta-nikkhepa'. One's own inclination is 'attajjhāsaya'; it is called 'attajjhāsaya' because that inclination exists as the cause for that Sutta. Or, it is called 'attajjhāsaya' because one's own inclination belongs to this Sutta. The same method applies to 'parajjhāsaya' (the inclination of others). The power of a question is 'pucchāvasa'; it is called 'pucchāvasika' because that power of a question belongs to this Sutta. The arising of a matter which is the cause for preaching a Sutta is 'atthuppatti'; 'atthuppatti' is indeed 'aṭṭhuppatti'; it is called 'aṭṭhuppattika' because that specific circumstance belongs to this Sutta.

Alternatively, it is called 'nikkhepa' because the Sutta is set down by the following reasons; thus, 'attajjhāsaya' and so forth are themselves 'nikkhepa'. In this alternative interpretation, one's own inclination is 'attajjhāsaya'. The inclination of others is 'parajjhāsaya'. It is called 'pucchā' because it is asked; it refers to the matter to be asked. The speech of those receiving the Dhamma which occurs by the power of asking is 'pucchāvasa'; that same term 'pucchāvasa', in consideration of the word 'nikkhepa', is stated in the masculine form as 'pucchāvasiko'. Similarly, 'atthuppatti' itself is 'aṭṭhuppattiko'; thus should the meaning be understood in this context.

Among these four types of Sutta-nikkhepa, it is appropriate to treat 'attajjhāsaya' as a separate category of Sutta-nikkhepa because it does not depend on causes such as the ripening of the faculties (indriya) of others, but is a discourse delivered solely by one's own inclination for the purpose of establishing the lineage of the Dhamma (dhamma-tanti). As for 'parajjhāsaya' and 'pucchāvasika', since they are delivered upon the arising of causes for the discourse such as the inclinations and questions of others, how could they not be included in 'aṭṭhuppatti'? Or, since 'pucchāvasika' and 'aṭṭhuppattika' are delivered in accordance with the inclinations of others, how could they not be included in 'parajjhāsaya'? This should not be questioned. This is because only the arising of a matter that serves as the cause for preaching a Sutta, which is free from the aspirations (abhinīhāra) and inquiries (paripucchā) of others, is taken as 'aṭṭhuppatti'; therefore, 'parajjhāsaya' and 'pucchāvasika' are taken separately. This is true: in the Brahmajāla Sutta, Dhammadāyāda Sutta, and others, the arising of praise, blame, or material gains is called 'aṭṭhuppatti' as the cause of the discourse. A Sutta preached by making only one's own inclination the cause, without depending on the questions of others, is called 'parajjhāsaya'; a Sutta preached by the power of a question is called 'pucchāvasika'. Thus this meaning is clear.

Among those Sutta-nikkhepas, the delivery (nikkhepa) of these Udānas—the three Bodhi Suttas beginning with the first, the Mucalinda Sutta, the Āyusaṅkhārossajjana Sutta, the Paccavekkhaṇa Sutta, and the Papañcasaññā Sutta—is called 'attajjhāsaya'. The delivery of these Udānas—the Huhuṅka Sutta, the Brāhmaṇajātika Sutta, and the Bāhiya Sutta—is called 'pucchāvasika'. The Rāja Sutta, the Sakkāra Sutta, the Ucchādana Sutta, the Piṇḍapātika Sutta, the Sippa Sutta, the Gopāla Sutta,
29:
the Sundarika Sutta, the Mātū Sutta, the Saṅghabhedaka Sutta, the Udapāna Sutta, the Tathāgatuppāda Sutta, the Moneyya Sutta, the Pāṭaligāmiya Sutta, and the two Dabba Suttas—the delivery of these Udānas is 'aṭṭhuppattika' (due to a specific circumstance). The Pālileyya Sutta, the Piya Sutta, the Nāgasamāla Sutta, and the Visākhā Sutta—the delivery of these Udānas is both 'attajjhāsaya' and 'parajjhāsaya'. The delivery of the remaining fifty-one Suttas is 'parajjhāsaya'. Thus, the distinction of delivery (nikkhepa-visesa) of these Udānas should be understood by way of one's own inclination and so forth.

Among these Udāna teachings, those Udānas preached by the Blessed One in the presence of the monks were mastered by those monks by word of mouth just as they were preached, reflected upon in the mind, and then told to the Treasurer of the Dhamma, the Venerable Ānanda. However, those Udānas preached by the Blessed One in the absence of the monks were later preached again by the Blessed One to the Treasurer of the Dhamma, the Venerable Ānanda. Thus, it should be understood that the Venerable Ānanda, having collected all of them together and preserved them, taught them to the monks, and later, at the time of the First Great Council, included them in the collection as 'Udāna'.

In the phrases beginning with 'Tena kho pana samayena', 'tena samayena' is the instrumental case used in the sense of the locative (the seventh case), 'kho pana' is a particle (nipāta), and it means 'at that time'. At what time? At the time when the Blessed One, having first attained supreme enlightenment, was dwelling at the foot of the Bodhi tree on the bank of the river Nerañjarā in Uruvelā. At that time. 'Sattāhaṃ' means seven days; this is the accusative case used in the sense of continuous duration (accanta-saṃyoga). Because the Blessed One dwelt for those seven days continuously and exclusively in the bliss of the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti-sukha), 'sattāhaṃ' is stated in the accusative case by way of continuous duration. 'Ekappallaṅkena' means from the time he sat on the noble Unconquerable Throne (Aparājita-pallaṅka), the Jewel Throne (Vajirāsana), on the full moon day of Visākha before the sun had even set, without rising even once, in that same single cross-legged position as originally assumed.

'Vimuttisukha-paṭisaṃvedī' means he sat experiencing the bliss of liberation, which is the bliss of the attainment of fruition. In that phrase, 'vimutti' (liberation) consists of five kinds: liberation by substitution of opposites (tadaṅga-vimutti), liberation by suppression (vikkhambhana-vimutti), liberation by eradication (samuccheda-vimutti), liberation by tranquilization (paṭippassaddhi-vimutti), and liberation by escape (nissaraṇa-vimutti). Among them, 'tadaṅga-vimutti' refers to the liberation or abandoning of opposing states through various factors of merit such as the renunciation of gifts, and through factors of insight (vipassanā) such as the discernment of mind and matter, as long as those respective factors do not decline.
30:
How is it so? Liberation by substitution of opposites (tadaṅgavimutti) is: liberation from stinginess, greed, and so forth through giving; from killing and so forth through the undertaking of virtue; from the view of self (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) through the definition of mentality-materiality; from the views of no-cause and wrong-cause through the discernment of conditions; from indecision through the knowledge of overcoming doubt which occurs after that discernment of conditions; from the grasping of 'I' and 'mine' through the comprehension of groups (aggregates); from the perception of the path in what is not the path through the definition of path and non-path; from the view of annihilation (ucchedadiṭṭhi) through the vision of arising; from the view of eternalism (sassatadiṭṭhi) through the vision of passing away; from the perception of safety in what is fearful through the vision of fear; from the perception of gratification through the vision of disadvantage; from the perception of delight through the vision of disenchantment; from the lack of desire for deliverance through the knowledge of desire for deliverance; from the lack of equanimity through the knowledge of equanimity; from being contrary to Nibbāna and the stability of Dhamma through conformity knowledge (anuloma); and from the sign of formations (saṅkhāranimitta) through change-of-lineage knowledge (gotrabhū).

Liberation by suppression (vikkhambhanavimutti) is the liberation by preventing the occurrence of the hindrances such as sensual desire, and opposing states such as initial thought (vitakka), by means of concentration—divided into access concentration and absorption concentration—for as long as that concentration does not decline.

Liberation by eradication (samucchedavimutti) is the liberation by means of the absolute cutting off and abandoning of the group of defilements belonging to the side of origination (samudaya), so that they never occur again, in the mental continuum of the Noble One who possesses each path, due to the development of the four Noble Paths, as stated in the method: 'for the abandoning of views,' and so forth.

Liberation by tranquilization (paṭippassaddhivimutti) is the subsiding of defilements at the moment of Fruition. Liberation by escape (nissaraṇavimutti) is Nibbāna, which is liberated from all formations because it has escaped from all conditioned things.

In this context, however, the Fruition-liberation (phalavimutti) of the Blessed One, which has Nibbāna as its object, is intended. Therefore, it is said that 'experiencing the bliss of liberation' means he was sitting while experiencing the bliss of fruition attainment (phalasamāpatti), which is the bliss of liberation.

Liberation (vimutti) is the state of the mind being liberated due to the tranquilization of defilements; or, the mind thus liberated should be understood as liberation itself. The bliss born of that liberation or associated with it is the bliss of liberation (vimuttisukha). Because of the statement, 'Venerable Sir, that equanimity which the Blessed One spoke of as peaceful bliss,' equanimity here should also be understood as bliss. Thus it is said in the Sammohavinodanī Commentary: 'Equanimity, because of its peacefulness, is spoken of as bliss.'

The Blessed One enters only the fruition attainment of Arahantship associated with the fourth jhāna, not any other. Alternatively, just as the stilling of the suffering of formations is called bliss in such passages as 'The stilling of those [formations] is bliss,' so too, the liberation by tranquilization obtained in the supreme Fruition due to the tranquilization of all suffering of defilements should be understood as bliss here. This bliss of liberation...
31:
...is of two kinds according to the occurrence of Fruition consciousness: in the Path-process (maggavīthi) and at other times (kālantara). Indeed, immediately after each Noble Path, three or two Fruition consciousnesses, which are the results of that specific path and have Nibbāna as their object, arise because supramundane wholesome states give results immediately.

In the impulsion-process (javanavāra) where the Noble Path arises, when there are two moments of conformity (anuloma), the third is change-of-lineage (gotrabhū), the fourth is the Path consciousness, and after that, three Fruition consciousnesses occur. However, when there are three moments of conformity, the fourth is change-of-lineage, the fifth is the Path consciousness, and after that, two Fruition consciousnesses occur. Thus, it occurs by way of absorption (appanā) at the fourth or fifth moment, and no further than that because of the proximity to the life-continuum (bhavaṅga). Some teachers say that even the sixth consciousness attains absorption, but that is rejected in the Commentaries. Thus should the Fruition in the Path-process be understood.

Fruition at other times is said to occur by way of fruition attainment (phalasamāpatti). The Fruition consciousness arising for one emerging from the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) is also included in this 'Fruition at other times.' That fruition attainment should be understood essentially as absorption having Nibbāna as its object, which is the result of supramundane wholesome states.

Who enters that attainment and who does not? All worldlings (puthujjana) cannot enter it because they have not attained it. Likewise, lower Noble Ones do not enter a higher Fruition, and higher Noble Ones do not enter a lower Fruition, because [the lower fruition] has been tranquilized by the transition to a different state of person. Those various Noble Ones enter only their own respective Fruition.

Some teachers say that Stream-enters (sotāpanna) and Once-returners (sakadāgāmī) do not enter fruition attainment, and only the two higher persons enter it because they are those who have perfected concentration. That is groundless. Why? Because even a worldling can enter the mundane concentration he has obtained. Or what is the use of speculating on the reason here? For it is said in the Paṭisambhidāmagga, in the answer to the questions: 'Which ten equanimities regarding formations arise by way of insight? Which ten change-of-lineage states arise by way of insight?' that the entering of fruition attainment by those Noble Ones is also taught, with the words 'for the sake of the attainment of the fruition of stream-entry, for the sake of the attainment of the fruition of once-returning.' Therefore, the conclusion should be reached here that all Noble Ones enter their own respective Fruition.

Why do they enter it? For the sake of dwelling happily in the present life. Just as kings enjoy the bliss of sovereignty and deities enjoy divine bliss, so too the Noble Ones...
32: "Let us experience supramundane happiness," they determine the duration and enter the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) at the desired moment. How is it entered, how is it maintained, and how is it emerged from? It is entered through two modes: non-attention to any object other than Nibbāna, and attention to Nibbāna. As it was said: "Friends, there are two conditions for the attainment of the signless deliverance of mind (animitta-cetovimutti): non-attention to all signs (nimitta) and attention to the signless element (animitta-dhātu)." The sequence of entering it is as follows: A noble disciple (ariyasāvaka) who desires the attainment of fruition, having gone into seclusion and staying solitary and peaceful, should practice insight (vipassanā) on formations (saṅkhāra) by way of their rise and fall (udayabbaya), and so forth. For such a person practicing insight in due order, immediately after the change-of-lineage knowledge (gotrabhū-ñāṇa) which takes formations as its object, the mind enters and becomes established in Nibbāna by way of fruition attainment. Due to the inclination toward fruition attainment, for a trainee (sekha) as well, only fruition (phala) arises, not the path (magga). To those teachers who say, "A Stream-enterer (sotāpanna), having developed insight with the thought 'I will enter my own fruition attainment,' becomes a Once-returner (sakadāgāmī), and a Once-returner becomes a Non-returner (anāgāmī)," this should be said: "If that were so, a Non-returner would become an Arahant, an Arahant would become a Paccekabuddha, and a Paccekabuddha would become a Sammāsambuddha," which would lead to absurd consequences. Therefore, because insight achieves its purpose according to one's resolve and disposition, for a trainee as well, only fruition arises, not the path. Furthermore, if that person attained the path associated with the first jhāna, only the fruition associated with the first jhāna arises. If they attained the path associated with any other jhāna such as the second, only the fruition associated with that particular jhāna arises. Why, in this process, does the change-of-lineage knowledge not take Nibbāna as its object, as it does when it precedes the path-knowledge? Because fruition knowledges are not emancipatory (niyyānika). Only the factors of the noble path are emancipatory. For it was said: "Which states are emancipatory? The four unincluded (apariyāpanna) noble paths are emancipatory." Therefore, since the knowledge that is the immediate condition for the path-knowledge—which is definitely emancipatory and occurs by way of emerging from both (formations and signs)—must itself have emerged from the sign of formations, it is appropriate for it to have Nibbāna as its object. But this is not the case for the knowledge preceding fruition.
33: Because the noble path has been developed, the fruition knowledges—which occur as its result—do not completely eradicate defilements, are not emancipatory (niyyānika), and do not have the nature of emerging from the sign of formations. Thus, the knowledge preceding them never takes Nibbāna as its object. This is because the conformity knowledges (anuloma-ñāṇa) in both the path-process and the fruition-attainment-process have dissimilar modes. In the noble path-process, the conformity knowledges arise as mundane knowledge reaching the peak of perfection, being conducive to path-knowledge by specially breaking through the very gross masses of greed and so forth that have never been broken through before. In the fruition-attainment-process, however, since those respective defilements have already been completely eradicated by the respective paths, those conformity knowledges have no effort in eradicating defilements; they arise merely as preliminary preparation (parikamma) for the noble ones to be endowed with the happiness of fruition attainment. Therefore, no emergence (vuṭṭhāna) from any formation is possible for those conformity knowledges. Since that is not possible, the knowledge at the end of those conformity knowledges (i.e., fruition) could not be one that emerges from the sign of formations and takes Nibbāna as its object. For this reason, when a trainee, for the sake of enjoying their own fruition attainment, contemplates formations by way of rise and fall (udayabbaya) and so forth, only fruition arises following the sequence of insight knowledge, not the path. This meaning is thus established. In this way, the entering of fruition attainment should be understood. "Friends, there are three conditions for the maintenance (ṭhiti) of the signless deliverance of mind: non-attention to all signs, attention to the signless element, and prior preparation (pubbe ca abhisaṅkhāro)." Because of this statement, the maintenance of that fruition attainment occurs through three modes. Among those three, "prior preparation" means the determination of the time duration before entering the attainment. Because it is determined as "I shall emerge at such a time," emergence from the attainment does not occur until that time arrives. "Friends, there are two conditions for the emergence (vuṭṭhāna) from the signless deliverance of mind: attention to all signs and non-attention to the signless element." Because of this statement, emergence from that fruition attainment occurs through two modes. Therein, "all signs" refers to the signs of materiality, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness. Although one does not actually attend to all these signs simultaneously, this was said in a comprehensive sense. Therefore, by attending to the object of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga)...
34:
Emergence from the attainment of fruition occurs; thus, the emergence from that attainment of fruition should be understood. This aforementioned entering and emerging is the fruition of Arahantship—

"With distress subsided, having the Deathless as object, beautiful,
With worldly baits vomited out, peaceful, the supreme fruit of recluseship."

Thus, he experienced the exceedingly pleasant bliss of liberation. Therefore, "experiencing the bliss of liberation" means he was sitting while experiencing the bliss of the attainment of fruition, which is the bliss of liberation.

"Atha" is a particle in the sense of a new topic. "Kho" is a particle used as a filler. Between them, "Atha" indicates a topic other than experiencing the bliss of liberation. What is that topic? It is the reflection on Dependent Origination. Alternatively, "Atha" is a particle meaning "afterwards"; by that meaning, it illuminates the sense to be mentioned later: "at the end of those seven days." "Tassa sattāhassa" refers to the seven days on the seat. "Accayena" means by passing away (at the end). "Tamhā samādhimhā" means from the concentration of the fruition of Arahantship. Right here, some teachers have elaborated on the seven weeks in sequence. We, however, shall explain those seven weeks later by showing how the Khandhaka text and this Udāna Pāḷi are not contradictory. "Rattiyā" is a genitive case in the sense of a part-whole relationship. "Paṭhamaṃ" is an accusative case in the sense of continuous duration. Indeed, the Blessed One was engaged in that very reflection throughout the entire first watch of that night.

"Dependent Origination" (Paṭiccasamuppāda) is the collection of causal factors. Causal factors such as ignorance (avijjā) and so on are called Dependent Origination. How is this to be known? It is known by the words of the Blessed One. For the Blessed One said: "Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this is the source, this is the origin, this is the condition for aging and death, namely, birth... ignorance is the condition for volitional formations" (DN 2.105, etc.). Thus, ignorance and so on are called causes. Just as there are twelve conditions, there are twelve factors of Dependent Origination.

In this context, this is the word-meaning: It is called "Paṭiccasamuppāda" because, depending on one another and facing each other, without rejecting the combination of causes, it produces the effects together. Alternatively, "paṭicca" means having gone towards a condition that is worthy of being met, and without being separated from that condition, the arising of the connected effect...
35:
## Dependent Origination.

In this context, "Paṭiccasamuppāda" should be understood as the cause endowed with the capacity to produce the effect, as understood by the expression of the basis of the term "samuppāda" in this Teaching; it should not be taken as merely the arising of conditions. Alternatively, it is "paṭicca" because it should be understood by the wise; it is "samuppāda" because it produces well by itself. Being both "paṭicca" (to be understood) and "samuppāda" (producing together), it is "Paṭiccasamuppāda"—thus the meaning here should be understood.

"Anuloma" (forward order) means the mode of conditions starting with ignorance, as taught in the method "With ignorance as condition, volitional formations [arise]," etc., is called "anuloma" because it performs its own required function. Alternatively, it is called "anuloma" because it is taught from the beginning to the end, or because it follows the order of the process of existence. He [reflected] on that forward order. "He reflected thoroughly" means he attended to it carefully in his mind. Whatever causal factor is a condition for whatever conditionally arisen phenomenon, in whatever way—as root-condition and so on—he attended to all that in his mind through the power of reviewing, without distortion, without omission, and in its entirety. To show briefly the manner in which the Blessed One reflected on the forward order of Dependent Origination, it was said: "Thus, when this exists, that is; with the arising of this, that arises."

In that text, "iti" means "thus" or "in this manner." "When this exists, that is" means when this condition such as ignorance exists, this effect such as volitional formations comes to be. "With the arising of this, that arises" means because of the arising of this condition such as ignorance, this effect such as volitional formations arises. By the words of the second and third suttas—"When this is not, that is not; with the cessation of this, that ceases"—the rule regarding this characteristic of conditionality is shown: "Only when this exists, [it occurs], not when it does not exist. Only with the arising of this, [it occurs], not without its arising. Only without cessation, [it occurs], not with cessation." Therefore, it should be understood that the rule inherent in the characteristic of Dependent Origination is stated here. "Cessation" (nirodha) means the non-arising and non-occurrence in the future through the attainment of dispassion (virāga) towards ignorance and so on. For it was said: "With the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease," and so on. The cessation and the opposite of cessation (arising) are stated as: "With the cessation of this, that ceases."
36:
Therefore, this point is shown: what is called non-cessation (anirodha) is indeed arising (uppāda); and this non-cessation is also called the state of existence (atthibhāva) in this context. Regarding the characteristic, "When this exists, this comes to be," by saying "With the arising of this, this arises" through another synonymous method, the latter statement specifies the former. Therefore, it is not spoken of with reference only to the state of being currently present, but indeed, it should be understood as referring to the state of not yet having ceased through the Path.

Furthermore, because in the explanation of the characteristic shown in two ways as "When this does not exist, this does not come to be; with the cessation of this, this ceases," only cessation (nirodha) is spoken of in such terms as "With the complete fading away and cessation of ignorance through the Path of Arahantship, formations cease," etc. Therefore, since the state of non-existence (natthibhāva) is also indeed cessation, it is shown that the state of existence (atthibhāva), which is the opposite of the state of non-existence, is non-cessation (anirodha). By that state of existence, which is called non-cessation, it specifies arising (uppāda). Therefore, in this context, it is not intended that the mere state of existence is arising; rather, this meaning is clarified: that the state of existence, which is called non-cessation, is indeed arising. Thus, these two statements of characteristics should be understood as being meaningful through their relationship as the specifier and the specified.

What is this non-cessation (anirodha) which is called "state of existence" and "arising"? It is the state of not yet being abandoned by the Path, and the state of being fit to produce a result because the fitness to produce a result that has not yet arisen has not been abandoned. For those unwholesome states (akusala dhamma) that should be abandoned, it is the state of not yet being eradicated by the Noble Path. For those wholesome (kusala) and indeterminate (abyākata) states that are not to be abandoned, it is the state of the fetters (saṃyojana) not yet being exhausted in those persons whose taints (āsava) are not yet exhausted. Indeed, the occurrence of the aggregates (khandha) together with fetters due to the state of having latent tendencies (anusaya) that have not been eradicated is called Dependent Origination (paṭiccasamuppāda).

And thus it has been said: "Bhikkhus, for the fool who is obstructed by ignorance and conjoined with craving, this body has been produced. That ignorance has not been abandoned by the fool, and that craving is not yet exhausted. Why is that? Bhikkhus, the fool has not lived the holy life (brahmacariya) rightly for the complete destruction of suffering. Therefore, with the breaking up of the body, the fool goes to another body; being one who has gone to another body, he is not released from birth, aging, and death," and so forth (SN 2.19).
37:
For those whose fetters are destroyed, because of the absence of ignorance, there is the non-occurrence of formations; and because of the absence of craving and clinging, there is the non-occurrence of clinging-existence (upādānabhava); thus the cutting off of the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa) will become manifest. For that very reason, it was said: "But, Phagguṇa, with the complete fading away and cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases; with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases," and so forth (SN 2.12).

Indeed, it is not that the six sense bases and so forth do not occur after the attainment of the supreme Path until Parinibbāna. However, because of the state of the destruction of fetters, which is a state of non-existence and can be called by the word "cessation," it is called cessation (nirodha). Alternatively, even kamma performed long ago is indeed said to be "existent" (santa) in the sense of being fit to produce a result, because its result has not yet been completed and its cause has not been abandoned by the Path; it is not that the result has already been produced, nor that its cause has been abandoned. The state of being fit to produce a result of ignorance, formations, etc., which are the causes for the arising of results, should be understood as non-cessation (anirodha) in the manner already stated. Thus, by this state of not having ceased, that cause without which the result cannot occur is spoken of by the words "When this exists," even if it is past. For that very reason, the arising of conditions (paccayuppāda) for one who has not yet lived the holy life—which has not yet reached the nature of non-occurrence—is spoken of as "With the arising of this," because it has not yet ceased, without considering the distinction of time. Alternatively, when the remaining conditions meet, even if it is not currently present, it is as if it were present; what to say of when it is already present? That state of being directed towards the arising of the result is spoken of as "With the arising of this." This is true. When directed towards that result, the cause arises because of that result. Therefore, the manifestation of the cause through its state of producing the result that is to occur at that moment is called "arising" (uppāda). Even if it is not currently present, that which is not of that moment being of that moment should be understood as "arising" (uppāda).

In that context, by the word "exists" (sati), the state of being a condition is spoken of by mere presence, showing the lack of agency (abyāpāratā) of Dependent Origination. By the word "arising" (uppādā), showing the nature of arising, the fact that it does not occur at all times, and the state of being directed towards the arising of the result, the impermanence (aniccatā) of Dependent Origination is shown. By the use of the locative and ablative cases having the sense of cause (hetu)—namely, "when existing, when not existing, from arising, from cessation"—the state of Dependent Origination as being fully endowed with source (nidāna), origin (samudaya), birth (jāti), and provenance (pabhava) is shown. Here, the causal sense in the locative case is to be understood where, upon the existence of something, the existence of a result that is inseparable from it is noted; it is known by that occurrence of the result. For example: "When wealth was not given to the poor, poverty became widespread," and "When the crops are accomplished, abundance of food occurs."

The causal sense of the ablative case is also known from its occurrence in the production of a result and in its natural state. For example: "From the kalala (embryo) the abbuda (foetus) arises; from the abbuda the pesi (piece of flesh) arises," and "From the Himalayas the Ganges flows," and "The Ganges is full from the rain." Similarly, when ignorance exists, formations etc. are noted as being inseparable from that ignorance; and from ignorance etc., formations etc. also arise excessively and are produced in various ways. Therefore, to show that meaning, the causal sense is indicated by the locative and ablative cases as "from arising" (uppādā). This is how it should be understood. Because the designations of Dependent Origination such as "With ignorance as condition, formations come to be," etc., are made based on what is shown in brief as "When this exists, this comes to be; with the arising of this, this arises; when this does not exist, this does not come to be; with the cessation of this, this ceases." Therefore, the aforementioned states such as provenance (pabhava) and arising...
38: 'From the foetus (abbuda) arises the piece of flesh (pesī)' (Saṃyutta Nikāya, Nidāna Vagga), and 'From the Himalayas the Ganges rivers flow, from the mountain peak the lake arises.' Just so, because of the existence of ignorance (avijjā) and so on, the state of volitional formations (saṅkhāra) and so on is to be understood as being inseparable from that ignorance. Because of ignorance and so on, volitional formations and so on arise and are conditioned in various ways. Therefore, to show the meaning that volitional formations and so on are the effects of ignorance and so on, and that ignorance is the primary cause (prakṛti) of volitional formations, the indications are made using the locative case (bhummā) and the ablative case (nissakka) in the sense of cause: 'When this exists, this comes to be.' Since, in this Dispensation, the Dependent Origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) which is briefly stated as 'When this exists, this comes to be; with the arising of this, this arises,' is explained in detail as 'With ignorance as condition, volitional formations [arise],' and so on, therefore, the aforementioned state of existence (atthibhāva) and arising (uppāda) are understood as the state of being a condition (paccaya-bhāva) for those respective conditionally arisen phenomena (paccayuppanna-dhamma). Indeed, apart from the meaning expressed by the restrictive statements—'Only when it exists, does it occur, not when it does not exist; only when it arises, does it occur, not when it ceases'—which signify the state of existence as non-disappearance and the arising as the nature of non-reversion or the moment of occurrence, there is no other thing called the state of being a condition (paccaya-bhāva). Therefore, the aforementioned state of existence and arising should be understood as the state of being a condition. The twenty-four conditions such as the root-condition (hetu) mentioned in the Paṭṭhāna should also be understood as specific distinctions of this state of being a condition. Thus, to show how the Blessed One reflected on the Dependent Origination in forward order (anuloma) in detail, He taught: 'Yadidaṃ avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā' and so on. In that Pali, 'yadidaṃ' is an indeclinable (nipāta) meaning 'that which is this.' In the terms such as 'avijjāpaccayā': it is called 'avijjā' (ignorance) because it finds (knows) what should not be found, such as bodily misconduct; it is called 'avijjā' because it does not find (know) what should be found, such as bodily good conduct. It is called 'avijjā' because it makes the non-perverted nature of phenomena unknown. It is called 'avijjā' because it causes beings to run through the rounds of rebirth (saṃsāra) which is without end. It is called 'avijjā' because it occurs in things that do not exist in the ultimate sense (such as persons and beings) and does not occur in things that do exist in the ultimate sense (such as aggregates, bases, and elements). It is called 'avijjā' because it is the opposite of knowledge (vijjā). That ignorance should be understood as being fourfold, such as 'non-knowledge regarding suffering.' It is called a condition (paccaya) because, depending on a cause and not being separate from it, the fruit arises and persists. Or, it is called a condition in the sense of being helpful (upakāra). Because it is both ignorance and a condition, it is 'avijjā-paccaya' (ignorance-condition); it means 'because of that condition which is ignorance.' They are called 'saṅkhāra' (volitional formations) because they condition; these are mundane wholesome and unwholesome volitions (cetanā). Those volitions should be understood as being threefold: meritorious volitional formations (puññābhisaṅkhāra), demeritorious volitional formations (apuññābhisaṅkhāra), and imperturbable volitional formations (āneñjābhisaṅkhāra). It is called 'viññāṇa' (consciousness) because it cognizes the object; it is of thirty-two types by way of mundane resultant consciousness. It is called 'nāma' (mentality/name) because it bends towards the object; it consists of the three mental aggregates such as feeling (vedanā). It is called 'rūpa' (form/matter) because it is deformed (oppressed); it consists of the primary elements (bhūta-rūpa) and derived matter (upādā-rūpa) such as the eye. Because it expands...
39:
It is called a sense base (āyatana) because it leads to the long suffering of saṃsāra. The nature of touching is contact (phassa). The nature of experiencing is feeling (vedanā). These two, contact and feeling, are of six kinds by way of the doors; if taken by way of resultants (vipāka), they are of thirty-six kinds. The nature of thirsting all around is craving (taṇhā); that craving is briefly of three kinds by way of sensual craving (kāma-taṇhā) and so forth, and in detail, it is of one hundred and eight kinds. The nature of grasping is clinging (upādāna); that clinging is of four kinds by way of clinging to sensuality (kāmupādāna) and so forth. The nature of becoming or causing to become is existence (bhava); that existence is of two kinds by way of kamma-existence (kamma-bhava) and rebirth-existence (upapatti-bhava). Arising is birth (jāti). Aging is decay (jarā). It is called death (maraṇa) because one dies by that state. Sorrowing is sorrow (soka). Weeping is lamentation (parideva). It is called pain (dukkha) because it causes suffering; alternatively, it is called dukkha because it destroys (khanati) the two moments by way of arising (uppāda) and presence (ṭhiti). The state of a bad mind is grief (domanassa). Intense exhaustion is despair (upāyāsa). 'Sambhavanti' means they arise. The word 'sambhavanti' should be connected not only with the words such as sorrow (soka) but with all the preceding words. In this way, it shows the definition of causes and their results as in 'with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise (avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā sambhavanti)'. This method applies in all instances.

Among those factors of dependent origination, ignorance (avijjā) has the characteristic of unknowing, the function of confusion, concealment as its manifestation, and the taints (āsava) as its proximate cause. Volitional formations (saṅkhāra) have the characteristic of forming, the function of striving, coordination as their manifestation, and ignorance as their proximate cause. Consciousness (viññāṇa) has the characteristic of cognizing the object, the function of being a precursor, rebirth-linking as its manifestation, and volitional formations as its proximate cause; or else, the physical base and object as its proximate cause. Name (nāma) has the characteristic of inclining towards the object, the function of association, being inseparable as its manifestation, and consciousness as its proximate cause. Form (rūpa) has the characteristic of being deformed (ruppana), the function of not grasping the object, the state of not being abandoned by the Path as its manifestation, and consciousness as its proximate cause. The sixfold sense base (saḷāyatana) has the characteristic of a sense base, the function of seeing and so forth, the state of being a base and door as its manifestation, and name-and-form as its proximate cause. Contact (phassa) has the characteristic of touching, the function of impingement, coincidence as its manifestation, and the sixfold sense base as its proximate cause. Feeling (vedanā) has the characteristic of experiencing, the function of enjoying the flavor of the object, pleasure and pain as its manifestation, and contact as its proximate cause. Craving (taṇhā) has the characteristic of being a cause, the function of delighting, insatiability as its manifestation, and feeling as its proximate cause. Clinging (upādāna) has the characteristic of seizing, the function of not releasing, intense craving and wrong view as its manifestation, and craving as its proximate cause. Existence (bhava) has the characteristic of kamma and the result of kamma, the function of becoming and causing to become, wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate states as its manifestation, and clinging as its proximate cause. Birth (jāti) has the characteristic of first arising in various types of existence, the function of handing over, the arising in this life from a past life or the variety of suffering as its manifestation. Decay (jarā) has the characteristic of the aging of the aggregates, the function of leading towards death, the destruction of youth as its manifestation. Death (maraṇa) has the characteristic of falling away (cuti).
40:
Death (maraṇa) has the characteristic of falling away (cuti), the function of disjunction, and separation from the destination (gati) as its manifestation. Sorrow (soka) has the characteristic of inner burning, the function of consuming the mind, and continual mourning as its manifestation. Lamentation (parideva) has the characteristic of wailing, the function of proclaiming virtues and faults, and confusion (sambhama) as its manifestation. Pain (dukkha) has the characteristic of oppressing the body, the function of causing mental displeasure to those of little wisdom, and bodily affliction as its manifestation. Grief (domanassa) has the characteristic of oppressing the mind, the function of mental distress, and mental suffering as its manifestation. Despair (upāyāsa) has the characteristic of mental combustion, the function of moaning, and dejection as its manifestation. Thus, these factors such as ignorance and so forth should be understood by way of their characteristics and so on. What has been said here is only a summary. For a detailed explanation with a complete decision in all aspects, one should consult the Vibhaṅga Commentary named Sammohavinodanī.

The word 'Evaṃ' (Thus) is an indication of the states pointed out. By that word, it shows that [this mass of suffering] arises only because of causes such as ignorance, and not because of creation by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and so forth. 'Etassa' (of this) refers to the states mentioned above. 'Kevalassa' (whole/only) means unmixed with other states like happiness, or it means the entire [mass]. 'Dukkhakkhandhassa' (of the mass of suffering) means of the collection of suffering; it is not of a being, nor of a soul (jīva), nor of beauty, happiness, and so forth. In the phrase 'the origin comes to be' (samudayo hoti), it means arising or production occurs.

'Having known this meaning' means having known in all aspects this meaning which was stated as: 'by the power of ignorance and so forth, the origin of the mass of suffering such as volitional formations and so forth occurs.' 'At that time' means at the time of knowing that meaning. 'He uttered this inspired utterance (udāna)' means that when this meaning was known, He uttered this inspired utterance which illustrates the power of fully knowing the cause and the states arisen from the cause, starting with 'Yadā have pātubhavanti dhammā' (When indeed dhammas become manifest), which originated from knowledge associated with joy; it means He spoke words of delight.

The meaning of that verse is: 'Yadā' means at which time. 'Have' is a particle used in the sense of 'certainly' or 'manifestly'. Some teachers, however, say that 'have' means 'āhave' (in battle), meaning at the time of fighting with the Maras of defilements, in accordance with the word: 'Fight Mara with the weapon of wisdom'. 'Pātubhavanti' means they arise. 'Dhammā' refers to the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhammā) which accomplish the penetration of the dependent origination in forward order. Alternatively, 'pātubhavanti' means they become clear, they become manifest and evident by the power of realization (abhisamaya). 'Dhammā' refers to the four Noble Truths. Energy (vīriya) is called 'ātāpa' in the sense of burning up the defilements. 'Ātāpino' means to one who possesses the energy of right exertion (sammappadhāna-vīriya). 'Jhāyato' means...
41:
For the Arahant who is contemplating with meditation on the object (ārammaṇūpanijjhāna) and meditation on the characteristics (lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna), who has abandoned evil and whose taints are destroyed—when these dhammas become manifest to him in such a way, all doubts vanish, depart, and cease. These doubts include those mentioned in the context of Dependent Origination (paṭiccasamuppāda), such as the Buddha's response, 'Venerable sir, who touches? That is not a valid question,' and 'Venerable sir, what is aging and death? To whom does this aging and death belong? That is not a valid question.' They also include the sixteen types of doubt that arise from not penetrating Dependent Origination, such as 'Was I in the past?' Why do they vanish? Because at that time, he understands the dhamma with its cause; he understands, knows, and penetrates this entire mass of suffering, such as formations (saṅkhāra), which arise from causes like ignorance (avijjā).

When do the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyadhamma) or the Four Noble Truths (catusaccadhamma) become manifest or arise for him? They arise at the moments of insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa) and path knowledge (magga-ñāṇa). There, mindfulness and other factors associated with insight knowledge, along with insight knowledge itself, arise individually according to their respective objects through the power of abandoning by substitution (tadaṅga-pahāna), discarding the perception of beauty (subha-saññā) and so on, through the power of the foundations of mindfulness (kāyānupassanā) and so forth. However, at the moment of the path (magga-khaṇa), they arise all at once, taking Nibbāna as their object, abandoning opposing states through the power of abandoning by eradication (samuccheda-pahāna), and achieving the non-deluded penetration of the four Noble Truths. Thus, first, the manifestation of the factors of enlightenment should be understood in the sense of their arising.

The manifestation of the Noble Truths should be understood in the sense of their becoming clear: for the mundane truths, through the power of making them the object of insight at the moment of insight; for the supramundane truths, through the power of being inclined towards them; at the moment of the path, through the power of penetrating the truth of cessation (nirodha-sacca) by taking it as an object; and for all truths, through the power of penetrating their respective functions.

Thus, although all dhammas in every aspect were already clear to the Blessed One's knowledge, because he had applied insight starting with Dependent Origination, he reflected on Dependent Origination—which is subtle, profound, and difficult to see—and with strong joy arising, he uttered this inspired utterance (udāna) here, demonstrating the absolute eradication of opposing states and the power of his own penetration of that Dhamma.
42:
"This inspired utterance was also spoken by the Blessed One; thus have I heard." This Pali text is found only in some manuscripts. In that text, the word "pi" in "ayampi" has the sense of conjunction (samuccaya), as in "This jewel in the Buddha is also excellent..." or "This person is also a defeated one (pārājika)." By this word "pi," the subsequent (second and third suttas) are to be included.

The word "vutta" in "vutto" is found in the senses of shaving hair, sowing seeds, leveling the soil, livelihood, release from bonds, making a noble utterance, learning, and speaking.

Indeed, it appears in the sense of shaving hair in phrases such as "a young man with a shaven head (vutta-siro)."

It appears in the sense of sowing in phrases such as "For him who does not betray friends, his cattle multiply, the seed sown (vuttaṃ) in the field flourishes, and he enjoys the fruit of what is sown (vuttānaṃ)."

It appears in the sense of leveling the soil with eight-pronged tools in phrases such as "not leveled (paṭivuttaṃ)."

It appears in the sense of livelihood in phrases such as "with hair removed, living on what is given by others (paradatta-vutto), I dwell with the mind of a deer."

It appears in the sense of release from bonds in phrases such as "A yellow leaf, released (pavuṭṭo) from its bond, is incapable of becoming green again."

It appears in the sense of making a noble utterance in phrases such as "The song was spoken (vuttaṃ), completed."

It appears in the sense of learning in phrases such as "The Pārāyana was learned (vutto)."

It appears in the sense of speaking in phrases such as "Monks, be my heirs in Dhamma, not my heirs in material things; thus the Blessed One spoke (vuttaṃ) this word."

In this context, it should be understood only in the sense of speaking (kathana). Therefore, it means "This inspired utterance was also spoken." "Iti" means "thus." The meaning of the two words "me sutaṃ" has been explained in every aspect in the commentary on the prologue (nidāna). The meaning previously stated as the prologue "evaṃ me sutaṃ" is here stated again as a conclusion "iti me sutaṃ." The restatement of what has already been said is called a conclusion (nigamana). The derivation of the meaning of the word "iti" is the same as the word "evaṃ," just as in "evaṃ me sutaṃ." Since we have already shown the construction of the meaning in the commentary on the Itivuttaka, it should be understood according to the method stated there.

## In the Commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya named Paramatthadီpanī,
## the Commentary on the Udāna, the Explanation of the First Bodhi Sutta, is finished.
43:
## 2. Commentary on the Second Bodhi Sutta

In the second sutta, 'paṭilomaṃ' (in reverse order) refers to the causal process beginning with ignorance, as stated in the method: 'With the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease,' and so on. It is called 'paṭiloma' because it ceases through absolute cessation (non-arising) and no longer performs its respective functions. Alternatively, it is called 'paṭiloma' because it is contrary or opposed to the process of saṃsāra. Since it is not described as starting from the end or the middle and reaching the beginning, the quality of being 'paṭiloma' (reverse) in this context is not appropriate in any sense other than the one just mentioned. The word 'paṭilomaṃ' is also a neuter designation of state (bhāvanapuṃsakaniddesa), as in passages such as 'The moon and sun revolve unevenly (visamaṃ).'

'When this is not, this does not come to be' means that when this cause, such as ignorance, is absent (having been abandoned by the Path), this result, such as volitional formations, does not occur or arise. 'With the cessation of this, this ceases' means that because of the cessation of this cause, such as ignorance (having been brought to the state of non-arising by the Path), this result, such as volitional formations, ceases and does not occur. In this second Bodhi Sutta, just as in the forward reflection (anuloma-manasikāra) passage—'When this exists, this comes to be; with the arising of this, this arises'—the inherent limitation is shown as: 'Only when this exists, it arises, not when it is absent; only with the arising of this, it arises, not with its cessation.' Similarly, it should be understood that the characteristic of inherent limitation in the reverse order (paṭiloma) is shown as: 'Only when this is absent, it does not arise, not when it exists; only with the cessation of this, it ceases, not with its arising.' All other matters to be discussed in this sutta should be understood according to the method already stated in the commentary on the first Bodhi Sutta.

Having thus briefly shown how the Blessed One reflected on dependent origination in reverse order, the passage beginning with 'With the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease' is now stated to show it in detail. Therein, 'with the cessation of ignorance' means through the cessation of ignorance without remainder by the Noble Path; the meaning is through the absolute eradication of ignorance by the Path of Arahatship by way of abandoning the underlying tendencies (anusaya). Although ignorance abandoned by the three lower paths is indeed abandoned by way of eradication, it is not abandoned without remainder. Indeed, ignorance leading to the states of deprivation (apāya) is abandoned by the first path. Similarly, ignorance that causes rebirth once more in this world, and ignorance that is the cause of arising in all places in the non-noble planes (anariyabhūmi), are abandoned respectively by the second and third paths, but not the rest. For that ignorance is abandoned without remainder only by the Path of Arahatship. 'Volitional formations cease' means there is the cessation of volitional formations by way of non-arising. To show that with the cessation of volitional formations thus ceased, consciousness ceases, and with the cessation of consciousness and so on, mentality-materiality and so on are also ceased, the passage beginning with 'With the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases' is spoken, ending with 'Such is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.' Whatever is to be said there is exactly as the method stated below.
44:
In this context of reverse reflection, although the cessation of the entire mass of suffering without remainder is stated by this much: "With the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases," nevertheless, just as in the forward order (anuloma), the passage "With ignorance as condition, volitional formations come to be... the mass of suffering arises" was stated to show the meaning that because of the existence of such and such a causal state, such and such a conditionally arisen state does not cease but continues to occur; so too, in this context, the passage "With the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases... the mass of suffering ceases" is stated to show that because of the absence of such and such a causal state, which is the opposite of that [forward order], such and such a conditionally arisen state ceases and no longer occurs. However, it is not for the purpose of showing the cessation of the mass of suffering pertaining to the three periods of time, as in the forward order. This distinction should also be understood: it is desired only to show the cessation, through the development of the Noble Path, of the mass of suffering that would have been liable to arise in the future if there were no development of the Noble Path.

"Having understood this matter" (etamatthaṃ viditvā) means having understood in every aspect this matter: that the cessation of the mass of suffering, such as volitional formations, occurs by way of the cessation of ignorance and so on. "He uttered this inspired utterance" (imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi) means that when this matter was understood, he uttered the inspired utterance that illuminates the power of the realization of the destruction of conditions such as ignorance, as manifested in the words "With the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease."

The summarized meaning in that inspired utterance is: because he has penetrated and realized the destruction—known as the non-arising cessation—of conditions such as ignorance, therefore, to that Brahmin (the Buddha) who is ardent and meditative in the manner described, the aforementioned factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyadhamma) or the truths of the Four Noble Truths become manifest, arise, or are revealed. Then, all the various kinds of doubts mentioned previously, which might arise due to not properly understanding the cessation of conditions, vanish and cease. The remaining words are exactly as the method stated below.

## The Commentary on the Second Bodhi Sutta is Finished.

## 3. Commentary on the Third Bodhi Sutta

In the third sutta, "anulomapaṭilomaṃ" means in forward order and in reverse order; the meaning is by way of the forward order and the reverse order as already described. Now, to raise an objection: previously also...
45:
In the previous two discourses, the occurrence of attention (manasikāra) on Dependent Origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) in the forward (anuloma) and reverse (paṭiloma) order has already been taught. Why is the occurrence of attention by way of both taught again in this discourse? It is stated again because attention occurred in that Dependent Origination for the third time by way of both. How was attention by way of both brought about? Is it not impossible to bring about attention on Dependent Origination in both forward and reverse order simultaneously, neither before nor after? Indeed, this meaning should not be understood as 'He attended to both together in mind'; rather, it was by way of turns.

The Blessed One, having first attended to Dependent Origination in the forward order, uttered the first inspired utterance (udāna) suitable to that forward order. In the second watch, having attended to it in the reverse order, He uttered the second inspired utterance suitable to that reverse order. In the third watch, however, He attended to it in both forward and reverse order by way of attending to the forward order at one time and the reverse order at another time. Therefore, I have said: 'Forward and reverse means both forward and reverse, by way of the aforementioned forward order and reverse order.' By this third watch, the proficiency, strength, and mastery (vasībhāva) of that attention are revealed. Here also, the distinction of these should be understood by way of the prior reflections (ābhoga) that occurred as: 'I shall attend to the forward order, I shall attend to the reverse order, I shall attend to both forward and reverse order.'

In that forward and reverse Dependent Origination, 'avijjāya tveva' means only of ignorance (cessation). 'Asesavirāganirodhā' means through total cessation by the path called dispassion (virāga), which is the Path of Arahantship; the meaning is the abandonment of non-arising without remainder by the Path of Arahantship. 'Saṅkhāranirodho' means the cessation of all formations (saṅkhāra) without remainder and without further arising. For, by the three lower paths, some formations cease and some do not cease, because ignorance ceases with a remainder. But by the Path of Arahantship, because that ignorance ceases without remainder, there are no formations that do not cease; all of them indeed cease.

'Etam-atthaṃ viditvā' means having understood this matter in every aspect—that the arising and cessation of the mass of suffering such as formations, etc., occurs by way of ignorance, etc., due to the arising and cessation of ignorance, etc. 'Imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi' means He uttered this inspired utterance of the aforementioned kind, which reveals the power of that Noble Path (ariya-magga) by which the matter called the arising and cessation of the mass of suffering was known by way of function and by way of the activity of the object.

In that third inspired utterance, the summary of the meaning is as follows: When indeed the four truths (catusacca-dhamma) become manifest to that Brahmin (Arahant) who is ardent (ātāpī) and meditative (jhāyī), then that Brahmin, by those factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma) that have arisen, or by the Noble Path where the four truths become manifest...
46:
...by those factors of enlightenment, or by that Noble Path where the four truths become manifest, he stands dispelling, crushing, and destroying the army of Māra of the kind described by the method beginning with 'Sensual pleasures are your first army' (Sn 438). How does he stand? Just as the sun illuminates the sky. Just as the risen sun stands dispelling the darkness while illuminating the sky with its own radiance, even so, that Brahmin whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), while penetrating the truths with those dhammas or with that Noble Path, stands dispelling the army of Māra.

Thus, the Blessed One uttered these three inspired utterances in the three watches of the night to reveal: by the first inspired utterance, the power of knowing the mode of conditions (paccayākāra); by the second, the power of attaining the destruction of conditions (Nibbāna); and by the third, the power of the Noble Path. In which night were they uttered? They were uttered on the seventh night after the Great Enlightenment. For, on the night of the full moon of Visākha, the Blessed One, having recollected his past lives (pubbenivāsanussati) in the first watch, having purified the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu) in the middle watch, and having applied his knowledge to Dependent Origination in the last watch, contemplated the formations of the three planes (tebhūmaka-saṅkhāra) through various methods, and reached the state of a Perfectly Enlightened Buddha (Sammāsambodhi) thinking, 'Now the dawn will rise.' Immediately after the attainment of Omniscience (sabbaññuta), the dawn rose. Thereafter, spending seven days at the foot of the Bodhi tree on that very seat, on the arrival of the seventh night, He attended to Dependent Origination in the three watches in the manner described and uttered these inspired utterances in sequence.

In the Khandhaka (Vinaya), however, because it is stated for all three times that 'He attended to Dependent Origination in forward and reverse order in mind,' it is said in the Khandhaka Commentary: 'Having attended in this way in all three watches, the Blessed One uttered these inspired utterances: the first by way of reviewing the mode of conditions, the second by way of reviewing Nibbāna, and the third by way of reviewing the Path.' That statement also is not contradictory. For, the Blessed One, excluding the seven days in the Jewel House (Ratanaghara), spent the remaining six weeks contemplating the Dhamma from time to time, mostly dwelling in the experience of the bliss of liberation (vimutti-sukha). But in the week at the Jewel House, He dwelt solely by way of familiarizing Himself with the Abhidhamma.

## The Commentary on the Third Bodhi Sutta is finished.
47:
## 4. Commentary on the Huṃhuṅka Sutta

In the fourth sutta, 'Ajapālanigrodhe' refers to the fact that goatherds (ajapāla) used to come and sit in the shade of that banyan tree; thus, the name 'Ajapālanigrodha' (The Goatherds' Banyan) arose for that tree. Some teachers, however, say: "Because old Brahmins, who were unable to recite the Vedas in that place, built houses surrounded by walls and all lived there, the name 'Ajapālanigrodha' arose." The word-definition (vacanattha) of this is: Because they could not recite the Vedas, they are called 'Ajapā' (non-reciters of the Vedas); since these Ajapā (old Brahmins) took up residence (lanti) in this place, it is called 'Ajapāla'. Alternatively, other teachers say: "Because it protects (pāleti) with its shade the goats (aja) that enter inside at noon, the name 'Ajapāla' became well-known." In every respect, this is the name of that tree, meaning 'near that tree'. This locative case (sattamī-vibhatti) in 'Ajapālanigrodhe' is used in the sense of proximity (samīpattha).

'Vimuttisukha-paṭisaṃvedī' means that he sat there as well, reflecting on the Dhamma and experiencing the bliss of liberation. This banyan tree is located to the east of the Bodhi tree. The word 'sattāhaṃ' (seven days) does not refer to the seven days immediately following the seven days on the throne (pallaṅka-sattāha). The Blessed One spent another three weeks (three sattāhas) near the Bodhi tree as well.

In this matter, the sequential account is as follows: It is said that when the Blessed One attained Supreme Enlightenment and sat for seven days on a single throne, a doubt arose in some deities: "The Blessed One does not rise yet; are there perhaps other qualities that make one a Buddha?" Then, on the eighth day, the Blessed One rose from his attainment, and knowing the doubt of the deities, he flew into the air to dispel their doubt and performed the Twin Miracle (Yamaka-pāṭihāriya), thereby dispelling the doubt of those deities. Thereafter, standing in the northern direction leaning slightly towards the east from the throne, he spent seven days gazing with unblinking eyes at the throne and the Bodhi tree, the place where he achieved the power of the perfections (pāramīs) accumulated for four incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons; that place became known as the 'Animisa-cetiya' (The Shrine of the Unblinking Gaze). Then, in the space between the throne and the place where he stood, he spent seven days walking back and forth on a long jeweled path (ratana-caṅkama) running from east to west; that place became known as the 'Ratana-caṅkama-cetiya' (The Jeweled Walk Shrine). Thereafter, in the western direction, the deities [created] a jeweled house...
48:
...the deities created a jeweled house in that place. Sitting there in a cross-legged posture, the Blessed One spent seven days reflecting on the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, especially the Samantapaṭṭhāna (The Great Book of Relations) which has infinite methods. That place became known as the 'Ratana-ghara-cetiya' (The Jeweled House Shrine). Having thus spent four weeks (sattāhas) near the Bodhi tree, in the fifth week, he approached the Ajapāla Banyan tree from the Bodhi tree and sat in a cross-legged posture at the foot of that banyan tree.

"Rose from concentration" means he rose from that concentration of the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti) according to the predetermined time. After rising, while the Blessed One was sitting there at the foot of the Ajapāla Banyan tree, a certain Brahmin approached the Blessed One and asked a question. Therefore, [the text] says "Atha kho aññataro" and so forth. In that passage, "aññataro" refers to a person who is not well-known by name or clan. "Huṃhuṅka-jātika" means that the Brahmin held the view of 'seen-omens' (diṭṭha-maṅgalika) and was stiff with pride. Due to the power of pride and the power of anger, whenever he saw anyone of an inferior birth, he would wander about making the sound "Huṃ huṃ" in disgust. Therefore, he is called "Huṃhuṅka-jātika". There is also a variant reading "Huhukka-jātika". "Brāhmaṇo" means he was a Brahmin by birth.

"Yena Bhagavā" refers to the direction where the Blessed One was staying. Here, the instrumental case is used in the sense of the locative (place). Alternatively, it means he approached by the direction through which the Blessed One should be approached. Or, "yena" is the instrumental case used in the sense of cause (hetu), meaning he approached because of the reason for which the Blessed One should be approached by devas and humans. And for what reason should the Blessed One be approached? Just as a multitude of people with afflicted bodies, being oppressed by various diseases and pains, approach a great and powerful physician for the treatment of their diseases, so too devas and humans with afflicted minds, being oppressed by the diseases of various defilements, should approach the Blessed One for the purpose of curing the disease of defilements through reasons such as hearing the Dhamma and asking questions. Therefore, this Brahmin also approached, desiring to cut off his own doubt.

"Upasaṅkamitvā" indicates the completion of the act of approaching. Alternatively, it means having gone to a place even closer and more immediate to the Blessed One than the place he first approached. "Sammodī" means he rejoiced harmoniously or well. The Blessed One rejoiced with him, and he also rejoiced with the Blessed One through the performance of courteous greetings (paṭisanthāra) such as "Is the Venerable One able to endure? Is he able to keep going?" and so forth. "Sammodanīyaṃ" refers to words worthy of rejoicing, suitable for generating joy. "Kathaṃ" means conversation. "Sāraṇīyaṃ" means...
49:
"Sāraṇီya" refers to that which is associated with being remembered by the virtuous, or that which should be reflected upon at other times. "Vītisāretvā" means having concluded or finished. "Ekamantaṃ" is a designation of a neutral state of being (bhāvanā-napuṃsaka); it means sitting in a certain place, avoiding the six faults of sitting, such as being too close, etc. "Etadavoca" means he uttered the words beginning with "Kittāvatā nu kho," which are to be spoken now.

In those words, "Kittāvatā" means by what measure. "Nu" is a particle in the sense of doubt. "Kho" is an expletive particle used to complete the sentence. "Bho" is a form of address (vocative) arising from the birth of Brahmins. Because it is so, it was said: "If there are stains of defilements, he is called a 'Bhovādī' (one who habitually says 'Bho')." "Gotama" is addressing the Blessed One by his clan name. One might object: "How does this Brahmin, who has just arrived, know the Blessed One's clan?" This Brahmin is not one who has just arrived. Whether during the six years of practicing austerities while being attended by the group of five monks, or later when he abandoned that practice and wandered alone for alms in the market town of Senāni in Uruvelā, he had previously seen and conversed with the Blessed One. Therefore, remembering the Blessed One's clan name as used by the group of five monks in the past, he addresses the Blessed One by clan as "Bho Gotama." Alternatively, from the time the Blessed One made the Great Renunciation and became a monk on the banks of the Anomā River, he became as well-known as the moon and the sun as "Samaṇa Gotama"; thus, there is no need to search for the reason why he knew the clan name.

"Brāhmaṇakaraṇa" means "they make one a Brahmin," thus it means the qualities that make one a Brahmin. Here, with the word "Kittāvatā," he asks about the extent of those qualities by which one becomes a Brahmin, and with the words "Katame ca pana," he asks about the nature (identity) of those qualities.

"Etamatthaṃ viditvā" means having understood the meaning of the question asked by the Brahmin, which had reached its peak, he uttered this inspired utterance (udāna) at that time. However, he did not preach the Dhamma to that Brahmin. Why? Because the Brahmin was not a suitable vessel (abhājana) for the Dhamma teaching. Indeed, even after hearing this verse, that Brahmin did not achieve the realization of the Four Noble Truths. Just as with this Brahmin, for the Ājīvaka Upaka, it was merely a manifestation of the Buddha's virtues. Before preaching the Dhammacakka...
50:
...for in the earlier part, the taking of refuge by the merchant brothers Tapussa and Bhallika, as well as others who heard the Dhamma preached by the Blessed One, was merely for the sake of future disposition (vāsanā), not for the sake of training (sekkha) or for the sake of penetration (nibbedha) that pierces the defilements. This is indeed the nature of things.

In that context, "Brāhmaṇa" refers to one who is a Brahmin because he has put away evil qualities. It does not refer to one who merely claims Brahminhood by birth while being endowed with evil qualities such as the prideful "huhuṃ" sound, the stain of defilements, and the view of auspicious sights (diṭṭhamangala). That true Brahmin is "Nihuhuṅka" because he has abandoned the pride called "huhuṃ" by putting away evil qualities. He is "Nikkasāva" because he is free from the stains of lust and so on. He is "Yatatta" because his mind is constantly engaged in meditation or because his mind is restrained by the restraint of virtue (sīla). He is "Vedantagū" because he has reached Nibbāna, the end of formations, through the knowledges (vedas) known as the four path-knowledges, or because he has reached the end of the Vedas. He is "Vusitabrahmacariya" because he has lived the holy life of the path. Such a person can rightfully say "I am a Brahmin" according to the Dhamma and with logical reason. A Brahmin is one who, though living in the entire world, has no obsessions (ussada) such as lust, hatred, delusion, pride, or views toward any single object, having abandoned them without remainder.

## The Commentary on the Fourth Sutta is finished.

## 5. Brāhmaṇasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the fifth sutta, "Sāvatthiyaṃ" means in the city of that name. That city is called "Sāvatthī" because it was built on the site where the sage named Savattha resided, just like the cities of Kākandī and Mākandī. This is the view of the grammarians. However, the teachers of the commentaries say: Sāvatthī is so called because everything (sabbaṃ) used and enjoyed by humans is there (atthi). Also, when people gathered at the merchant assemblies were asked "What goods are here?", the reply "Everything is here" (sabbaṃ atthi) led to the name Sāvatthī.

"At all times, all requirements are gathered in Sāvatthī;
Therefore, because everything is there, it is called Sāvatthī."
51:
In the phrase 'in that Sāvatthī,' the locative case (bhummavacana) denotes proximity. Regarding the word 'Jetavane'—he is called 'Jeta' because he conquers (jināti) his own enemies. Or, he is called 'Jeta' because he was born when the King conquered his enemies. Or, he was named 'Jeta' for the sake of auspiciousness. It is called 'Vana' because it causes beings to resort (vanayati) to it. This means that by its own excellence, it produces devotion and respect in the minds of beings towards itself. Alternatively, 'Vana' also denotes 'requesting.' It is called 'Vana' because, with the songs of birds such as cuckoos intoxicated by the scents of various flowers, and with the hands of tree branches and sprouts swaying in the gentle breeze, it seems to be requesting beings, 'Come here and enjoy me.' Because it was the grove of Prince Jeta, it is called 'Jetavana.' Indeed, that grove was planted, nurtured, and protected by Prince Jeta, and he himself was its owner; therefore, it is called 'Jetavana.' In that Jetavana (He dwelt).

'Anāthapiṇḍikassa Ārāme'—although his name given by his parents was 'Sudatta,' that great merchant is called 'Anāthapiṇḍika' because he was endowed with all sensual fulfillments, free from the stain of stinginess, and possessed of virtues such as compassion, and thus constantly gave alms (piṇḍa) to the helpless (anātha). 'Ārāma'—it is called 'Ārāma' because beings, especially those who have gone forth (monks), come from various places and delight (ramanti) there without weariness, due to its beauty with flowers and fruits, and its possession of the five factors of a dwelling, such as being neither too far nor too near. Or, it is called 'Ārāma' because, due to such excellences, it attracts those who have gone there and causes them to delight. That monastery was purchased by the householder Anāthapiṇḍika from the hand of Prince Jeta for eighteen crores of gold pieces by spreading them over the ground; he had the dwellings constructed at a cost of eighteen crores; and he completed the dedication ceremony of the monastery with another eighteen crores. Thus, having renounced a total of fifty-four crores of gold pieces, it was dedicated to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha; therefore, it is called 'Anāthapiṇḍikassa Ārāma.' In that monastery of Anāthapiṇḍika (He dwelt).

Here, the mention of 'Jetavane' is to acknowledge the former owner, and 'Anāthapiṇḍikassa Ārāme' is to acknowledge the later owner. The mention of both is to show the exceptional renunciation of these two virtuous people, so that those who desire merit in the future may follow their example. Among them, the renunciation of Prince Jeta consisted of the construction of the gateway and the towers, the eighteen crores received from the sale of the land, and the trees worth many crores. The renunciation of Anāthapiṇḍika was fifty-four...
52:
...crores. Thus, by praising the renunciation of those virtuous ones, the Treasurer of the Dhamma (Venerable Ānanda), showing that 'those who desire merit perform merits in this way,' encourages other seekers of merit to follow their example.

In this regard, there might be an objection: If the Blessed One is dwelling in Sāvatthī, it should not be said 'in Jetavana.' If He is dwelling in Jetavana, it should not be said 'in Sāvatthī.' For it is not possible to dwell in two places at the same time. However, it should not be viewed in this way. Did we not say that 'this locative case denotes proximity (samīpattha)'? Therefore, since this Jetavana is in the vicinity of Sāvatthī, it is said of Him dwelling there: 'He dwells in Jetavana, in Sāvatthī.' The mention of Sāvatthī is to indicate the alms-resort (gocaragāma), while the remaining words are to indicate the dwelling place (nivāsaṭṭhāna) suitable for those who have gone forth.

In the words 'Venerable Sāriputta' and so on, 'Āyasmā' (Venerable) is a term of endearment. The word 'ca' (and) has the sense of conjunction (samuccayattha). He is called 'Sāriputta' because he is the son of the Brahmin woman named Rūpasārī. 'Mahāmoggallāna' is a term of honor. He is called 'Mahāmoggallāna' because he is a Moggallāna who is great (mahanta) due to his special qualities. 'Revata' refers to Revata of the Acacia Forest (Khadiravanika Revata), not Kaṅkhārevata. For on one occasion, the Blessed One was seated in the midst of the four assemblies to preach the Dhamma, appearing like a golden pillar surrounded by red blankets, like a golden mountain surrounded by coral banners, like the swan-king Dhataraṭṭha surrounded by ninety thousand swans, like a Cakkavatti King surrounded by a fourfold army resplendent with the seven jewels, and like the moon rising in the middle of the sky surrounded by the great Saṅgha of monks. At that time, these Chief Disciples and Great Disciples approached to pay homage at the feet of the Blessed One.

'He addressed the monks'—this means He spoke to the monks sitting around Him, pointing out those Venerable ones as they were coming. Indeed, the Blessed One, seeing those Venerable ones approaching—who were endowed with virtues such as virtue (sīla), concentration (samādhi), and wisdom (paññā), possessed of supreme tranquility, and gifted with the highest perfection of deportment—with a clear and confident mind, addressed the monks to praise their special qualities: 'Monks, these Brahmins are coming; monks, these Brahmins are coming.' This repetition (āmeḍita) is due to His appreciation, and it is also appropriate to say it is due to His praise. When it was thus said by the Blessed One...
53:
When the Blessed One addressed those venerable ones as "Brahmins": "Aññatara" refers to a certain monk sitting in that assembly whose name and clan were not well-known. "Brāhmaṇajātika" means one born into a Brahmin family. He had gone forth from a wealthy Brahmin Mahāsāla family.
