The following thought occurred to that monk: "Worldly people say that one is a Brahmin only through being well-born on both sides for seven generations and through the perfection of Brahmin training, and not otherwise. Yet the Blessed One addresses these venerable ones as 'Brahmins'. Let me ask the Blessed One about the characteristics of a Brahmin." The Blessed One addressed those elders as "Brahmins" at that time for that very purpose. The etymology for those who are Brahmins by birth is "one who recites (anati) the Vedas (brahmam)." However, Noble Ones (Ariyas) are called Brahmins because they have warded off (bāhita) evil. For it is said: "One is called a Brahmin because he has warded off evil; one is called a recluse (samaṇa) because of his even conduct (samacariyā)." And it will be said later: "Having warded off evil states..."

"Knowing this matter" means knowing the meaning of the word 'Brahmin' which has reached the pinnacle in the ultimate sense. "This inspired utterance" means he uttered this inspired utterance that clarifies the state of being a Brahmin in the ultimate sense.

In that inspired utterance, "having warded off" (bāhitvā) means having put outside, having removed from one's own continuity, having abandoned by way of the abandonment by cutting off (samuccheda-pahāna). "Evil states" (pāpake dhamme) means low states: the three types of misconduct (duccarita), the twelve types of unwholesome consciousness (akusala-cittuppāda), the ten unwholesome courses of action (akusala-kammapatha), and all unwholesome states divided into many categories. "Those who always wander mindful" means those who, having attained abundance of mindfulness, are mindful at all times through constant dwelling (satata-vihāra) regarding the six objects such as forms, and wander in the four postures. Here, by taking mindfulness, clear comprehension (sampajañña) is also included. "Those whose fetters are destroyed" means those whose fetters are completely exhausted because the ten types of fetters have been cut off by the four noble paths. "Buddhas" means those who are awakened through the penetration of the Four Noble Truths. There are three types of Buddhas: Disciple Buddhas (Sāvaka-buddha), Private Buddhas (Pacceka-buddha), and Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas (Sammāsambuddha). Here, Disciple Buddhas are intended. "They indeed are Brahmins in the world" means they are born of the noble birth in the states called 'Brahmin' in the sense of being excellent, or they are the breast-born sons (orasaputta) of the Blessed One who is a Brahmin. Thus, in this world of beings, they are called Brahmins in the ultimate sense, not merely by birth or clan, nor merely by wearing matted hair, etc. Thus in these two suttas—
54:
The states that make one a Brahmin were taught leading up to Arahantship. However, the diversity in the teaching (desanā-nānatta) should be understood as being due to the diverse inclinations (āsaya) of beings, the elegance of the teaching (desanā-vilāsa), and the diversity of expression (abhilāpanā-nānatta).

## The Commentary on the Fifth Sutta is finished.

## 6. Commentary on the Mahākassapa Sutta

In the sixth sutta, "at Rājagaha" means in the city of that name. It is called "Rājagaha" because it was possessed by kings such as Mandhātu and Mahāgovinda. Others explain it in another way: "It is Rājagaha because it is the house (gaha) of kings, being difficult for rival kings to overcome." Nevertheless, it is just the name of that city. That city is a city only during the time of a Buddha or a Cakkavatti king; at other times, it is empty, possessed by Yakkhas, and remains as their dwelling place.

In the phrase "at Veluvana, in the Kalandakanivāpa": "Veluvana" is the name of that monastery. It is said to have been surrounded by a wall eighteen cubits high. It was adorned with a great Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭi) suitable for the Blessed One's dwelling, and with other mansions, huts, caves, pavilions, walkways, and gate-towers. Because it was surrounded on the outside by bamboo trees (veḷu), appearing dark green and delightful to the heart, it is called "Veluvana." Because they gave food (nivāpa) to squirrels (kalandaka) there, it is called "Kalandakanivāpa."

Formerly, a certain king entered that garden to play, became intoxicated with liquor, and fell asleep during the day. His attendants, thinking "The king is asleep," were lured away here and there by flowers, fruits, and so on. Then, a black cobra came out of a tree hollow due to the smell of liquor and approached the king. Seeing this, a tree deity thought, "I will save the king's life," went in the form of a squirrel, and made a sound near his ear. The king woke up, and the black cobra turned back. Seeing the squirrel, the king thought, "This little black one has given me my life," and established a feeding ground for squirrels there, and had a proclamation of safety (abhayaghosa) announced. Therefore, from that day on, it became known as "Kalandakanivāpa." "Kalandaka" is the name for squirrels. In that Veluvana, in the Kalandakanivāpa.

"Mahākassapa": He is "Great Kassapa" because he is endowed with the great aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha) and so on. Alternatively, in relation to the Elder Kumārakassapa, this elder...
55:
The Great Elder is called "Mahākassapa." Regarding the phrase "Pipphaliguhāyaṃ" (in the Pipphali Cave), it is said that there was once a Pipphali tree near the entrance of that cave; because of that tree, the cave was known as the "Pipphali Cave." In that Pipphali Cave. "Ābādhiko" means one who has an affliction, meaning one who is ill. "Dukkhito" means one in whom bodily suffering has arisen, meaning one who has reached a state of suffering. "Bāḷhagilāno" means having extreme illness; yet, even with such intense painful feelings, he endured them with mindfulness and clear comprehension. Then, the Blessed One, knowing the Elder Mahākassapa's condition, went to that place and recited the Bojjhaṅga Paritta (the Protection of the Factors of Enlightenment). Because of that recitation, the Elder's illness was subsided. This account is stated in the Bojjhaṅga Saṃyutta as follows:

"At that time, the Venerable Mahākassapa was staying in the Pipphali Cave, afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill. Then, in the evening, the Blessed One rose from his seclusion and approached the Venerable Mahākassapa. Having approached, he sat down on the prepared seat. Having sat down, the Blessed One ... (pe) ... said this: 'Kassapa, are you keeping well? Are you enduring? Are the painful feelings receding and not increasing? Is their receding apparent and not their increasing?' 'Venerable Sir, I am not keeping well, I am not enduring. Intense painful feelings are increasing for me, not receding. Their increasing is apparent, not their receding.'

'Kassapa, these seven factors of enlightenment have been well-expounded by me, developed, and frequently practiced; they lead to higher knowledge, to awakening, and to Nibbāna. Which seven? Kassapa, the enlightenment factor of mindfulness has been well-expounded by me, developed, and frequently practiced; it leads to higher knowledge, to awakening, and to Nibbāna ... (pe) ... the enlightenment factor of equanimity has been well-expounded by me, developed, and frequently practiced; it leads to higher knowledge, to awakening, and to Nibbāna. Kassapa, these seven factors of enlightenment have been well-expounded by me, developed, and frequently practiced; they lead to higher knowledge, to awakening, and to Nibbāna.' 'Indeed, Blessed One, they are the factors of enlightenment! Indeed, Sugata, they are the factors of enlightenment!'

The Blessed One said this. The Venerable Mahākassapa was uplifted and rejoiced in the Blessed One's words. And the Venerable Mahākassapa rose (from that illness)."
56:
As soon as the Venerable Mahākassapa rose from that illness, that illness of the Venerable Mahākassapa was abandoned. Therefore, it is said (in the Bojjhaṅga Saṃyutta), "Then, at a later time, the Venerable Mahākassapa rose from that illness."

Regarding the phrase "This thought occurred": In the previous days of his illness, he had stayed only in the monastery, consuming the alms-food brought by his fellow residents. Then, after rising from that illness, this thought occurred to the Venerable Mahākassapa: "What if I were to enter Rājagaha for alms?"

"Five hundred celestial maidens" refers to the five hundred dove-colored nymphs who were the attendants of Sakka, the King of Devas. "They were striving" means that, intending to offer alms to the Elder, they prepared five hundred portions of alms-food, took them in golden bowls, and stood along the path, saying, "Venerable Sir, please accept this alms-food; please show us favor," being very diligent in the act of offering alms. Therefore, it is said, "For the sake of the Venerable Mahākassapa obtaining alms-food."

It is said that Sakka, the King of Devas, knowing the Elder's thought, sent those celestial maidens, saying, "Go, offer alms to the Venerable Mahākassapa and establish your own support (merit)." For Sakka thought, "If the Elder accepts alms-food from even one of these maidens as they go, it will be for her welfare and happiness for a long time." The Elder refused. To the celestial maidens who were saying, "Venerable Sir, please accept my alms-food; please accept my alms-food," he said, "Go away, you who have performed merit and possess great wealth; I will show favor to the poor." When they pleaded again even after being refused, unwilling to leave, he said, "You do not know your own measure; go away!" and snapped his fingers. Hearing the sound of the Elder's finger-snap, the maidens were terrified, and unable to remain, they fled and returned to the celestial realm. Therefore, it is said, "Having refused the five hundred celestial maidens."
57:
"Pubbaṇhasamayaṃ" means at a certain time in the morning, at a certain period. "Nivāsetvā" means having firmly dressed the undergarment by way of rearranging it over the monastery-wear. "Pattacīvaramādāya" means having donned the robe and taken the bowl in hand. "Piṇḍāya pāvisi" means he entered for the purpose of alms-gathering. "Daliddavisikhā" is the place where poor people live. "Kapaṇavisikhā" is the dwelling place of those who are destitute due to the loss of wealth. "Pesakāravisikhā" is the dwelling place of weavers.

How did the Blessed One see? While dwelling at Veḷuvana Monastery, reflecting, "My son Kassapa, who has recovered from illness, what is he doing?", the Blessed One saw with his divine eye (dibbacakkhu).

Having known this matter: Having known this matter regarding the practice of Venerable Mahākassapa, who rejected the divine alms-food consisting of various curries and dishes offered by five hundred celestial nymphs, in order to favor the destitute people, he uttered this inspired utterance (udāna) which demonstrates the power of the "such-like" nature (tādibhāva) of an Arahant whose taints are destroyed, by way of showing supreme fewness of wishes.

In that verse of the inspired utterance, "ananyaposiṃ": one who supports others is called "aññaposī"; one who does not support others is "ananyaposiṃ." It means one who supports only himself, being alone without others to be supported by him. By this term "ananyaposiṃ," the Elder's quality of being easy to support (subhara) is shown. Indeed, the Elder Mahākassapa lived as a person of supreme fewness of wishes, supporting only himself with the robe carried on his body and the alms-food carried in his stomach. He did not support anyone among relatives, friends, etc., because of his lack of attachment anywhere. Alternatively, he is "ananyaposiṃ" because there is no state of being supported by any other person. One whose four requisites are tied to only a single donor is not called "ananyaposiṃ" because his livelihood depends on one person.

Venerable Mahākassapa, following the method stated in the verse "Just as a bee [collects nectar from] a flower" (Dhp. 49), wandered for alms relying on the strength of his legs, being always like a newcomer in the houses of donors, and subsisted on mixed alms-food. Because he practiced in such a way, the Blessed One praised that Venerable Mahākassapa for his "moon-like practice" (candūpamappaṭipadā). "Aññātaṃ" means well-known, having fame spread due to genuine virtues. Or else, it means one known by gods and humans due to those qualities of being self-supporting, fewness of wishes, and contentment. Alternatively, "aññātaṃ" means one who is not known by way of making himself known to others for the sake of gain, honor, and fame, because of having completely abandoned craving in every way.
58:
Indeed, one who is not free from craving and has evil wishes makes himself known to others with the intention of being highly regarded through deceit. "Danta" (tamed) refers to one who is disciplined through the supreme restraint of the faculties by way of six-factored equanimity (saḷaṅgupekkhā). "Sāre patiṭṭhita" (established in the essence) refers to one who is established in the essence of liberation (vimutti), or one who is established in the essence of virtue, etc., such as the aggregate of virtue of one beyond training (asekkhasīlakkhandha). "Khīṇāsavaṃ vantadosaṃ": he is called "khīṇāsava" because he has completely abandoned the four taints (āsava), such as the taint of sensual desire. Because he has thus abandoned them, he is called "vantadosa" because he has spat out faults such as lust in every way. The Blessed One said: "I call such a person, a 'Paramattha Brāhmaṇa' (Brahmin in the ultimate sense) who is endowed with the aforementioned qualities, a 'Brāhmaṇa'." In this discourse also, the diversity of the teaching should be understood according to the method previously mentioned.

## The Commentary on the Sixth Sutta is Finished.

## 7. Commentary on the Ajakalāpaka Sutta

In the seventh discourse, "Pāvāyaṃ" means in the city of the Malla kings of that name. "Ajakalāpake cetiye" means in a place revered by people, which received the name "Ajakalāpaka" because it was possessed by a Yakkha named Ajakalāpaka. It is heard that this Yakkha receives offerings together with groups of goats tied in bundles, and not in any other way; therefore, he is known as "Ajakalāpaka." Some, however, say: he is called "Ajakalāpaka" because he makes beings scream like young goats. When people bring offerings to that Yakkha and present them while making the sound of a goat, only then is that Yakkha pleased; therefore, he is called "Ajakalāpaka." That Yakkha is endowed with great power, is fierce, harsh, and rough, and he constantly resides there. Therefore, people revere that place and present offerings from time to time. Thus it is said, "Ajakalāpake cetiye." "Ajakalāpakassa yakkhassa bhavane" means in the mansion of that Yakkha.

At that time, the Teacher, wishing to discipline that Yakkha, went alone without a companion in the evening, taking his bowl and robes, to the door of the mansion of the Yakkha Ajakalāpaka. He asked the gatekeeper of that mansion for permission to enter. The gatekeeper said, "Venerable Sir, the Yakkha Ajakalāpaka is fierce and harsh; he has no respect for recluses or brahmins. Therefore, only you would know (the risk). As for me, it is not proper to remain without informing the Yakkha." Having said this, he went with the speed of the wind to the Yakkha Ajakalāpaka, who had gone to an assembly of Yakkhas. Meanwhile, the Blessed One entered the mansion and sat on the prepared seat in the pavilion of the Yakkha Ajakalāpaka. The Yakkha's female attendants approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and sat in suitable places. The Blessed One preached a Dhamma talk appropriate for the occasion to those attendants. Therefore, the Recensionists (Saṅgītikāras) said in the Pali text: "He was staying in the mansion of the Yakkha Ajakalāpaka at the Ajakalāpaka Shrine in the city of Pāvā." Then, while the Yakkha kings Sātāgiri and Hemavata were traveling through the sky above the mansion of the Yakkha Ajakalāpaka to the assembly of Yakkhas, their journey was interrupted. When they reflected, "Why is this?", they saw the Blessed One sitting in the mansion of the Yakkha Ajakalāpaka.
59: He went to the presence of Ajakalāpaka with the speed of the wind. The Teacher entered the mansion and sat on the seat prepared in the sitting hall of the yakkha Ajakalāpaka. The yakkha's retinue approached the Teacher, paid homage, and stood to one side. The Teacher gave them a timely Dhamma talk. Therefore, it is said: "He was staying at the Ajakalāpaka Shrine in Pāvā, in the mansion of the yakkha Ajakalāpaka." At that time, the yakkha chiefs Sātāgiri and Hemavata, while traveling above the mansion of Ajakalāpaka to a gathering of yakkhas, found their progress hindered. Wondering "What is the cause?", they looked down and saw the Teacher sitting in Ajakalāpaka's mansion. They went there, paid homage to the Blessed One, and said, "Venerable Sir, we are going to the gathering of yakkhas." Having asked permission and circumambulated him, they departed. Seeing Ajakalāpaka at the gathering, they joyfully announced: "Friend Ajakalāpaka, it is a great gain for you! The Blessed One, the foremost person in the world with its devas, is sitting in your mansion. Approach and attend upon the Blessed One, and listen to the Dhamma." Hearing their words, the yakkha thought, "These chiefs are talking about that shaven-headed ascetic sitting in my mansion." Overcome with anger, he thought, "Today there will be a battle between me and that ascetic." Rising from the gathering, he lifted his right foot and stepped on a mountain peak sixty leagues high, which split into two. The rest of what should be said here should be understood according to the method given in the commentary on the Āḷavaka Sutta. Indeed, the encounter with Ajakalāpaka is similar to the encounter with Āḷavaka, except for the asking and answering of questions and the three-fold exiting and entering of the mansion. Ajakalāpaka, even as he was coming, thought, "I will drive away that ascetic with these whirlwinds and rains." He conjured up rains including whirlwinds, but was unable to cause even a slight movement in the Blessed One. Then he created a host of ghosts with various weapons and terrifying forms. Approaching the Blessed One and moving around him, he caused various disturbances throughout the night, yet he could not move the Blessed One even a hair's breadth from his seat. However, he burned with anger, thinking, "This ascetic entered and sat in my mansion without asking me." Then the Blessed One, knowing the state of his mind, thought, "Just as if one were to split the gall bladder on the nose of a fierce dog, it would become even more enraged, so too this yakkha will commit more offenses in his heart if I remain inside the mansion. I shall go outside the mansion." Thinking thus, he himself left the mansion and sat in the open air. At that time, it is preached that the Blessed One was sitting in the open air during the darkness of the night. In that Pali text, "during the darkness of the night" means in a thick darkness so dense that one cannot see with the eyes. At that time, the darkness endowed with four factors occurred. Rain was falling drop by drop. Then the yakkha Ajakalāpaka thought, "I will drive away this ascetic by terrifying him with a fearful sound."
60: ...just as if one were to split the gall bladder on the nose of a fierce dog, it would become even more enraged, so too this yakkha will commit more offenses in his heart if I remain inside the mansion. I shall go outside the mansion." Thinking thus, he himself left the mansion and sat in the open air. Therefore, it was said: "At that time, the Blessed One was sitting in the open air during the darkness of the night." In that Pali text, "rattandhakāratimisāyaṃ" means in the darkness that causes blindness at night, in a thick darkness devoid of the arising of eye-consciousness. It should be known that at that time, the darkness endowed with four factors prevailed. The rain fell drop by drop. Then the yakkha Ajakalāpaka thought, "I will drive away this ascetic by terrifying him with this fearful sound." He went near the Blessed One and made that terrifying sound, starting with "Akkulo". Therefore, the words "Atha kho ajakalāpako" etc., were said. In those words, "bhayaṃ" means the terror of the mind. "Chambhitattaṃ" means the trembling of the body where the thighs become stiff like pillars. "Lomahaṃsaṃ" means the bristling of the hairs. By these three terms, only the arising of fear is shown. "Upasaṅkami" (he approached) — if it is asked: "Why did this yakkha approach with such an intention? Did he not already perform the disturbances he could do before?" — it is true that he did. However, that yakkha thought, "I could not do anything to him while he was staying on the firm ground in a safe place inside the mansion. Now, I can terrify and drive away the Blessed One who is staying outside." Truly, this yakkha regarded his mansion as "firm ground," thinking, "Because he stays on that ground, this ascetic is not afraid." "Three times he made the sound 'Akkulo Pakkulo', the Akkula-Pakkulika sound" means that out of a desire to terrify, he made such a sound three times. This is an onomatopoeic sound. At that time, that yakkha, as if lifting Mount Sineru, as if overturning the great earth, with great effort, made a sound like a hundred thunderclaps gathered in one place, like the trumpeting of the elephants of the directions, the roar of maned lions, the 'hiṃ' sound of yakkhas, the loud laughter of ghosts, the clapping of asuras, the crash of the thunderbolt of Sakka the king of devas. By its depth, pervasiveness, and terrifying nature, his sound seemed to mock and overwhelm all other sounds, like the roar of the great whirlwind at the end of an aeon, as if splitting the hearts of worldlings. Three times he let out his yakkha-roar, a great and fearful sound with indistinct syllables...
61:
The Yakkha roared, thinking, "With this sound, I will terrify this ascetic and make him flee." Wherever that sound spread, mountains cracked into layers. Starting from the great trees, leaves, fruits, and flowers fell from all trees, vines, and bushes. Even the great Himavanta mountain range, three thousand yojanas in extent, shook, trembled, and quaked violently. From the earth-dwelling deities (bhummadevatā) onwards, many deities experienced fear, trembling, and horripilation; let alone human beings. For other footless, two-footed, and four-footed creatures, it was a great and terrifying moment, as if the great earth were breaking apart. A great tumult arose throughout the entire island of Jambudīpa. The Blessed One, however, sat motionless, not paying attention to that sound as if asking "What is this sound?" He made a resolution (adhiṭṭhāna): "May no one be harmed by this sound."

Because that sound reached the ears of beings in the manner of "Akkula Pakkula," it is called "Akkulo Pakkulo" by way of imitation. Considering that the Yakkha produced the "Akkula Pakkula" sound in making that intense noise, the redactors of the Council included it as "Akkulapakkulikaṃ akāsi" (he made the Akkula-Pakkula sound). Some teachers, however, say that "Akkulo Bakkulo" is spoken as a synonym for the two words "ākula" (confused) and "byākula" (disturbed), similar to "ekaṃ ekakaṃ." A being born only once, due to its first arising, is called "ākula"; the letter "ā" is shortened and the letter "ka" is added to become "akkula." A being born twice is called "bakkula." Here, the word "kula" is a synonym for "birth" (jāti), as in "kolaṃkola" and so on. Following the stated meaning, the first word refers to the viviparous (jalābuja) such as lions and tigers, and the second word refers to the oviparous (aṇḍaja) such as venomous cobras. Therefore, other teachers say that the Yakkha shows this meaning with these two words: "I am one who will take your life, like a lion or like a cobra." Still other teachers, stating the Pali as "akkhulo bhakkhulo," give the meaning: "He is called akkhulo because he can exhaust or destroy life, and bhakkhulo because he can devour." Who is he? He is any one of the Yakkhas, Rakkhasas, Pisācas, lions, tigers, etc., who brings harm to humans. Here too, the connection of meaning should be understood in the same way as previously stated.
62:
"O ascetic, this is a Pisāca (flesh-eater) for you," the Yakkha said, referring to himself, after creating a great and terrifying form and standing before the Blessed One.

"Etam-atthaṃ viditvā" means: having known that distorted behavior produced by the Yakkha through body and speech, and having known in every way his own state of being free from defilements regarding worldly conditions (lokadhamma), which is the cause of his being unsubduable by that distortion. "Tāyaṃ velāyaṃ" means: at the time of performing that distorted behavior. "Imaṃ udānaṃ" means: not paying attention to that distortion, he uttered this inspired utterance (udāna) which illustrates the power of the Dhamma, the cause for not paying attention to it.

In that inspired utterance, "yadā sakesu dhammesu" means: at the time when, in the five aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandha) known as one's own individual existence (attabhāva). "Pāragū" means: one who has gone to the further shore due to the fulfillment of full understanding (pariññābhisamaya); and for that very reason, one who has gone to the further shore due to the fulfillment of the realization of abandoning, realizing, and developing (pahāna-sacchikiriyā-bhāvanā-abhisamaya) regarding the origin (samudaya) which is the cause of those aggregates, the cessation (nirodha) which has the characteristic of their non-occurrence, and the path (paṭipadā) leading to cessation. "Hoti brāhmaṇo" means: he is called a Brahmin because he has barred (bāhita) evil in every way; and by understanding his own individual existence in every way, he is one who has realized the Four Noble Truths. It is also said: "In this very fathom-long carcass, endowed with perception and mind, I declare the world and the origin of the world," and so forth. Alternatively, "sakesu dhammesu" means: in one's own qualities. One's own qualities refer to the qualities such as virtue (sīla) of a person who desires their own welfare. Indeed, the pure qualities such as virtue, concentration, wisdom, and liberation are called a man's own qualities because they definitely bring about welfare and happiness; they are not "non-own qualities" like the defiled qualities that bring harm. "Pāragū" means: one who has reached the shore, the end, by the fulfillment of those qualities such as virtue.

Among those qualities, virtue (sīla) is first of two kinds: mundane (lokiya) and supramundane (lokuttara). Of these, mundane virtue is the virtue of the preliminary stage (pubbabhāga-sīla). Briefly, it is of four kinds, such as the restraint of the Pātimokkha (pātimokkha-saṃvara-sīla), and in detail, it has many varieties. Supramundane virtue is of two kinds by way of the Path and Fruit; in essence, it is Right Speech, Right Action, and Right Livelihood. Just as virtue, so too concentration (samādhi) and wisdom (paññā) are of two kinds: mundane and supramundane. Therein, mundane concentration consists of the eight attainments (samāpatti) together with access concentration (upacāra). Supramundane concentration...
63:
(Supramundane concentration) is concentration included in the Path. Wisdom is also of two kinds: mundane wisdom, which consists of wisdom based on learning (sutamaya-ñāṇa), wisdom based on reflection (cintāmaya-ñāṇa), and wisdom based on mental development (bhāvanāmaya-ñāṇa), and is subject to taints (sāsava); and supramundane wisdom, which is associated with the Path and the Fruit. Liberation (vimutti) refers to the liberation of the Fruit (phala-vimutti) and Nibbāna; therefore, that liberation is strictly supramundane. The knowledge and vision of liberation (vimuttiñāṇadassana) is purely mundane because it is of the nature of reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇāñāṇa), which is of nineteen types. Thus, because these qualities such as virtue (sīla) and so on have arisen in their entirety without remainder through the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship in one's own continuity, one is called a "paragū"—one who has gone to the far shore (pāra) or limit (pariyanta) of one's own qualities.

Alternatively, one is a "paragū" in virtue through the attainment of the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpattiphala). For that Stream-enterer is said to be "one who fulfills the virtues." By taking the Stream-enterer here, the Once-returner (sakadāgāmī) is also included. One is a "paragū" in concentration through the attainment of the fruit of Non-returning (anāgāmiphala). For that Non-returner is said to be "one who fulfills concentration." One is a "paragū" in the remaining three qualities (wisdom, liberation, and knowledge and vision of liberation) through the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship. For an Arahant is called a "paragū" in wisdom, liberation, and knowledge and vision of liberation because of having reached the fullness of wisdom, having attained the foremost unshakable liberation of mind (cetovimutti), and having reached the end of reviewing knowledge. Thus, in every way, because of the completion of the sixteen functions such as full understanding (pariññā) and so on through the power of the four Paths regarding the four Noble Truths, one has gone to the far shore of one's own qualities at those respective times as mentioned.

"He is a Brahmin" (brāhmaṇo hoti) means that at that time, he is a Brahmin in the ultimate sense (paramattha-brāhmaṇa) because he has excluded evil qualities. "Then he transcends this demon and the akkula-pakkulika sound" (atha etaṃ pisācañca pakkulañcātivattati) means that after reaching the far shore as mentioned, "O Ajakalāpaka, you transcend, overcome, and surpass this demon who came to eat flesh as shown by you, and that akkula-pakkulika sound created by you to cause fear; you are not afraid of it."

This verse was also spoken in praise of the fruit of Arahantship alone. Then the demon Ajakalāpaka, seeing that such nature of the Blessed One was unshakable even by such terrifying intimidation created by himself, had a mind full of faith, thinking, "Oh, what an amazing man!" and manifesting the faith of a worldling (puthujjana) established within him, he declared his status as a lay follower (upāsaka) in the presence of the Teacher.

## The Commentary on the Seventh Sutta is finished.
64:
## 8. Saṅgāmajisutta-vaṇṇanā

In the eighth sutta, Saṅgāmaji is the name of this venerable one. This venerable one was the son of a certain very wealthy merchant in Sāvatthī. When he reached the proper age, his parents married him to a suitable wife, handed over the wealth to him, and he was bound by the bondage of household life. One day, he saw the lay followers (upāsakas) living in Sāvatthī, having given alms and undertaken the precepts in the morning, wearing clean clothes and clean upper robes in the evening, and carrying perfumes, garlands, etc., in their hands, heading towards Jetavana to listen to the Dhamma. When he asked, "Where are you going?" and was told, "To the presence of the Blessed One at Jetavana to listen to the Dhamma," he said, "In that case, I will go too," and went to Jetavana with them. At that time, the Blessed One, like a maned lion roaring a lion's roar in a golden cave, was sitting on the noble Buddha-seat prepared in the Pavilion of the True Dhamma (Saddhamma-maṇဍapa), teaching the Dhamma in the midst of the fourfold assembly.

Then those lay followers, having paid homage to the Blessed One, sat down at one side. The clansman Saṅgāmaji also sat down at the edge of that assembly, listening to the Dhamma. The Blessed One gave a gradual discourse (anupubbikathā) and proclaimed the four Truths. At the conclusion of the Truths, there was the realization of the Dhamma (dhammābhisamaya) for many thousands of living beings. The clansman Saṅgāmaji also attained the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpattiphala), and when the assembly rose, he approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and requested ordination, saying, "Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One ordain me." "But have you been permitted by your parents to ordain?" "Venerable Sir, I have not been permitted." "Saṅgāmaji, the Tathāgatas do not ordain a son who is not permitted by his parents." "Venerable Sir, I will act in such a way that my parents will permit me to ordain." Having paid homage to the Blessed One and circumambulated him, he approached his parents and said, "Mother and father, please permit me to ordain." What follows should be understood according to the method mentioned in the Raṭṭhapāla Sutta (M. Ni. 2.293 etc.).

Then, having given a promise, "I will show myself after ordaining," and having received permission from his parents, he approached the Blessed One and requested ordination. He received the novice ordination (pabbajjā) and the higher ordination (upasampadā) in the presence of the Blessed One. Not long after his higher ordination, striving and exerting for the sake of the higher paths, he spent the rainy season living in a certain forest dwelling, became one with the six supernormal powers (abhiññā), and after the rainy season, in order to see the Blessed One and also to his parents...
65:
To be released from the promise given to his parents, he went to Sāvatthī. With reference to this journey, it is stated in the Pali: "At that time, the Venerable Saṅgāmaji was staying at Sāvatthī."

The Venerable Saṅgāmaji, having wandered for alms in a nearby village and finished his meal, returned from his alms round and entered the Jetavana monastery to approach the Blessed One. After exchanging pleasant greetings with the Blessed One, he reported his attainment [of the fruit of Arahantship]. Then, having paid homage to the Blessed One and circumambulated him, he departed and sat at the foot of a certain tree for the day’s abiding. At that time, the parents, relatives, and friends of the Venerable Saṅgāmaji heard of his arrival. Overjoyed, saying, "It is said that Saṅgāmaji has arrived here," they went quickly to the monastery. Searching for him, they saw him sitting at the foot of that tree. They approached him, exchanged greetings, and pleaded: "Do not let the kings seize this heirless wealth, nor let unloved heirs take it. It is not yet time for you to be a recluse. Come, dear son, return to the lay life!"

Hearing these words, the Elder thought: "These people do not know that I have no desire for sense pleasures. Just as dung-carrying dogs or pigs desire only to cling to a heap of dung, they desire only to cling to sense pleasures. It is not possible to make them understand through a Dhamma talk." Thinking thus, he sat as if he did not hear.

Seeing that he did not comply with their words despite their various pleas, the parents returned home and sent Saṅgāmaji’s former wife along with their young son and a retinue. They said, "We have returned without winning his heart despite our various pleas. Go, lady! Show your husband the son, plead with him, and make him understand." It is said that the Venerable One had ordained while she was pregnant. She accepted, saying "Very well," and taking the child, went to the Jetavana monastery with a large retinue. With reference to her going, the passage beginning with "The former wife of Venerable Saṅgāmaji heard..." was spoken.

In that passage, "purāṇadutiyikā" means the former wife who used to serve at his feet during his previous life as a layman. "Ayya" (Noble Sir) is a term used to address monks, though she would have previously called him "husband" (ayyaputta). "Kira" is a particle indicating hearsay, to be understood in connection with "it is said he has arrived." "O recluse, support your little son" means: "You ordained and left me while I was pregnant. Now I have this little son. It is improper for you to abandon me like this and practice the life of a recluse. Therefore, O recluse, support me and the little son with food, clothing, and so on." However, the Venerable Saṅgāmaji kept his senses restrained, neither looking at them nor speaking. Therefore, it is said: "When this was said, the Venerable Saṅgāmaji remained silent."
66:
Although she spoke thus three times, seeing the Elder remain silent, she thought: "Men may be indifferent toward their wives, but they are usually affectionate toward their sons. Love for a son pierces to the very marrow of the bones. Therefore, he might come under my influence through love for his son." Thinking thus, she placed the young son in the Elder’s lap and walked a short distance away, saying, "O recluse, this is your son; support him!" It is said that she was unable to stand before the Elder due to his ascetic power. The Elder neither looked at the child nor spoke. Then the woman, standing not far away and turning her head to look back, realized the Elder's state of mind. She returned, took the child, and departed, thinking: "This recluse has no desire even for his own son; how much less would he desire a wife, gold, silver, and so on?" Therefore, it is said: "Then the former wife of Venerable Saṅgāmaji..."

In that passage, "even for the son" means: if this recluse has no desire even for his own biological son, how much less for others? In the term "divine" (dibba), it is called divine because it is like that of the devas. Devas possess a divine sensitive eye (pasāda-cakkhu) produced by wholesome kamma, which is not clouded by bile, phlegm, blood, etc., and is capable of perceiving distant objects. This eye of direct knowledge (abhiññā-cakkhu) produced by the concentration of the fourth jhāna is also called "divine" because it is similar to that. Alternatively, it is called divine because it is obtained by relying on a divine abiding (dibba-vihāra), or because of its great radiance and great range. "With that divine [eye]" is the meaning. "Pure" means perfectly pure due to the absence of defilements such as the hindrances. "Surpassing that of humans" means exceeding the scope of human vision. "Such a manner" refers to the improper and unseemly act of placing a son in the lap of a monk as mentioned before.

"That matter" means having known in every way that matter, namely, the Venerable Saṅgāmaji’s state of being indifferent toward all sense pleasures such as his son and wife. "This inspired utterance" means he uttered this inspired utterance which illustrates the Elder's quality of steadfastness (tādi) toward desirable and undesirable objects.

In that verse, "coming" refers to the former wife who approached him. "Does not rejoice" means he did not feel joy or delight, thinking, "She has come to see me." "Departing" refers to her leaving, thinking, "This former wife is leaving because I did not welcome her." "Does not grieve" means he did not fall into mental distress. To show the reason why the Elder neither rejoiced nor grieved, it is said: "Released from bonds, Saṅgāmaji..." There, "bonds" refers to the fivefold bonds of lust, hatred, delusion, conceit, and views, which the Elder Saṅgāmaji had cut off through abandonment by uprooting (samuccheda-pahāna), thereby becoming released.
67:
I call the Elder Saṅgāmaji a Brāhmaṇa, who is liberated through tranquility and liberation, and who has conquered attachment. I call that Arahant, who has attained such a state of 'tādi' and whose taints (āsavas) are destroyed, a Brāhmaṇa because he has completely discarded all evil.

## The Commentary on the Eighth Sutta is finished.

## 9. Commentary on the Jaṭila Sutta

In the ninth sutta, the Jaṭila Sutta, in the phrase 'at Gayā' (Gayāyaṃ), 'Gayā' refers to both a village and a bathing ghat (tittha). Because the Blessed One was staying not far from the village of Gayā, it is said that he 'dwells at Gayā'; likewise, because he was near the Gayā ghat. Regarding the Gayā ghat, there is a pond and also a river not far from the village of Gayā. The worldly masses call both of them the 'ghat for washing away evil' (pāpapavāhanatittha). Regarding 'at Gayāsīsa' (Gayāsīse), there is a mountain there named Gayāsīsa with a peak resembling an elephant's head. On that mountain, there is a stone plateau resembling an elephant's frontal globe (kumbha) which has enough space for a thousand monks; the Blessed One was staying there. Therefore, it is said, 'He was dwelling at Gayā, at Gayāsīsa.'

'Jaṭilas' refers to ascetics (tāpasas). They are called 'Jaṭilas' here because they wear matted hair (jaṭā). 'During the time of snowfall in the Antaraṭṭhaka' (antaraṭṭhake himapātasamaye) refers to the period of eight days when snow falls—the last four days of the month of Māgha and the first four days of the month of Phagguṇa, occurring within the winter season. 'They emerge at Gayā' (Gayāyaṃ ummujjanti) means some people first submerge their entire bodies in the water designated as a 'ghat' and then emerge, rise up, or float up. 'They submerge' (nimujjanti) means they sink into the water including their heads. 'They also perform emerging and submerging' (ummujjanimujjampi karonti) means they repeatedly perform the acts of emerging and submerging.

In this regard, some hold the view that 'purification from evil occurs by a single emergence.' Therefore, they depart after performing only one emergence. However, since there is no emerging without submerging, they also perform submerging due to their inseparable nature. Those who hold the view that 'purification from evil occurs by a single submergence' also depart after submerging only once and then emerging, as the two are inseparable in the manner described. But those who hold the view that 'purification from evil occurs only by staying submerged in that ghat' submerge in that ghat, hold their breath, and reach the end of their lives right there, like those who have fallen from a mountain precipice...
68:
...reach the end of their lives right there in that submerged place, like those who have fallen from a mountain precipice. Others hold the view that 'purification from evil occurs when one bathes by repeatedly emerging and submerging'; thus, they perform emerging and submerging from time to time. With reference to all of them, it is said: 'They emerge, they submerge, and they also perform emerging and submerging.' Here, although submerging precedes emerging, 'emerging' (ummujjanaṃ) is mentioned first to show the prevalence of those who perform emerging and both acts, as those who only submerge are few. Similarly, in the phrase 'many Jaṭilas,' it is said so because the matted-hair ascetics were the majority; however, at that time, Brahmins named Muṇḍikas and Sikhaṇḍikas, who also believed in purification by water, acted in the same way at that ghat.

'They pour' (osiñcanti) means some take the water of the Gayā river with their hands and pour it over their heads and bodies. Others take water with jars and, standing on the bank, do the same. 'They sacrifice to the fire' (aggiṃ juhanti) means some prepare a sacrificial altar on the bank of the Gayā river, bring ritual implements such as smoke and sacrificial grass (dabbha), and perform the fire sacrifice or attend to the sacrificial fire. 'Purification through this' (iminā suddhī) means they hold the view that 'purification from the stain of evil, the washing away of evil, or purification from saṃsāra occurs through this emerging and submerging in the Gayā river and by attending to the fire.'

In this context, 'emerging' and so on should be understood as being mentioned as mere examples. Among them, some practice living in water, some offer palm-salutations (añjali) in the water, some stand in the water and revolve according to the course of the moon and sun, some chant mantras like the Sāvittī many thousands of times, some invoke vidyā-mantras saying 'O Indra, come!' and so on, and some perform great services. While doing so, some descend into the water, some ascend from the water, some perform ritual rinsing (ācamana) for purification after ascending, and some stand inside the water playing strings or playing the lute, thus displaying various kinds of activities. Alternatively, since they perform such distorted activities only after first submerging and emerging in that water, all of that is included within submerging and emerging, and thus it is said 'they emerge' and so on. While such chaotic activities were taking place there, the Blessed One, staying on the hilltop, heard their commotion and, looking to see 'What is this?', saw those peculiar activities. With reference to that sight, it is said: 'The Blessed One saw... pe... purification through this.' This has the meaning already stated.
69:
"Having understood this matter" means having understood in every aspect their wrong assumption of the path to purification in what is not the path to purification, such as descending into water, and his own unerring realization of the path to purification in such things as the Truth. "This inspired utterance" means he uttered this inspired utterance which shows that purification by water is not the path to purification, and shows that things such as the Truth are the true path to purification.

In that verse, in the phrase "one does not become pure by water," "by water" refers to [the act of] emerging from water and so forth. In the term *udakummubjanādi*, the final part is dropped and it is called "*udaka*" (water). It is like calling the *rūpabhava* (fine-material existence) simply "*rūpa*." Alternatively, it means that there is no such thing as the purification of a being by means of water, which is the instrument for completing actions such as emerging [from water]. Or else, a being does not become pure from the stains of evil by that aforementioned water. Why? Because many people bathe in this water. If purification from evil were to occur through the aforementioned descending into water and so forth, then those who commit evil deeds such as matricide, others who kill cows and buffaloes, and even down to fish and tortoises, would all become pure from evil. But it is not so. Why? Because bathing does not have the nature of opposing the causes of evil. Whatever destroys something is the opposite of that thing, just as light is the opposite of darkness, and knowledge (*vijjā*) is the opposite of ignorance (*avijjā*). Bathing is not like that in relation to evil. Therefore, the conclusion should be reached here that "one does not become pure by water."

To show that by which one becomes pure, he said: "In whom there is truth," and so forth. Therein, "in whom" means in which person. "Truth" (*sacca*) means both truth of speech and truth of abstinence. Alternatively, "truth" means both truth of knowledge and ultimate truth. "Dhamma" means the Dhamma of the Noble Path and the Dhamma of the Fruit. If all that is found in a person, he is pure, and he is a Brahmin (*brāhmaṇa*). Specifically, an Arahant, whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*), is pure and a Brahmin due to ultimate purification. Why is "truth" mentioned separately from "Dhamma" in this discourse? Because truth is of great benefit. Indeed, it is said: "Truth is indeed the immortal word," "Truth is indeed the sweetest of tastes," "The virtuous, established in truth and meaning and Dhamma, are said to be firm," "Ascetics and Brahmins are established in truth," and so forth; the virtues of truth are revealed in many scriptural passages. Regarding falsehood, which is the opposite of truth, it is revealed: "For the person who has transgressed one law, who speaks falsely, [he goes to hell]," and "The speaker of untruth goes to hell," and so forth.

## Commentary on the Ninth Sutta is finished.
70:
## 10. Commentary on the Bāhiya Sutta

In the tenth discourse, "Bāhiya" is his name. "Dārucīriya" is because he wore clothing made of bark. He lived in the seaport named Suppāraka. Who was this Bāhiya, why did he become Dārucīriya, and why did he live in the Suppāraka seaport?

Here is the sequential account. It is said that a hundred thousand eons ago, during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, a certain clansman in the city of Haṃsavatī, while listening to the Dhamma teaching of the Ten-Powered One, saw the Teacher appointing a certain monk to the foremost position (*etadagga*) of those with swift intuition (*khippābhiññā*). He thought, "Great indeed is this monk, who is thus appointed to the foremost position by the Teacher. Oh, may I too, in the future, having gone forth in the dispensation of such a Buddha, be appointed by the Teacher to such a foremost position as this monk." Having aspired to that position, he performed corresponding meritorious deeds, and after performing merit throughout his life, he was destined for heaven and wandered through the realms of gods and humans. Having gone forth in the dispensation of Kassapa Buddha, while practicing the recluse's Dhamma with perfect virtue, he reached the end of his life and was reborn in the celestial realm. Having lived in the celestial realm for the interval between two Buddhas, in this Buddha-arising period, he took rebirth in a noble family in the country of Bāhiya. Because he was born in the country of Bāhiya, he was known as Bāhiya. When he reached maturity, while living the household life, he filled a ship with many goods for trade, entered the ocean, and traveled back and forth, reaching his own city safely with his retinue seven times.

On the eighth occasion, however, thinking "I will go to Suvaṇṇabhūmi," he loaded goods and boarded the ship. When the ship reached the great ocean, before reaching the desired destination, it was wrecked in the middle of the ocean. The multitude of people became food for fish and tortoises. Bāhiya, however, grabbing a plank of the ship and swimming, was gently tossed by the force of the waves and reached the shore of the Suppāraka seaport on the seventh day. Since his clothes had slipped off and fallen into the ocean, he lay on the shore of the ocean just as he was born. Having relieved his exhaustion and gained some relief, he stood up and, out of shame, entered a thicket. Seeing no other clothing to cover himself, he cut [bark from] *akka* trees and, binding them with fibers, made a garment to cover himself. (Some teachers say that he bored holes in wooden planks, stitched them with fibers, and wore them as a garment.) Thus, because he always wore clothing made of wood, he was famous as Dārucīriya, and by his former name as Bāhiya. That Dārucīriya took a broken bowl and wandered for alms in the Suppāraka seaport in the manner mentioned. People saw him and thought, "If there are Arahants in the world, they must be like this person. If we offer this venerable one clothing, will he take it, or will he not take it because of his fewness of desires?" Wishing to test him, they brought clothes from various places. That Dārucīriya thought, "If I come in this manner, these people will not have faith in me. This person, having rejected clothes, by this way of living alone..."
71:
He wrapped himself in bark fibers (from the Madhuca tree), making lower and upper garments to cover himself. Some teachers, however, say: "He bored holes in wooden planks, threaded them with bark fibers, and made lower and upper garments to wear." Because he habitually wore clothes made of wood in every way, he became well-known as "Dārucīriya," and by his old name as "Bāhiya."

Holding a broken pot and wandering for alms at the Suppāraka seaport in the manner mentioned, people saw him and thought: "If there are indeed Arahants in the world, such a person must be one. Will this venerable one accept offered clothes, or will he not accept them due to his fewness of wishes?" Desiring to test him, they brought clothes from various directions. That Dārucīriya thought: "If I do not come in this manner, these people will not be so devoted to me. If I reject these clothes and live only in this way, gains, honors, and offerings will arise for me." Having thought thus, he stood in a state of pretension and did not accept the clothes. People thought, "Oh, how few are the wishes of this venerable one!" and with hearts exceedingly devoted, they performed great offerings and acts of respect.

After finishing his meal, that Dārucīriya went to a shrine in a nearby place. The multitude of people followed him, cleaned that shrine, and offered it to him. He thought: "These people are so devoted to me just for wearing bark that they perform such offerings and acts of respect; I should be one who has an excellent livelihood for them." Thus, he lived with few requisites and fewness of wishes. Being esteemed by those people as an "Arahant," he also considered himself an "Arahant." Offerings and honors towards that Dārucīriya increased more and more, and he became one who easily obtained the four excellent requisites. Therefore, it was said (in the Pāḷi): "At that time, Bāhiya Dārucīriya lived at Suppāraka on the seashore, honored, revered..." and so on.

In that passage, "sakkato" means honored by way of respectful attendance and service. "garukato" means revered like a stone parasol, with the intention that he is endowed with special qualities. "mānito" means esteemed by way of mental appreciation. "pūjito" means worshipped by way of offerings such as flowers and scents. "apacito" means respected by those with devoted minds through acts such as giving way on the path and bringing seats. "lābhi cīvara... pe... parikkhārānaṃ" means one who gains by way of receiving the four requisites, such as robes, which are most excellent and brought repeatedly.
72:
Another way of explanation: Sakkato means having attained honor. Garukato means having attained reverence in connection with special qualities. Mānito means being esteemed and loved by many in their minds. Pūjito means being worshipped with the great worship of the four requisites. Apacito means having attained respect. Indeed, one to whom people respectfully offer well-prepared and most excellent requisites is called sakkato. One in whom people establish a sense of reverence and then make offerings is called garukato. One whom people love in their minds and highly esteem is called mānito. One for whom people perform all these by way of worship is called pūjito. One for whom people perform supreme humility by way of salutation, rising to greet, and pressing the palms together is called apacito. They performed all these for Bāhiya. Therefore, it is said: "Bāhiya Dārucīriya lived at Suppāraka, honored..." and so on. In this context, although Bāhiya did not accept the robes, he is still called a "gainer" (lābhi) of robes because people approached him and offered them, saying, "Come, Bhante, please accept this cloth."

Rahogatassa means of one who has gone into seclusion. Paṭisallīnassa means of one who is alone in solitude. To that Bāhiya, who was called an "Arahant" by many people, there arose a reflection in his mind (a wrong thought) in the following manner. How? He thought: "Whoever in the world are Arahants or have entered the path to Arahantship, I am one of them." The meaning of that is: "Among those who are Arahants in this world of beings because they have slain the enemies of defilements and are worthy of offerings and honors, and those who have entered the path to Arahantship by slaying the defilements, I am one."

Purāṇasālohitā refers to a deity who was like a blood relative in a previous life and who practiced the ascetic Dhamma together with him. Some teachers, however, say: "Purāṇasālohitā is a certain goddess who was his mother in a previous life in ancient times." That view is rejected in the Commentary, and only the first meaning is accepted.

It is heard that: Long ago, when the Dispensation of the Buddha Kassapa was declining, seven bhikkhus, seeing the corrupt behavior of novices and others, were moved by spiritual urgency (saṃvega). Thinking, "Before the Dispensation disappears, we will make a support for ourselves," they paid homage to the Golden Cetiya and entered the forest. Seeing a mountain, they said, "Let those who have attachment to life turn back; let those without attachment [climb] this..."
73: "Those who have attachment to life, turn back; those without attachment, climb this mountain," they said. Having constructed a ladder, they all climbed the mountain, then threw the ladder down and practiced the ascetic Dhamma. Among those monks, the Elder of the Saṅgha attained Arahantship after just one night. That Elder brought almsfood from Uttarakuru and said to the monks, "Friends, partake of this almsfood." The monks replied, "Venerable sir, you have achieved this through your own spiritual power. If we also attain the special Dhamma like you, we will bring and consume it ourselves," and they did not wish to eat. Then, on the second day, the second Elder attained the fruit of Anāgāmī (Non-Returner). He also brought almsfood in the same manner, went to that place, and invited the remaining monks, but they refused in the same way. Among them, the Elder who attained Arahantship passed into Parinibbāna, and the Anāgāmī Elder was reborn in the Suddhāvāsa realm. The remaining five men, though they strove and exerted themselves, were unable to attain the special Dhamma. Being unable to do so, they withered away right there on the mountain, passed away, and were reborn in the deva world. They wandered only in the deva worlds for the duration of one buddhantara (the interval between two Buddhas). When this Buddha appeared, they passed away from the deva world and were reborn in various families. Among them, one became King Pukkusāti, one became Kumārakassapa, one became Dabba Mallaputta, one became Sabhiya the Wanderer, and one became Bāhiya Dārucīriya. Regarding the Anāgāmī person reborn in the Brahma world, it is said, "a deity who was a former kinsman." A son of the devas (devaputta) is also called a "deity" (devatā) because he is a divine being, just like a daughter of the devas (devadhītā), as seen in passages such as "Atha kho aññatarā devatā" (Then a certain deity...). In this context, however, a Brahma is intended by the term "deity." Immediately after being reborn in that realm, that Brahma looked at his own Brahma-splendor and reflected on the cause of his arrival. The fact that the seven men climbed the mountain to practice the ascetic Dhamma, that one of them attained Parinibbāna, and that he himself attained the fruit of Anāgāmī and was reborn in this realm, became clear to him. While reflecting, "Where are the remaining five men?", he knew they were reborn in the sense-sphere deva worlds. Later, from time to time, he would observe their progress, thinking, "What are they doing?" At this time, while reflecting, "Where are they?", he saw Bāhiya living near the port of Suppāraka, wearing bark garments and making a living through deception. [He thought,] "This man, while practicing the ascetic Dhamma with me in the past after constructing a ladder and climbing the mountain, lived with extreme austerity and [no regard] for life..."
74:
In the past, while Bāhiya was practicing the ascetic Dhamma with me after constructing a ladder and climbing the mountain, he had no regard for life and did not even eat the almsfood brought by the Arahant, practicing with great austerity. Yet now, desiring praise, he wanders about claiming to be an Arahant when he is not, craving gains, honors, and fame. He does not even know that the Sammāsambuddha has appeared. "I shall strike terror into this Bāhiya and make him aware of the Buddha's appearance," thinking thus, he immediately descended from the Brahma world and appeared before Dārucīriya at the port of Suppāraka during the night. Bāhiya, seeing the magnificent radiance at his dwelling place, wondered, "What is this?" and went outside to look. Seeing the Great Brahma standing in the sky, he raised his hands in salutation and asked, "O divine king, who are you?" Then the Brahma spoke to Bāhiya:

"I am your former companion of old. At that time, I attained the fruit of Anāgāmī and was reborn in the Brahma world. You, however, were unable to attain any special Dhamma, died as a worldling, and wandered through Saṃsāra. Now, wearing the garb of a sectarian, you wander about holding the view 'I am an Arahant' while not being one. Knowing this, I have come. Bāhiya, you are certainly not an Arahant. Abandon this evil wrong view. Bāhiya, let it not be for your harm and suffering for a long time. The Sammāsambuddha has appeared in the world. That Blessed One alone is truly an Arahant. Go to that Blessed One and pay homage to Him."

Thus it was said: "Atha kho bāhiyassa dārucီriyassa purāṇasālohitā devatā" and so forth. In that Pali, 'anukampikā' means one who habitually favors others, one with excessive compassion (karuṇā). 'Atthakāmā' means one who desires welfare, one with excessive loving-kindness (mettā). Here, by the first term, the Brahma shows his desire to remove Bāhiya's suffering, and by the second term, his desire to bring about Bāhiya's welfare. 'Cetasa' means 'with his own mind.' Here, taking the mind as the lead, it should be understood as the knowledge of encompassing the minds of others (cetopariya-ñāṇa). 'Cetopariyavitakkaṃ' refers to the occurrence of Bāhiya's mental reflections. 'Aññāya' means 'having known.'

'Tenupasaṅkami' means approaching, just as a strong man might stretch out his bent arm or bend his outstretched arm; likewise, vanishing from the Brahma world and appearing before Bāhiya. 'Etadavoca' means the Brahma spoke these words now to be mentioned, such as "Bāhiya, you are certainly not an Arahant," like catching a thief red-handed with the stolen goods, to Bāhiya who had such wrong reflections as "Whoever in the world are Arahants..." and so forth. By the words "Bāhiya, you are certainly not an Arahant," he rejects Bāhiya's status as an asekha (Arahant) at that time. By the words "nor are you one who has reached the path of Arahantship," he rejects his status as a sekha (trainee). By both these phrases, he shows only Bāhiya's status as a non-noble one (non-ariya). By this Pali text, "Bāhiya, you are certainly not an Arahant, nor are you one who has reached the path of Arahantship," Bāhiya's...
75:
With the words "You are not an Arahant, Bāhiya," his status as an asekha (one beyond training) is denied. With the words "Nor have you entered the path to Arahantship," his status as a sekha (one in training) is denied. By both statements, only his status as a non-noble (anariya) is shown. With the words "You do not even have the practice that leads to the fruit of Arahantship," his status as a noble worldling (kalyāṇa-puthujjana) is also rejected.

In this context, "practice" (paṭipadā) refers to the six purifications, beginning with the purification of virtue (sīla-visuddhi). It is called paṭipadā because one practices and ascends to the Noble Path through these purifications. "Assa" means "should be."

Based on what did this false notion (arahattādhimāna) that "I have attained the fruit of Arahantship" arise in Bāhiya? Some teachers say, "The conceit of Arahantship arose because his defilements were suppressed by the power of temporary abandonment (tadaṅga-pahāna) due to his fewness of wishes, contentment, austerity, and his long-standing merits." Other teachers, however, say, "Bāhiya had attained the four jhānas, and because his defilements did not manifest due to abandonment by suppression (vikkham-bhana-pahāna), the conceit of Arahantship arose." Both of these are merely the opinions of those teachers. This is because the commentary states, "He was desiring gain, offerings, and fame, with the intention of being esteemed." Therefore, the meaning should be understood only according to the method already mentioned.

Then Bāhiya, looking at the Great Brahmā standing in the sky and speaking, thought: "How grave a matter indeed! I thought of myself as an Arahant, but this Brahmā says, 'You do not even have the practice that leads to the fruit of Arahantship.' Are there any Arahants in the world?" After thinking thus, he questioned the Brahmā. Therefore, he asked the words: "O deity, who are the Arahants in the world now, or those who have entered the path to Arahantship?"

In that passage, "atha" is a particle used to begin a question. "Ke carahi" means "Who now?" "Loke" refers to the world of sentient beings (okāsaloka). The meaning of this question is: "In the whole of Jambudīpa, which is the physical world (bhājanaloka), in what place do Arahants or those who have entered the path to Arahantship live now, so that we may approach them, abide by their instructions, and be liberated from the suffering of Saṃsāra?" "Uttaresu" refers to the north-east direction from the port of Suppāraka.

He is "Arahaṃ" because of being remote (āraka) from defilements. This is true. The Blessed One stands very far from all defilements because he has destroyed defilements along with their residual traces (vāsanā) by means of the Path. Alternatively, he is "Arahaṃ" because he has killed the enemies (arīnaṃ hata). The Blessed One has killed and eradicated the enemies of defilements without remainder by the Noble Path. Therefore, the Blessed One is called "Arahaṃ." Alternatively, he is "Arahaṃ" because he has destroyed the spokes (arānaṃ hata) of the wheel of Saṃsāra. There is the wheel of Saṃsāra...
76:
...There is the wheel of Saṃsāra that has been turning for time without beginning, joined to the chariot of the three realms by an axle made of the origin of taints (āsava-samudaya), with spokes made of volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra) such as ignorance and craving for existence, and a rim made of aging and death. The Blessed One, standing on the ground of virtue (sīla) with his feet of energy (vīriya) at the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), took the axe of knowledge that brings the end of kamma with the hand of faith (saddhā), and all the spokes were broken, destroyed, and shattered. He is also called "Arahaṃ" because he is worthy (arahati) of receiving special offerings. Since the Blessed One is the supreme field of merit in the world with its devas, he is worthy of receiving excellent requisites such as robes and special offerings. Alternatively, he is "Arahaṃ" because of the absence of secrecy (rahābhāva). Because the Blessed One has completely cut off defilements like greed and because evil defilements can no longer arise, he is called "Arahaṃ" due to the absence of secrecy in doing evil.

He is called "Sammāsambuddha" because he has fully (sammā) and by himself (sāmaṃ) awakened to all phenomena (dhamma). The Blessed One awakened to things that should be known by direct knowledge (abhiññeyya) through direct knowledge, things that should be fully understood (pariññeyya) through full understanding, things that should be abandoned (pahātabba) by abandoning, things that should be realized (sacchikātabba) by realization, and things that should be developed (bhāvetabba) by development. Thus it was said: "What should be known is known by me, what should be developed has been developed, what should be abandoned has been abandoned; therefore, O Brahmin, I am a Buddha."

Alternatively, this meaning should be understood through the power of all the triads (tika) and dyads (duka), such as wholesome states being blameless and having happy results, and unwholesome states being blameworthy and having painful results. In short, he is "Sammāsambuddha" because he has awakened to all phenomena in all their aspects through his self-evolved knowledge (sayambhū-ñāṇa) without error. Details should be understood as given in the Visuddhimagga. "Arahattāya" means for the attainment of the supreme fruit. "Dhammaṃ deseti" means he points out and teaches the practice of virtue, etc., which are endowed with the qualities of being good in the beginning, etc., or the practice of calm (samatha) and insight (vipassanā), according to the inclinations of those to be led.

"Saṃvejito" means he was struck with spiritual urgency (saṃvega): "Alas, the state of a worldling is indeed loathsome! I, who am not an Arahant, thought of myself as an Arahant. I did not know the Fully Self-Enlightened One who has arisen in the world and is teaching the Dhamma. This life is difficult to know; this death is difficult to know." Thus, his mind was agitated by the words of the deity. "Tāvad-eva" means at that very moment. "Suppārakā pakkāmi" means he departed from Suppāraka with joy directed toward the Buddha, which arose just by hearing the name "Buddha"...
77:
Bāhiya, with a heart urged by spiritual urgency (saṃvega), set out from the port of Suppāraka towards Sāvatthī. "Staying one night at every [stop]" means he traveled while sleeping for only one night on the entire journey. In truth, Sāvatthī is one hundred and twenty yojanas away from the port of Suppāraka, and he traveled that long distance by staying for only one night. Some say that on the very day he left Suppāraka, he arrived in Sāvatthī.

Indeed, how could this Bāhiya travel like that? It is said that he was able to go because of the power of the deities (devatā) or "by the power of the Buddha." However, because it is stated "staying one night at every [stop]" and because the journey is one hundred and twenty yojanas, it might seem to mean that in whatever village, market town, or royal capital he stayed during the night along the way, he did not let the second dawn rise there, thus reaching Sāvatthī by staying only one night at each place. This should not be understood in that way. It is because the intended meaning is "by staying only one night" for the entire journey of one hundred and twenty yojanas. That Bāhiya, having stayed for only one night on that entire journey, arrived at Sāvatthī in the morning of the final day.

The Blessed One also, knowing that Bāhiya was coming, thought, "His faculties (indriya) are not yet mature; they will become mature in a moment," and while waiting for the maturation of his faculties, He entered Sāvatthī for alms at that moment, surrounded by a large community of monks. Bāhiya, having entered Jetavana and seeing many monks walking back and forth in the open air to relieve the weariness of their bodies after finishing their morning meal, asked, "Where is the Blessed One now?" The monks replied, "The Blessed One has entered Sāvatthī for alms," and asked in return, "But where have you come from?" "I have come from the port of Suppāraka," Bāhiya replied. "You have come from a far distance; sit down for a while, wash your feet, apply oil, and rest for a bit. You will see the Teacher when He returns," they said. "Venerable sirs, I do not know the danger to my own life. I have come the journey of one hundred and twenty yojanas in only one night, without stopping for long or sitting down anywhere. I will rest only after I have seen the Teacher," he said, and with a sense of haste, he entered Sāvatthī and saw the Blessed One, who was radiant with incomparable Buddha-glory. Therefore, it was said: "At that time, many monks were walking back and forth in the open air. Then Bāhiya Dārucīriya approached those monks," and so forth.

In that Pali, "kahaṃ" means "in what place." The word "nu" is used in the sense of doubt (saṃsaya). The word "kho" is a mere particle to complete the sentence. It means "in what certain place?" "Dassanakāmamhā" means "we desire to see." For we [see] that [Blessed One]...
78:
We desire to see and approach the Blessed One just as a blind man desires sight, as a deaf man desires hearing, as a mute man desires the ability to speak well, as a person with deformed limbs desires limbs, as a poor man desires wealth, as a traveler in a wilderness desires a safe place, as one afflicted by disease desires health, and as one shipwrecked in the great ocean desires a great raft. 'Taramānarūpo' means one who is in a hurried state.

'Pāsādika' (inspiring confidence) means one who brings about confidence in all respects to the multitude of people who strive to behold his physical body (rūpakāya), because he is adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, the eighty minor marks, the fathom-wide radiance (byāmappabhā), and the crest of light (ketumālā), and is thus endowed with the perfection of physical beauty that is entirely pleasing. 'Pasādanīya' (worthy of confidence) means one who is worthy of being revered, or who is fit to inspire confidence, or who is worthy of confidence by those who behold him, because he is endowed with the perfection of the Dhamma-body (dhammakāya) consisting of the Ten Powers (dasabala), the Fourfold Intrepidity (caturvesārajja), the Six Uncommon Knowledges (asādhāraṇa-ñāṇa), the eighteen special qualities of a Buddha (āveṇika-buddhadhamma), and other immeasurable virtues. 'Santindriya' (calm senses) means one whose five senses, such as the eye, are tranquil due to the absence of restlessness and agitation. 'Santamanasa' (calm mind) means one whose mind, the sixth sense-base, is tranquil due to having reached the state of being free from defilements. 'Uttamadamasathasamathamanuppatta' means one who has reached and stands in the supreme self-control and tranquility known as the supramundane wisdom-liberation and mind-liberation. 'Danta' (tamed) means one who is tamed in body because of his perfectly pure bodily conduct, the absence of restlessness of hands and feet, and the absence of playfulness and such. 'Gutta' (guarded) means one who is guarded in speech because of his perfectly pure verbal conduct, the absence of useless talk, and the absence of playfulness and such. 'Yatindriya' (restrained senses) means one who has restrained senses by the power of the mind-faculty because of his perfectly pure mental conduct and the state of having effortless equanimity through the application of noble psychic power. 'Nāga' means he is called Nāga for these reasons: because he does not go by the power of desire and such, because the abandoned defilements such as lust do not return, because he never performs any evil (āgu) at any time, and because he does not return to a new existence. In this context, the word 'Pāsādika' shows the Buddha's state as a standard (pramāṇa) by way of his physical body; 'Pasādanīya' shows it by way of his Dhamma-body; and the remaining terms such as 'Santindriya' show his state as a standard in other respects. By showing this, it should be understood that the Buddha's state as a standard for all beings without exception in the world of the four types of standards is revealed.

Seeing the Blessed One, who is endowed with such qualities, walking in the street, he thought, "It has been a long time indeed since I have seen the Sammāsambuddha," and being filled with great joy and rapture of five colors, with his whole body suffused with rapture, with eyes wide and unblinking due to the diffusion of rapture, he bowed his body from the moment he saw him and entered into the aura of the Blessed One's physical radiance as if diving into it. Approaching the Blessed One, he paid homage with the fivefold prostration, massaged and kissed his feet, and said, "Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One teach me the Dhamma; may the Sugata teach me the Dhamma." Therefore, it is taught in the Pāḷi: "Having prostrated with his head at the feet of the Blessed One... it would be for my welfare and happiness." He prostrated with his head at the feet of the Blessed One and spoke these words to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One teach me the Dhamma of the Path and Fruit; O Blessed One who speaks well, may you teach me that Dhamma which would be for my welfare and happiness for a long time."
79:
That person, with his whole body suffused with rapture, with eyes wide and unblinking due to rapture, bowed his body from the moment he saw [the Buddha] and entered into the aura of the Blessed One's physical radiance as if diving into it, and approached the Blessed One. Then, having paid homage with the fivefold prostration, massaged and kissed the feet of the Blessed One, he requested, "Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One teach me the Dhamma." Referring to that, it is stated in the Pāḷi: "Having prostrated with his head at the feet of the Blessed One, he spoke thus to the Blessed One: 'Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One teach me the Dhamma; may the Sugata teach me the Dhamma, that Dhamma which would be for my welfare and happiness for a long time.'"

In that passage, "Sugata" means he is called Sugata because of his beautiful going, because he has gone to a beautiful place, because he has gone rightly, and because he has spoken rightly. Going is also called "gata," and that going of the Blessed One is beautiful, pure, and faultless. What is that going? It is the Noble Path (ariya magga). Indeed, by that going, he has gone to the safe region [Nibbāna] without clinging, and he also causes others to go; thus he is Sugata because of his beautiful going. Furthermore, he is Sugata because he has gone to a beautiful place, which is the Deathless Nibbāna (amata nibbāna). He is Sugata because he has gone rightly, in that the defilements abandoned by each respective path do not return again. Thus it is said:

"Those defilements that have been abandoned by the Path of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga) do not return to him, do not come back, do not arrive again; thus he is Sugata. Those abandoned by the Path of Once-returning... the Path of Arahantship... do not return; thus he is Sugata."

Alternatively, he is Sugata because he has gone by practicing rightly in all three stages; the meaning is that he is one of good conduct (suppaṭipanna). Indeed, from the time at the feet of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara until the Great Seat of Enlightenment (mahābodhi-maṇḍa), having reached the pinnacle of right practice by fulfilling the thirty perfections, and through conduct for the benefit of kin (ñātattha-cariyā), conduct for the benefit of the world (lokattha-cariyā), and conduct for the benefit of Buddhahood (buddhattha-cariyā), he promoted only the welfare and happiness of the entire world of beings. He is Sugata because he has gone or practiced with the right practice that is not the domain of all [ordinary] beings, respecting the supramundane Dhamma attained in succession, and by the Middle Way (majjhimā paṭipadā) known as the incomparable development of the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga-bhāvanā), which does not approach the two extremes of eternalism (sassata-diṭṭhi) and annihilationism (uccheda-diṭṭhi), or the devotion to sensual indulgence (kāmasukhallikānuyoga) and self-mortification (attakilamathānuyoga), in the Noble Truths. Furthermore, he is Sugata because he speaks rightly; he speaks only appropriate words in appropriate places. Thus it is also said:
80:
The Blessed One is one who speaks at the right time (kālavādī), one who speaks what is factual (bhūtavādī), one who speaks what is beneficial (atthavādī), one who speaks according to the Dhamma (dhammavādī), and one who speaks according to the Vinaya (vinayavādī). He speaks words that are worth treasuring, timely, reasoned, well-defined, and connected with the goal.

It is also stated in other scriptures: "The Tathāgata does not speak such words that are false, not connected with the goal, and are unloved and displeasing to others," and so forth. Because he speaks rightly in this way, he is called the Sugata.

"That the teaching of this Dhamma may be for my long-term welfare and happiness" means: may the teaching of this Dhamma, even within a short time, be for my benefit such as jhāna and vimokkha (liberation), and for the happiness that is to be attained through that Dhamma. "It is not the time, Bāhiya, for teaching Dhamma" means: since it is the time for alms-round, it is not yet the time to teach the Dhamma.
