A question may be raised: Can there be an "unsuitable time" (akāla) for the Blessed One who acts for the welfare of beings? Why is the Blessed One called a kālavādī? It is said: Here, "time" (kāla) refers to the time when the faculties (indriya) of those to be led (the veneyya) have reached maturity. However, since it was difficult for Bāhiya himself to know whether his own faculties were mature or not at that time, the Blessed One did not mention that reason. Instead, pointing to the fact that he was standing in the middle of the street, he said, "We have entered among the houses [for alms]."

"Hard to know" (dujjānaṃ) means difficult to understand. "Dangers to life" (jīvitantarāyānaṃ) refers to the occurrence or non-occurrence of things that cause danger to life; he said "jīvitantarāyānaṃ" due to a sense of urgency and agitation. For indeed, life is dependent on many conditions, and its dangers are of many forms. Thus it is said:

"Today itself the effort should be made,
Who knows if death will come tomorrow?
For there is no bargaining for us
With Death and his great army."

Why does this Bāhiya prioritize the danger to life first? Some say, "Because of his knowledge of signs or his skill in the unseen." Others say, "Because he heard about the danger to life from a deity." In truth, being one in his last birth (pacchimabhavika) and being urged by the perfection of his supporting conditions (upanissaya), he spoke thus. Indeed, for such persons, the end of life does not occur until they have attained Arahantship.

For what reason did the Blessed One, though wishing to teach him the Dhamma, refuse twice? The Blessed One had this thought: "From the moment he saw me, rapture (pīti) has pervaded his entire body without interval. As long as the force of rapture is excessively strong, he will not yet be able to penetrate the Dhamma even upon hearing it. He will only be able to know the Dhamma when neutral equanimity (majjhattūpekkhā) is established. Furthermore, the physical distress (daratha) in his body is strong because he has come a journey of a hundred leagues; let that also subside first." For this reason, he refused twice. Some teachers say, "The Blessed One did this to generate reverence for hearing the Dhamma." When requested for the third time, seeing that neutral equanimity had been established in Bāhiya, his physical distress had subsided, and seeing the danger to his life, the Buddha thought, "Now is the time for the Dhamma teaching," and began the Dhamma teaching with the words beginning with "Tasmā tiha."
81:
[The Buddha thought,] "From the moment he saw me, rapture (pīti) has pervaded his entire body without interval. As long as the force of rapture is excessively strong, he will not yet be able to penetrate the Dhamma even upon hearing it. Let him wait until neutral equanimity (majjhattūpekkhā) is established. Having traveled a journey of a hundred leagues, the physical distress (daratha) in his body is also strong; let that also subside first." For this reason, he refused twice. Some teachers say, "The Blessed One did this to generate reverence for hearing the Dhamma." When requested for the third time, seeing that neutral equanimity was present and the physical distress had subsided, and seeing the danger to his life, he thought, "Now is the time for the Dhamma teaching," and began the Dhamma teaching with "Tasmā tiha," and so forth.

In that [teaching], "tasmā" means: because you are making an effort and requesting me so much, or because you speak of the difficulty of knowing the dangers to life, and because your faculties have reached maturity (therefore). "Tiha" is merely a particle. "Te" means "by you." "Evaṃ" refers to the manner that is now to be spoken.

"Sikkhitabbaṃ" means the training should be done by way of the three trainings, such as the training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā). To show how one should train, he spoke the words beginning with "diṭṭhe diṭṭhamattaṃ bhavissati" (in the seen, there will be only the seen).

Therein, "diṭṭhe diṭṭhamattaṃ" means in the sphere of forms (rūpāyatana), there is only the seeing by eye-consciousness. Just as eye-consciousness sees only the form in the form, and does not see its nature such as impermanence, etc., even so, it should be trained: "Through the consciousness at the eye-door, there will be for me only the seen." This is the meaning. Or, in the seen object, "diṭṭhaṃ" means the cognizing of the form by eye-consciousness. "Mattaṃ" means the measure (pamāṇa). "Diṭṭhamattaṃ" means this [thought-process] has the measure of the seen; the meaning is that the mind will be only the measure of eye-consciousness. What is meant is this: Just as eye-consciousness is not lustful, not hateful, and not deluded regarding a form that has come into range, even so, the javana (impulsion) will be for me only the measure of eye-consciousness, being free from lust and so forth; I will keep the javana only within the measure of eye-consciousness.

Alternatively, "diṭṭhaṃ" is the form seen by eye-consciousness, and "diṭṭhamattaṃ" is the triad of minds known as receiving (sampaṭicchana), investigating (santīraṇa), and determining (votthabbana) that arise regarding that very form. Just as that triad of minds is not lustful, not hateful, and not deluded, even so, regarding a form that has come into range, I will produce the javana only with the measure of that receiving consciousness and so forth; I will not allow it to arise by way of lust and so forth, exceeding that measure. This is how the meaning should be understood here. In this same way...
82:
In the heard and in the sensed. The 'sensed' (muta) should be understood as the bases of smell, taste, and touch (gandhāyatana, rasāyatana, phoṭṭhabbāyatana) together with the registration consciousnesses (tadārammaṇa-viññāṇa) that have those as their objects. In the phrase 'In the cognized, there will be only the cognized,' the 'cognized' (viññāta) refers to the mental objects (dhammārammaṇa) known by mind-door advertence (manodvārāvajjana). 'In that cognized, there will be only the cognized' means the group of states that are merely the measure of advertence. The meaning here is: 'Just as the advertence-consciousness does not lust, does not hate, and is not deluded, so too, I will maintain the mind merely at the measure of advertence, not allowing it to arise by way of lust and so forth.' 'Thus, Bāhiya, you should train yourself' means: Bāhiya, you should train by following the three trainings (sikkhā) through this practice.

In this way, the Blessed One, for the sake of Bāhiya who desired a brief teaching, analyzed the object of insight (vipassanā)—which is divided into the six objects along with the six classes of consciousness—into four groups beginning with the 'seen' (diṭṭha), and showed him the full understanding of the known (ñātapariññā) and the full understanding by investigation (tīraṇapariññā) regarding those four groups. How did He show it? In these four groups, the visible base (rūpāyatana) is called 'seen' because it is to be seen; eye-consciousness (cakkhuviññāṇa), together with the consciousnesses occurring at that door, is also called 'seen' because of the act of seeing. Both of these are merely phenomena (dhamma) occurring according to their conditions; herein, there is no doer (kattā) or instigator (kāretā) whatsoever. Since that phenomenon is impermanent (anicca) in the sense of non-existence after having been, suffering (dukkha) in the sense of being oppressed by rise and fall, and non-self (anattā) in the sense of not being subject to one's will, where would there be an opportunity for a wise person to have lust and so forth toward it? This is the intention here. The meaning should be understood in the same way regarding the 'heard' (suta) and so forth.

Now, in order to show the full understanding by abandoning (pahānapariññā) together with the Path and Fruit to Bāhiya, who is established in the full understanding of the known and investigation, the Buddha began the words: 'Bāhiya, when for you...' and so forth. In that passage, 'yato' means 'when' or 'because.' 'Te' means 'your.' 'Tato' means 'then' or 'therefore.' 'Tena' means 'by that seen and so forth' or 'by the lust and so forth connected with the seen and so forth.' This is what is meant: Bāhiya, at the time when, or for the reason that, you practice according to the method I have stated regarding the seen and so forth, there will be merely the seen and so forth through the penetration of the undistorted nature of things; at that time, or for that reason, you will not exist together with the lust and so forth connected with the seen and so forth; you will not be one who lusts, hates, or is deluded; because lust and so forth have been abandoned, you will not be one bound together with that seen and so forth. 'Bāhiya, then you are not therein' means: when or because you are not one who lusts through that lust, or hates through that hatred, or is deluded through that delusion, then or therefore you will not be in that seen and so forth; you will not be one who stays attached to that seen, heard, sensed, or cognized by way of craving, conceit, and views (taṇhā, māna, diṭṭhi) as 'This is mine, this I am, this is my self.' By this much of the Dhamma teaching, He brought the full understanding by abandoning to its peak and showed the stage of the one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsavabhūmi), which is Arahantship.
83:
Bāhiya, at that time you will not be bound to that seen and so forth by that lust and so forth; then you are neither in this world, nor in the world beyond, nor in between the two. 'This itself is the end of suffering' means this is the end of the suffering of defilements and the suffering of the round of rebirths, the state of not revolving again. This is the meaning here. As for those teachers who, taking the phrase 'ubhayaman-tarena,' desire an intermediate state (antarābhava), their view is wrong. The existence of an intermediate state is indeed rejected in the Abhidhamma. The word 'antarena' (in between) is merely used to indicate another alternative. Therefore, the meaning here is: 'Neither here, nor beyond, nor in the other alternative of both.'

Alternatively, the word 'antarena' indicates the non-existence of another alternative. Its meaning is: 'Neither here, nor beyond, and between the two there is no other place.' Also, those teachers who, having improperly grasped the meaning of the sutta terms 'antarāparinibbāyī' and 'sambhavesī,' say 'There is indeed an intermediate state,' they too are mistaken. Because the meaning of the first sutta term is that one is an 'antarāparinibbāyī' (one who attains Nibbāna in the interval) because one attains Nibbāna through the complete cessation of defilements by attaining the supreme Path in the interval, without exceeding half the lifespan in those respective realms such as Aviha; it is not because of being in an intermediate state. 

Regarding the meaning of the latter sutta term: those who have already become and will not become again, those Arahants are called 'bhūta' (beings) in the preceding term. Those who are the opposite of 'bhūta' and seek a new existence are called 'sambhavesī' (seekers of birth); because they have not yet abandoned the fetters of existence, Trainees (sekha) and worldlings (puthujjana) are called 'sambhavesī.' Alternatively, among the four modes of birth, egg-born and womb-born beings are called 'sambhavesī' as long as they have not yet broken through the eggshell or the membrane of the womb; when they have come out from the eggshell or the womb, they are called 'bhūta.' Moisture-born and spontaneously born beings are called 'sambhavesī' in their first thought-moment; from the second thought-moment onwards, they are called 'bhūta.' Or, they are 'sambhavesī' as long as they are in the posture in which they are born and have not yet reached another posture; after that, they are 'bhūta.' Therefore, the intermediate state should be rejected as non-existent. When there is a straightforward meaning in accordance with the Pali text, what is the use of imagining an intermediate state whose efficacy is not evident?

As for those teachers who argue the logic: 'The manifestation of phenomena proceeding as a continuity is seen in other places without interruption, as in the case of non-conscious continuities like rice and so forth; so too, in a conscious continuity, there must be manifestation in other places without interruption. And this method is logical only if there is an intermediate state, not otherwise.' If that were so, then logic should also be stated for a person of psychic power who has attained mastery over the mind, regarding the manifestation from the Brahma world to this human world, or going from this human world to the Brahma world within the blink of an eye, in accordance with the mind. If the uninterrupted occurrence of phenomena in all aspects is not desired, it is taught that 'The range of psychic power (iddhivisaya) of those with psychic power is unthinkable.' If it does occur, then that statement is also evidence here. This is because it is taught that 'The result of kamma (kammavipāka) is unthinkable.' Therefore, the words of those teachers are merely a view. Natural phenomena have an unthinkable nature. In some places, they occur by being interrupted by causes; in some places, they occur without interruption. Therefore, just as the reflection of a face and an echo are seen to arise due to causes such as the face in other places like a mirror or a mountain, one should not apply everything to every place. This is the summary here. For the detail, see the investigation of the intermediate state completed with the simile of the reflection of a face.
84:
For a person who has attained mastery over the mind, when resolving upon a body that follows the mind, it is appropriate to say that he can travel from the Brahma realm to this human world, or from this human world to the Brahma realm, in the blink of an eye. If it is not desired that the occurrence of phenomena happens in an uninterrupted sequence in every way, it is said that the range of psychic powers (iddhivisaya) of those with psychic powers is unthinkable. This statement is also a point of comparison here, because it is said that the ripening of kamma (kammavipāka) is unthinkable. Therefore, the words of those other teachers are merely their own opinions. Indeed, natural phenomena (sabhāvadhamma) are unthinkable in nature. These phenomena appear in some places as interrupted by the power of causes, and in some places as uninterrupted. Indeed, just as through causes such as the face and sound, the results such as reflections and echoes are seen to arise in other places like mirrors or mountains. Therefore, one should not assume that everything is the same in every case; this is the summary here. The detailed investigation of the intermediate state (antarābhava), established through the example of a reflection, should be taken from the commentary (ṭīkā) on the Kathāvatthu.

Other teachers say: "idha" (here) refers to the sensual realm (kāmabhava), "huraṃ" (beyond) refers to the formless realm (arūpabhava), and "ubhayamantare" (in between) refers to the fine-material realm (rūpabhava). Others say: "idha" refers to the internal sense bases (ajjhattikāyatana), "huraṃ" refers to the external sense bases (bāhirāyatana), and "ubhayamantare" refers to the mind and mental factors (citta-cetasika). Alternatively, they say: "idha" refers to causal phenomena (paccayadhamma), "huraṃ" refers to resultant phenomena (paccayuppannadhamma), and "ubhayamantare" refers to conceptual phenomena (paññattidhamma). All these statements are not found in the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā). Thus, through the words "In the seen, there will be only the seen," etc., the phenomena of the three planes are gathered in four ways according to the "seen" and so forth. In that gathering, by way of abandoning the grasping of beauty, pleasure, permanence, and self, and by showing the repeated contemplation of foulness, suffering, impermanence, and non-self, Vipassanā (insight) is taught in brief along with the lower purifications (visuddhi). By the words "Then, Bāhiya, you are not by that (lust, etc.)," the Path (magga) is taught because of the intended total cutting off of lust and so forth. By the words "Then, Bāhiya, you are not in that (seen, etc.)," the Fruit (phala) is taught. By the words "Neither here," etc., the Nibbāna element without residue (anupādisesa nibbānadhātu) is taught. Therefore, it is said in the Pali: "Then the mind of Bāhiya... was liberated from the taints (āsavas)."

At the very end of this brief teaching (tāvad-eva), at that very moment and not at another time. "Anupādāya" means without grasping. "Āsavehi" means from the taints called sensual lust and so forth, which are named "āsavas" because they flow up to the peak of existence and up to the change-of-lineage (gotrabhū), and because they resemble fermented spirits like wine due to being long-stored. "Vimucci" means he was liberated and released through the liberation of cutting off (samuccheda-vimutti) and the liberation of tranquilization (paṭippassaddhi-vimutti). For that Dārucīriya, while listening to the Teacher's Dhamma, purified his virtues, and based on the mental concentration he had attained, he established insight. Being one of swift intuition (khippābhiññā), at that very moment, with all taints exhausted, he reached the Fruit of Arahantship together with the four analytical knowledges. That Dārucīriya, having cut the stream of saṃsāra and being one who bears his final body, while the seventy-nine reviewing knowledges were occurring by nature...
85:
Bāhiya, having exhausted the taints, reached Arahantship together with the four analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). Having cut the stream of saṃsāra, reached the end of the round of rebirths, and bearing his final body, being urged by the nature of reviewing knowledges (paccavekkhaṇā), he requested the Buddha for ordination. When asked, "Are your bowl and robes complete?", he replied, "They are not complete, Bhante." Then the Teacher said, "If so, seek a bowl and robes," and departed. Regarding this, it is said in the Pali: "Then the Blessed One... departed."

It is heard that while practicing the Dhamma of a recluse for twenty thousand years during the dispensation of the Buddha Kassapa, he thought, "A monk should only use the requisites he receives himself without giving to others," and thus he never supported even a single monk with a bowl or a robe. Because of that, there was no supporting condition (upaniśśaya) for the "Come, bhikkhu" (ehibhikkhu) ordination in his continuity. However, some teachers say: "It is said that in a world empty of Buddhas, he was a thief. While committing robbery in the forest, equipped with a bow and arrows, he saw a Paccekabuddha. Desiring the bowl and robes, he shot him with an arrow and took them. Because of that unwholesome deed, the bowl and robes created by psychic power would not arise for him. The Teacher, knowing this, did not grant him ordination by the 'Come, bhikkhu' method." While Bāhiya was wandering in search of a bowl and robes, a cow with a young calf ran swiftly and struck him, causing his death. Referring to this, it is said in the Pali: "Then, not long after the Blessed One had departed, a cow with a young calf attacked Bāhiya Dārucīriya and deprived him of life."

In that Pali, "acirapakkantassa" means not long after the Blessed One had departed. "Gāvī taruṇavacchā" refers to a certain yakkhinī (ogress) in the form of a cow with a young calf. "Adhipatitvā" means having overcome and trampled. "Jīvitā voropesi" means that because of a grudge from a previous life, upon merely seeing him, a vengeful mind arose, and she struck him with her horns and deprived him of life.

The Teacher, after wandering for alms and finishing his meal, was leaving the city with many monks when he saw Bāhiya's body lying in a rubbish heap. He commanded the monks: "Bhikkhus, take a couch from a house, carry this body out of the city, cremate it, and build a stupa (thūpa)." The monks did so. Having done so, they returned to the monastery, approached the Teacher, reported what they had done, and asked about Bāhiya's future destination. Then the Blessed One informed them of Bāhiya's final parinibbāna. The monks said, "Bhante, you say that Bāhiya Dārucīriya attained Arahantship; when did he attain Arahantship..."
86:
"Has he attained the fruit of Arahantship?" they asked. "He attained it even while listening to my Dhamma," the Buddha replied. "But when did you preach the Dhamma to him, Bhante?" they asked again. "Today, while walking for alms, standing in the middle of the street," he said. "Bhante, that Dhamma preached while standing in the middle of the street was very brief. How could he attain such a distinctive distinction with just that much Dhamma?" they asked. To show them, "Monks, why do you measure my Dhamma as 'little' or 'much'? Better than thousands of verses not connected with the goal, a single word of a verse connected with the goal is indeed superior," the Blessed One spoke this verse in the Dhammapada:

"Though there be a thousand verses composed of meaningless words, better is a single word of a verse, hearing which one is stilled." (Dhp. 101)

To show that "Not only did Bāhiya attain Parinibbāna, but he is also the foremost among my disciple monks who possess quick intuition (khippābhiññā) and is worthy of offerings," he placed that venerable one in the position of foremost (etadagga), saying: "Monks, among my disciple monks who possess quick intuition, Bāhiya Dārucīriya is the foremost." (A.N. 1.216). Referring to that, it was said: "Then the Blessed One, having wandered for alms in Sāvatthī... Monks, Bāhiya Dārucīriya has attained Parinibbāna."

In that text, 'pacchābhattaṃ' means the period after the meal. 'Piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto' means having returned from seeking alms. By both words, it is meant that the meal-duty was finished. 'Nīharitvā' means having carried [the body] outside the city. 'Jhāpetha' means "cremate [him]." 'Thūpañcassa karotha' means "having taken the bodily relics of Bāhiya, build a stupa." He stated the reason for doing so: "Monks, your fellow practitioner (sabrahmacārī) has passed away." The meaning is: You practice the Dhamma of practice such as higher virtue (adhisīla), which is called 'Brahma' because of its noble meaning; Bāhiya also practiced that same noble Dhamma as you, thus he is called a 'fellow practitioner' (sabrahmacārī). He has passed away, having reached the time of death. Therefore, carry him on a couch, cremate him, and build a stupa.

'Tassa kā gati' means "Among the five destinations, what is his destination, his rebirth, his state of being?" or 'gati' means the finality—is he a Noble One (ariya) or a worldling (puthujjana)?—what is the conclusion? 'Abhisamparāyo' means the arising of a new existence after death, or the cessation of existence. Although the meaning of his Parinibbāna was already made clear by the command to build a stupa, those monks who did not understand by that much asked, "What is his destination...?"
87:
The monks asked about Bāhiya's destination. Or, they asked the Blessed One in that way because they wished to make it more manifest. He is called a wise man (paṇḍita) because he has attained the wisdom of the highest path (arahatta-magga-paññā). He spoke the truth and practiced accordingly. 'Dhammassa' means for the supramundane Dhamma (lokuttara-dhamma). 'Anudhammaṃ' means the Dhamma of practice, such as the purification of virtue (sīlavisuddhi). Or, 'dhammassa' means for the Dhamma of Nibbāna, and 'anudhammaṃ' means the Dhamma of the Noble Path and Fruit (ariyamagga-phala). "He did not trouble me because of the Dhamma teaching" means he did not trouble the Buddha because he practiced according to the instruction. Indeed, if one hears the Dhamma from the Teacher or takes a meditation subject but does not practice according to the instruction, he is said to trouble the Teacher. Referring to this, it was said: "O Brahma, thinking it would only be wearisome among men, I did not preach the refined Dhamma that I had mastered." (Maha-va. 9; M.N. 1.283, 2.339). Alternatively, "He did not trouble me because of this Dhamma" means he did not trouble the Buddha because he practiced well this teaching (sāsana-dhamma) which is the cause of deliverance from the suffering of the round (vaṭṭa-dukkha). One who practices wrongly, destroying the Dispensation, is said to strike the Dhamma-body (dhammakāya) of the Teacher. But this Bāhiya, having brought the right practice to its culmination, attained Parinibbāna through the Nibbāna element without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbāna-dhātu). Therefore, it was said: "Monks, Bāhiya Dārucīriya has attained Parinibbāna."

Having known in every aspect the fact that the Elder Bāhiya attained Parinibbāna through the Nibbāna element without remainder, and the fact that the destination of the Arahants who have thus attained Parinibbāna is difficult for ordinary people to understand, he uttered this inspired utterance (udāna) which illuminates the power of this Parinibbāna. In that inspired utterance, 'yattha' means in which Nibbāna water, earth, fire, and air do not find a footing, they do not stay. Why? Because Nibbāna is of an unconditioned nature (asaṅkhata-sabhāva). Indeed, not even a trace of conditioned things (saṅkhata-dhamma) can exist there. The groups of stars and constellations, called 'sukka' because of their white color, do not shine. Even the sun, which is capable of spreading light over three islands at once, does not appear there by way of radiance. Even the moon, with its pleasant and cool rays, despite its brilliance, does not shine with its moonlight in that Nibbāna because it does not exist there. Referring to the doubt, "If there are no sun, moon, etc., in that Nibbāna, will it be a place of perpetual darkness like the Lokantarika hell?", he said, "There is no darkness in that Nibbāna." Where there is no matter (rūpa), there can be no darkness. When the Brāhmaṇa, a noble disciple endowed with the knowledge of the four truths (mona), realizes Nibbāna for himself, setting aside hearsay, then he is liberated from mind-and-matter (nāma-rūpa) and from pleasure and pain (sukha-dukkha).
88:
With reference to the doubt whether that Nibbāna would be a state of perpetual and dense darkness (due to the absence of the sun and moon), the Blessed One preached: "Darkness does not exist in that Nibbāna." Indeed, where there is no materiality, darkness cannot exist.

"When the sage, the Brahmin, has known by himself through silence" (yadā ca attanā vedi, muni monena brāhmaṇo) means: the noble disciple Brahmin, who is called a "sage" (muni) because he is endowed with the knowledge of the path called "silence" (mona) through the realization of the Four Truths, and is endowed with bodily silence and so forth—at the moment of the path of Arahatship, having abandoned hearsay and so forth, and having personally realized it, he has known and penetrated Nibbāna. There is also a variant reading "avedī", which means "he has known".

"Then from the material and the immaterial, and from pleasure and pain, he is set free" (atha rūpā arūpā ca, sukhadukkhā pamuccati) means: after thus knowing Nibbāna (it refers to the liberation from the round of suffering). "From the material" (rūpā) refers to material phenomena, and by this term, five-constituent existence (pañcavokāra-bhava) and one-constituent existence (ekavokāra-bhava) are taken. "From the immaterial" (arūpā) refers to immaterial phenomena, and by this term, immaterial existence (arūpa-bhava) which is unmixed with materiality is taken. That immaterial existence is also called "four-constituent existence" (catuvokāra-bhava). "From pleasure and pain" (sukhadukkhā) means liberation from the round of rebirth consisting of pleasure and pain arising in all planes.

Alternatively, "from the material" means from rebirth in the fine-material realm (rūpa-loka); "from the immaterial" means from rebirth in the immaterial realm (arūpa-loka); and "from pleasure and pain" means from rebirth in the sense realm (kāmāvacara-loka). This is because the sense-sphere existence is a mixture of pleasure and pain. Thus, by these two verses, the Blessed One shows: "Such is the attainment of Nibbāna of my son Bāhiya," who is completely liberated from the entire round of rebirth in this manner.

## The Explanation of the Tenth Sutta is finished.

## The Explanation of the Bodhi Chapter is also finished.
89:
After thus knowing (Nibbāna). "Rūpā" refers to material phenomena. By this term, the five-constituent existence and the one-constituent existence are included. "Arūpā" refers to mental phenomena. By this term, the immaterial existence which is unmixed with materiality is included. That existence is also called "four-constituent existence". "Sukhadukkhā" means liberation from pleasure and pain that arises in all planes, and from the round of rebirth. Alternatively, "rūpā" means liberation from rebirth in the fine-material sphere; "arūpā" means liberation from rebirth in the immaterial sphere; and "sukhadukkhā" means liberation from rebirth in the sense-sphere. Indeed, the sense-sphere existence is a mixture of pleasure and pain. Thus, as described, he is forever liberated from the entire mass of the round of rebirth. By these two verses, the Blessed One shows: "Such is the destination of my son Bāhiya." The commentary on the tenth sutta is finished. The commentary on the Bodhi Chapter is finished.

## 2. Mucalinda Chapter

## 1. Commentary on the Mucalinda Sutta

In the first sutta of the Mucalinda Chapter, in the phrase "Mucalinda-mūle", "Mucalinda" refers to the Nipa tree (Barringtonia acutangula). It is also called "Nicula". (The Buddha stayed) near that tree. Some teachers, however, say that "Mucala" is the name of that tree, and it is called "Mucalinda" because it is the chief of the forest. 

"Mahā akālamegho" refers to a great cloud that arose before the rainy season had arrived. That cloud arose in the last month of the hot season (the beginning of the month of Āsāḷha), filling the entire world-system. "Sattāha-vaddalikā" means that when that great cloud arose, there were raindrops falling continuously for seven days. "Sītavāta-duddinī" means that during those seven days of rain, the days were gloomy due to the cold wind mixed with raindrops blowing from all directions. 

"Mucalindo nāma nāgarājā" refers to the Naga King of great power who was born in the Naga realm beneath the pond near that Mucalinda tree. "Sakabhavanā" means (coming out) from his own Naga realm. "Sattakkhattuṃ bhogehi parikkhipitvā" means encircling the Blessed One's body seven times with the coils of his own body. "Uparimuddhani mahantaṃ phaṇaṃ vihaccā" means spreading his great hood over the Blessed One's head. There is also a reading "phaṇaṃ karitvā", which has the same meaning.

It is said that this thought occurred to that Naga King: "The Blessed One is sitting at the foot of the tree near my abode, and this seven-day storm is occurring; it is proper to provide a dwelling for the Blessed One." Although that Naga King was capable of creating a palace made of the seven jewels, he thought, "If I do it that way, I will not gain the essence of bodily merit (kāyasāra); I will perform personal service (veyyāvacca) to the Blessed One with my own body." Thus, creating a large physical form, he encircled the Teacher seven times with his coils and held his hood over him. "The interior of the coils was about the size of the treasury chamber in the Lohapāsāda," it is said in the Khandhaka Commentary. The Majjhima Commentary, however, says, "It was about the size of the ground floor of the Lohapāsāda." "The Blessed One will stay in whatever posture he desires" was the Naga King's intention. The Blessed One, however, spent the seven days in the same cross-legged posture. That place became like a gabled house with well-closed windows and a well-fitted bolt. The words "Let not cold (disturb) the Blessed One" and so forth show the reason for the Naga King acting in that way. That Naga King...
90: Truly, that Naga King remained there having acted thus, thinking: "May cold not afflict the Blessed One, may heat not afflict him, may the touch of gadflies and such not afflict him." Although it is true that there was no heat during those seven days of rainy weather, it was appropriate for the Naga King to think, "If the clouds should clear from time to time, there might be heat; may that heat also not afflict him." However, some teachers say that the mention of 'heat' (uṇha) here is to state the reason for making the Naga's coils extensive. For if the coils were small, the heat generated from the Naga's body might afflict the Blessed One; therefore, by making the coils extensive, he remained having acted thus so that "heat may not afflict him." 'Viddha' means rising upwards, or becoming distant due to the clearing of clouds. 'Vigatavalāhaka' means cloudless. 'Deva' refers to the sky. 'Viditvā' means knowing that "now the clouds in the sky have cleared, and there is no longer any danger of cold and so forth for the Blessed One." 'Viniveṭhetvā' means having removed. 'Sakavaṇṇa' means his own Naga form. 'Paṭisaṃharitvā' means having made it disappear. 'Māṇavakavaṇṇa' means (taking) the form of a young man. 'Etam-atthaṃ' means having known in every respect this meaning: that for one who experiences the bliss of seclusion, there is only happiness wherever they may be. 'Imam udānaṃ' means he uttered this inspired utterance which illustrates the power of the bliss of seclusion. In those inspired verses, 'sukho viveko' means the seclusion from acquisitions (upadhiviveka), known as Nibbāna, is bliss. 'Tuṭṭhassa' means for one who is content with the contentment associated with the knowledge of the four paths. 'Sutadhammassa' means for one who has the Dhamma clearly revealed or for one who has heard the Dhamma. 'Passato' means for one who sees that seclusion, or whatever is to be seen, with the eye of knowledge obtained through the power of one's own energy. 'Abyāpajja' means the state of non-anger; by this, the preliminary stage of loving-kindness (mettā) is shown. 'Pāṇabhūtesu saṃyamo' means restraint and non-violence towards living beings is bliss. By this, the preliminary stage of compassion (karuṇā) is shown. 'Sukhā virāgatā loke' means dispassion in the world is also bliss. What kind of dispassion? It is said that the transcending of sensual pleasures is dispassion; that dispassion is also bliss. By this, the path of Non-returning (anāgāmimagga) is spoken of. By the phrase 'asmimānassa yo vinayo', the fruit of Arahatship (arahattaphala) is spoken of. The fruit of Arahatship is called the subduing and removal of the conceit "I am". There is no bliss superior to this fruit of Arahatship; therefore, he said, "This indeed is the supreme bliss." Thus, he took the climax of the teaching with the fruit of Arahatship. ## The Commentary on the First Sutta is finished.
91:
## 2. Commentary on the Rāja Sutta

In the second sutta, regarding the word "sambahulānaṃ", according to the Vinaya method, three persons are called "sambahula" (many); beyond three, it is a "Saṅgha". However, according to the Suttanta method, three are just three; only beyond three are they called "sambahula". Therefore, in this context, "sambahulā" should be understood according to the Suttanta method. "Upaṭṭhānasālāyam" means in the pavilion of the Dhamma assembly. This is true; it is called "upaṭṭhānasālā" because it is the place where monks assemble for the Blessed One who has come to teach the Dhamma. Alternatively, the hall or pavilion where monks decide on Vinaya matters, discuss the Dhamma, engage in inquiries, and normally stay by way of assembly is also called "upaṭṭhānasālā". In that assembly place, the Buddha's seat is always prepared. This was the custom of the monks during the lifetime of the Buddhas.

"Sannisinnānaṃ" refers to those who are staying together by way of sitting. "Sannipatitānaṃ" refers to those who have come from various places and are staying by way of assembly. Alternatively, "sannisinnānaṃ" refers to those who sit respectfully as if in the presence of the Teacher, having placed the Buddha's seat in front. "Sannipatitānaṃ" refers to the monks who, having similar inclinations, assemble very well and properly with mutual inclination. "Ayaṃ" points to the talk that is about to be spoken now. "Antarākathā" means another single talk occurring in the interval between meditation practice, learning the Pali text, or learning the commentary, etc. Alternatively, it is called "antarākathā" because it occurs in the interval between the advice of the Sugata received at noon and the hearing of the Dhamma to be received in the evening. Or, it is called "antarākathā" because it is another single talk occurring in the interval of the monks' good practices. "Udapādi" means it arose.

"Imesaṃ dvinnaṃ rājူnaṃ" is the genitive case used in the sense of selection, meaning "among these two kings". In the phrase "mahaddhanataro vā" and so forth, he is called "mahaddhana" because he possesses great wealth consisting of the collection of the seven kinds of treasures buried in the earth. Between the two kings, this king is "mahaddhanatara" because he has exceedingly great wealth. The word "vā" has the sense of alternative (vikappa). In the remaining words also, this same method should be understood. This is the distinction: he is called "mahābhoga" because he has great possessions by way of constant use. He is called "mahākoso" because he has a great treasury which is the daily incoming revenue. Other teachers, however, say that the property consisting of various items like gems, essence, and wood, which is the daily incoming revenue, is called "dhana", and that same wealth stored in treasury rooms and so forth is called "kosa".

Vajira, mahānīla, indanīla, marakata, veḷuriya, padumarāga, phussarāga, kakketana, pulāka, vimala, jotirasa, sugandhika, bālasūriya, abhishyāsa, gomedaka, saṅkhagaḷika, muttā, saṅkha, añjanamūla, vajira, amataṃsa, sayaka, and brāhmaṇi—these twenty-four kinds of gems are called "maṇi" (gems). Besides the two kinds, gold and silver, and the various types of metals, the coins (kahāpaṇa) are called "dhana". Bedding, seating, clothing, ornaments, ivory, and wealth other than the twenty-four kinds of gems are called "bhoga". Sandalwood, aloe-wood, musk, valerian, camphor, and so forth are called "kuppa". Among those four kinds of wealth, starting from the special treasures such as hill paddy, green gram, and black gram, whatever objects there are that serve as internal or external utilities for beings, all of them should be included. He is called "mahārājā" because he has a kingdom where great authority prevails. He is called [a king with great vehicles] because he has vehicles such as elephants and horses...
92:
There are twenty-four types of gems: Lohitaṅka, Phalika, Pavāḷa, Jotirasa, Gomuttaka, Gomedaka, Saugandhika, Muttā, Saṅkha, Añjanamūla, Rājapaṭṭa, Amataṃsaka, Piyaka, and Brāhmaṇī. The seven types of metals, such as gold and silver, and the Kahāpaṇa (coins) are called Sāra (essential wealth). Bedding, floor coverings, clothing, ivory, stone, and so forth are called Pheggu (non-essential wealth). Sandalwood, aloe-wood, saffron, tagara, camphor, and so forth are called Gumba (clustered wealth). Among these, by the word 'ādisadda' (and so forth) mentioned first, one should include all objects used by beings for consumption and utility, beginning with various types of grains (dhanya) such as Sāli rice, paddy, mung beans, and black grams, categorized as Pubbaṇṇa and Aparanna.

He is called Mahāvijita because he possesses a vast conquered territory. He is called Mahāvāhana because he possesses great vehicles such as elephants and horses. He is called Mahabbala because he possesses great military strength and physical strength. He is called Mahiddhika because he possesses great psychic power born of meritorious deeds that can fulfill his desires. He is called Mahānubhāva because he possesses great majesty, known as energy (ussāha), counsel (manta), and lordly power (pabhusatti).

In this context, the first term illustrates the attainment of revenue (āyasampadā); the second, the attainment of resources (vittūpakaraṇasampadā); the third, the attainment of wealth (vibhavasampadā); the fourth, the attainment of territory (janapadasampadā); the fifth, the attainment of vehicles (yānasampadā); the sixth, the attainment of retinue (parivārasampadā) along with personal attainment (attasampadā); the seventh, the attainment of merit (puññakammasampadā); and the eighth, the attainment of majesty (pabhāvasampadā) for those kings. Therefore, it should be understood that all seven natural assets (pakatisampadā) desired by kings—namely, excellence of the lord, excellence of ministers, excellence of the army, excellence of the territory, excellence of wealth, excellence of friends, and excellence of fortresses—are appropriately illustrated.

He is called Rājā because he gladdens the assembly with the four bases of sympathy (saṅgahavatthu), such as giving (dāna). He is called Māgadha because he rules over the Magadha country. He is called Seniya because he is endowed with a large army or because he belongs to the Seniya clan. Bimbī means gold; therefore, he is called Bimbisāra because his complexion is like the color of pure gold. Some, however, say that this is merely the name of that king. He is called Pasenadi because he conquers the enemy's army. He is called Kosala because he is the lord of the Kosala country. In the phrase 'ayañcarahi', 'carahi' is merely a particle (nipāta). 'Vippakatā' means an unfinished conversation. The meaning is that the intervening conversation of those monks was not yet concluded.

'Sāyanhasamayaṃ' means at a certain time in the evening. 'Paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito' means having arisen from the withdrawal of the mind from various objects such as forms, or from the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti). In detail, the Blessed One, in the morning, surrounded by the community of monks, entered Sāvatthī for alms. Having obtained alms easily and finished his meal, he departed from Sāvatthī with the monks, entered the monastery, and stood in front of the Gandhakuṭi. He then gave advice suitable to the temperaments of the monks who stood waiting to perform their duties. After directing them to places for the day's seclusion, such as the forest or the foot of a tree, he entered the Gandhakuṭi and spent the day in the bliss of the attainment of fruition. At the designated time, he arose from that attainment.
93:
The Blessed One arose at the designated time from the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti), also known as seclusion (paṭisallāna). To explain in detail: in the morning, the Blessed One, surrounded by the community of monks, entered Sāvatthī. Having ensured that alms were easily obtained for the monks and having finished his meal, he departed from Sāvatthī with the monks, entered the monastery, and stood in front of the Gandhakuṭi. He gave the 'Sugata's advice' as appropriate to the monks who stood there after performing their duties. When those monks had departed for their daytime resting places, such as the forest or the foot of a tree, he entered the Gandhakuṭi and spent the afternoon in the bliss of the attainment of fruition. Arising from the attainment at the designated time, he thought, 'The four assemblies, waiting for my arrival, are sitting and filling the entire monastery; it is now time for me to go to the circle of the Dhamma Hall to preach the Dhamma.'

He then rose from his seat and departed from the fragrant Gandhakuṭi like a Kesara lion king emerging from a golden cave, or like a noble elephant in rut approaching the herd. He walked with a graceful gait, without any bodily agitation. He approached the assembly hall, illuminating the entire monastery with the perfection of his physical body (rūpakāya), which was radiant with the thirty-two marks of a great man and adorned with the eighty minor marks. He was endowed with a fathom-long aura (byāmappabhā) and adorned with the brilliant crest-aura (ketumālā) from his head. He emitted the six-colored Buddha-rays—blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, and brilliant—possessing inconceivable power and incomparable Buddha-grace. Referring to this, it is said in the Pali: 'Atha kho bhagavā... pe ... tenupasaṅkami' (Then the Blessed One... approached there).

Having approached and shown the proper conduct, he saw those monks sitting in silence and thought, 'If I do not speak, these monks, out of respect for the Buddha, will not speak even for an entire aeon.' To initiate the conversation, he said, 'Monks, for what [talk] are you [sitting]?' and so forth. Here, 'Kāya nuttha' means 'With what kind of talk are you sitting together in discussion?' There is also a Pali reading 'Kāya nottha', which has the same meaning. Some also read 'Kāya nvettha', meaning 'With what kind of talk are you sitting together in this assembly?' In brief, the meaning is: 'Monks, for what kind of talk are you sitting here? What talk of yours was unfinished because of my arrival? I shall conclude that talk.' In this way, he invited them with the invitation of an Omniscient One.

'Na khvetaṃ' should be grammatically resolved as 'Na kho etaṃ'. Or this is simply the reading. Some also read 'Na khotaṃ', which is also resolved as 'Na kho etaṃ'. 'Kulaputtānaṃ' means for you, sons of good family, who are endowed with noble birth and good conduct. 'Saddhā' means with faith—faith in the results of kamma and faith in the Triple Gem. 'Agārasmā' means from the home, or from the state of being a householder. 'Anagāriyaṃ' means into homelessness, or the state of a monk. 'Pabbajitānaṃ' means for those who have entered the monkhood.
94:
To those who have approached the state of a monk (upagatānaṃ). The word 'yaṃ' refers to the consideration of the action. The connection of words in that sentence is as follows: 'Monks, you did not go forth as monks because you were oppressed by kings, nor because you were oppressed by robbers, nor because you were in debt, nor for the sake of a livelihood. Indeed, it was out of faith, having left the household life, that you went forth in my Dispensation (sāsana). Yet now, monks, why do you engage in such pointless talk (tiracchānakathā) related to kings, which is contrary to the Path and Fruition? Engaging in such talk is not proper for you; it is indeed not suitable.'

Having rejected what was improper for the monks thus assembled, and now wishing to allow them the proper practice, he said: 'Monks, when you are assembled, there are two things to be done: either Dhamma talk or Noble Silence.' In that statement, 'vo' means 'for you.' In relation to the word 'karaṇīyaṃ' (to be done), the genitive case is used in the sense of the agent, thus it means 'by you.' 'Dvayaṃ karaṇīyaṃ' means only two things should be done. 'Dhammī kathā' refers to talk that is not divorced from the Four Noble Truths, a Dhamma teaching that illustrates the process of arising and ceasing. Even the Dhamma talk known as the ten subjects of talk (kathāvatthu) is merely a part of that Truth. 'Ariyo' is called noble because it brings about absolute welfare, or because it is especially pure and sublime. 'Tuṇhībhāvo' refers to the non-speaking which constitutes the development of tranquility (samatha) and insight (vipassanā). Some teachers say that the second jhāna is Noble Silence (ariya-tuṇhībhāva) because it is the opposite of verbal formations (vacīsaṅkhāra). Other teachers say that the fourth jhāna is Noble Silence.

The meaning in this Pali is: 'Monks, living in a secluded dwelling with a secluded body for the purpose of increasing mental seclusion (citta-viveka), if you should ever assemble, you who are thus assembled and living together should either engage in Dhamma talk related to the impermanence of the five aggregates and so forth, for the sake of mutual benefit—in the manner stated as "making one hear what has not been heard, or purifying what has been heard"—or you should dwell in Jhanic attainments for the sake of not harming one another.'

Among those two things to be done, by the first statement of what is to be done, he shows the means of entering the Dispensation for those who have not yet entered. By the latter statement, he shows the means of escape from saṃsāra for those who have already entered. Alternatively, by the first task, he enjoins them to proficiency in the scriptures (āgama-veyyatti), and by the latter task, to proficiency in realization (adhigama-veyyatti). Or, by the first task, he points out the primary cause for the arising of Right View (sammādiṭṭhi), and by the second task, the second cause. For it has been said: 'Monks, there are two causes, two conditions for the arising of Right View. Which two? The voice of another (paratoghosa) and wise attention (yoniso manasikāra)' (A. Ni. 2.127).
95:
Alternatively, by the first task, he clarifies the root cause of Mundane Right View (lokiya-sammādiṭṭhi), and by the second task, the root cause of Supramundane Right View (lokuttara-sammādiṭṭhi); in this way and so forth, the connection of meaning here should be understood.

Having understood in every aspect this matter that the attainment of jhāna and so forth is more peaceful and more sublime than the attainment of fame desired by those monks, he uttered this inspired utterance (udāna) which illustrates the power of the happiness of the Noble Dwellings (ariya-vihāra).

In that verse of inspired utterance, in the phrase 'yañca kāmasukhaṃ loke' (and whatever sensual pleasure there is in the world), the word 'loka' (world) appears in the sense of conditioned things (saṅkhāra) in such passages as 'the world of aggregates, the world of sense bases, the world of elements.'

In passages such as:
'As far as the sun and moon revolve,
And the quarters shine in their radiance,
So far the world extends a thousandfold,
Therein your power holds sway.'
—it appears in the sense of the world of space (okāsa-loka). In passages such as 'The Blessed One, surveying the world with the Buddha-eye, saw...' it appears in the sense of the world of sentient beings (satta-loka). Here, however, it should be understood in both senses: the world of sentient beings and the world of space. Therefore, in this world from the Avīci hell upwards to below the Brahma realm, whatever pleasure there is that arises through the power of the defilement of sensuality (kilesa-kāma) in dependence on the objects of sensuality (vatthu-kāma), that is sensual pleasure.

'And whatever divine pleasure there is' (yañcidaṃ diviyaṃ sukhaṃ) refers to whatever pleasure of the fine-material attainments (rūpa-samāpatti) of Brahmas and humans is to be obtained by way of the divine dwellings (dibba-vihāra) in the heavenly realms.

'To the happiness of the destruction of craving' (taṇhakkhayasukhassa) means: that happiness of the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti) which occurs by way of the subsiding of craving, having made Nibbāna the object—in dependence on which craving is destroyed—is called the happiness of the destruction of craving; (it refers) to that happiness of the destruction of craving. 'Ete' (these) is a designation with a change of gender, meaning 'these pleasures.' Some teachers, taking both as a general type of happiness, read it as 'etaṃ'; according to their view, the reading should be 'kalaṃ nāgghati'.

'Soḷasiṃ' means the sixteenth part that completes the whole. Here is the summary of the meaning: starting from the happiness of a Universal Monarch, the human happiness in the entire human world, the happiness to be experienced by Nagas, Garudas, etc., in their respective worlds, and the sixfold sensual pleasure in the six deva realms—thus, the sensual pleasure arising in the elevenfold sensual realm (kāmaloka), as well as this pleasure arising in the fine-material and immaterial jhānas which are the divine dwellings of the fine-material and immaterial devas...
96:
The term 'diviya' refers to the happiness of mundane jhāna. Both types of happiness (mundane and heavenly) are said to be not worth even a sixteenth part of the happiness of the attainment of fruition (phala-samapatti), which takes the cessation of craving (Nirvāṇa) as its object.

This explanation is given in terms of the attainment of fruition in general. Since the Pāḷi text mentions 'the cessation of craving' without specification, even a sixteenth part of the happiness of the attainment of the first fruition (sotāpatti-phala) is not equaled by mundane happiness. Thus it was said:

'Better than sole sovereignty over the earth, or going to heaven, or lordship over all the worlds, is the fruit of Stream-entry.' (Dhammapada 178).

It was also stated in the Sotāpatti-saṃyutta:

'Monks, although a Wheel-turning Monarch (Cakkavatti) exercises sovereignty and lordship over the four great continents and, with the breaking up of the body after death, is reborn in a happy destination, the heavenly world, in the company of the Tāvatiṃsa devas; and there in the Nandana Grove, surrounded by a host of nymphs, he enjoys himself, supplied and endowed with the five types of celestial sensual pleasures; yet, he is not endowed with four things. Therefore, that Wheel-turning Monarch is not yet free from hell, not free from the animal realm, not free from the realm of ghosts, and not free from the plane of misery, the bad destination, the nether world.

Monks, although a noble disciple (ariya-sāvaka) subsists on scraps of alms-food and wears coarse, discarded rags, yet that noble disciple is endowed with four things. Therefore, that noble disciple is free from hell, free from the animal realm, free from the realm of ghosts, and free from the plane of misery, the bad destination, the nether world.

What are the four? Here, monks, a noble disciple is endowed with unwavering confidence in the Buddha: "The Blessed One is such because he is an Arahant... the Buddha, the Blessed One." He is endowed with unwavering confidence in the Dhamma: "The Dhamma is well-expounded... to be experienced by the wise for themselves." He is endowed with unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha: "The Saṅgha is the unsurpassed field of merit for the world." He is endowed with virtues dear to the noble ones, which are unbroken... and lead to concentration. He is endowed with these four things. Monks, the obtaining of the four continents by a Wheel-turning Monarch is not worth a sixteenth part of the obtaining of these four things by a noble disciple.'

In this way, the Blessed One analyzed and taught that in every respect, supramundane happiness is far superior and incomparably more excellent than mundane happiness.

The commentary on the second sutta ends.
97:
'The obtaining of the four things is not worth a sixteenth part of the obtaining of the four continents' (as stated in the Saṃyutta Nikāya). In this way, the Blessed One analyzed that while mundane happiness is superior and excellent in all worldly respects, supramundane happiness alone is unsurpassed and most excellent.

## Commentary on the Second Sutta Ends.

## 3. Commentary on the Daṇḍa Sutta

In the third sutta, the Daṇḍa Sutta, 'kumāraka' means boys. In the phrase 'antarā ca sāvatthiṃ antarā ca jetavanaṃ', the word 'antarā' is used in the sense of 'reason' or 'cause' in passages such as 'Who knows the reason for that, except the Tathāgata?' and 'People meet and consult; what is the reason between me and you?'. It is used in the sense of 'moment' or 'occasion' in passages such as 'I saw, venerable sir, a certain woman washing a vessel in a lightning flash (vijjantarikāya)'. It is used in the sense of 'mind' or 'heart' in passages such as 'In whose heart (yassantarato) there is no anger'. It is used in the sense of 'middle' in passages such as 'He reached the end in the middle (antarā)'. It is used in the sense of 'interval' or 'space' in passages such as 'Monks, this Tapodā river flows through the interval (antarikāya) between two great hells'. Here also, it should be understood in the sense of 'interval' or 'space'. Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as 'in the space between Sāvatthī and the Jetavana monastery'. Because of the association with the word 'antarā', the accusative case is used as in 'antarā ca sāvatthiṃ antarā ca jetavanaṃ'. In such contexts, grammarians usually use the word 'antarā' only once, as in 'antarā gāmañca nadiñca gacchati' (he goes between the village and the river), and that word is to be connected with the second term as well. In this Pāḷi text, however, it is stated by repeating the word.

'Ahiṃ daṇḍena hananti' means they were chasing and striking with sticks a black cobra that had come out of its hole and was traveling in search of food, being hungry within. At that time, the Blessed One, while entering Sāvatthī for alms, saw those boys striking the snake with sticks on the way and asked, "Boys, why are you striking this snake with sticks?" When they replied, "Venerable sir, because we are afraid of being bitten," the Blessed One felt spiritual urgency (dhamma-saṃvega), thinking, "Although these boys strike this snake to seek their own happiness, they will only experience suffering in their future births; oh, how wondrous is the deceptive skill of ignorance!" With that spiritual urgency, he uttered an inspired utterance. Therefore, it is said, "Atha kho bhagavā..." and so forth.
98:
In that Pali, 'Etamatth၁ viditvā' means: 'Knowing this matter, that "these children, by causing suffering to others for their own happiness, will not obtain their own happiness in the hereafter,"' so some teachers say. Other teachers, however, say: 'Seeking happiness for those who practice wrongly leads to future suffering; for those who practice well, it leads certainly to happiness. Therefore, the Teacher uttered this inspired utterance out of joy, thinking, "Indeed, those who follow my instruction, being free from harming others, will surely have a share of happiness."' Still other teachers say: 'Having known the harm of the oppression caused by those children in every way, and wishing to explain the danger of harming others and the benefit of compassion for others in due order, he uttered this inspired utterance.'

In those verses of the inspired utterance, 'sukhakāmāni' means those who long for happiness because they certainly desire their own happiness. 'Bhũtāni' refers to living beings. In the passage 'yo daၑၑena vihi၁sati', the word 'daၑၑena' is just a teaching [metaphor]; it means by a stick, or by striking with a clod of earth, a weapon, the palm of the hand, and so on. Alternatively, 'daၑၑena' means by way of punishment. This is the meaning: whichever person harms, oppresses, or brings suffering to all beings who desire happiness—whether by the 'stick of speech' (vacĩdaၑၑa) by attacking their lineage and so on, or by the 'stick of the body' (kāyadaၑၑa) through the power of beating, striking, cutting, etc., with hands, clubs, weapons, and so on, or by the 'stick of wealth' (dhanadaၑၑa) by imposing a fine of a hundred or a thousand—while seeking his own happiness, that person, seeking, searching for, or yearning for his own happiness, does not obtain the threefold happiness—human happiness, divine happiness, and the happiness of Nibbāna—in the hereafter. On the contrary, the meaning is that he obtains only suffering because of that punishment.

'Pecce so labhate sukhanti' means: being endowed with patience, loving-kindness, and compassion, and thinking, 'Just as I desire happiness and recoil from suffering, so do all beings,' and established in 'coincidental abstinence' (sampatta-virati) and so on, he does not harm or oppress any beings with any kind of stick in the manner mentioned. That person, in the hereafter, obtains human happiness if born as a human, divine happiness if born as a deva, and surpassing both, obtains the happiness of Nibbāna. In this teaching, because that happiness will inevitably occur for such a person, the word 'labhate' (obtains) is used to show that happiness as if it were occurring in the present. In the previous verse also, the method is the same.

## The Commentary on the Third Sutta is finished.
99:
## 4. Commentary on the Sakkāra Sutta

In the fourth sutta, "At that time, the Blessed One was honored" means that due to the result of the extraordinary accumulation of merit fulfilled throughout four incalculables and a hundred thousand eons, the Blessed One received the honor and respect of humans, devas, and Brahmas through offerings and such that increased progressively, as if an effort had arisen thinking, "Beyond this state, there is no further opportunity for me to bear fruit."

Just as great twin clouds might rise in all directions and cause a great flood, all the perfections (pāramĩs) seemed to gather together, thinking, "We shall show our fruit in this single existence as a Buddha," and generated a great flood of gains and offerings for the Blessed One.

At that time, Khattiyas, Brahmins, and others, carrying food, drinks, clothing, vehicles, flowers, perfumes, and ointments, came and searched for the Blessed One, asking, "Where is the Buddha? Where is the Blessed One? Where is the God of gods? Where is the Bull among men? Where is the Lion among men?"

Even though they brought requisites in hundreds of carts, they did not get the opportunity to make their offerings, and like the Brahmin of Andhakavinda and others, they stood with the poles of their carts touching each other within an area of about a league (gāvuta) all around, and they followed [the Buddha] continuously. All this should be understood according to the method mentioned in the Mahāvagga Khandhaka and in various suttas. As it was for the Blessed One, so it was for the Sa၅gha of monks. For it was said:

"Cunda, among the communities or groups that have arisen in the world at present, I do not see any other single Sa၅gha that has reached such a pinnacle of gains and fame as this Sa၅gha of monks."

That gain and honor which arose for the Blessed One and the Sa၅gha of monks together became immeasurable, like the flood of water from two great rivers. Therefore, it is stated in the Pali: "At that time, the Blessed One was honored with requisites... the Sa၅gha of monks was also honored with requisites."

The sectarians (titthiyas), however, were not honored or respected because of their lack of past merit and their wrong practice. But especially upon the arising of the Buddha, their splendor was ruined like fireflies at sunrise; they became lusterless, powerless, and their gains and honor declined. Those sectarians, being envious and jealous of such gains and honor of the Blessed One and the Sa၅gha, thinking, "We will drive them away by attacking them with harsh words," went about abusing and threatening the monks in various places, vomiting the poison of their malice.
100:
Those heretics wandered about. Therefore, it is said in the Pali: "The wandering ascetics of other sects are not respected ... (pe) ... they do not receive requisites. Then, those wandering ascetics of other sects, unable to endure the honor given to the Blessed One, upon seeing the monks in the village or in the forest, abuse, threaten, provoke, and harass the community of monks and the monks with harsh and improper words that are unfit to be spoken among virtuous people."

In that Pali text, "asabbhāhi" means with harsh words that are unfit to be spoken in an assembly or among a group of virtuous people. "Pharusāhi" means with words that are rough and cutting to the core. "Akkosanti" means they abuse and revile using grounds for abuse such as birth and so on. "Paribhāsanti" means they threaten by creating fear through quarreling. "Rosenti" means they provoke anger by excessive harassment so that anger arises in others. "Vihesenti" means they harass and cause discomfort in various ways.

How did these heretics come to practice abuse and so on toward the Blessed One and the community of monks, who are worthy of devotion from all sides? Since the appearance of the Blessed One, their gains and honor had declined, and their minds were ruined. Like someone digging the earth and stumbling, or like someone trying to create a blemish on a flawless beryl gem, they persuaded a female wandering ascetic named Sundarī. Through her, they spread dispraise of the Teacher and the monks and practiced abuse and so on. This story of Sundarī will appear later in the Sundarī Sutta of the Pali text. Therefore, what should be said here, I will explain only in that Sundarī Sutta.

The monks approached the Blessed One and reported that matter. Therefore, it is said: "Then many monks approached the Blessed One ... (pe) ... they harass." This has the meaning already stated.

"Etam-atthaṃ viditvā" means having known in every way that misconduct of the heretics who were overcome by envy. "Imaṃ udānaṃ" means he uttered this inspired utterance which demonstrates the power of the quality of being "tādi" (steadfastness), which is unshaken by the misconduct committed by those with wrong views and the help provided by those with clear faith.

In that verse of the inspired utterance, "gāme araññe sukhadukkha-phuṭṭho" means being touched by pleasure or pain in any place, whether in a village or a forest, while experiencing pleasure and pain, or being endowed with the causes of that pleasure and pain. "Nevattato no parato dahetha" means "I..."
101:
...am happy, I am suffering, my happiness, my suffering, another has caused this happiness and suffering for me"—in this way, one should not regard that happiness and suffering as being due to oneself or due to others. Why? Because in these five aggregates, there is nothing at all that should be seen as "I", "mine", "another", or "another's"; there are only conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra) which arise according to causes and perish moment by moment. In this teaching, the mention of happiness and suffering is merely the head of the discourse; the meaning should be understood by way of all worldly conditions (lokadhamma). Thus, the Blessed One clarified the fourfold emptiness (catukoṭika suññatā): "I am not anywhere, for anyone, in any way; nor is there anything of mine anywhere, for anyone, in any way."

Now, to show the reason for not regarding it as from self or from others, he said: "Contacts touch based on acquisition (upadhi)." These contacts, known as those to be experienced as pleasant and those to be experienced as painful, touch their respective objects when that acquisition, called the five aggregates, exists; they occur only in that acquisition. Since neutral feeling (adukkhamasukha-vedanā) has a peaceful nature, it is included within pleasant feeling; therefore, this explanation of the meaning is made only by way of the two kinds of contact.

To show how those contacts do not touch, he said: "How could contacts touch one without acquisition?" When the acquisition of the aggregates is absent in every way, by what cause could those contacts touch? There is no such cause. If you do not desire the happiness and suffering that arise due to abuse and so on, you should strive only for the state of being without acquisition in every way. Thus, he concluded the verse with the Nibbāna element without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbāna-dhātu). In this way, by this inspired utterance, the round of suffering (vaṭṭa) and the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa) were taught.

## The Commentary on the Fourth Sutta is finished.

## 5. Upāsaka Sutta Commentary

In the fifth sutta, "Icchānaṅgalako" refers to a certain Brahmin village named Icchānaṅgala in the Kosala country. One is called "Icchānaṅgalaka" because of living there or being born and raised there. "Upāsako" (lay follower) refers to a lay follower who has declared his status as a lay follower in the presence of the Blessed One through the three refuges, who possesses the five precepts, and who regards the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha as his own. "By some business or other" (kenacid-eva karaṇīyena) means...
102:
It means having completed the tasks to be done, such as clearing and cleaning. This lay follower used to approach and attend upon the Blessed One regularly in the past. Due to being very busy with many tasks, he was unable to find the opportunity to see the Blessed One for some time. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Lay follower, you have taken a long time to make this turn, that is, for coming here."

In that passage, 'cirassaṃ' means after a long time. 'Pariyāyaṃ' refers to a turn or occasion. 'Yadidaṃ' is an indeclinable meaning "which is this turn." The intended meaning is: "This turn that was made today for the purpose of coming here to my presence, you have made it after a long delay." 'Cirapaṭikāhaṃ' should be connected as "I have had the desire to approach since a long time ago." 'Kehi ci kehi ci' means by some or other persons, or by any whatsoever. By saying this, he shows respect. For one who is extremely devoted to the Teacher does not have the same regard for others as he does for seeing the Teacher and hearing the Dhamma. In the phrase 'kiccakaraṇīyehi', an obligatory task is called 'kicca', and the remaining work is called 'karaṇīya'. Alternatively, a task to be done first is 'kicca', and one to be done later is 'karaṇīya'. Or, a small task is 'kicca', and a large one is 'karaṇīya'. 'Byāvaṭo' means being occupied or busy. 'Evāhaṃ' means "In this manner, I was unable to approach, not because of disrespect, but because of being busy."

"Knowing this matter" means knowing in every aspect that for beings, during the rare appearance of a Buddha and the rare attainment of human life, being possessed of impediments and being occupied with tasks becomes an obstacle to merit, whereas for one without impediments, there is no such obstacle. Having known this, he uttered this inspired utterance (udāna) that clarifies that meaning.

In that Udāna verse, "Happy indeed is he who has nothing" means that for a person who does not possess even a single object among the sense bases like forms, thinking "this is mine" through craving, it is truly a state of happiness for that person. There is also a reading 'na hosi', which should be understood in the past tense. Some teachers explain 'kiñcana' as "one who has no impediments such as lust (rāga)," but this is not very appropriate because this teaching is presented based on the nature of possession (pariggaha). However, if one considers that lust and so on are included within the objects to be possessed, then it would be appropriate. Alternatively, because the absence of impediments like lust results in the absence of even the slightest obstructive impediment (palibodha), that state of having nothing is the cause of happiness, hence the meaning "Oh, how happy!"
103:
...because it is the cause, "Happy indeed, oh, how happy!" is the meaning. If one asks, "Who is it that has no impediments?", the answer is given: "For one who has understood the Dhamma and is learned." One who has understood the Dhamma (saṅkhātadhamma) is one who has completed his tasks by fulfilling the sixteen functions through the four paths. For that reason, he is "learned" (bahussuta) through the great learning of penetration (paṭivedha-bāhusacca).

Thus, the Blessed One, having shown the benefit of the state of having nothing, said "See the one who has impediments" (sakiñcanaṃ passa) to show the danger of the state of having impediments. The meaning is: one is called 'sakiñcana' because of the existence of impediments of lust and impediments of material things. Because of having impediments, one is troubled and falls into distress through the performance of tasks for the sake of seeking and protecting sensual pleasures—both those not yet obtained and those already obtained—and through the grasping of "I" and "mine". Seeing the multitude of people in this state, the Teacher, having reached spiritual urgency (dhamma-saṃvega), spoke to his own mind. "People are bound to people" means that while being another person oneself, one becomes bound to another person through the power of craving, thinking "I belong to this person, this person belongs to me," and thus falls into distress. There is also a variant reading 'paṭibaddhacitto' (with a bound mind). This meaning should be illustrated by such scriptural verses as: "Sons I have, wealth I have, thus the fool is troubled; when even one's own self does not belong to oneself, how then sons? How then wealth?" (Dhp 62).

## The Commentary on the Fifth Sutta is finished.

## 6. Gabbhinī Sutta Vaṇṇanā (Commentary on the Pregnant Woman Sutta)

In the sixth sutta, "aññatarassa paribbājakassa" means to a certain householder wanderer. "Daharā" means young. "Māṇavikā" is a term for a brahmin girl. "Pajāpatī" means wife. "Gabbhinī" means pregnant. "Upavijaññā" means that the time of delivery is very near, such as today or tomorrow. It is said that he was a brahmin by birth who lived in a forest hermitage with his wife; therefore, they address him as a wanderer (paribbājaka) along with his wife. His wife, being of brahmin birth, addresses him as "Brahmin". "Telaṃ" refers to sesame oil. Here, with oil as the primary item, he orders her to "bring everything" that is needed to remedy the suffering of childbirth after delivery, such as ghee (sappi), salt (loṇa), and so on.
104:
"It will be" (bhavissati) refers to the oil and such that will be useful to me when I have given birth and the fetus has come out. There is also a variant reading "paribbājikāya". "From where?" (kuto) means from what place; the meaning is that there is no place, such as a relative's house or a friend's house, from where I could bring oil and so forth. "I bring oil" (āharāmi) is spoken in the present tense because the future is near; it means "I will bring oil". In the phrase "to a recluse or a brahmin, or ghee or oil," the word "vā" (or) has a conjunctive sense (samuccaya), similar to its use in "from fire or from water or from internal dissension." The genitive case in "sappissa vā telassa vā" is used in the sense of the accusative (paccatta), meaning that ghee and oil are given to be drunk as much as desired. Others say that "sappissa vā telassa vā" is a genitive of relation to a part (avayavasambandha); here, the part of the whole mass of ghee and oil is expressed by the word "yāvadattha" (as much as needed).

"Not to be taken out" (no nīharituṃ) means it is not given to be taken outside by means of a vessel or by hand. "Ucchadditvāna" means having vomited; it should be connected as "it would be good if I could vomit it out." This thought occurred to that brahmin: "I will go to the King's granary, drink oil up to my throat, return home immediately, vomit what I have drunk into a vessel, place it on the stove and cook it. I will let the fire burn away the bile, phlegm, and so forth mixed with it, and then I will take the oil and use it for this female wanderer's childbirth."

"To make it go upwards" (uddhaṃ kātuṃ) means to bring it up by vomiting. "But not downwards" (na pana adho) means he is unable to bring it out downwards by purging. That brahmin thought, "The oil drunk in excess will come out of the mouth by itself," but because the stomach was empty, it did not come out. Not knowing or not obtaining the procedure for vomiting or purging, he was afflicted by intense painful feelings and rolled to and fro. "Dukkhāhi" means feelings that are hard to endure. "Tibbāhi" means thick or intense feelings. "Kharāhi" means harsh feelings. "Kaṭukāhi" means feelings that are very unpleasant and cruel. "Āvaṭṭati" means being unable to stay still in one place, pulling one's body here and there and rolling. "Parivaṭṭati" means even while lying in one place, throwing one's limbs all around and rolling. Alternatively, rolling forward is called "āvaṭṭati," and rolling all around is called "parivaṭṭati."

"Having known this matter" means having known in every aspect this matter: "This arising of suffering occurs to one with encumbrances due to inconsiderate consumption; however, for one without encumbrances, this does not exist in any way." Having known this in all its aspects, he uttered this inspired utterance (udāna) explaining that meaning.
105:
In that inspired verse, "Happy indeed" (sukino vata) means "The virtuous are indeed happy." Who are they? They are those without encumbrances (akiñcana). They are called "without encumbrances" because of the absence of the encumbrance of defilements like lust (rāga) and the encumbrance of possession (pariggaha). The Blessed One said, "People who have reached the end of knowledge (vedaguno) are without encumbrances." Those who have reached the knowledge known as the Path of the Noble Ones (ariyamagga-ñāṇa), or who have reached Nibbāna through that knowledge, are "vedagū". These noble ones, the Arahants, are called "without encumbrances" because the encumbrances of lust and so forth have been completely cut off by the Highest Path. Indeed, when the encumbrance of lust and so forth is absent, how could the encumbrance of possessing material things arise?

Thus, with the first half of the verse, he praises the Arahants, and with the second half, starting with "See the one with encumbrances" (sakiñcanaṃ passa), he censures the blind worldlings. The meaning of those words is exactly as stated in the previous sutta. Thus, by this verse also, the round of suffering (vaṭṭa) and the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa) are taught.

## The Commentary on the Sixth Sutta is finished.

## 7. Ekaputtaka Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the seventh sutta, "ekaputtako" means an only son. That son is called "ekaputtaka" because he is to be pitied, "piya" because he is dear, and "manāpa" because he increases the joy of the mind. Alternatively, he is "piya" because he is lovely to look at due to the perfection of his physical beauty, and "manāpa" because he has a good nature due to the perfection of his virtue and conduct. Because it consumes beings, it is called "kāla" (time/death). Because he has reached that death, he is "kālaṅkata". Alternatively, because he has reached destruction and invisibility caused by time or the King of Death, he is "kālaṅkata," meaning he has died.

"Many lay followers" (sambahulā upāsakā) means many lay followers living in Sāvatthī, sharing the grief with the lay follower whose son had died, followed him to the cemetery. After performing the necessary funeral rites for the body, they returned. Upon returning, they entered the water just as they were, washed their heads, squeezed their clothes, and without letting them dry, wore one garment and used another as an upper robe. Placing that lay follower in front, they approached the Blessed One, thinking, "We will listen to the Dhamma that dispels grief in the presence of the Teacher." Therefore, it is said, "with wet hair," and so forth.

In those words, "allavatthā" means those with clothes wet with water. "Divā divassa" means in the day of the day, which means at the time of midday. Since the Tathāgatas, though they know, they ask; though they know, they do not ask; knowing the time, they ask; knowing the time, they do not ask. Therefore, the Blessed One, though he knew, in order to initiate a conversation, said, "Lay followers, on other days you... of mine..."
106:
Because of the sorrow of the lay follower whose son had died, they followed the body to the cemetery and performed the necessary rites for the corpse. Upon returning, they descended into the water and washed their heads as usual.
