Without wringing out their clothes to dry them, wearing one garment and using another as an upper robe, they approached the Blessed One, placing that lay follower at the front, thinking, "We shall listen to the Dhamma of the Blessed One which can dispel sorrow." Therefore, the Blessed One spoke the words beginning with "allakesā" (with wet hair) in the Pali. In that context, "allavatthā" means having clothes wet with water. "Divā divassa" means at the time of midday within the day itself.

The Buddhas, even though they know, they ask; even though they know, they do not ask. Knowing the proper time, they ask; knowing the proper time, they do not ask. Therefore, the Blessed One, though knowing, asked, "How is it, lay followers?" and so on, for the purpose of initiating a conversation. The meaning of those words is: "Lay followers, on other days when you come to me, you come in the evening with clean clothes dried in the sun. But today, you have come here at midday with wet clothes and wet hair. What is the reason for this?"

The words "For that reason, we..." mean: "We, who have reached such a state because of the mental distress caused by separation from a beloved son and being overwhelmed by the powerful fire of sorrow, approach this place."

"Knowing this matter" means: Because of the existence of beloved objects, sorrow, suffering, and grief, etc., arise; if there were no beloved objects, these [sorrows] would not exist in any way. Knowing this matter in all its aspects, he uttered this inspired utterance (udāna) which clarifies that meaning.

In that inspired verse, "piyarūpassādagadhitāse" refers to those whose minds are attached and bound by relishing the pleasant feeling in the aggregates of form (rūpakkhandha), etc., which are of a beloved nature. "Gadhitāse" has the same meaning as "gadhitā". Or, the syllable "se" is merely a particle (nipāta). What are called "pleasant forms" (piyarūpa) are the eye, etc., and sons, wives, etc. For it is said: "What in the world is of a pleasant nature and a delightful nature? The eye in the world is of a pleasant nature and a delightful nature... (pe) ... craving for mental objects (dhamma-taṇhā) in the world is of a pleasant nature and a delightful nature."

"Fields, lands, gold, or silver, cattle, horses, slaves, and workmen, women, kinsmen, and many sensual pleasures—the person who greedily pursues these..."

Therefore, the meaning is: those who are greedy, infatuated, and obsessed with the relish of those pleasant forms. Who are those "bound by the relish of pleasant forms"? He shows them with "groups of devas and many humans" (devakāyā puthumanussā ca). This refers to the many groups of devas such as those of the Four Great Kings (Cātumahārājika), and the many humans such as those of Jambudīpa. "Aghāvino" means those who have reached suffering through bodily and mental pain. "Parijunnā" means those who have declined from the attainment of youth and health due to the ruin of old age and disease, etc. Or, this meaning should be understood among devas and humans according to what is applicable.

Alternatively, although suffering, old age, and disease do not manifestly occur to devas who are entirely endowed with sensual happiness, they are still called "aghāvino" and "parijunnā" because they have a nature that cannot transcend old age and disease. Or, it should be understood that suffering, etc., arise for those devas due to the appearance of the five premonitory signs (pubbanimitta), hidden old age, and mental disease. "They go under the power of the King of Death" means that because they have not abandoned craving for beloved objects, they repeatedly...
107:
Because they have not yet abandoned the craving for pleasant objects, they repeatedly enter the mother's womb and wander in the three rounds of existence, thus falling into the hands of death, known as the King of Death.

Having shown the round of existence (vaṭṭa) with this much, he now shows the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa) with the verse beginning with "Ye ve divā." In that verse, "Ye ve divā ca ratto ca appamattā" means they fulfill the practice of diligence, being steadfastly diligent by day and by night, in the manner stated: "Throughout the day, by walking and sitting, they purify the mind from obstructive states," and so on. "Jahanti piyarūpaṃ" means that by exerting effort in the meditation on the Four Noble Truths and attaining the Noble Path, they abandon pleasant forms—such as the eye and other pleasant objects—by abandoning the desire and lust (chandarāga) associated with those objects. "Te ve khaṇanti aghamūlaṃ maccuno āmisaṃ durativattaṃ" means those Noble Ones (ariyas), with the hoe of Noble Path-knowledge, dig up craving along with ignorance, which is the root of the suffering of the round, the bait to be touched by death, and which is difficult to overcome because it cannot be averted by any recluses or brahmins outside this Dispensation. They uproot it without leaving even a trace. This meaning should be expanded upon with such sutta verses as:

"Diligence is the path to the Deathless; negligence is the path to death. The diligent do not die; the negligent are as if already dead."

This should be understood in detail through such sutta passages.

## The Commentary on the Seventh Sutta is finished.

## 8. Suppavāsāsutta-vaṇṇanā

In the eighth sutta, "Kuṇḍikāyaṃ" means in the city of the Koliyans of this name. "Kuṇḍadhānavane" means in the forest called Kuṇḍadhāna, not far from that city.

In the past, it is said, a yakkha named Kuṇḍa lived in that forest grove. He delighted in offerings mixed with broken rice (kuṇḍa); therefore, people offered such oblations to him there. Because of this, that forest grove became known as Kuṇḍadhāna. Not far from that forest, there was a principal village. That village was also called Kuṇḍikā because it was situated within the sphere of that yakkha's authority and was protected by him.
108:
That village was also called "Kuṇḍikā" because it was situated within the sphere of that yakkha's authority and was protected by him. Later, the Koliyan kings built a city in that place. That city was also called "Kuṇḍikā" according to the former usage. In that forest grove, the Koliyan kings established a monastery for the residence of the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of monks. That monastery also became known as "Kuṇḍadhānavana." Later, while the Blessed One was wandering on a walking tour through the countryside, he eventually reached that monastery and stayed there. Therefore, it is said: "At one time the Blessed One was staying at Kuṇḍikā in the Kuṇḍadhāna forest."

"Suppavāsā" is the name of that laywoman. "Koliyadhītā" means she was the daughter of a Koliyan king. That laywoman was a Noble Disciple (ariyasāvikā), a Stream-enterer (sotāpanna), who was placed in the foremost rank (etadagga) among the female disciples of the Blessed One who give choice alms. If there was any suitable food, snack, or medicine for the Blessed One that others could not provide, she would personally arrange everything with her own wisdom and respectfully offer it after preparing it perfectly. Daily, she would give 108 meals, consisting of meals for the Saṅgha and for individual monks. Any monk or nun who entered that family for alms would not leave empty-handed. Thus, she was one who was liberal in giving, open-handed, delighting in relinquishment, devoted to those who ask, and delighting in the distribution of gifts. In the womb of this laywoman Suppavāsā, a disciple-to-be (sāvakabodhisatta) who had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and was in his final existence, took rebirth. Due to some past unwholesome kamma, Suppavāsā carried that fetus in her womb for seven years, and for seven days she experienced a confused birth. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "She carried the fetus for seven years; for seven days she had a difficult birth."

In that passage, "satta vassāni" means for seven years. This term is in the accusative case (accantasaṃyoga) in the sense of continuous duration. "Gabbhaṃ dhāreti" means she carries the fetus, meaning she was pregnant. "Sattāhaṃ mūḷhagabbhā" means for seven days she had a confused/obstructed fetus. To explain: when the fetus is mature and ready for birth, it is moved by the birth-winds (kammajavāta) and turns so that its feet are up and its head is down, facing the birth canal. In this way, it comes out without getting stuck anywhere. However, when things go wrong, due to an abnormal turn, it lies across the birth canal, blocking it, or the birth canal itself closes. That fetus, turning this way and that due to the birth-winds and becoming confused, is called "mūḷhagabbha." For Suppavāsā, this happened for seven days. Therefore, it is said: "For seven days she had a difficult birth."

This fetus was the Elder Sīvali. Why did he have to suffer the pain of staying in the womb for seven years and reach the state of a difficult birth for seven days? And why did his mother, though she was a Noble Disciple and a Stream-enterer, have to experience such suffering?
109:
If it is asked why that noble disciple Suppavāsā experienced such suffering—it is said: In the past, while the King of Kāsi was reigning in Bārāṇasī, a certain King of Kosala came with a great army, captured Bārāṇasī, killed that king, and made his chief queen his own chief queen. However, the son of the King of Bārāṇasī escaped through a drainage gate at the time of his father's death. Having gathered his relatives and friends and gradually building up his strength, he returned to Bārāṇasī. He established a large camp not far from the city and sent a message to that king: 'Either give up the kingdom or fight.' When the prince's mother heard this news, she sent a message saying, 'There is no need for war. Cut off all movement from every direction and surround the city of Bārāṇasī. Then, the people in the city, exhausted by the depletion of wood, water, and food, will capture the king and hand him over without a fight.' Listening to his mother's advice, the prince guarded the four main gates and besieged the city for seven years. The people in the city would exit through small gates to bring in wood and water and perform all their tasks.

Then, when the prince's mother heard about this situation, she sent a secret message to her son, saying, 'My son is foolish; he does not know the strategy. Go and tell him to close those small gates as well and blockade the city.' Hearing his mother's message, the prince did so for seven days. Since the citizens could no longer go outside, on the seventh day, they took the head of that king and presented it to the prince. The prince entered the city and took over the kingdom. Due to the result of the kamma of blockading the city for seven years at that time, he now stayed for seven years in the 'blood-pot' known as the mother's womb. Due to the remaining kamma of blockading the city completely for seven days, he fell into the state of a mūḷhagabbha (obstructed labor) for seven days. However, in the Jātaka Commentary, it is said: 'Due to the result of the kamma of capturing the city after blockading it for seven days, he stayed in the blood-pot for seven years and fell into the state of a mūḷhagabbha for seven days.' Because he had made a great offering (mahādāna) at the feet of Padumuttara Buddha and made an aspiration, 'May I be the foremost among those who receive gains,' and because during the time of Vipassī Buddha he had offered molasses-curd worth a thousand pieces of money together with the citizens and made an aspiration, he became the foremost among those who receive gains through the power of that merit. Suppavāsā, too, because she had sent the message, 'Dear son, capture the city by blockading it,' carried the fetus in her womb for seven years and for seven days...
110: ...suffered an obstructed birth. Thus, the mother and son experienced such suffering in accordance with their own kamma. "With three kinds of thoughts" means with three right thoughts associated with the recollection of the qualities of the Triple Gem. "Endures" means she bears the suffering arisen from the obstructed birth. Indeed, that laywoman Suppavāsā, by repeatedly recollecting the Buddha's state of perfect enlightenment, the good practice of the Noble Saṅgha, and Nibbāna as the escape from suffering, overcomes and endures the suffering arising within her by not attending to it. Therefore, it was said, "She endures with three kinds of thoughts." "The Blessed One is indeed perfectly enlightened" and so forth shows the manner in which those thoughts occur. Its meaning is: The Blessed One, the Protector of the World, is called "Bhagavā" because he is endowed with reasons such as the six glories. That Blessed One has indeed realized all dhammas correctly and unerringly by himself. That Blessed One teaches the Dhamma for the sake of abandoning and for the ultimate non-arising cessation of this entire mass of round-of-suffering (vaṭṭa-dukkha) of such a nature as I am experiencing now and others of the same kind; he teaches the unerring Dhamma. Indeed, the Teacher's attainment of Perfect Enlightenment (Sammāsambodhi) is established by his teaching of the unerring Dhamma. The group of eight noble persons, known by the name "Saṅgha of Disciples" because they were born at the end of hearing the Dhamma of the Blessed One who is endowed with the aforementioned qualities and because they are united by the commonality of virtue and view, is indeed "well-practiced" (suppaṭipanna); oh, they have indeed practiced rightly! This Noble Saṅgha has practiced the non-retreating path for the sake of abandoning and for the non-arising cessation of such round-of-suffering. Nibbāna, which is the escape from all conditioned things, is indeed "truly blissful"; oh, it is indeed thoroughly blissful! In that Nibbāna, such round-of-suffering is not found. In this context, even one who is still practicing is called "practiced" (paṭipanna) because of the non-retreating nature of the practice. Alternatively, like the word "uppanna" (arisen), the word "paṭipanna" should be understood as having a present meaning. Therefore, it was said, "One practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry." "To her husband" refers to her own husband, the Koliyan prince. "Addressed" means she spoke. "Pay homage to the Blessed One's feet with your head in my name" means: "With your head, pay homage to the feet of the Blessed One, which are adorned with the marks of the wheel and possess the splendor of a blooming lotus; perform the salutation with the highest limb (the head) according to my words." In the words beginning with "free from affliction" (appābādha), "affliction" (ābādha) refers to a disagreeable sensation which, even if it arises in one part, takes hold of the entire body as if binding it with an iron plate. "Ailment" (ātaṅka) is a disease that makes life difficult. Alternatively, a manageable disease is called "ātaṅka", while the other is "ābādha". Or, a minor disease is called "ātaṅka"...
111:
A severe illness is called ābādha. Some teachers, however, say, "An internal illness is called ābādha, and an external illness is called ātaṅka." He says to inquire about the absence of both these types of illness. The rising of a sick person is difficult; there is no strength in the body. Therefore, he says to inquire about the quick rising of the body, characterized by ease of movement due to the absence of illness, and the strength of the body. Phāsuvihāraṃ means living happily in the four postures: standing, sitting, walking, and lying down. Then, showing the manner in which the prince should inquire, he says, "Venerable Sir, Suppavāsā..." and so on. "Speak thus" indicates the manner of speaking now.

Paramaṃ is a word of acceptance. By that, he shows, "Very well, sister, I will do as you have said." Koliyaputta is the Koliyan prince, the husband of Suppavāsā. Sukhinī hotu: The Blessed One, the Teacher of gods and humans, worthy of the highest offerings in the world including the devas, accepted the salutation sent by Suppavāsā. Immediately after that, showing his own dwelling in loving-kindness (mettāvihāra), which is the habit of the Buddhas to bring happiness, he generally declared it to Suppavāsā. Then, by way of rejecting the suffering caused by the pregnancy complication for her son, and showing the bringing of the benefit of happiness, he said, "May Suppavāsā be happy, may she be healthy, and may she give birth to a healthy son."

Saha vacanā means simultaneously with the words of the Blessed One. At the very moment the Blessed One spoke in that manner, that kamma came to an end. Seeing the exhaustion of that kamma, the Teacher spoke thus. Other teachers say, "If the Blessed One had not spoken in that way, that suffering would have followed the mother and son for some time longer." Because the Blessed One said, "May Suppavāsā be happy, may she be healthy, and may she give birth to a healthy son," at the same time as those words, the fetus gave up its tangled state and came out easily. Thus, there was safety for both mother and son. The power of the Buddhas is indeed inconceivable. Just as for Paṭācārā, who went mad due to grief from separation from loved ones:

"Both sons have died, my husband died on the road;
Mother, father, and brother are burning on a single funeral pyre."
112:
"Sister, regain your mindfulness." At the end of these words of the Blessed One, the madness of Paṭācārā, who was wandering naked, ceased. Similarly, the laywoman Suppiyā, who was unable to rise and was lying on her bed due to a great wound she had inflicted on her own thigh, at the end of the words "Let her come and salute me," the wound became normal, and she went herself to salute the Blessed One. Such stories should be cited here as examples.

"Venerable Sir, let it be so" means: "Venerable Sir, just as the Blessed One said, wishing for the health of the mother and son, 'May she be happy, may she be healthy, and may she give birth to a healthy son,' let it be so." Indeed, the words of the Blessed Buddhas never turn out otherwise. Some teachers say, "May it be so." Others explain by bringing out the meaning of the word hotu.

"Having greatly rejoiced" means: Having obtained joy and gladness at those words spoken by the Blessed One with a Brahma-voice as sweet as the call of the Karavīka bird, she rejoiced in his presence. "Having appreciated" means: Producing appreciation afterwards. Or, rejoicing with the mind and appreciating with speech. Or, rejoicing at the perfection of the words and appreciating the perfection of the meaning.

"She returned to her own home" means she went back to her house. For those who read "yena sakaṃ gharaṃ," because of the connection between the words ya and ta, the word tena is already included, but the remaining text paṭiyāyitvā should be joined and read.

"Giving birth" (vijāta) means the act of bearing a child (pasuta). "It is wonderful" (acchariyaṃ): It is called acchariya because it is something that does not happen constantly, like a blind person climbing a mountain. This is the grammatical method. In the Commentaries, it is said, "That which is worthy of snapping one's fingers is acchariya." "Vata" is a particle used in praise, meaning "Indeed, it is wonderful!" "Bho" is a term of address used righteously. Because it is something that has not happened before, it is called abbhuta (marvelous).

"Tathāgata" means the Blessed One is called Tathāgata for eight reasons: (1) He has come in the same way as previous Buddhas; (2) He has gone in the same way; (3) He has arrived at the true characteristics; (4) He has fully awakened to the true dhammas as they really are; (5) He is a seer of truth; (6) He is a speaker of truth; (7) He acts as he speaks; (8) He overcomes all in the sense of surpassing.
113:
In what way is the Blessed One called 'Tathāgata' because he has 'thus come' (tathā āgato)? Just as the former Fully Enlightened Buddhas came, exerting themselves for the welfare of the entire world, so too has this Blessed One come. What is meant by this? In the same way those Blessed Ones came with an aspiration (abhinīhāra) endowed with eight qualities, this Blessed One also came with an aspiration endowed with those same eight qualities. And just as those Blessed Ones, having fulfilled the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramī), and the ten perfections, ten sub-perfections, and ten ultimate perfections—namely virtue, renunciation, wisdom, energy, patience, truthfulness, determination, loving-kindness, and equanimity—thus fulfilling the thirty perfections; having made the five great sacrifices (mahāpariccāga); and having fulfilled the previous applications, previous conduct, preaching of the Dhamma, conduct for the benefit of relatives, and so forth, reaching the pinnacle of the conduct for enlightenment (buddhi-cariyā), they came; so too has this Blessed One come. And just as those Blessed Ones came having developed and augmented the four foundations of mindfulness... (and so forth) ...the Noble Eightfold Path; so too has this Blessed One come. Thus, he is the 'Tathāgata' because he has 'thus come'.

In what way is he called 'Tathāgata' because he has 'thus gone' (tathā gato)? Just as those Blessed Ones, immediately after being born, stood on the earth with level feet, and facing the north, went forward with a stride of seven steps; while a white parasol was being held over them, they surveyed all directions and uttered a bold speech (āsabhī vāca) proclaiming their supremacy and excellence in the world; and just as that going of theirs was true (tatha) and unerring, serving as a precursor for the attainment of many distinctions; so too did this Blessed One go. And his going was also true and unerring, serving as a precursor for the attainment of those very same distinctions. Thus, he is the 'Tathāgata' because he has 'thus gone'.

Alternatively, just as those Blessed Ones went having abandoned sensual desire through renunciation (nekkhamma), ill-will through non-ill-will (abyāpāda), sloth and torpor through the perception of light (āloka-saññā), restlessness and remorse through non-distraction (avikkhepa), and doubt through the definition of phenomena (dhamma-vavatthāna); and went having pierced ignorance with knowledge, dispelled discontent with joy (pāmojja), and abandoned various opposing states through the eight attainments, the eighteen great insights, and the four Noble Paths; so too has this Blessed One gone. In this way also, he is the 'Tathāgata' because he has 'thus gone'.

In what way is he called 'Tathāgata' because he has 'arrived at the true characteristics' (tatha-lakkhaṇaṃ āgato)? The characteristic of hardness of the earth element, the characteristic of flowing of the water element, the characteristic of heat of the fire element, the characteristic of supporting of the air element, the characteristic of non-contact of the space element, the characteristic of changing of form (rūpa), the characteristic of feeling of sensation (vedanā), the characteristic of perceiving of perception (saññā), the characteristic of constructing of mental formations (saṅkhāra), the characteristic of cognizing of consciousness (viññāṇa)...
114:
...the characteristic of cognizing the object, and so forth; thus for the five aggregates, the twelve sense bases, the eighteen elements, the twenty-two faculties, the four truths, the twelve-linked dependent origination, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the Noble Eightfold Path, the seven purifications, and Nibbāna which is plunged in the deathless—whatever is the individual essence and characteristic (sabhāva-sarasa-lakkhaṇa) of each of those phenomena, he has arrived at that true, unerring, and non-otherwise characteristic through the 'going' of knowledge, reaching and attaining it without fail. Thus, he is the 'Tathāgata' because he has 'arrived at the true characteristics'.

In what way is he called 'Tathāgata' because he has 'perfectly awakened to the true phenomena as they really are' (tatha-dhamme yāthāvato abhisambuddho)? True phenomena (tatha-dhamma) are the Four Noble Truths. As it was said: "Monks, these four are true (tatha), unerring (avitatha), and not otherwise (anaññatha). Which four? 'This is suffering'—monks, this is true, this is unerring, this is not otherwise," and so forth in detail. And the Blessed One has perfectly awakened to those truths; therefore, because of perfectly awakening to the true phenomena, he is the 'Tathāgata'.

Furthermore, the fact that aging and death arise with birth as a condition is true, unerring, and not otherwise... (and so forth) ...the fact that mental formations arise with ignorance as a condition is true, unerring, and not otherwise. Likewise, the fact that ignorance is the condition for mental formations... (and so forth) ...the fact that birth is the condition for aging and death is true, unerring, and not otherwise. The Blessed One has perfectly awakened to all of that. Therefore, also because of perfectly awakening to the true phenomena, he is the 'Tathāgata'. For in this context, the word 'gata' (gone) means 'perfectly awakened' (abhisambuddha). Thus, he is the 'Tathāgata' because he has 'perfectly awakened to the true phenomena as they really are'.

In what way is he called 'Tathāgata' because of 'true seeing' (tatha-dassitāya)? In the world with its devas... (and so forth) ...among the generation of beings including devas, humans, and Brahmās, in the infinite world systems, there exists what is called a visible object (rūpārammaṇa) that comes into the range of the eye door of infinite beings. The Blessed One knows and sees that object in every aspect. To the one who thus knows and sees, whether by way of its being pleasant or unpleasant, or by way of the categories found among the seen, heard, sensed, and cognized, when it is analyzed by many names such as "What is that form which is the form-base? It is that form which, depending on the four great elements, is colored and bright, visible and impinging, blue, yellow, etc.", and through thirteen turns (vāra) and fifty-two methods, it is only true (tatha) and there is no error. This same method applies to sounds and so forth that come into the range of the ear door and other sense doors. For this was said by the Blessed One:
115:
“Monks, in the world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among the generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans, whatever is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought, and pondered by the mind—that I know, that I have fully realized. That is known to the Tathāgata, but the Tathāgata does not abide [clinging] in it,” thus it was stated (in the Aṅguttara Nikāya).

Thus, because of seeing truly (tathadassitāya), he is called the Tathāgata. In that sentence, the formation of the word 'Tathāgata' should be understood in the sense of seeing truly.

How is he the Tathāgata because of speaking truly (tathavāditāya)? From the night the Blessed One fully realized the supreme self-enlightenment until the night he attained Parinibbāna in the element of Nibbāna without remainder—during this interval of forty-five years—whatever the Blessed One spoke, uttered, or taught such as Sutta, Geyya, and so forth, all that is pure, complete, crushing lust and intoxication, entirely consistent, true, and unerring. Therefore, it was said—

“Cunda, on the night the Tathāgata fully realizes the supreme self-enlightenment, and on the night he attains Parinibbāna in the element of Nibbāna without remainder, whatever he speaks, utters, or points out in this interval, all that is just so and not otherwise. Therefore, he is called ‘Tathāgata’” (in the Dīgha Nikāya).

In this context, the word 'gata' has the meaning of 'gada' (speaking). Thus, because of speaking truly, he is called the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, 'āgadana' is called 'āgada', meaning speech. Because the Blessed One has true, unerring, and non-perverted speech (āgada), by changing the letter 'd' to 't', the word formation as 'Tathāgata' should be understood in this context.

How is he the Tathāgata because of acting as he speaks (tathākāritāya)? For the Blessed One’s bodily actions conform to his speech, and his speech conforms to his bodily actions. Therefore, he acts as he speaks and speaks as he acts. For the Blessed One who is such, his bodily actions proceed (pavatta) just as his speech is, and his speech proceeds just as his bodily actions are; thus he is the Tathāgata. Therefore, it was said—

“Monks, as the Tathāgata speaks, so he acts; as he acts, so he speaks. Thus, because he acts as he speaks and speaks as he acts, he is called ‘Tathāgata’” (in the Aṅguttara Nikāya).
116:
Thus, because of acting as he speaks, he is called 'Tathāgata'.

How is he the Tathāgata in the sense of surpassing (abhibhavanaṭṭhena)? Because from the highest point of existence above down to the Avīci hell below, and across the boundless world systems, he surpasses all beings in virtue, in concentration, in wisdom, in liberation, and in the knowledge and vision of liberation. There is no measure or comparison for that Blessed One; rather, he is incomparable, immeasurable, supreme, the God of gods, the Sakka beyond Sakkas, the Brahma beyond Brahmas, the most excellent of all beings. Therefore, he is called 'Tathāgata'. Therefore, the Blessed One said—

“Monks, in the world with its devas... among the generation with its devas and humans, the Tathāgata is the vanquisher, the unvanquished, the one who sees everything, the wielder of power. Therefore, he is called ‘Tathāgata’” (in the Aṅguttara Nikāya).

In that sentence, the word formation is: he is called 'agada' because he is like a medicine (agada). The elegance of his teaching and the abundance of his merit are called 'agada'. Just as a powerful physician overcomes snakes with divine medicine, so the Blessed One surpasses all proponents of external views and the world with its devas. In this sense of surpassing the whole world, he has the aforementioned true, unerring, and non-perverted medicine (agada); by changing the letter 'd' to 't', it should be understood as 'Tathāgata'. Thus, he is the Tathāgata in the sense of surpassing.

Furthermore, he is 'Tathāgata' because he has gone/known truly (tathāya gato) and he is 'Tathāgata' because he has arrived at the truth (tathaṃ gato). In that variation, he is 'Tathāgata' because he has known (avagata) the entire world through the full understanding of investigation (tīraṇa-pariññā). He is 'Tathāgata' because he has transcended (atīta) the origin of the world through the full understanding of abandoning (pahāna-pariññā). He is 'Tathāgata' because he has attained (adhigata) the cessation of the world, Nibbāna, through realization. He is 'Tathāgata' because he has practiced (paṭipanna) the path leading to the cessation of the world. For this was said by the Blessed One—

“Monks, the world has been fully realized by the Tathāgata; the Tathāgata is detached from the world. Monks, the origin of the world has been fully realized by the Tathāgata; the origin of the world has been abandoned by the Tathāgata. Monks, the cessation of the world has been fully realized by the Tathāgata; the cessation of the world has been realized by the Tathāgata. Monks, the path leading to the cessation of the world has been fully realized by the Tathāgata; the path leading to the cessation of the world has been developed by the Tathāgata. Monks, whatever in the world with its devas... all that the Tathāgata has fully realized; therefore, he is called ‘Tathāgata’.”
117:
"Monks, in the world with its devas... the Tathāgata has fully awakened to all that. Therefore, he is called 'Tathāgata'." (A. Ni. 4.23).

The Blessed One is also called 'Tathāgata' for eight other reasons: (1) He is called 'Tathāgata' because he has come to the state of Buddhahood through a true and unerring resolution. (2) He is called 'Tathāgata' because he has acted for the welfare of beings through the true and unerring Great Compassion he holds for them. (3) He is called 'Tathāgata' because he has known the characteristics and so forth of the entire group of the true and unerring Four Noble Truths. (4) He is called 'Tathāgata' because he has reached the path that is constant and unerring, just as the previous Buddhas did. (5) He is called 'Tathāgata' because he is endowed with qualities similar to those of the previous Buddhas. (6) He is called 'Tathāgata' because he possesses a body and mind that function according to his will. (7) He is called 'Tathāgata' because he is endowed with the true and unerring qualities of the requisites of enlightenment (bodhi-sambhāra) and does not fall into inferior states. (8) He is called 'Tathāgata' by virtue of having the practice of going in the Ariyan Path.

How is he called 'Tathāgata' because he has come through a true and unerring resolution? When the Blessed One was the hermit Sumedha, at the feet of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara—
"The aspiration for Buddhahood succeeds only when these eight factors meet: human birth, the male sex, the necessary cause (merit), the sight of a Teacher, renunciation, possession of qualities (such as jhāna), great dedication (adhikāra), and a strong desire." (Bu. Vaṃ. 2.59) —
While fulfilling the resolution endowed with these eight factors as stated, he made the Great Aspiration: "Having crossed over, I will help the world with its devas to cross; having been freed, I will free others; having been tamed, I will tame others; having been calmed, I will calm others; having been comforted, I will comfort others; having attained Nibbāna, I will help others attain Nibbāna; having awakened, I will awaken others." For this was said by the Blessed One:

"What is the use of me crossing alone, a man who has seen his own strength? Having reached omniscience, I will help the world with its devas to cross over."
"By this great dedication of mine, performed before the Supreme Man (Dīpaṅkara), having reached omniscience, I will help many people to cross over."
"Having cut the stream of Samsara, having destroyed the three realms of existence, and having embarked on the raft of the Dhamma (the Eightfold Path), I will help the world with its devas to cross over."
"What is the use of me realizing the Dhamma here in this life in the guise of an unknown disciple? Having reached omniscience, I will become a Buddha in the world with its devas."

Without failing in that Great Aspiration, which is the root cause for the investigation, reflection, and undertaking of the entire collection of qualities that make one a Buddha, the Leader of the World, for four incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons, with respect, continuously, and without omission, [fulfilled] the perfection of giving and so forth...
118:
“What is the use of me, who has seen my own strength, crossing over the ocean of Saṃsāra alone as a Great Man? Having reached Omniscience, I shall rescue the world including the devas from Saṃsāra.

By this deed of laying myself down as a bridge for the Great Man, the Buddha Dīpaṅkara, I shall reach Omniscience and rescue many people from Saṃsāra.

Cutting the stream of Saṃsāra, destroying the three realms of existence, and embarking on the raft of the Eightfold Path, I shall rescue the world including the devas from Saṃsāra.

What is the use of me realizing the Dhamma in the form of an unknown disciple in the dispensation of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara? Having reached Omniscience, I shall truly become a Buddha in the world including the devas.” Thus it was said.

Without failing that Great Aspiration (Mahāpaṭiññā), which is the root of investigating, reflecting upon, and undertaking the qualities that make one a Buddha, the Lord, the Chief of the World, fulfilled the thirty perfections such as the Perfection of Giving (Dāna-pāramī) respectfully, continuously, and without remainder for four incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons. He renounced the five great sacrifices such as the sacrifice of limbs, greatly developed the four resolutions such as the resolution of truth (Saccādhiṭṭhāna), and accumulated the requisites of merit (Puṇṇasambhāra) and wisdom (Ñāṇasambhāra). He brought to their peak the previous applications (Pubbayoga), previous conduct (Pubbacariya), the teaching of the Dhamma (Dhammakkhāna), and conduct for the benefit of relatives (Ñātattha-cariya), and having brought the conduct of wisdom (Buddhicariya) to its ultimate climax, he penetrated and realized the unsurpassed Supreme Enlightenment (Sammāsambodhi). Therefore, that Great Aspiration of the Blessed One is true, unfailing, and not otherwise. In that aspiration, there is not even a hair’s breadth of falsehood.

Indeed, that word is true. As the twenty-four Buddhas—namely, the Buddha Dīpaṅkara, Koṇḍañña, Maṅgala, ... up to the Blessed One Kassapa—appeared in succession, they gave the prophecy: “You shall become a Buddha.” Thus, having received the prophecy in the presence of the twenty-four Buddhas, he arrived having obtained the benefits (ānisamsa) that are to be obtained by Bodhisattas who have made their resolution. Because he arrived (āgata) at the state of a Buddha through that aforementioned Great Aspiration (Tathā), he is called ‘Tathāgata’. Thus, because he arrived through the unchanging Great Aspiration, he is called ‘Tathāgata’.

How is he ‘Tathāgata’ because he went (gata) by a true way? The Lord, the Refuge of the World, seeing the multitude of beings who had fallen into great suffering, hardship, and confinement, with a mind full of exertion, made the Great Resolution: “There is no other refuge for these beings; I alone, having first been liberated from the suffering of Saṃsāra, shall liberate them.” Having made this resolution, he strove to fulfill the welfare of all beings in the world according to his vow. Disregarding his own body and life, he practiced well the difficult practices (dukkharacariyā) which cause terror even to others who merely hear of them. In practicing thus, his practice for the Great Bodhi was not of the nature of decline, defilement, or mere stagnation; rather, he practiced in a manner that led only to higher and higher distinction. Gradually fulfilling the requisites of enlightenment (bodhisambhāra) without remainder, he reached the state of an Omniscient Buddha.

Even after that, with a mind urged by that same Great Compassion (Mahākaruṇā), he renounced the delight of seclusion and the supreme, peaceful bliss of liberation (vimokkhasukha). In a world full of foolish people, disregarding the various kinds of honor, contempt, and mistreatment produced by them, he completed the Buddha-duties (Buddhakicca) without remainder by disciplining those who were fit to be disciplined. In performing those Buddha-duties, the manner of the Blessed One’s descent into practice through Great Compassion for beings will be revealed later.

Just as the Blessed One, the Refuge of the World, had Great Compassion for beings when he was a Buddha, so too, from the time of his aspiration as a Bodhisatta, he was consistent in every way at all times. Because that consistency at all times is true and unchanging, he practiced for the benefit of the entire world of beings with a Great Compassion that was equal and unchanging throughout the three periods of time. Therefore, he is called ‘Tathāgata’. For this reason, because he practiced for the benefit of beings with unchanging Great Compassion, he is called ‘Tathāgata’. Because he also realized the four Noble Truths which are true and unchanging, he is called ‘Tathāgata’. How is this so? The things that are true and unchanging are the four knowledges of the Noble Path (Ariya-magga-ñāṇa). These Noble Truths, the Blessed One, in this way...
119:
The Great Compassion (Mahākaruṇā) of the Lord Buddha, the Refuge of the World, towards sentient beings, and likewise, the Great Compassion of the Bodhisatta from the time of the Great Resolve (Mahābhinihāra) onwards, is consistent in every way and at all times. It is true (tatha), unerring (avitatha), and not otherwise (ananyathā). Therefore, because He acted for the benefit of the entire world of beings with that true Great Compassion, which has a uniform flavor towards all beings in those three stages, He is called 'Tathāgata'. Thus, because He has gone (gata) in a true (tatha) manner, He is called 'Tathāgata'.

In what way is He called 'Tathāgata' because He has realized (āgata) the true (tatha) dhammas? The true dhammas are the four Noble Path Knowledges (Ariya-magga-ñāṇa). Indeed, those knowledges encompass all knowable things (ñeyya-dhamma) and the four Noble Truths, which are the causes of both the process of existence (pavattī) and its cessation (nivattī), namely: "This is suffering (dukkha), this is the origin of suffering (dukkha-samudaya), this is the cessation of suffering (dukkha-nirodha), and this is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering (dukkha-nirodha-gāminī paṭipadā)." They realize the nature of suffering in its sense of oppression, being conditioned, burning, and change; the nature of origin in its sense of accumulation, source, bondage, and hindrance; the nature of cessation in its sense of escape, seclusion, being unconditioned, and deathlessness; and the nature of the path in its sense of leading out, cause, seeing, and predominance. By completely cutting off the defilements that obstruct the realization of the true nature of these truths and their divisions, and by the occurrence of an unerring mode of realization known as non-delusion (asammoha-abhisamaya), these truths are true (tatha), unerring (avitatha), and not otherwise (ananyathā) because the individual essence and characteristic (sabhāva-sarasa-lakkhaṇa) of the dhammas do not fail. The Blessed One, without being led by others, has realized and attained those truths by Himself. Therefore, because He has realized (āgata) the true (tatha) dhammas, He is called 'Tathāgata'.

Just as with the Path Knowledges, the Blessed One's unobstructed knowledges (appaṭihata-ñāṇa) regarding the three periods of time, the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā), the four intrepidities (vesārajja), the five knowledges of defining the destinations (gati), the six uncommon knowledges (asādhāraṇa-ñāṇa), the seven knowledges of analyzing the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), the eight knowledges of analyzing the path factors (maggaṅga), the nine knowledges of the successive meditative attainments (anupubba-vihāra-samāpatti), and the ten powers (dasabala) should also be understood as having a true nature.

In this regard, the detailed explanation is as follows: In the infinite world-systems, one should know the names, lineages, and so forth, connected with the aggregates (khandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu) of the past, which are divided into inferior, superior, and so forth, of infinite beings, along with their specific states such as natural functions. Also, in the case of non-sentient (anindriyabaddha) matter, and in the case of material phenomena that are extremely subtle, concealed, or in very distant places, whatever distinction there is in color, shape, smell, taste, touch, and so forth, which arise due to their respective specific conditions—in all those things, just like an emblic myrobalan (āmalaka) placed on the palm of the hand...
120:
...just like an emblic myrobalan on the palm of the hand, the Blessed One's knowledge occurs clearly and without obstruction in the past, and similarly in the future and the present. These are called the unobstructed knowledges regarding the three periods of time. As it was said:

"In the past, the knowledge of the Buddha, the Blessed One, is unobstructed; in the future, the knowledge of the Buddha, the Blessed One, is unobstructed; in the present, the knowledge of the Buddha, the Blessed One, is unobstructed."

Those knowledges are true (tatha), unerring (avitatha), and not otherwise (ananyathā) because they do not fail in the individual essence, function, and characteristic of the dhammas in those respective times. The Blessed One attained those knowledges through His self-evolved knowledge (sayambhū-ñāṇa). In this way also, because He has arrived at (āgata) the true (tatha) knowledges, He is called 'Tathāgata'.

Furthermore, there are the four analytical insights: the analytical insight into meanings (attha-paṭisambhidā), the analytical insight into dhammas (dhamma-paṭisambhidā), the analytical insight into language (nirutti-paṭisambhidā), and the analytical insight into perspicacity (paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā). Among these, the knowledge that reaches the distinction of meanings and is capable of noting, clarifying, and defining the variety of meanings is called 'attha-paṭisambhidā'. The knowledge that reaches the distinction of dhammas and is capable of noting, clarifying, and defining the variety of dhammas is called 'dhamma-paṭisambhidā'. The knowledge that reaches the distinction of linguistic expressions and is capable of noting, clarifying, and defining the variety of linguistic expressions is called 'nirutti-paṭisambhidā'. The knowledge that reaches the distinction of perspicacity and is capable of noting, clarifying, and defining the variety of perspicacity is called 'paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā'.

Indeed, it was said: "Knowledge in meanings is attha-paṭisambhidā; knowledge in dhammas is dhamma-paṭisambhidā; knowledge in the linguistic expression of those meanings and dhammas is nirutti-paṭisambhidā; knowledge in knowledges is paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā."

Among these four, in brief, the result of a cause is called 'attha' because it arises following a cause and because it is to be reached. In detail, however, these five things are called 'attha': conditioned things (paccayuppanna), Nibbāna, the meaning of what is spoken, resultant (vipāka), and functional (kiriya). For one who contemplates that 'attha', the knowledge that reaches the distinctions within that 'attha' is called 'attha-paṭisambhidā'.

'Dhamma', in brief, is the cause. Because that cause arranges, produces, and leads to the respective result (attha), it is called 'dhamma'. In detail, however, these five things are called 'dhamma': any cause that produces a result, the Noble Path (ariya-magga), the spoken teaching, the wholesome (kusala), and the unwholesome (akusala). For one who contemplates that 'dhamma', the knowledge that reaches the distinctions within that 'dhamma' is called 'dhamma-paṭisambhidā'.

It was also said thus:
121:
“The knowledge of the Truth of Suffering is called Atthappaṭisambhidā; the knowledge of the cause of suffering (the Truth of Origin) is called Dhammappaṭisambhidā; the knowledge of the cessation of suffering (the Truth of Cessation) is called Atthappaṭisambhidā; the knowledge of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering (the Truth of the Path) is called Dhammappaṭisambhidā,” so it is taught in the Vibhaṅga Pāḷi. 

Alternatively, the knowledge of the cause is called Dhammappaṭisambhidā, and the knowledge of the result of the cause is called Atthappaṭisambhidā. Whatever (resultant) phenomena have arisen, have become, have been produced, have been generated, have been manifested—the knowledge of these phenomena is called Atthappaṭisambhidā. The knowledge of the causes from which those phenomena have arisen, have become, have been produced, have been generated, have been manifested—the knowledge of those (causal) phenomena is called Dhammappaṭisambhidā. 

Knowledge of aging and death (jarāmaraṇa) is Atthappaṭisambhidā; knowledge of the origin of aging and death is Dhammappaṭisambhidā. Knowledge of the cessation of aging and death is Atthappaṭisambhidā; knowledge of the practice leading to the cessation of aging and death is Dhammappaṭisambhidā. Knowledge of birth (jāti), existence (bhava), clinging (upādāna), craving (taṇhā), feeling (vedanā), contact (phassa), the six sense bases (saḷāyatana), mind-and-matter (nāmarūpa), consciousness (viññāṇa), and volitional formations (saṅkhāra) is Atthappaṭisambhidā; knowledge of the origin of volitional formations is Dhammappaṭisambhidā. Knowledge of the cessation of volitional formations is Atthappaṭisambhidā; knowledge of the practice leading to the cessation of volitional formations is Dhammappaṭisambhidā. 

“Here, monks, in this Dispensation, a monk knows the Dhamma: the Sutta, Geyya ... Vedalla; this knowledge is called Dhammappaṭisambhidā. He knows the meaning of each of those spoken words: ‘This is the meaning of this statement; this is the meaning of that statement’; this knowledge is called Atthappaṭisambhidā.” 

“Which phenomena are wholesome? At a time when a wholesome consciousness of the sense sphere has arisen, accompanied by joy, associated with knowledge, having a form as object ... or a mental phenomenon as object, or whatever object it may be; at that time there is contact ... there is non-distraction (avikkhepa) ... these phenomena are called wholesome. Knowledge of these (wholesome) phenomena is called Dhammappaṭisambhidā; knowledge of the result (vipāka) of those wholesome phenomena is called Atthappaṭisambhidā,” and so on, the details should be understood. 

Furthermore, in regard to the aforementioned meaning and Dhamma, whatever natural expression (sabhāvanirutti), unerring designation, naming, or direct address exists; in that expression of natural language, the knowledge that reaches distinction in the Magadhan language—the original language of all beings—saying “This is the natural expression, this is not the natural expression,” is called Niruttippaṭisambhidā. For one who reviews all those aforementioned knowledges by making them an object, in terms of their range and function in detail, the knowledge that reaches distinction within that knowledge is called Paṭibhānappaṭisambhidā. Thus, these (four analytical knowledges occur).
122:
The Blessed One himself attained the four analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa). Because these knowledges occur in their respective domains such as meaning (attha) and law (dhamma) without deviation and in an unerring manner, they are true (tatha), unfailing, and not otherwise. For this reason also, the Blessed One is called ‘Tathāgata’ because he has arrived at the true dhammas.

Likewise, the Blessed One has known, seen, attained, and fully realized all knowable things (ñeyyadhamma) in every aspect. This is because the Blessed One has fully realized the dhammas to be known with higher knowledge through higher knowledge, the dhammas to be fully understood through full understanding, the dhammas to be abandoned through abandoning, the dhammas to be realized through realization, and the dhammas to be developed through development. Therefore, there is no ascetic, brahmin, deva, Māra, or Brahmā who is capable of investigating and questioning him with reason, saying, “These dhammas have not yet been fully realized by you.”

Whatever dhammas are to be abandoned, the Blessed One has abandoned them all without remainder at the foot of the Bodhi tree, and they are of the nature not to arise again. There is no further task to be done for the sake of abandoning those dhammas. Indeed, for the Blessed One, the one thousand five hundred defilements (kilesa)—including greed (lobha), hatred (dosa), delusion (moha), wrong attention, lack of shame (ahirika), lack of dread (anottappa), sloth (thina), torpor (middha), anger (kodha), enmity (upanāha), contempt (makkha), domineering (palāsa), envy (issā), avarice (macchariya), deceit (māyā), fraud (sāṭheyya), obstinacy (thambha), impetuosity (sārambha), pride (māna), arrogance (atimāna), intoxication (mada), negligence (pamāda), the three unwholesome roots, misconduct, irregular and wrong perception, stains (mala), thought (vitakka), proliferation (papañca), seeking (esanā), craving (taṇhā), the fourfold wrong perversions (vipariyesa), taints (āsava), ties (gantha), floods (ogha), yokes (yoga), wrong courses (agati), clinging (upādāna), the fivefold excessive delight (abhinandana), hindrances (nīvaraṇa), mental barrenness (cetokhila), mental shackles (vinibandha), the six roots of dispute (vivādamūla), the seven underlying tendencies (anusaya), the eightfold wrongness (micchatta), the nine grounds for resentment (āghātavatthu), the ten unwholesome courses of action (akusalakamma-patha) rooted in craving, the twenty-one kinds of improper search (anesana), the sixty-two views, and the one hundred and eight varieties of craving—have been abandoned along with their habitual tendencies (vāsanā), completely cut off, and uprooted. Therefore, there is no ascetic, brahmin, deva, Māra, or Brahmā who is capable of investigating and questioning him with reason, saying, “These named defilements have not yet been abandoned by you.”

The Blessed One has taught the dhammas that constitute obstacles, such as those involving action (kamma), result (vipāka), defilement (kilesa), reproach (upavāda), and transgression of authority (āṇāvītikkama). For one who indulges in those dhammas, they are certainly sufficient to cause an obstacle. Therefore, there is no ascetic, brahmin, deva, Māra, or Brahmā who is capable of investigating and questioning him with reason, saying, “For one who indulges in those dhammas, they are not capable of causing an obstacle.”

The Blessed One, for the sake of complete escape from the suffering of the round of rebirths (vaṭṭa-dukkha), has [taught the path] comprised of virtue, concentration, and wisdom, consisting of seven groups, having thirty-seven factors, and preceded by the Noble Path...
123:
The Blessed One has taught the peerless Dhamma that leads out of the round of suffering. This Dhamma indeed leads one who practices it to liberation from the suffering of the round of rebirths. No ascetic, brahmin, deva, Māra, or Brahmā is able to justly challenge the Blessed One, saying, 'This Dhamma taught by you as leading out of suffering does not lead out of suffering.' Nor can anyone say, 'These things are not fully understood by you who claim to be a Perfectly Enlightened One.' Thus, because of his realization of the unerring nature of his own knowledge, the things to be abandoned, and the things to be taught, the Blessed One's Fourfold Grounds of Self-Confidence (Vesārajja-ñāṇa) are true, unerring, and not otherwise. In this way also, because he has arrived at the truth, the Blessed One is called 'Tathāgata.'

Furthermore, there are five destinations (gati): the realm of hell (niraya-gati), the animal realm (tiracchāna-gati), the realm of hungry ghosts (peta-gati), the human realm (manussa-gati), and the celestial realm (deva-gati). Among these five, the eight great hells beginning with Sañjīva, the sixteen auxiliary hells (ussada-niraya) beginning with Kukkuḷa, and the Lokantarika hell are called 'Niraya' because they are of the nature of absolute suffering and because they are devoid of any gratification. They are also called 'Gati' because they are destinations to be reached according to one's kamma. Therefore, they are called 'Niraya-gati.' The cold hells of intense darkness are also included within these hells.

Beings such as worms, maggots, reptiles, birds, dogs, leopards, and jackals are called 'Tiracchāna' (animals) because of their nature of moving horizontally. Since these animals are themselves a destination, they are called 'Tiracchāna-gati.' Petas (hungry ghosts) such as the Nijjhāmatanhika, who live depending on what others give because of their hunger and thirst, are called 'Peta' because they are far removed from manifest happiness due to their great suffering. Since these petas are themselves a destination, they are called 'Peta-gati.' The Kāḷakañjika Asuras are also included within these petas.

Those who dwell in the four great islands such as Jambudīpa, along with the two thousand small islands, are called 'Manussa' (humans) because of the nobility of their minds compared to those in the four woeful planes. Since these humans are themselves a destination, they are called 'Manussa-gati.' The groups of devas in the twenty-six planes, starting from the Cātumahārājika up to the plane of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (Nevasaññānāsaññāyatana), are called 'Deva' because they sport and shine with their own psychic power and majesty. Since these devas are themselves a destination, they are called 'Deva-gati.'

Since these five destinations are specific types of rebirth-existence (upapatti-bhava) produced by various kammas, they consist essentially of resultant aggregates (vipāka-kkhandha) and kamma-born matter (kammaja-rūpa). Among those destinations, the Blessed One's knowledge functions by way of defining the distinction between cause and effect, such as: 'This particular destination arises because of this particular kamma,' and 'These groups of beings are thus distinguished separately because of the specific conditions of that kamma.' Therefore, the Blessed One said:

'Sāriputta, there are these five destinations. Which five? Hell, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, the human realm, and the celestial realm. Sāriputta, I know hell, and I know the path leading to hell, and I know the practice leading to hell. I also know how one, by practicing that way, with the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in a state of misery, a bad destination, a lower realm, in hell.' The Blessed One's knowledges that know these five destinations are true, unerring, and not otherwise, because they arise without distortion regarding their respective objects and because they are unfailing.
124:
“Sāriputta, there are these five destinations. Which five? Hell, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, the human realm, and the celestial realm. Sāriputta, I know hell, the path leading to hell, and the practice leading to hell. I also know how one, by practicing that way, with the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in a state of misery, a bad destination, a lower realm, in hell.” Thus it was taught in (M. Ni. 1. 153), and so forth.

These knowledges of the Blessed One are true, unerring, and not otherwise, because they function without distortion regarding their respective objects and because they are unfailing. In this way also, because he has arrived at the truth, the Blessed One is called 'Tathāgata.'

Similarly, the Blessed One's knowledge which functions through fifty modes of wisdom, making manifest the distinctions such as those with little dust and those with much dust by penetrating the presence or absence (the deficiency or sufficiency) of faith and so forth in beings, is called 'Knowledge of the higher and lower faculties of beings' (Indriyaparopariyatta-ñāṇa). This is true: 'A person with faith has little dust; a person without faith has much dust,' as taught in detail in (Paṭi. Ma. 1. 111).

Furthermore, the Blessed One's knowledge which functions by way of making manifest the inclinations and so forth of beings as they really are, is called 'Knowledge of inclinations and latent tendencies' (Āsayānusaya-ñāṇa). It functions in such ways as: 'This person has little dust; this person has an eternalist view; this person has an annihilationist view; this person is established in conformable patience (anulomika-khanti); this person is established in knowledge of things as they really are; this person has an inclination for sensual pleasure and not for renunciation; this person has an inclination for renunciation and not for sensual pleasure.' Also: 'In this person, sensual lust is very strong, not aversion; in this person, aversion is very strong, not sensual lust.' Also: 'In this person, meritorious volitional formations (puññābhisaṅkhāra) are predominant, not demeritorious or imperturbable formations; in this person, demeritorious volitional formations (apuññābhisaṅkhāra) are predominant, not meritorious or imperturbable formations; in this person, imperturbable volitional formations (āneñjābhisaṅkhāra) are predominant, not meritorious or demeritorious formations. In this person, good bodily conduct is predominant; in this person, good verbal conduct; in this person, good mental conduct. This person has low aspirations; this person has noble aspirations. This person is possessed of the obstruction of kamma (kammāvaraṇa); this person is possessed of the obstruction of defilement (kilesāvaraṇa); this person is possessed of the obstruction of result (vipākāvaraṇa). This person is not possessed of the obstruction of kamma, nor the obstruction of defilement, nor the obstruction of result.' Referring to that knowledge, it was said:
125:
'In this world, the Tathāgata knows the dispositions (āsaya) of beings, knows their underlying tendencies (anusaya), knows their temperaments (carita), knows their inclinations (adhimutti), and knows those beings who are capable or incapable [of liberation],' and so forth—thus is the Knowledge of Underlying Tendencies and Dispositions (Āsayānusaya-ñāṇa) taught in the Paṭisambhidāmagga.

There is also the Buddha's Knowledge of the Twin Miracle (Yamaka-pāṭihāriya-ñāṇa), which produces various unique psychic transformations not shared with disciples, causing streams of fire and water to proceed from the upper body, lower body, front of the body, back of the body, from the right and left eye-sockets, ear-canals, nostrils, shoulders, arms, palms, and soles of the feet, and from the intervals between fingers and toes, and from the pores of the skin. Regarding this knowledge, it is said: 'In this world, the Tathāgata performs the Twin Miracle, which is not shared with disciples: from the upper body a mass of fire proceeds, and from the lower body a stream of water proceeds. From the lower body a mass of fire proceeds, and from the upper body a stream of water proceeds,' and so forth.

There is also the Knowledge of the Attainment of Great Compassion (Mahākaruṇā-samāpatti-ñāṇa), which is the cause for the Buddha's descent into Great Compassion, occurring through various methods with the desire to deliver the multitude of beings oppressed by many painful states such as passion (rāga) and birth (jāti). As it is said: 'What is the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the attainment of Great Compassion? Great compassion descends upon the Buddhas, the Exalted Ones, as they see beings in many ways. Great compassion descends upon the Buddhas, the Exalted Ones, as they see: "The world of living beings is aflame." Great compassion descends upon the Buddhas, the Exalted Ones, as they see: "The multitude of beings is constantly anxious and striving in many affairs, they are passing away, they have entered upon a wrong path; the world is led away [by old age and death], it is unstable; the world is without protection, without a master; the world has nothing of its own, one must go leaving everything behind; the world is deficient, never satisfied, a slave to craving."' 

'The world of living beings is without protection, without a shelter, without a refuge, having become helpless. The world is devoid of wholesome states, it is not at peace; the world of living beings is with a dart, pierced by the seven darts of defilements, blinded by ignorance...'
126:
The multitude of beings wandering in the world is as if cast into the narrow cage of defilements (kilesa) that obstructs the arising of wholesome states. They exist only within ignorance (avijjā), which, like an eggshell, remains enveloping and covering them from all sides. Unwholesome states are extremely tangled, like a weaver's tangled cloth or like a matted ball of thread that is difficult to clean after being sprayed with sour liquid. Like the tangled pabbaja and muñja grasses, this multitude of beings cannot transcend the cycle of rebirth (saṃsāra), the four woeful planes (apāya), and the miserable destinations (duggati). They are well-smeared with the poison of ignorance. They are submerged in the mire of defilements. They are firmly bound and entwined by the tangles of lust (rāga), hatred (dosa), and delusion (moha), which arise through the reversal of the six sense objects such as forms.

This multitude of beings is enveloped on all sides by the cloak of craving (taṇhā), which arises repeatedly. They are surrounded and caught in the net of craving. They are being swept away by the stream of craving. They are bound by the fetter of craving. The latent tendency of craving (taṇhānusaya) follows them continuously. They suffer because of the burning nature of craving. They are scorched on all sides by the intense heat of craving. 

Similarly, they are enveloped by the cloak of wrong view (diṭṭhi). They are surrounded and caught in the net of wrong view. They are being swept away by the stream of wrong view. They are bound by the fetter of wrong view. The latent tendency of wrong view (diṭṭhānusaya) follows them continuously. They suffer intensely because of the burning of wrong view. They are scorched on all sides by the intense heat of wrong view. 

Birth (jāti) follows them. Aging (jarā) pursues them. Sickness (byādhi) overwhelms them. Death (maraṇa) strikes them down. They remain established in suffering (dukkha). They are completely dominated by craving. They are surrounded on all sides by the wall of aging. They are encircled by the snare of death. They are bound by a great bond. Bound by the bonds of lust, hatred, delusion, conceit (māna), wrong view, defilements, and misconduct, they have reached a great state of confinement. They are obstructed by the great impediments (palibodha) such as lust, which prevent them from striving for wholesome states. They fall into the great abyss of the five destinations or of aging and death. They have reached the great wilderness of birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. They must wander in the great cycle of existence. They revolve repeatedly in the difficult journey of saṃsāra, which is hard to cross. They are submerged in the foul mire of sensuality (kāma), which is like a great swamp.

The multitude of beings wandering in the world is oppressed and ablaze with the fire of lust, the fire of hatred, and the fire of delusion, as well as with birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. They are carried away toward the dangers of aging and so forth. They are oppressed so as to be objects of pity for the virtuous. They are like criminals who, always lacking protection, suffer punishments from kings. They commit cruel acts such as robbery and plunder. Bound by the bonds of faults like lust, they stand facing the place of execution by death. Without a refuge, they have reached a most pitiable state. Because the nature of suffering is so oppressive, they are constantly tormented by calamities throughout the long cycle of saṃsāra. They are filled with longing through the bodily tie of covetousness (abhijjhā-kāyagantha) and so forth. They are always parched and hungry with the thirst of craving.
127:
A being is like one naturally blind, lacking the vision of wisdom; he is equal to one without the eye of wisdom; he remains with the eye of wisdom destroyed; he is bereft of a guide or attendant; he tends to run towards the path of wrong view, which is not the true way; straying and deviating from the straight path of the Noble Path, they cross over to the improper way of the unrighteous; they enter into the four great floods.

He is beset by two types of wrong views; he has practiced wrongly with three types of misconduct; he is bound by the four yogas; he is tied by the four knots (gantha); he is strongly clinging with the four types of grasping (upādāna); he has descended into the five destinations (gati); he lusts after the five cords of sensual pleasure; he is obstructed by the five hindrances (nīvaraṇa); he is contentious with the six roots of dispute; he lusts after the six groups of craving; he is beset by six types of wrong views; he is followed by the seven underlying tendencies (anusaya); he is fettered by the seven fetters (saṃyojana); he is haughty with seven types of conceit (māna); he revolves with the eight worldly conditions (lokadhamma); he is led away by the eight wrongnesses (micchatta); he is corrupted by the eight faults of man; he harbors resentment with the nine grounds for resentment; he is haughty with nine types of conceit; he lusts after the nine things rooted in craving; he is defiled by the ten grounds of defilement (kilesa); he harbors resentment with the ten grounds for resentment; he is possessed of the ten unwholesome paths of action; he is fettered by the ten fetters; he is led away by the ten wrongnesses; he is possessed of wrong view based on ten matters; he is possessed of the view of extremes (antaggāhikadiṭṭhi) based on ten matters; he is entangled by the one hundred and eight proliferations of craving; he is beset by the sixty-two types of wrong views. Seeing thus, 'Such is the world of beings (loka-sannivāsa),' Great Compassion (Mahākaruṇā) descends upon the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, towards beings.

'I have crossed over, but the world has not crossed over. I am liberated, but the world is not liberated. I am tamed, but the world is not tamed. I am at peace, but the world is not at peace. I am comforted, but the world is not comforted. I am extinguished (attained Nibbāna), but the world is not extinguished. Having crossed over, I am able to help others cross over; being liberated, I am able to liberate others; being tamed, I am able to tame others; being at peace, I am able to bring peace to others; being comforted, I am able to comfort others; being extinguished, I am able to bring others to extinction.' Seeing thus, Great Compassion descends upon the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, towards beings.
128:
Thus, the analysis has been made through eighty-nine modes. Whatever the extent of the totality of things to be known (dhammadhātu), in all those things, conditioned (saṅkhata) and unconditioned (asaṅkhata), etc., the knowledge of the Blessed One is independent of another's instruction, capable of penetrating in every way, occurring immediately upon wish, and not shared by others. Because that knowledge penetrates and knows without remainder the conditioned, the unconditioned, and conventional truths (sammuti-sacca) in every way, it is called Omniscience (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa). Because there is no obstruction (āvaraṇa) in that Omniscience, it is also called Unobstructed Knowledge (Anāvaraṇa-ñāṇa) based on its occurrence without attachment. In reality, although that knowledge is one, it is presented in two ways to show its unshared nature through the manner of its occurrence regarding objects. Otherwise, Omniscience and Unobstructed Knowledge would become identical in their scope of all objects, which is not appropriate. Even if it were not appropriate, this is the logic, and here is the Pali text:

'He knows all conditioned and unconditioned things without remainder, thus it is Omniscience; there is no obstruction therein, thus it is Unobstructed Knowledge. He knows all the past, thus it is Omniscience; there is no obstruction therein, thus it is Unobstructed Knowledge. He knows all the future, thus it is Omniscience; there is no obstruction therein, thus it is Unobstructed Knowledge. He knows all the present, thus it is Omniscience; there is no obstruction therein, thus it is Unobstructed Knowledge.' Thus the detail should be understood.

Thus, these six unique knowledges (asādhāraṇa-ñāṇa) of the Blessed One are true, unerring, and not otherwise, because they occur in an undistorted manner and are non-discrepant regarding their respective objects. For this reason also, the Blessed One is called 'Tathāgata' because he has arrived at (āgata) the true (tatha) unique knowledges.

Likewise:

'Monks, these are the seven factors of enlightenment: the enlightenment factor of mindfulness, the enlightenment factor of investigation of states, the enlightenment factor of energy, the enlightenment factor of rapture, the enlightenment factor of tranquility, the enlightenment factor of concentration, and the enlightenment factor of equanimity.' Thus by way of enumeration, and also: 'There is the harmony of states such as mindfulness, etc., which arises at the moment of the supramundane path, and which is the opposite of many afflictions such as sluggishness, restlessness, standing still, striving, devotion to sensual pleasure, devotion to self-mortification, the view of annihilation, and the view of eternalism. By this harmony of states, the noble disciple (ariya-sāvaka) awakens from the sleep of defilements, or rises up. Or, he penetrates the Four Noble Truths, or realizes Nibbāna itself. Therefore, that harmony of states is called Bodhi (Enlightenment). Because they are factors of that Bodhi, they are called Bojjhaṅga (Factors of Enlightenment). Or, the noble disciple, by the aforementioned harmony of states...'
129:
It is called 'Bodhi' (Enlightenment) because it knows the [Four Noble] Truths. It is called 'Bojjhaṅga' (Factors of Enlightenment) because these are the constituent parts of that Bodhi; thus it is described by way of its general characteristic. By way of its specific characteristics, it should be understood as follows: the mindfulness factor of enlightenment (sati-sambojjhaṅga) has the characteristic of establishing; the investigation-of-states factor of enlightenment (dhammavicaya-sambojjhaṅga) has the characteristic of investigation; the energy factor of enlightenment (vīriya-sambojjhaṅga) has the characteristic of upholding; the rapture factor of enlightenment (pīti-sambojjhaṅga) has the characteristic of pervading; the tranquility factor of enlightenment (passaddhi-sambojjhaṅga) has the characteristic of calming; the concentration factor of enlightenment (samādhi-sambojjhaṅga) has the characteristic of non-distraction; and the equanimity factor of enlightenment (upekkhā-sambojjhaṅga) has the characteristic of reflection.

'Among those seven factors of enlightenment, what is the mindfulness factor of enlightenment? Here, a monk is mindful, possessed of the highest mindfulness and skill; he is one who remembers and recalls what was done and said long ago.' By this statement from the Vibhaṅga Pali, it is shown that the seven factors of enlightenment arise simultaneously through mutual assistance. Furthermore, by the statement, 'Among those seven factors of enlightenment, what is the mindfulness factor of enlightenment? Here, monks, there is mindfulness regarding internal states, and there is mindfulness regarding external states,' their occurrence is shown through the classification of their objects. By the statement, 'Among those seven factors of enlightenment, what is the mindfulness factor of enlightenment? Here, monks, a monk develops the mindfulness factor of enlightenment that is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and ripening in relinquishment,' the method of cultivation (bhāvanā) is shown. By the statement, 'What are the seven factors of enlightenment? Here, a monk, at the time he develops supramundane jhāna... at that time there are the seven factors of enlightenment: the mindfulness factor of enlightenment... the equanimity factor of enlightenment. Therein, what is the mindfulness factor of enlightenment? That which is mindfulness... recollection...' their classification is shown through ninety-six thousand methods. Thus, the Blessed One's knowledges that clarify the factors of enlightenment, which occur in various modes, are 'tatha' (true), 'avitatha' (not false), and 'ananyatha' (not otherwise) because they do not deviate from their respective meanings. In this way also, the Blessed One is the 'Tathāgata' because He has arrived at (āgata) these truths (tatha).

Likewise, 'Among those eight path factors, what is the Noble Truth of the Way Leading to the Cessation of Suffering? It is this Noble Eightfold Path. Namely, Right View... Right Concentration.' Thus, He showed them by way of their individual forms. It is 'Ariya' (Noble) because it is far from all defilements, because it makes one a Noble One, and because it brings about the attainment of the Noble Fruit. It is 'Aṭṭhaṅgika' (Eightfold) because it has eight factors and because it is the absolute cause for the attainment of Nibbāna. It is 'Magga' (Path) because it goes along killing the defilements, because it is sought by those desiring Nibbāna, or because it itself seeks Nibbāna. This is the general characteristic. Right View (sammā-diṭṭhi) has the characteristic of seeing rightly; Right Intention (sammā-saṅkappa) has the characteristic of directing rightly; Right Speech (sammā-vācā) has the characteristic of embracing rightly; Right...
130:
Right Action (sammā-kammanta) has the characteristic of originating rightly; Right Livelihood (sammā-ājīva) has the characteristic of purifying rightly; Right Effort (sammā-vāyāma) has the characteristic of upholding rightly; Right Mindfulness (sammā-sati) has the characteristic of establishing rightly; Right Concentration (sammā-samādhi) has the characteristic of non-distraction rightly. Thus, by way of specific characteristics, [the Blessed One's knowledges are true].

Right View abandons wrong view along with other defilements that are its opposites; it takes Nibbāna as its object; and by destroying the delusion that covers that Nibbāna, it sees the associated states without confusion. Likewise, Right Intention and the others abandon wrong intention and so forth, take Nibbāna as their object, and perform the functions of rightly directing, embracing, originating, purifying, upholding, establishing, and concentrating the conascent states (sahajāta-dhamma). Thus, by way of the classification of functions (kicca), [the Blessed One's knowledges are true].

In the preliminary stage (pubba-bhāga), Right View occurs at different moments and has various objects such as suffering; however, at the time of the Path (magga-kāla), it occurs in a single moment, taking only Nibbāna as its object, and receives four names according to its function, such as 'Knowledge of Suffering' (dukkhe ñāṇa). Right Intention and the others also occur at different moments and have various objects in the preliminary stage, but at the time of the Path, they occur in a single moment and have the same object.

Among those path factors, Right Intention receives three names according to its function, such as 'Thought of Renunciation' (nekkhamma-saṅkappa). The three factors beginning with Right Speech are, in the preliminary stage, both abstinences (virati) and volitions (cetanā) through classifications such as 'Abstinence from False Speech' (musāvādā veramaṇī). At the moment of the Path, however, they are only abstinences. Right Effort and Right Mindfulness receive four names according to their functions as Right Strivings (sammappadhāna) and Foundations of Mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna). Right Concentration, even at the moment of the Path, is diverse according to the First Jhāna and so forth. Thus, by way of the classification of occurrence in the preliminary and subsequent stages (pubba-bhāga, para-bhāga), [the Blessed One's knowledges are true].

By the method of cultivation such as, 'Here, monks, a monk develops Right View based on seclusion...'; and by the classification through eighty-four thousand methods such as, 'Among those factors of enlightenment, what is the Eightfold Path? Here, a monk, at the time he develops supramundane jhāna... with the painful practice and slow intuition, at that time there is the Eightfold Path consisting of Right View, Right Intention...'; thus, the Blessed One's knowledges that clarify the Noble Path, which occur in many modes, are all 'tatha' (true), 'avitatha' (not false), and 'ananyatha' (not otherwise) because they do not deviate from the meaning.
