In this way also, the Blessed One is the 'Tathāgata' because He has arrived at those true knowledges.

Likewise, there is the attainment of the First Jhāna and the attainment of Cessation (nirodha-samāpatti). In these successive dwellings and attainments (anupubba-vihāra-samāpatti), the Blessed One's knowledges—which occur by way of accomplishment and reflection, and by way of appropriate association for the purpose of dwelling in them and attaining them—are true, not false, and not otherwise for the realization of those meanings.
131:
Similarly, the knowledge of what is a cause and what is not a cause, accurately knowing "this is the cause of this result, this is not the cause"; the knowledge of the specific results of the various types of kamma undertaken by various beings—past, etc.—exactly as they are and without remainder; the knowledge of the distinction between kamma with taints and kamma without taints, knowing even at the moment of exertion, "this practice leads to hell... this practice leads to Nibbāna"; the knowledge of the diversity of elements according to the many natures, such as the internal and external aggregates and sense-bases of that world, in the manner of "because this specific element is predominant, this distinction arises in this continuity of phenomena," exactly as it is; the knowledge of the low and superior inclinations and dispositions of beings without remainder; the knowledge of the keenness or dullness of the faculties such as faith; the knowledge of the distinctions of jhāna, liberation, etc., along with their defilements; the knowledge of the continuity of aggregates previously lived in countless births of beings, along with their connections, without remainder; the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings along with their low and superior divisions; and the knowledge of the Four Truths in the manner previously stated, such as "this is suffering"—these Ten Powers of Knowledge (Dasabala-ñāṇa) of the Blessed One are called "True" (tathā) because they penetrate their respective objects without error, because they accomplish the desired purpose, and because they occur exactly as things are; they are unerring and not otherwise. For it is said:
"Here, the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the possible as possible and the impossible as impossible," and so forth.

In this way also, the Blessed One is called Tathāgata because he has come (āgata) to the true things (tathā).

Just as by the power of these knowledges, so too by the power of the specific wisdoms—infinite and immeasurable, and not shared with others—such as the knowledge that analyzes the foundations of mindfulness and right efforts, the Blessed One has come to (āgata), or attained (adhigata), the true knowledges. Thus also, he is Tathāgata because he has come to the true things.

How is he Tathāgata because he has gone (gata) in a true way (tathā)? The Blessed One's birth, his supreme enlightenment, his proclamation of the Dhamma and Vinaya, and the Nibbāna element without remainder—these are called "True" (tathā). What does this mean? Because the purpose for which the Lord of the World aspired to and practiced for enlightenment is certainly accomplished, because it is unerring, and because it has a non-perverted meaning, it is true (tathā), unerring, and not otherwise. Indeed, this Blessed One, while being a Bodhisatta, fulfilled all the causes for Buddhahood, such as the thirty perfections in their various forms, and while residing in the Tusita heaven, heard the "Buddha-uproar" (Buddha-kolāhala). Deities from ten thousand world-systems gathered and approached him, pleading: "O Great Hero, the time has come for you to become a Buddha; please take conception in a mother's womb. Save the world of devas and humans and let them realize the deathless Nibbāna." Having been thus requested, and seeing the omens that had appeared, he made the Five Great Observations (Mahāvilokana) and resolved, "Now I shall be born in the human world and become a Buddha." On the full-moon day of Āsāḷha, he took conception in the womb of Queen Mahāmāyādevī of the Sakyan royal line. Having been attended to by the service of devas and humans for ten months, he reached birth at the time of dawn on the full-moon day of Visākha. At the moment of his birth, just as at the moment of his conception, thirty-two omens appeared.
132:
Having fulfilled all the causes for Buddhahood, while residing in the Tusita heaven, he heard the "Buddha-uproar"—the announcement that a Buddha would soon appear in the world. Deities and Brahmas from ten thousand world-systems gathered together, approached him, and pleaded:
"O Great Hero, Deva-son of the Bodhisatta, the time has come for you to become a Buddha. Please descend and take conception in a mother's womb. Save the world of devas and humans from the whirlpool of Saṃsāra and realize the deathless Nibbāna."
Having been thus requested, and seeing the omens that had arisen, he made the Five Great Observations (Mahāvilokana) and resolved, "Now I shall be born among the human race in the human world and become a Buddha." On the full-moon day of Āsāḷha, he took conception in the womb of Queen Mahāmāyādevī, the chief consort of King Suddhodana of the Sakyan royal line. Having received the great service of devas and humans for ten months, he reached birth at the time of dawn on the full-moon day of Visākha.

At the moment of his birth, just as at the moment of his conception, thirty-two omens appeared. This ten-thousandfold world-system shook, shook violently, and trembled greatly. Immeasurable light and radiance spread throughout the ten thousand world-systems. As if wishing to see the glory of the Bodhisatta, those born blind regained their sight. The deaf heard sounds. The mute were able to speak well. The hunchbacked became straight-bodied. The lame regained the ability to walk on foot. All beings in bondage were released from shackles, prisons, and other ties. In all the hells, the fires were extinguished. In the realm of hungry ghosts (peta), hunger and thirst were appeased. There was no more fear for animals. The diseases and ailments of all beings were cured. All beings spoke endearing words to one another. Horses neighed with a pleasant manner. Elephants trumpeted like the sound of cranes. All musical instruments emitted their own echoes spontaneously. Human ornaments such as bracelets and rings made sweet sounds without being struck or played. All directions became clear and bright. Gentle, cool breezes that bring happiness to beings blew. A great unseasonal rain fell. Water also burst forth from the earth and flowed. Birds gave up flying in the sky and rested. Rivers stopped flowing and stood still. The water in the great ocean became sweet. While the pure sun was shining, all the stars in the sky shone brightly. Except for the formless (arūpa) Brahmas, all other devas, Brahmas, and even the denizens of hell became visible to one another. Obstructions such as trees, walls, doors, and rocky mountains disappeared and became unobstructed. The passing away and rebirth of beings ceased for a moment. Overpowering all foul odors, divine fragrances wafted through the air. All fruit-bearing trees became laden with fruit.
133:
The Great Ocean had its surface covered in all directions with five-colored lotuses. All flowers, both land-grown and water-grown, bloomed. Lotuses bloomed on the trunks of trees, on the branches, and on the creepers. On the surface of the earth, breaking through the rocky ground, lotuses called daṇḍapaduma (stalk-lotuses) emerged, appearing in seven layers one above the other. In the sky, olambakapaduma (hanging lotuses) appeared like dangling ornaments. A rain of flowers fell all around. Divine musical instruments played in the sky. The entire ten-thousandfold world-system became like a released garland of flowers, like a compressed bouquet, and like a decorated seat of flowers; it was adorned with a single garland of flowers, with shimmering fly-whisks, and was perfumed with the scent of flowers and incense, reaching the pinnacle of supreme beauty. These premonitory signs were indeed signs of the attainment of many distinctions, such as the Fruition of Arahantship, to be achieved later. This conception, adorned with the manifestation of many such wonders, was for the purpose of attaining the Supreme Enlightenment (Abhisambodhi) which he had aspired for; because of the certain accomplishment of that Enlightenment, it was thus 'tathā' (true), 'avitathā' (not false), and 'anaññathā' (not otherwise).

Likewise, all those kinsmen who were buddha-veneyya (to be guided by the Buddha) and bodhaneyya (capable of enlightenment), the Blessed One himself guided without exception. Those who were sāvaka-veneyya (to be guided by disciples) and dhamma-veneyya (to be guided by the Dhamma) were guided and will be guided by the disciples and others. Because of the certain accomplishment of that purpose for which the Blessed One aspired to Supreme Enlightenment, the attainment of Omniscience is true, not false, and not otherwise.

Furthermore, whatever nature of a knowable thing (ñeyyadhamma) is to be realized, the Blessed One perfectly enlightened himself to that thing through his own knowledge, which is bound merely by reflection (āvajjanamaṭṭa), like an āmalaka (myrobalan) fruit placed in the palm of the hand, without any distortion and without exception. For this reason also, the attainment of Omniscience is true, not false, and not otherwise.

Likewise, having well observed the various ways in which those various teachings should be taught, and the inclinations, underlying tendencies, characters, and dispositions of those various beings, the Blessed One guided the veneyya beings and caused them to reach the Noble Plane (ariyabhūmi). He did this without abandoning the natural order (dhammatā), without overstepping the path of conventional designations and expressions (paññatti-naya-vohāra), but by clarifying the natural order and instructing them according to their faults, according to their inclinations, and according to the Dhamma. This proclamation of the Dhamma and Vinaya by the Blessed One is also true, not false, and not otherwise, because of the accomplishment of that purpose and because it is stated as it truly is.
134:
Likewise, the Deathless Great Element of Nibbāna (amata-mahānibbāna-dhātu), which the Blessed One attained, is free from the nature of form and formless things such as contact (phassa) and feeling (vedanā) beginning with the earth element. It transcends the nature of the world because it is free from the state of disintegration and non-existence. It cannot be illuminated by any light because it is unmixed with the darkness (of defilements). It is free from states such as destiny (gati), having no foundation and no object, because it is devoid of the nature of the world. It is called 'anupādisesa' (without remainder) because there is not even a trace of the fuel of grasping called the aggregates. Referring to that Nibbāna, the Blessed One said:

'There is, O monks, that sphere where there is neither earth, nor water, nor fire, nor air; nor the sphere of infinite space, nor the sphere of infinite consciousness, nor the sphere of nothingness, nor the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; neither this world, nor the next world, nor both sun and moon. There, O monks, I say there is no coming, no going, no staying, no passing away, and no arising. It is without foundation, without occurrence, and without object. This itself is the end of suffering.'

That Nibbāna is the ceasing of all aggregates of grasping, the stilling of all formations (saṅkhāra), the relinquishing of all attachments (upadhi), the calming of all suffering, the uprooting of all clingings (ālaya), the cutting off of all rounds of rebirth (vaṭṭa). Because its nature, which is characterized by absolute peace, never fails, it is 'tathā' (true), 'avitathā' (not false), and 'anaññathā' (not otherwise). Thus, because he has gone to (gata), approached (upagata), attained (adhigata), practiced (paṭipanna), and reached (patta) these states such as the high birth (abhijāti) in such a way (tathā), he is called the 'Tathāgata'. In this way, the Blessed One is the 'Tathāgata' because he has reached the truth.

In what way is he 'Tathāgata' because he is of such a nature? Just as the former Fully Enlightened Buddhas were of such a nature, so too is this Blessed One of such a nature. What does this mean? Those Blessed Ones were endowed with Path-virtue, Fruition-virtue, and all mundane and supramundane virtue; with Path-concentration, Fruition-concentration, and all mundane and supramundane concentration; with Path-wisdom, Fruition-wisdom, and all mundane and supramundane wisdom; with the two thousand four hundred billion (2,400,000,000,000) meditative attainments (samāpatti-vihāra) to be resorted to daily; and in brief, with liberation by substitution of opposites (tadaṅga-vimutti), liberation by suppression (vikkhambhana-vimutti), liberation by eradication (samuccheda-vimutti), liberation by tranquillization (paṭippassaddhi-vimutti), and liberation by escape (nissaraṇa-vimutti). In detail, they were endowed with all the qualities of Omniscience, which have infinite and immeasurable divisions and inconceivable majesty.
135: Our Blessed One is also of such a nature. Although there may be differences among all the Fully Enlightened Buddhas in these five aspects: difference in lifespan, difference in physical stature, difference in clan, difference in the practice of austerities, and difference in radiance, there is no difference whatsoever in the purities such as the purity of virtue (sīlavisuddhi), in the practice of tranquility and insight (samatha-vipassanā), or in the qualities attained by themselves. Indeed, like gold split in the middle, those Blessed Buddhas are indistinguishable from one another. Therefore, just as the previous Fully Enlightened Buddhas were of such a nature, this Blessed One is also of such a nature. Being of such a nature (tathā-vidha), He is called 'Tathāgata'. Here, the word 'gata' has the sense of 'vidha' (manner/nature). For this reason, worldly scholars say that the word 'gata' used in conjunction with 'vidha' carries the meaning of 'pakāra' (manner). How is He called 'Tathāgata' because He has proceeded (pavattita) in such a way? Because He is endowed with psychic powers and majesty not shared by others, because He has reached the excellence of perfections such as the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā), and because He has obtained unobstructed knowledge (anāvaraṇañāṇa), there is no obstruction anywhere in the Blessed One's bodily conduct and so forth. Thus, He has such movement, occurrence, and the proceeding of body, speech, and mind according to His will. Therefore, He is called 'Tathāgata'. In this way, because He has proceeded in such a way, He is 'Tathāgata'. How is He called 'Tathāgata' because He has come (āgata) through unerring knowledges? In fulfilling the requisites of enlightenment (bodhisambhāra), there is no conduct contrary to those requisites; thus He is 'agata' (not gone [to the wrong path]). This state of not going [astray] occurs through knowledges that contemplate the faults [of defilements] and the benefits [of perfections] unerringly in the perfection of giving and so on. Thus, because He has come through such unerring knowledges, He is 'Tathāgata'. Alternatively, He does not have the going (gata) into the five destinations (gati) which is called the occurrence of defilements and volitional formations, or the occurrence of the aggregates; thus He is 'agata' (not gone). This state of not going [into rebirth] occurs through the unerring knowledge of the Noble Path (ariya-magga-ñāṇa) by which He attains Nibbāna with residues and Nibbāna without residues. Thus, the Blessed One is 'Tathāgata' because He has come through unerring knowledges. How is He 'Tathāgata' by having arrived at the truth (tathā-gata-bhāva)? 'Tathā-gata-bhāvena' means because of the existence of the Tathāgata according to His true nature. What is this 'Tathāgata' by whose existence the Blessed One is called 'Tathāgata'? It is the True Dhamma (Saddhamma). The True Dhamma, namely the Noble Path, first uproots the entire side of defilements by the power of tranquility and insight joined in tandem (yuganaddha-samatha-vipassanā), and by the power of abandonment by eradication (samuccheda-pahāna)...
136: ...must be reached; thus it is 'Tathā-gata' (arrived at the truth). The Dhamma of Fruition (phala-dhamma) is 'Tathā-gata' (proceeded thus) because it is reached through the power of abandonment by tranquilization (paṭippassaddhi-pahāna) in accordance with its respective Path. As for the Dhamma of Nibbāna, it is 'Tathā-gata' because it is penetrated by wisdom for the sake of stilling all the suffering of the round of rebirth, and because it is realized by the Buddhas and others in that way. The Dhamma of Scriptural Study (pariyatti-dhamma) is also 'Tathā-gata' because it was set forth by previous Buddhas in the form of Sutta, Geyya, etc., and by demonstrating the origin and so forth, in accordance with the inclinations (āsaya) of those to be led (veneyya); and our Blessed One has likewise spoken and set it forth. Or, He is 'Tathāgata' because it is understood (avagata) by the Blessed One's disciples just as it was taught by the Blessed One. Thus, the entire True Dhamma is 'Tathāgata'. Therefore, Sakka, the Lord of Devas, said: 'We revere the Dhamma, the Tathāgata (the Truth), honored by gods and men; may there be safety!' Because He possesses that Dhamma, the Blessed One is 'Tathāgata'. Just as with the Dhamma, so too with the Noble Saṅgha: because they have reached their respective Fruitions through their respective Paths, having placed at the forefront the extremely pure preliminary practice of tranquility and insight while practicing for their own benefit and the benefit of others, they are 'Tathā-gata'. Or, because the Blessed One has known the Four Truths, Dependent Origination, and so forth as they were taught, and because He speaks (gadana) accordingly due to His Buddhahood, He is 'Tathāgata'. Therefore, Sakka, the King of Devas, said: 'We revere the Saṅgha, the Tathāgata (the Truth), honored by gods and men; may there be safety!' Because He has such a Saṅgha of disciples, the Blessed One is 'Tathāgata'. Thus, He is 'Tathāgata' by being of the nature of a Tathāgata. This explanation is merely an introduction to illustrating the 'Tathāgata-hood' of the Tathāgata. In all its aspects, only a Tathāgata could describe the 'Tathāgata-hood' of a Tathāgata. For this word 'Tathāgata' is of great meaning, of great destination, and of great scope. Like the word 'appamāda' (heedfulness), a Dhamma teacher who logically brings forth the meaning of the Buddha's word from the Three Piṭakas should not be said to be 'one who has plunged into what is not a landing place'. In this regard, it is said: 'Just as the previous Great Sages, the Munis in this world, attained the state of Omniscience and came [to this world], so too has this Sakyan Sage come; therefore, the One with Vision is called the Tathāgata.'
137:
Only the Blessed One can truly explain the nature of the Tathāgata. This statement is true. The term 'Tathāgata' possesses many meanings, a noble destination, and a vast scope. Because it has a vast scope like the term 'appamāda' (heedfulness), it cannot be said that a Dhamma preacher who applies the meaning inappropriately to the Buddha's words—the Three Piṭakas—is one who strays into what is not the case. Therefore, regarding this term 'Tathāgata', it is said:

Just as the former Victors (Buddhas) who appeared in the past came after completely abandoning defilements such as sensual desire through the knowledge of concentration, so too did our Sakyamuni Buddha, the possessor of radiant splendor, come in that same manner. Because he came in such a way, he is known as the 'Tathāgata'.

This Victor, the pinnacle of the Sakyan princes, is called the 'Tathāgata' because he realized, through his self-enlightened knowledge (sayambhū-ñāṇa), the true and unerring characteristics of elements (dhātu), bases (āyatana), and so forth, in terms of their specific and general characteristics.

Because he clearly realized, through his universal vision (samantacakkhu), the four true and unerring Noble Truths, as well as the principle of this-conditionality (idappaccayatā) and dependent origination in all its aspects, without needing the guidance of others, the Victor is called the 'Tathāgata'.

In the numerous world systems, the Victor's vision of the diverse and varied sense objects such as forms and so forth is truly accurate. Because he sees thus accurately, the All-Seeing Buddha is called the 'Tathāgata'.

Because he speaks the Dhamma exactly as it is, acts in accordance with his own words, and exists having overcome the world with his virtues, for these reasons, the Buddha, the Leader of the World, is called the 'Tathāgata'.

He fully understood the world in all its aspects through the three unerring full understandings (pariññā), transcended ignorance (avijjā) which is the cause of the world, reached Nibbāna through direct realization, and attained the Noble Path; therefore, he is called the 'Tathāgata'.

For the welfare of the world, he came in all aspects according to his unerring vow. The Victor, the Refuge of the world, always conducts the welfare of the world with unerring compassion. For these reasons also, he is called the 'Tathāgata'.

Because the Victorious Buddha knows the object exactly as it is through his unerring knowledge, he is called the 'Tathāgata'. Just like those previous Buddhas, because he accomplishes the benefit and has arrived through unerring direct knowledge (abhijānāti) and so forth, he is called the 'Tathāgata'. In the same manner as the Buddhas who appeared in the past, through virtue, concentration, and so forth...
138:
Because he arrived at this state of Buddhahood through unerring knowledges, because he understands the object according to its true nature, because he arrived through noble birth (abhijāti) and so forth, and because he accomplishes that purpose, he is called the 'Tathāgata'.

Just as those former Great Sages (Buddhas) were of such a nature, so too is this Gotama Buddha of such a nature. Because his speech and mind function according to his will, that Supreme Person is called the 'Tathāgata'.

For that Refuge who has seen the end of existence, there was no occurrence of anything contrary to the requisites of enlightenment (sambodhi-sambhāra) in the past, nor is there any occurrence in Saṃsāra due to the Noble Path knowledges. Therefore, the Buddha who is free from such occurrences is called the 'Tathāgata' (Agata).

Just as the defilements to be abandoned by the Buddha are abandoned, through that abandoning, the Noble Dhamma arises. Just as the defilements are abandoned by the Buddha through a certain path, through that path, the Noble Group (Sangha) also exists. Because he is endowed with that Noble Dhamma and Noble Group, he is called the 'Tathāgata'.

'Mahiddhikata' means being endowed with great psychic power, which is defined as the ability to produce extraordinary transformations of phenomena through supreme mastery over the mind and engagement with the modes of psychic power (iddhividha). 'Mahānubhāvata' (Great Majesty) means being endowed with the power of merit, which has existed for a long time, has distant opposites, is the cause for the accomplishment of desired goals, and possesses great brilliance. The word 'yatra' is an indeclinable (nipāta) used in the sense of the nominative case, expressing wonder, praise, excitement, joy, and faith. Because it is associated with that indeclinable, the future tense verb 'vijāyissati' (will give birth) expresses only the past tense meaning. The meaning here is: this Suppavāsā, who was thus immersed in suffering and had fallen into distress, at the very moment the Blessed One spoke, became happy and free from illness, and gave birth to a healthy son. 'Attamano' means having one's own mind, meaning a mind free from defilements due to faith in the Blessed One. A mind overwhelmed by defilements cannot be called 'attamano' because it does not follow one's own will. Alternatively, it means a mind possessed by joy and happiness. 'Pamudito' means being associated with joy and happiness, or it means the occurrence of intense delight.

When two or three days had passed after the birth, 'sattabhattāni' refers to the alms-food offered for seven days. 'Svetanaya' means the merit that will arise through the offering and attending to the Sangha headed by the Buddha on the very next day for the sake of merit. At that time, the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna. Why did he address him? He did so to increase the faith of the prince, who was Suppavāsā's husband. Suppavāsā herself already possessed unwavering faith. It was the responsibility of the Elder Mahāmoggallāna to look after the faith of the lay devotee (dāyaka). Therefore, the Buddha spoke to have the prince perform the service. In that Pali text 'svetanaya', the word 'sve' should be analyzed as 'tuyhaṃ' (your), and it should be understood as 'tomorrow is your service'.
139:
Filled with joy. "Pītisomanassajāta" means the arising of intense joy and happiness. "Atha" means afterwards, when two or three days had passed after giving birth. "Sattabhattāni" means the alms-food to be offered for seven days. "Svātanāya" is for the merit to be performed tomorrow. It refers to the merit that will arise from offering alms and attending to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha tomorrow.

Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna. Why did he address him? To protect (or increase) the devotion of Suppavāsā's husband. Suppavāsā herself already possessed unshakable devotion, but protecting the devotion of the lay follower was the responsibility of the Elder Mahāmoggallāna. Therefore, he said, "This person is your attendant." In that phrase, "tuyheso" should be analyzed as "tuyhaṃ eso" (this person of yours). "Tiṇṇam dhammānam pāṭibhogo" indicates: "If the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna can guarantee that my three things, such as wealth and so on, will not be destroyed, I will be able to give the alms after seven days." The Elder, seeing that there was no danger to the lay follower's wealth and life during those days, said, "Friend, I guarantee two of those things: wealth and life." As for faith, since it is connected to the mind, he left it as the lay follower's own responsibility, saying, "But for faith, you yourself must be the guarantor." In truth, that lay follower was one who had seen the Four Noble Truths (a Stream-enterer), and since there was no reason for his faith to change, it was spoken thus. For that very reason, the Blessed One said, "Make him understand that you will do it later too."

The lay follower, out of respect and obedience toward the Teacher and the Elder, and wishing for the increase of Suppavāsā's merit, consented, saying, "Let Suppavāsā, the Koliyan princess, give alms for the first seven days; I will do it afterwards." After eleven days had passed from the day the child was born, they fed the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha for seven days, and on the seventh day, they had the seven-year-old child pay homage to the Buddha and the Saṅgha. "Satta me vassāni" means for seven years; the accusative case is used here in the sense of continuous duration (accantasaṃyoga). "Lohitakumbhiyaṃ vutthāni" means dwelling in a jar of blood, which is the mother's womb; it is said in reference to the suffering of his own stay in the womb. "Aññānipi evarūpāni satta puttāni" means "I would like seven more sons like this"; the gender is changed in this expression. Thus, although she reached great suffering through carrying the pregnancy for seven years and the difficult labor for seven days, it shows how she could not be satisfied due to craving and attachment for the son.

Knowing the nature of craving—that even after experiencing great suffering for seven years and seven days, one still desires a son—and wishing to show the disadvantage of craving, the Blessed One uttered this inspired utterance (udāna). The meaning of that inspired utterance is: "Asātaṃ" means that which is unpleasant, bad, or undesirable suffering, yet it appears in the form of the pleasant, the form of the beloved, or the form of happiness. In reality, it is merely a collection of formations (saṅkhāra) that is unpleasant suffering, but for those who have not yet abandoned perversions (vippallāsa)...
140:
...it means sons who are born after causing great suffering. By this, it is shown that women, due to their attachment to sons, are never satisfied by obtaining a son.

"Knowing this meaning" means knowing the meaning of what Suppavāsā said, having forgotten in an instant the great suffering that occurred due to carrying the pregnancy for seven years and seven days, through the power of attachment to the son. "This inspired utterance" means he uttered this inspired utterance which shows the great harmfulness of the affection of craving, deceiving negligent persons with desirable appearances as if they had reached mental happiness.

In that inspired utterance, "asātaṃ" means unpleasant, not good, undesirable. "Sātarūpena" means in a pleasant nature. "Piyarūpena" means in a lovable nature. "Sukhassa rūpena" means in the nature of happiness. This is what is meant: because the entire collection of formations (saṅkhāra) within the round of rebirths, being unpleasant, unloved, and only suffering, appears as if it were desirable, lovable, and happy through improper attention (ayoniso manasikāra) because perversions (vippallāsa) have not been abandoned, it overcomes, overwhelms, and subdues the negligent person who lacks mindfulness. Therefore, it also overwhelms this Suppavāsā with the happiness of the object of love called "son," which is a counterfeit of pleasure, even though it is such unpleasant, unloved suffering, for the seventh time.

## The Commentary on the Eighth Sutta is finished.

## 9. Visākhāsutta-vaṇṇanā

In the ninth sutta, "Pubbārāme" means in the monastery built in a place similar to the Uttamadevī Monastery of Anurādhapura, in the eastern direction of Sāvatthī. "Migāramātupāsāde" means in the palace of Migāra's mother.

In this context, this is the sequential story: One hundred thousand eons ago, a certain female lay follower, seeing the Buddha Padumuttara appoint another female lay follower to the position of his chief female attendant, invited the Blessed One and gave alms to a hundred thousand monks headed by the Buddha. Having paid respect to the Blessed One, she made a wish: "In the future, may I become the chief female attendant of a Buddha like you." That lay follower wandered through the worlds of devas and humans for a hundred thousand eons, and in the time of our Buddha, she was conceived in the womb of Sumanadevī, in the house of the treasurer Dhanañjaya, the son of the treasurer Meṇ္ဍka, in the city of Bhaddiya. When she was born, they named her Visākhā. When the Blessed One arrived at the city of Bhaddiya, Visākhā, along with five hundred young girls, went to welcome the Blessed One and became a Stream-enterer upon first seeing him. Later, she went to the house of the youth Punnavaḍḍhana, the son of the treasurer Migāra, in the city of Sāvatthī. In that father-in-law's house, the great treasurer Migāra, because of her great kindness, placed her in the position of a mother. Therefore, she is called "Migāramātā" (Migāra's Mother). That lay follower Visākhā, having given up her mahallatā ornament, for nine crores, to the Buddha and the community of monks...
141:
She made the aspiration: "May I become the chief female lay attendant of a Buddha like you." Having wandered through the realms of devas and humans for a hundred thousand aeons, she was reborn in the womb of Sumanadevī, the daughter of the financier Dhanañjaya and granddaughter of the financier Meṇḍaka, in the city of Bhaddiya during the time of our Blessed One. At the time of her birth, they named her Visākhā. When the Blessed One arrived at the city of Bhaddiya, Visākhā, along with five hundred young maidens, went out to welcome the Blessed One and became a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna) upon her first sight of Him.

Later, she went to the house of the young man Puṇṇavaddhana, the son of the financier Migāra in Sāvatthī. There, because she was of great service, her father-in-law, the financier Migāra, placed her in the position of a mother. Therefore, she is called "Migāramātā" (Migāra's Mother). She sold her Mahālatā ornament for ninety million and, for the residence of the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of monks, she built a mansion (pāsāda) adorned with a thousand rooms—five hundred rooms on the upper floor and five hundred rooms on the lower floor—on a piece of land measuring about eight karīsas. Therefore, it is called the "Migāramātupāsāda."

"Kocideva attho" means some purpose or matter. "Raññe" means in the king. "Paṭibaddho" means connected with or dependent (āyatta). From Visākhā's relatives' house, such goods adorned with rubies, pearls, and so on, were sent as a gift for her. When they reached the city gate, the customs officers, while collecting tax there, did not take an appropriate amount but took an excessive amount. Hearing of this, Visākhā, wishing to report the matter to the King, went to the royal palace with a suitable retinue. At that moment, the King had entered the inner palace with Queen Mallikā. Visākhā, not getting an opportunity for an audience, waited, thinking, "I will get it now, I will get it now," until the mealtime had passed, and she returned having missed her meal. In this way, even after going for two or three days, she did not get the opportunity. Thus, although the King had not yet been informed, because he did not provide the opportunity to settle the case, it is said, "It cannot be concluded as desired."

In that passage, "yathādhippāyaṃ" means according to one's wish, and "na tīreti" means does not conclude or complete. In truth, the great lay devotee wished only to pay the King the appropriate tax and have the excess released, but because she did not meet the King, that wish was not fulfilled. "Handa" is an exclamatory particle (nipāta) in the sense of relinquishing. "Divā divassa" means in the day of the day, which means at the time of midday. Having gone to the palace gate for two or three days for some business, because that matter was not concluded, it was in vain. Therefore, reflecting that approaching the Blessed One would be beneficial because of the attainment of the supreme sight (dassanānuttariya) and so on, she spoke the words beginning with "Idha me, bhante," wishing to show the meaning: "Venerable Sir, I have come here at this midday hour." "Etamatthaṃ viditvā" means having known this matter.
142:
The great lay devotee Visākhā said, "Venerable Sir, I have come here at this time," and so on, wishing to show this meaning: that approaching the Blessed One is beneficial because it is the cause for obtaining the supreme sight and other blessings. Having known this matter—namely, the failure to fulfill one's wish due to dependence on others—the Blessed One uttered this inspired utterance (udāna) which illuminates the disadvantages of living in dependence on others and the advantages of living independently.

In that inspired utterance, "All dependence on others is suffering" (Sabbaṃ paravasaṃ dukkhaṃ) means that whatever purpose or matter is dependent on others, because of the inability to accomplish it according to one's own will, it is suffering or brings about suffering. "All self-mastery is happiness" (Sabbaṃ issariyaṃ sukhaṃ) refers to two kinds of mastery (issariya): mundane and supramundane. Mundane mastery includes the sovereignty of kings and the mastery over the mind resulting from mundane meditative absorptions (jhāna) and direct knowledge (abhiññā). Supramundane mastery is the mastery over cessation (nirodha) which is the mark of attaining the paths and fruits. Among these, the sovereignty among humans culminating in the status of a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti), and the sovereignty that is the lordship over various groups of devas such as Sakka and others—both of these, although they are happiness in the sense of being a cause for happiness through the accomplishment of one's desires by the power of kamma, are entirely suffering because they are subject to the suffering of change (vipariṇāma-dukkha). Likewise, the mastery over the mind resulting from mundane jhāna is also suffering because it is ultimately impermanent. Only the mastery associated with the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) is called absolute happiness, because it is unshakeable by worldly conditions (lokadhamma) and is of a nature that does not return to saṃsāra. However, here the Teacher said, "All self-mastery is happiness," referring to the mental happiness one obtains through independence in all matters.

"In common concerns, they are troubled" (Sādhāraṇe vihaññanti) is an explanation of the meaning of the phrase "All dependence on others is suffering." The meaning here is: when there is a common purpose to be accomplished, because of its dependence on others and the inability to fulfill it according to one's wish, these beings are troubled, they meet with frustration, and they are weary. Why? "For bonds are hard to overcome" (Yogā hi duratikkamā), because the bond of sensual desire (kāmayoga), the bond of existence (bhavayoga), the bond of views (diṭṭhiyoga), and the bond of ignorance (avijjāyoga), which have been cultivated throughout beginningless time, are hard to overcome as they cannot be abandoned by those who have not accumulated the requisites of merit. Among these four bonds, the bond of views is to be overcome by the first path (Sotāpatti-magga), and the bond of sensual desire by the third path (Anāgāmi-magga). The others are to be overcome by the highest path (Arahatta-magga). Thus, because the Noble Paths are difficult to attain, these bonds are hard to overcome. Therefore, due to the failure to obtain what is desired by the power of the bond of sensual desire and so on, beings are troubled. However, in the case of the uncommon (asādhāraṇa) happiness of the mind and the mastery associated with the attainment of cessation, there is no such trouble.
143:
The meaning is that when there is mastery over the mind and mastery over the attainment of cessation, there can never be any distress or suffering.

Alternatively, "all that is subject to another" means whatever is called a mode of existence dependent on something other than oneself; all that is suffering because of its impermanent nature. For it was said: "Whatever is impermanent is suffering." "All mastery" refers to Nibbāna, which is called "mastery" (issariya) because it is the state of supremacy, being liberated from all conditioned things; all that is happiness, categorized as Nibbāna with residue and so forth. For it was said: "Nibbāna is the supreme happiness."

"Common" (sādhāraṇa): although suffering and happiness are thus defined, these beings, being immersed in the causes of suffering common to many, are distressed. Why? Because "the bonds (yogas) are difficult to overcome." Since the bonds of sensual desire (kāmayoga) and so forth, which are the causes of being immersed in all [suffering], are difficult to overcome, the meaning is: "Visākhā, you too, desiring an object dependent on others and not obtaining it, are distressed."

## The Explanation of the Ninth Sutta is finished.

## 10. The Explanation of the Bhaddiya Sutta

In the tenth sutta, "at Anupiyā" (anupiyāyaṃ) means in the city of that name. "In the Mango Grove" (ambavane) means there was a mango grove belonging to the Malla kings not far from that city; in that mango grove, the Malla kings had a monastery built for the Blessed One, and it is called simply "Ambavana". The Blessed One dwelt there, making the town of Anupiyā his resort for alms; hence it is said, "He was dwelling at Anupiyā in the Mango Grove."

"Bhaddiya" is the name of that elder. "The son of Kāḷīgodhā" means he was the son of the Sakiyan princess named Kāḷīgodhā, a queen of the Sakiyan kings, a noble disciple (ariyasāvikā) who had attained the fruit [of the path] and understood the Teaching. The procedure of his going forth is already mentioned in the Khandhaka. After going forth and establishing insight, he became an Arahat endowed with the six higher powers (chaḷabhiñña) before long; he also practiced by undertaking the thirteen ascetic practices (dhutaṅga). The Blessed One also placed him in the foremost position (etadagga) among those of high birth, saying: "Monks, the foremost among my monk disciples who are of high birth is Bhaddiya, the son of Kāḷīgodhā." Thus, he was among the eighty great disciples.

"Gone to an empty place" (suññāgāragato): excluding the village and its precincts, the remaining forest is called "forest" (arañña); excluding that and the foot of a tree, other places suitable for recluses such as mountain caves, which are not crowded with people, should be known as "empty places" (suññāgāra). Alternatively, a house that is quiet because of the absence of sounds, which are like thorns to the ear, is also called an "empty place".

When he reached such a secluded place, "exceedingly" (abhikkantaṃ) means he "uttered an inspired utterance" (udānaṃ udānesi) many times. When that Venerable Bhaddiya reached a place for the day or a place for the night, he mostly spent his time in the bliss of the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti) and the bliss of the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti). Therefore, with reference to that bliss, and out of loathing for the royal happiness he had previously experienced which was accompanied by danger and anxiety, he well uttered the inspired utterance: "O, what happiness! O, what happiness!" (aho sukhaṃ, aho sukhaṃ), which was accompanied by joy (somanassa) and associated with zest (pīti) born of knowledge.
144:
Because the place of residence is not crowded with people, it is intended here as "suññāgāra" (empty dwelling). Alternatively, any secluded house that is free from sounds, which are thorns to jhāna, should also be known as "suññāgāra." He went to such an empty place. "Abhikkhaṇaṃ" means many times. "Udānaṃ udānesi" (uttered an inspired exclamation) means that whether that Venerable Bhaddiya went to a place for the day's stay in the forest or a place for the night's stay, he mostly spent his time in the bliss of the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti) and the bliss of cessation (nirodha). Therefore, referring to that bliss, and being disgusted with the royal happiness he had previously experienced, which was accompanied by danger and anxiety, he uttered the inspired exclamation, "Oh, what happiness! Oh, what happiness!" which was born of joy (somanassa), knowledge, and zest (pīti).

When those monks heard it, "nesaṃ etadahosi" (this thought occurred to them) means when many monks heard the Venerable Bhaddiya uttering the exclamation, "Oh, what happiness! Oh, what happiness!", they thought, "Undoubtedly, this person is living the holy life dissatisfied (anabhirata)." Those monks, being worldlings (puthujjanas), did not know the exclamation uttered by the Venerable Bhaddiya in reference to the bliss of seclusion (viveka-sukha) and thus thought in this way; therefore, it is said, "undoubtedly," and so on. In that context, "nissaṃsayaṃ" means without doubt, certainly. After stating the Pali "yaṃ so pubbe agāriyabhūto samāno," some explain the meaning with the remaining verb "anubhavī" (experienced). Others read it as "yaṃ sā." However, the Pali is "yaṃsa pubbe agāriyabhūtassa." In that Pali, "yaṃsa" is a sandhi of "yaṃ assa," occurring through the dropping of the letters 'a' and 'sa,' as in "evaṃsa te" and "pupphaṃsā uppajjī." Its meaning is: the royal happiness experienced by this Venerable Bhaddiya when he was a householder before ordaining. "Sā tamanussaramāno" means (the monks thought) that he was now recollecting that happiness with the power of longing.

Those monks told this to the Blessed One; many monks, having the nature of speaking out, told this to the Blessed One with the intention of helping that Venerable Bhaddiya, and not out of a desire to complain. "Aññataraṃ" means a certain monk who was not well-known by name or clan. The Blessed One, wishing to inform those monks, ordered that monk to call him. The word "evaṃ" is an acceptance, meaning "very well." Again, after promising "evaṃ," Venerable Bhaddiya admitted his own exclamation, saying that he constantly uttered this exclamation, "Oh, what happiness! Oh, what happiness!" exactly as those monks had said. One might ask, "Why did the Blessed One ask, 'Bhaddiya, why (do you utter this)?' Did He not know his mind?" It was not that He did not know. Rather, He asked because He wished to have Venerable Bhaddiya himself speak about that matter.
145:
Does he know? It is not that he does not know; he knows. However, he asks in order to have that matter spoken and to make those monks understand. For it has been said: "The Tathāgatas ask even though they know; they do not ask even though they know," and so on. "Atthavasaṃ" means the reason.

"Antepure" means in the inner part of the palace, which is the place where the women of the harem move about, and where the king bathes, eats, and sleeps. "Rakkhā susaṃvihitā" means that protection by men such as bodyguards is well-arranged all around. "Bahipi antepure" means in the royal residence outside the inner palace, such as the court of justice and so on. Thus, being protected and guarded in many places, both inside and outside the palace, the capital, and the kingdom, by hundreds of well-arranged guards, protections, and defenses, for the sake of one's own safety and living in comfort. The words beginning with "bhīto" are synonyms of one another.

Alternatively, "bhīto" means being afraid of other kings. "Ubviggo" means being agitated and shaken by the fear that naturally arises even in one's own kingdom. "Ussaṅkī" means, according to the saying "A king should never be careless," being apprehensive, looking upwards due to lack of trust everywhere and suspicion regarding the causes of various duties to be performed. "Utrāsī" means being terrified with a terror capable of causing the body to tremble, which arises thinking, "Even those who serve closely might sometimes do me harm while I am unaware." There is also a reading "utrasto." "Vihāsiṃ" means "I lived being of such a nature."

"Etarahi" means now, starting from the time of becoming a monk. "Eko" means alone, without a companion; by this, he shows physical seclusion. The meaning of the words beginning with "abhīto" should be understood as the opposite of the meanings mentioned before. Because of the absence of possession (pariggaha), which is the cause of fear and so on, and the absence of defilements (kilesa), which are the cause of that possession, fearlessness and so on arise for that elder. By this, he shows mental seclusion (cittaviveka). "Appossukko" means being unconcerned about the protection of the body. "Pannalomo" means having the hair lying flat because of the absence of agitation that causes horripilation. By these two words, he shows living at ease (serivihāra). "Paradattavutto" means living on requisites such as robes given by others; by this, through the manifestation of the absence of all attachment, he shows the absence of any remaining cause of fear. "Migabhūtena cetasā" means with a mind that has become like a deer's because of living trustfully. For a deer, in the forest where there are no humans...
146:
(A deer), when living, stands, sits, and lies down without apprehension, and goes wherever it desires with unobstructed movement; "in the same way, I also live," thus he shows. For this was said by a Paccekabuddha:

"Just as a deer in the forest is unbound,
And goes for fodder wherever it desires,
A wise man, looking for independence,
Should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros."

"Venerable Sir, I, seeing well this reason, namely, the supreme bliss of seclusion (vivekasukha) and the bliss of the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpattisukha) which are now occurring to me, uttered this inspired utterance: 'Oh, what happiness! Oh, what happiness!'" thus he said.

"Etam-atthaṃ" means having known in every aspect that meaning called the bliss of seclusion, which is beyond the reach of worldlings, of the Elder Bhaddiya. "Imaṃ udānaṃ" means he uttered this inspired utterance which illustrates the power of the departure of fear and sorrow along with their causes.

In that verse, "yassantarato na santi kopā" means that in the interior, in the mind of that noble person (ariya), there are no angers (kopa), such as lust and so on which cause mental turbidity and thus destroy the mind, or the many types of anger (dosa-kopa) arising from various causes like the grounds for resentment (āghātavatthu), because they have been abandoned by the Path. Indeed, this word "antara" is seen in the sense of "reason" in such passages as "What is the reason (antara) between me and you?"; in the sense of "middle" in "In the middle of the eight [days] (antaraṭṭhake) during the snowy season"; in the sense of "interval" in "Between (antarā) Jeta’s Grove and Sāvatthī"; and in the sense of "mind" in "Fear is born from within (antarato)." Here too, it should be understood as "mind." Therefore, it is said, "in one's own mind within."

"Itibhavābhavatañca vītivatto" means because "bhava" is success (sampatti) and "abhava" is failure (vipatti). Likewise, "bhava" is growth, "abhava" is decline. Or "bhava" is eternalism (sassata), "abhava" is annihilationism (uccheda). Or "bhava" is merit, "abhava" is demerit. Or "bhava" is a happy destination, "abhava" is a miserable destination. Or "bhava" is small, "abhava" is large. Therefore, by way of these successes and failures, growth and decline, eternalism and annihilationism, merit and demerit, happy and miserable destinations, small and large, and rebirth in a new existence, this state of being and non-being (bhavābhava) of many kinds is spoken of.
147:
By means of the four Ariya paths, in accordance with the respective methods, one has transcended and overcome such various states of existence (itibhavābhava). The grammatical inflection (vibhakti) should be modified in reading according to the sense.

'Taṃ vigatabhayaṃ' means that such an Arahant, endowed with the aforementioned qualities, is one who is free from fear because the causes of fear have vanished—both due to the absence of defilements that corrupt the mind and due to having fully transcended various states of existence. He is one who possesses happiness through the bliss of seclusion (vivekasukha) and the bliss of the fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala), and being free from fear, he is without sorrow.

'Devā nānubhavanti dassanāya' means that, setting aside the devas who have attained the Path, even all the devas by rebirth (upapatti-devā), though they may strive, are not able, not capable, and not empowered to see [the Arahant's mind] by way of perceiving the mental processes; what then to say of human beings? Indeed, even those in training (sekha) do not know the mental process of an Arahant, just like worldlings (puthujjana).

## The commentary on the tenth sutta is finished.

## The commentary on the Mucalinda Vagga is finished.
148:
## 3. Nanda Vagga
## 1. Commentary on the Kammavipākaja Sutta
In the first sutta of the Nanda Vagga, "aññataro bhikkhu" refers to an Arahant monk who is not well-known by name or clan. This venerable Arahant was a clansman living in Rājagaha who, having been stirred by the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna and seeing the faults of saṃsāra, went forth in the presence of the Teacher. Having purified his virtue and taken up the meditation subject of the Four Noble Truths, he soon applied himself to insight and attained the fruit of Arahantship. Later, a harsh illness arose in that Arahant whose taints were destroyed, and he dwelt enduring it with reflection. For Arahants, there is no such thing as mental suffering, but physical suffering does indeed occur. One day, he sat down cross-legged, enduring the painful feeling, at a place not far from the Blessed One who was teaching the Dhamma. Therefore, it was said: "He was sitting not far from the Blessed One," and so forth.

In that text, "pallaṅka" means sitting with the thighs bound all around (sitting cross-legged). "Ābhujitvā" means having folded [the legs]. "Ujuṃ kāyaṃ paṇidhāya" means keeping the upper body straight, aligning the eighteen vertebrae of the spine end to end. For one sitting in this way, the skin, flesh, and sinews do not bend; therefore, that monk sat in that cross-legged posture. "Purāṇakammavipākajaṃ" means that which has arisen as the result of kamma performed in the past, or that which has arisen as a part of the round of results (vipākavaṭṭa) consisting of various types of pleasure and pain, which are the results of past kamma. What is that? It is suffering (dukkha). By the term "purāṇakammavipākajaṃ," showing that the illness is caused by kamma, [the commentary] rejects the idea that it is caused by external effort or seasonal changes (utu-vipariṇāma), etc. "Dukkha" means a nature that ordinary people cannot endure. "Tibba" means sharp, or powerful/abundant because it occurs by overwhelming [the mind]. "Khara" means harsh. "Kaṭuka" means unpleasant. "Adhivāsento" means enduring, bearing, or allowing it to remain above.

"Sato sampajāno" means being mindful and clearly comprehending by the power of mindfulness and clear comprehension that grasp feelings. This means: "This feeling is impermanent (anicca) because it does not exist after having come to be; it is dependently arisen (paṭiccasamuppanna) because it arises depending on causes such as undesirable objects; because it has the nature of definitely breaking up after having arisen, it is of the nature of wasting away (khayadhamma), of the nature of vanishing (vayadhamma), of the nature of fading away (virāgadhamma), and of the nature of ceasing (nirodhadhamma)." Thus, by being mindful through the observation of the characteristic of impermanence in feeling...
149:
Being mindful (*sato*), one is also endowed with clear comprehension (*sampajāno*) by way of penetrating the non-perverted nature of reality. Alternatively, because of attaining the fullness of mindfulness, one is 'mindful' (*sato*) due to mindfulness being well-established in all the foundations of mindfulness—body, feelings, mind, and mental objects. Similarly, because of attaining the fullness of wisdom, one is 'clearly comprehending' (*sampajāno*) due to discerning conditioned phenomena.

'Avihaññamāno' (not being distressed) means: as it was said, 'Monks, when an uninstructed blind worldling is touched by any painful state, he sorrows, grieves, laments, beats his breast, and falls into confusion.' Unlike such a blind worldling, the Arahant is not distressed. Having completely uprooted [mental suffering] through the Noble Path, he does not produce mental distress; merely enduring the physical suffering born of kamma-result, he sits like one who has entered a meditative attainment. 'Addasā' (he saw) means the Buddha saw that venerable one sitting in such a manner with the patience of endurance (*adhivāsana-khanti*).

'Etam-atthaṃ' (this matter) means: having known in every aspect this meaning—characterized by the fact that Arahants are not smeared by worldly conditions and have no reason to strive for treatment by doctors and so on, even when such a disease occurs. 'Imaṃ udānaṃ' (this inspired utterance) means he uttered this inspired utterance which clarifies the attainment of non-affliction by any painful states among conditioned things.

In that verse, 'sabbakammajahassa' means 'of one who has abandoned all kamma.' Indeed, from the moment the Path of Arahantship arises, all wholesome and unwholesome kammas of an Arahant are said to be abandoned because they are unable to produce rebirth. Therefore, the knowledge of the Noble Path is called 'the knowledge that makes an end of kamma.' 'Bhikkhuno' (of a monk) means he is called a monk because of having destroyed the defilements. 'Dhuna-mānassa pure kataṃ rajaṃ' (shaking off the dust created before) means: of one who is shaking off or destroying, through the experiencing of the result (*vipāka*), the kamma that leads to painful feelings, which is called 'dust' because it was mixed with the dust of lust and so on, performed prior to the attainment of Arahantship. After the attainment of Arahantship, the occurrence of faulty unwholesome functional [kamma] is impossible. Even blameless wholesome functional [kamma] becomes merely functional (*kiriya*) because the root of existence has been utterly cut off; like a flower on a tree whose roots are cut, it is unable to produce fruit.

'Amamassa' (of one without 'mine') means of one who is free from 'mine-making' (*mamaṅkāra*), having no grasping of anything such as form and so on as 'mine.' For one who has 'mine-making', out of love for self, has the body looked after by doctors and so on. But an Arahant is without 'mine'; therefore, he is indifferent even towards the care of the body. 'Ṭhitassa' (of one who is steady) means of one who has crossed the four floods and stands on the dry land of Nibbāna. Or, because of the absence of running on by way of taking rebirth...
150:
...of one who is steady. For worldlings and trainees (*sekha*), because they have not abandoned the defilements and volitional formations, they run on in Saṃsāra by way of death and rebirth. But an Arahant, because of the absence of that, is called 'steady' (*ṭhita*). Alternatively, it means of one who stands on the dry land of Nibbāna having crossed the four floods, or of one who is established in the ten noble qualities (*ariya-dhamma*) of an Arahant.

'Tādino' (of the such-like) means: of one who possesses the state of 'suchness' (*tādibhāva*) characterized by being the same towards desirable and undesirable objects, being endowed with the fivefold noble power (*ariyiddhi*) described in the manner beginning with 'he dwells perceiving the unrepulsive in the repulsive,' and with the six-factored equanimity (*chaḷaṅgupekkhā*) which is unshakable by the eight worldly conditions.

'Attho natthi janaṃ lapetave' (there is no need to speak to people) means: because of having no regard for the body, there is no need or purpose to speak to or tell people, 'Do provide me with medicines and so on.' Like a yellow leaf that has fallen from its bond, the intention of the Arahants is: 'Let this body break and fall of its own accord.' For it has been said:

'I do not long for death, I do not long for life;
I await my time, like a laborer awaiting his wages.'

Alternatively, it means the Arahant has no need to make people invite him with the four requisites by showing some sign and speaking to them, 'What does the venerable one need?' This is because such wrong livelihood (*micchā-ājīva*) has been utterly uprooted by the Path. Thus, the Blessed One revealed the reason for that Elder not seeking treatment to the monks who were thinking, 'Why does this Elder sit near the Blessed One without having his disease treated by doctors?'

## The Commentary on the First Sutta is Finished.

## 2. Commentary on the Nanda Sutta

In the second sutta, 'Nanda' is the name of that prince. He received the name 'Nanda' because he was born possessing the marks of a Universal Monarch, bringing joy (*nandento*) to his parents, attendants, and the entire circle of relatives. 'The Blessed One's brother' means he was a brother because of being the son of the same father as the Blessed One. Indeed, siblings born of the same mother do not arise for the Blessed One; therefore, it is said 'the son of his maternal aunt,' meaning the son of his junior mother. For he was the son of Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī. 'Anabhirato' (dissatisfied) means not taking delight.
151:
Brahmacariya means the noble, especially the supreme practice, eating in one sitting, sleeping alone, and abstaining from sexual intercourse. Sandhāretuṃ means to maintain or to carry out perfectly and purely from the first thought until the last thought. By this second term 'brahmacariya', the noble practice of the Path (maggabrahmacariya) should also be understood as included. Sikkhā paccakkhāya means rejecting and abandoning the three trainings that were undertaken and established along with the state of a monk at the time of higher ordination. Hīnāya refers to the state of a householder (lay life). Āvattissāmi means "I will return" (to the lay life).

Why was this stated? Here is the chronological account (anupubbikathā): After the Blessed One set the noble Wheel of Dhamma in motion, he went to Rājagaha and stayed at the Veluvana monastery. King Suddhodana sent ten messengers, each with a thousand followers, saying, "Bring my son to see me." All of them, along with their followers, attained Arahantship. Finally, the Elder Kāludāyi, who had also attained Arahantship, knew the proper time for the journey. He praised the beauty of the route and requested the Buddha to visit his birthplace. Accompanied by twenty thousand Arahants, the Buddha went to the city of Kapilavatthu. In the assembly of his kinsmen, he caused the Pokkharavassa rain to fall as a special event and preached the Vessantara Jātaka. On the following day, while entering for alms, he established his father in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti) with the verse beginning with "Uttiṭṭhe nappamajjeyya." After going to the palace, he established Mahāpajāpati in the Fruit of Stream-entry and the King in the Fruit of Once-returning (Sakadāgāmi) with the verse beginning with "Dhammañcare."

After the meal, he preached the Candakinnarī Jātaka based on the virtues of Rāhula's mother. On the third day, while Prince Nanda's consecration, house-warming, and marriage ceremonies were taking place, the Buddha entered for alms, placed the bowl in Prince Nanda's hands, spoke words of blessing, and rising from his seat, departed without taking the bowl back from the Prince's hand. Out of respect for the Tathāgata, the Prince did not dare to say, "Venerable Sir, please take your bowl." He thought, "He will take the bowl at the head of the stairs," but the Teacher did not take it there. He then thought, "He will take it at the foot of the stairs," but the Teacher did not take it there either. He thought, "He will take it in the royal courtyard," but the Teacher still did not take it. Although the Prince wished to turn back, he followed unwillingly. Unable to say "Take the bowl" due to respect, he continued following, thinking, "He will take it here, he will take it there."
152:
At that moment, the palace ladies told Princess Janapadakalyāṇī, "Lady, the Blessed One has taken Prince Nanda away; he will separate him from you." Princess Janapadakalyāṇī, with her hair only half-combed and water still dripping from it, quickly ascended the palace, stood at the lion-cage window (siha-pañjara), and said, "Noble son, please return quickly." Her words remained as if lodged crosswise in Nanda's heart. The Teacher, without taking the bowl from the Prince's hand, led him to the monastery and asked, "Nanda, will you ordain?" Out of deep respect for the Buddha, he did not dare to say "I will not ordain," but instead said, "Yes, I will ordain." The Teacher then said, "In that case, ordain Nanda." Thus, on the third day after arriving at Kapilavatthu, he had Nanda ordained. On the seventh day, Prince Rāhula, who had been adorned and sent by his mother saying, "Ascetic, give me my inheritance," followed the Buddha to the monastery and was also ordained. On another day, the Buddha preached the Mahādhammapāla Jātaka and established the King, his father, in the Fruit of Non-returning (Anāgāmi).

Thus, the Blessed One established Mahāpajāpati Gotamī in the Fruit of Stream-entry and his father in the three higher Fruits. Surrounded by the community of monks, he returned to Rājagaha. From there, having accepted Anāthapiṇḍika's invitation to come to Sāvatthī, he went and stayed at the Jetavana Great Monastery when it was completed. While the Teacher was staying at Jetavana, the Venerable Nanda, who had ordained against his will, could not see the danger in sensual pleasures. Constantly remembering the words of Princess Janapadakalyāṇī, he became dissatisfied and informed the monks of his discontent. Therefore, it was said: "At that time, the Venerable Nanda... said, 'I will return to the lower life.'"

Why did the Blessed One have him ordained in this way? The Teacher, skilled in disciplining those who are to be tamed, thought: "It is not possible to separate Nanda from sensual pleasures merely by showing their danger beforehand. Only after he is ordained can I, through a skillful means, separate him from sensual pleasures and cause him to attain the higher distinction (of the Path and Fruit)." Thus, he had Prince Nanda ordained first.

Sākiyānī refers to a Sakyan princess. Janapadakalyāṇī refers to a woman who is the most beautiful in the land, free from the six bodily defects and endowed with the five beauties. She was free from the six bodily defects because she was neither too tall, nor too short, nor too thin, nor too stout, nor too dark, nor too fair—surpassing human beauty without yet reaching divine beauty. She was endowed with the five beauties: beauty of skin, beauty of flesh, beauty of nails, beauty of bones, and beauty of age.
153:
This princess creates light in an area of twelve cubits (or ten cubits) with the radiance of her own body. She possesses a complexion similar to the color of the piyangu flower or the color of gold. This is her beauty of skin (chavikalyaṇā). Her four limbs and her lips, including the edges of her mouth, are like red coral or red blankets, as if treated smoothly with lac-dye. This is her beauty of flesh (maṃsakalyaṇā). Her twenty nails appear as if surrounded by lac-dye where they are attached to the flesh, and where they are free, they resemble the color of milk. This is her beauty of nails (nakhakalyaṇā). Her thirty-two teeth are well-aligned; they appear like a row of very pure coral or a row of diamonds. This is her beauty of bones (aṭṭhikalyaṇā). Although she is twenty years of age, she appears as if she were sixteen. There is no graying of hair. This is her beauty of age (vayakalyaṇā). Being endowed with such qualities, she is beautiful in appearance. Therefore, she is called "Janapadakalyāṇī" (The Beauty of the Country).

The phrase "Gharā nikkhamantassa" is a word ending in the genitive case (chaṭṭhī vibhatti) in the sense of disregard (anādara), meaning "of one who has left the house." Some also recite it as "Gharā nikkhamantaṃ." The phrase "Upāḍḍhullikhitehi keseehi" is a word ending in the instrumental case (tatiyā vibhatti) in the sense of a characteristic of such a state (itthambhūtalakkhaṇa), meaning "marked by hair that is not yet fully combed." Some also recite it as "Aḍḍhullikhitehi." "Ullikhana" refers to the proper grooming of hair with combs and such. Some also call it "Aḍḍhakāravidhāna." "Apaloketvā" means looking as if binding with half-closed eyes that indicate the diffusion of the essence of affection. "Maṃ bhante" means that having said "maṃ" previously, and having a mind clouded by weariness in the Dispensation, he said again, "maṃ etadavoca." "Tuvaṭaṃ" means quickly. "Tamanussaramāno" means repeatedly reflecting on those words of the princess Janapadakalyāṇī, or those words together with her gestures.

The Blessed One, hearing the words of the Venerable Nanda, thought, "I will appease this monk's passion by a skillful means." While conveying the Venerable Nanda to the Tāvatiṃsa realm by psychic power, He showed him a burnt and mutilated female monkey with severed ears, nose, and tail, sitting on a charred tree stump in a burnt field along the way, and then proceeded to the Tāvatiṃsa realm. In the Pali text, it is stated as if the Teacher went to the Tāvatiṃsa realm in a single moment; that statement refers to the arrival at the Tāvatiṃsa realm without mentioning the journey. In truth, while traveling, the Blessed One showed that burnt and mutilated monkey to the Venerable Nanda along the way. If so, how should the reference to the bending of the arm, etc., be understood? That statement should be taken as indicating the disappearance from that place. Thus, the Blessed One, having conveyed the Venerable Nanda to the Tāvatiṃsa realm, showed him five hundred celestial nymphs with feet like those of a dove (kakuṭapādāni) who had come to attend upon Sakka, the king of gods, and were standing there after paying homage to Him. Then, comparing the perfection of beauty of the princess Janapadakalyāṇī and those nymphs...
154:
...showing them standing there, He asked about the difference in the perfection of beauty between the princess Janapadakalyāṇī and those five hundred celestial nymphs. Regarding that matter, it is said: "Then the Blessed One, taking the Venerable Nanda by the arm... (nymphs) with feet like those of a dove."

In that passage, "bāhāyaṃ gahetvā" means as if taking him by the arm. In fact, at that time, the Blessed One performed a psychic feat such that it was as if the Venerable Nanda was being led by the Blessed One holding his arm. In this regard, if the Blessed One had only desired to show or enter the Tāvatiṃsa heaven for the Venerable monk, He could have shown that heaven even while he was sitting, as during the time of the psychic feat of opening the worlds (lokavivaraṇa), or He could have sent him there by psychic power. However, because He wished to show that monkey along the way so that Nanda would easily perceive the lowly and loathsome nature of the human state compared to the divine state, and because He wished to show the celestial glory and wealth by letting him experience them, He took him by the hand and led him there. (He thought) that by doing so, Nanda would find special delight in living the holy life for that purpose.

"Kakuṭapādāni" means those who have feet like pigeons because of their reddish color. It is said that all those nymphs had such delicate feet because of the merit of offering oil for massaging the feet of the disciples of the Buddha Kassapa. "Passasi no" means "Do you see?" "Abhirūpatarā" means having a more exceedingly excellent form. "Dassanīyatarā" means more worth seeing because one cannot be satisfied even by looking all day long. "Pāsādikatarā" means more inspiring of confidence from all aspects due to the beauty of all limbs.

Why did the Blessed One make the Venerable Nanda, whose mind was soaked with defilements, look at the celestial nymphs? It was to remove his defilements even through pleasant means. Just as a skilled physician, when treating a person with an excess of humors (dosa), first saturates the humors with the drinking of oil and so on, and later removes the disease properly through emetics and purgatives; in the same way, the Blessed One, who is skilled in disciplining those to be tamed, showed the celestial nymphs to the Venerable Nanda, who had great passion, to saturate (his passion), and then wished to remove it without remainder with the medicine of the Noble Path (Ariyamagga). This is how it should be understood.

"Paluṭṭhamakkaṭī" means a female monkey with burnt limbs. "Evameva kho" means "Venerable Sir, the old burnt monkey with severed ears and nose that You showed me is just like this when compared to the princess Janapadakalyāṇī."
155:
## 
'Upādāya' means 'taking into account' or 'comparing' the Janapadakalyāṇī with these five hundred celestial nymphs. In the phrase 'pañcannaṃ accharāsatānaṃ,' the genitive case is used in the sense of the accusative; therefore, it is interpreted as 'the five hundred celestial nymphs.' Alternatively, this genitive case relates to the connection of parts (avayava-sambandha); therefore, it should be understood as taking into account the perfection of the beauty of the five hundred celestial nymphs. 'Upanidhāya' also means 'placing near' (comparing) or 'upādāya' (taking into account). 'Saṅkhyā' refers to being counted (included) as a woman. 'Kalabhāga' refers to a fraction of a fraction; it means that if one part is divided into sixteen parts, and one of those is taken and again divided into sixteen, each resulting part is desired as a 'kalabhāga.' It means she cannot even reach such a small fraction. 'Upanidhi' refers to taking as a simile, 'this woman is like that woman,' and placing them near each other.

Regarding the holy life (brahmacariya) in this Dispensation in which the Venerable Nanda was dissatisfied, since that holy life was mentioned previously and is well-known, it is not directly touched upon. Instead, to generate respect (ādara) for delighting in that holy life, the Buddha said, 'Nanda, delight! Nanda, delight!' by way of repetition (āmeḍita). 'I am your guarantor'—why did the Blessed One, while desiring the Venerable Nanda's stay in the holy life, become a guarantor for the unholy life (sensual enjoyment)? He became a guarantor with the thought that Nanda's lust, which was firmly fixed on the object of the Janapadakalyāṇī, could be easily abandoned after shifting it to a new object (the celestial nymphs). The 'Talk on Heaven' (saggakathā) in the 'Gradual Discourse' (anupubbikathā) illustrates this meaning.

'They heard'—how did they hear? At that time, after the Blessed One had shown the duty to the Venerable Nanda and went to his day-retreat, he told that matter to the monks who came to attend on him. For example, just as a skilled man might extract a splinter that has not come out by using another splinter, and then remove that splinter by moving it with his hands and so on; in the same way, the Blessed One, desiring to extract the Elder's lust for the familiar object (the Janapadakalyāṇī) by means of a new object (the celestial nymphs), and then to remove that new object as well by making it a cause for the holy life, commanded: 'Come, monks, address the monk Nanda with the word hireling and with the word one who is bought.' Thus the monks heard. Some teachers, however, say, 'The Blessed One performed such a feat of psychic power that those monks came to know that matter.'

'Bhatakavādena' means by the word 'hireling.' One who performs work for wages is called a hireling (bhataka). This Venerable Nanda, too, was like a hireling because he was practicing the holy life for the sake of union with the celestial nymphs.
156:
## 
'Bhatakavādena' means by the word 'hireling.' 'Upakkītakavādena'—one who buys something with money and so on is called 'upakkītaka' (one who is bought). This Venerable Nanda, too, 'buys' his holy life for the sake of the celestial nymphs; therefore, he is addressed with the word 'upakkītaka.' Alternatively, by the command of the Blessed One, he was leading a life consisting of the practice of the holy life for the 'wage' consisting of union with the celestial nymphs; since he was subsisting on that wage, he was like one being supported by the Blessed One, and thus called 'bhataka' (hireling). Likewise, by making the union with celestial nymphs the 'merchandise' to be obtained and staying under the Blessed One's instruction, he was like one bought by the Blessed One through that merchandise, and thus called 'upakkītaka.'

'Aṭṭīyamāno' means being oppressed and thus coming to suffering. 'Harāyamāno' means being ashamed. 'Jigucchamāno' means regarding as loathsome. 'Eko' means being without a companion. 'Vūpakaṭṭho' means being withdrawn physically and mentally from sensual objects (vatthu-kāma) and defilements (kilesa-kāma). 'Appamatto' means not abandoning mindfulness in the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna). 'Ātāpī' means one who has effort, which is the heat produced in body and mind. Because it burns away defilements, effort is called 'ātāpa.' 'Pahitatto' means having a mind sent towards the meditation subject without regard for body or life, or having a mind sent towards Nibbāna. 'Na cirasseva' means not long after starting the meditation subject. 'Yassatthāya' means for the sake of which (the fruit of Arahantship). 'Kulaputtā'—there are two kinds of sons of good family: by birth (jāti-kulaputta) and by conduct (ācāra-kulaputta); this Venerable Nanda was a son of good family in both ways. 'Sammadeva' means properly, by way of reason and cause. 'Agārasmā' means from home. 'Anagāriyaṃ' means the state of homelessness (monkhood). Since activities belonging to the home, such as plowing and trading, do not exist in this monkhood, it is called 'anagāriya.' 'Pabbajanti' means they go forth. 'Tadanuttaraṃ brahmacariyapariyosānaṃ' means the fruit of Arahantship, which is the culmination of the holy life of the path. For the sake of that fruit of Arahantship, sons of good family go forth in this Dispensation. 'Diṭṭheve dhamme' means in that very life. 'Sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā' means realizing for oneself through one's own wisdom and knowing without depending on others. 'Upasampajja vihāsī' means he lived having attained or having fulfilled it. While living thus, in the statement 'Birth is exhausted... he knew,' this shows the stage of his reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇā).

In that context, 'Birth is exhausted' does not mean past birth is exhausted, as it was already exhausted; nor does it mean future birth, as it has not yet arrived; nor does it mean the present life, as it still clearly exists. However, because the path has been developed, the births that would have occurred in the one-constituent, four-constituent, and five-constituent realms have reached the state of not arising again; therefore, it is said 'exhausted.' The Venerable Nanda, having reviewed that birth as having its defilements abandoned through the development of the path, knew through higher knowledge that although kamma exists, since there are no defilements, there is no more birth now. 'Vusitaṃ' means lived or completed. 'Brahmacariyaṃ' is the holy life of the path. Although worldlings and the seven types of trainees (sekha) are still practicing the holy life, an Arahant is called 'one who has lived' (vusitavā) it.
157:
In that text, 'khīṇā jāti' (birth is exhausted) means that past birth cannot be exhausted because it has already ceased; future birth cannot be exhausted because it has not yet arrived; and the present existence cannot be exhausted because it is currently manifest. However, the birth consisting of one, four, or five aggregates in the realms of one-constituent existence (ekavokāra-bhava), four-constituent existence (catuvokāra-bhava), and five-constituent existence (pañcavokāra-bhava), which would have arisen because the Path had not yet been developed, is now exhausted because it has reached the state of non-arising through the development of the Path. The Elder Nanda, having reflected on the defilements abandoned by the development of the Path, understood with higher knowledge that although karma is still manifest, it will no longer lead to rebirth because of the absence of defilements.

'Vusitaṃ' means lived, practiced, or completed. 'Brahmacariyaṃ' refers to the holy life of the Path. This is because the seven types of trainees (sekha) along with the noble worldlings (kalyāṇa-puthujjana) are said to be 'living' the holy life, whereas the Arahant is one who 'has lived' it.
