Therefore, the Elder Nanda, reflecting on his own practice of living the holy life in the Dispensation, understood: "The holy life has been lived."

'Kataṃ karaṇီyaṃ' means that the sixteen-fold task—consisting of full understanding (pariññā), abandoning (pahāna), realization (sacchikiriyā), and development (bhāvanā) regarding the Four Noble Truths through the four Paths—has been completed. This is because noble worldlings and others are still 'doing' that task, whereas the Arahant is one who 'has done' what was to be done. Therefore, the Elder Nanda, reflecting on his own duty, understood: "Done is what was to be done."

'Nāparaṃ itthattāya' means he understood: "Now, for this kind of state, there is no further task for me to develop the Path for the sake of the sixteen-fold duty or for the exhaustion of defilements." Alternatively, 'nāparaṃ itthattāya' means he understood: "There is no further succession of aggregates for me beyond this present succession of aggregates of this kind. These five aggregates, having been fully understood, remain like a tree with its roots cut; they will be extinguished like a fire without fuel upon the cessation of the final consciousness, and will reach the state of being indescribable."

'Aññataro' means a certain person. 'Arahataṃ' means he became one of the great disciples among the Arahant disciples of the Blessed One.

'Aññatarā devatā' refers to a certain Brahma deity who had attained the Path. This is because that deity, being an adept (asekha) herself, understood the domain of an adept. Trainees (sekha) understand their respective trainee-domains, and worldlings (puthujjana) understand only their own worldling-domain.

'Abhikkantāya rattiyā' means when the night was far spent, in the middle watch. 'Abhikkantavaṇṇā' means having a most excellent complexion. 'Kevalakappaṃ' means entirely, from all around. 'Obhāsetvā' means having illuminated the entire Jetavana monastery at once with her own radiance, like the moon or the sun. 'Tenupasaṅkamī' means that, having known that the Venerable Nanda had reached the fruit of Arahantship and being filled with joy and appreciation, she approached the Blessed One with the intention of reporting this matter. In the phrase 'āsavānaṃ khayā', the etymological definition is as follows: those states which...
158:
(The deity), having known that the Venerable Nanda had reached the fruit of Arahantship and being filled with joy and appreciation, approached the Blessed One with the intention of reporting that matter.

In the phrase 'āsavānaṃ khayā', the term 'āsava' (taints) is so called because they arise and flow out from the eye-door and so forth. Alternatively, they are called 'āsava' because they flow up to the change-of-lineage (gotrabhū) or up to the peak of existence (bhavagga); meaning they occur by including these states and this spatial world within their scope. They are called 'āsava' in the sense of being long-fermented, like the 'āsava' (fermented liquor) made from mango juice and the like. Their state of being long-fermented should be understood from such sayings as: "Bhikkhus, the preceding starting point of ignorance is not evident" (A.N. 10.61). Alternatively, they are called 'āsava' because they produce (flow) the long suffering of saṃsāra. Among these meanings, the first applies to defilements (kilesa), and the latter also applies to karma. Not only karma and defilements are called 'āsava', but indeed various kinds of afflictions (upaddava) are also called 'āsava'. This is true: in the passage, "Cunda, I do not teach the Dhamma only for the restraint of taints belonging to the present life" (D.N. 3.182), the defilements which are the root of disputes are intended as 'āsava'.

"That taint by which one would arise as a god, or as a gandhabba, or a bird,
By which one would go to the state of a yakkha, or reach the human state,
Those taints of mine are exhausted, destroyed, and brought to ruin."

In this passage (A.N. 4.36), karma belonging to the three planes of existence and the remaining unwholesome states are intended as 'āsava'. In the phrase, "For the restraint of taints belonging to the present life, for the warding off of taints belonging to the future life" (Pārājika 39), it refers to various afflictions such as the harming of others, remorse, killing, and imprisonment, as well as the various afflictions that constitute the suffering of the states of deprivation (apāya).

Furthermore, these taints appear as two kinds in the Vinaya: "Taints belonging to the present life and taints belonging to the future life." In the Saḷāyatana Saṃyutta, they appear as three kinds: "Friends, there are these three taints: the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava), the taint of existence (bhavāsava), and the taint of ignorance (avijjāsava)" (D.N. 3.305). The same is true in other Suttas. In the Abhidhamma, they appear as four kinds by adding the taint of views (diṭṭhāsava) to those three. In the Nibbedhika Sutta, they appear as five kinds, starting with: "Bhikkhus, there are taints leading to hell" (A.N. 6.63). In the Chakka Nipāta, they appear as six kinds, starting with: "Bhikkhus, there are taints to be abandoned by restraint" (A.N. 6.58).
159:
In terms of method, they are presented in six ways. In the Sabbāsava Sutta, those same taints (āsavas) are presented in seven ways, together with the things to be abandoned by the Path of Stream-entry and so forth. However, here, according to the Abhidhamma method, the four taints should be understood.

Regarding the word "khayā": In passages such as "the destruction (khaya), breaking up, and complete breaking up of the taints," the destruction of the self-nature of the taints is called the destruction of taints (āsavakkhaya). In passages such as "Monks, I say the destruction of the taints is for one who knows and sees," the non-arising of taints in the future is called the destruction of taints.

In verses such as:
"For the trainee (sekha) who is practicing, following the straight path,
First knowledge arises in the destruction [of taints], and immediately after that, the final knowledge,"
the Path (magga) is called the destruction of taints. In passages such as "By the destruction of the taints, one becomes a recluse (samaṇa)," the Fruit (phala) is meant.

In verses such as:
"For one who constantly observes the faults of others and is always intent on blaming,
His taints increase; he is far from the destruction of taints,"
Nibbāna is called the destruction of taints. But in this context, the absolute destruction, or non-arising, or the Path of the taints is called "the destruction of the taints" (āsavānaṃ khayo).

"Anāsavaṃ" means one who has completely abandoned the taints through the power of subsiding. "Cetovimuttiṃ" refers to the concentration of the Fruit of Arahantship. "Paññāvimuttiṃ" refers to the wisdom of the Fruit of Arahantship. The use of both terms is to show the yoking together (yuganandha) of serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā) in the Fruit, just as in the Path. "Ñāṇaṃ" refers to omniscient knowledge (sabbaññutañāṇa). Immediately after the deity's words, as the Blessed One was reflecting, "How is it?" omniscient knowledge arose in Him: "Nanda has realized the Fruit of Arahantship."

Indeed, when the Venerable Nanda was thus teased by his companion monks, he felt spiritual urgency (saṃvega), thinking, "It is a very heavy thing I have done, that having gone forth in this well-expounded Dhamma-Vinaya, I have made the Teacher a guarantor for the sake of obtaining celestial nymphs." Establishing shame and fear of wrongdoing (hiri-ottappa), and striving with effort, he reached the Fruit of Arahantship and thought, "What if I were to release the Blessed One from that promise?" He approached the Blessed One and informed the Teacher of his intention. Therefore, it was said: "Then the Venerable Nanda... from that promise." In that text, "paṭissavā" means the guarantee or promise, based on the acknowledgment: "I am the guarantor for the sake of obtaining celestial nymphs."
160:
Then the Blessed One said to the Venerable Nanda: "I know that you have realized the Fruit of Arahantship; a deity has also informed me. Therefore, I am now released from the promise, because you have been released by reaching the Fruit of Arahantship; I am no longer a guarantor." Therefore, He spoke the words beginning with "Yad eva kho te nanda." In that text, "yad eva" means "at the very time." "Te" means "your." "Mutto" means "released." This is the meaning: At the very time your mind was released from the taints, immediately after reaching that Fruit of Arahantship, I, the Buddha, was released from that guarantee.

The Venerable Nanda himself, at the very time of practicing insight, became energetic, thinking, "Because of my lack of restraint of the sense faculties, I have come to this state of perversion; I shall thoroughly subdue that lack of restraint." Having strong shame and fear of wrongdoing (hiri-ottappa), and because of his past aspirations regarding the virtue of restraint of the sense faculties (indriyasaṃvara-sīla), he reached the highest practice in guarding the sense faculties. For it was said:

"Monks, if Nanda has to look towards the eastern direction, having concentrated his whole mind, Nanda looks towards the eastern direction, thinking, 'While I am looking towards the eastern direction in this way, may no evil unwholesome states of covetousness and grief follow and afflict me.' Thus, he is one with clear comprehension (sampajāna) in that matter."

"Monks, if Nanda has to look towards the western direction... northern... southern... upward... downward... or the intermediate directions, having well-collected his whole mind, he looks, reflecting, 'While I am looking in this way... (and so forth).' Thus, he is one with clear comprehension in that matter," He said. For that reason, the Teacher placed the Venerable Nanda in the foremost position (etadagga), saying: "Monks, among my disciple monks who guard the doors of the sense faculties, Nanda is the foremost."

"Etam-atthaṃ viditvā" means having known in every way that meaning, which is the attainment of the state of being steadfast (tādi) in the face of happiness and so forth, after the Venerable Nanda had exhausted all taints. "Imaṃ udānaṃ" means He uttered this inspired utterance which explains that meaning.

In that verse of inspired utterance, "yassa nittiṇṇo paṅko" means that noble person who, by the bridge of the Noble Path, has crossed the mire of all views or the deep mire of saṃsāra by going to the further shore of Nibbāna. "Maddito kāmakaṇḍako" means that person has, with the staff of Path-knowledge, struck and crushed all the thorns of defilements and the thorns of objective sensuality, which are called "thorns of desire" because they pierce beings; he has destroyed them without remainder. Having reached the Nibbāna of the Fruit of Arahantship where delusion is exhausted, that monk who has destroyed the defilements is unshaken by happiness arising in connection with pleasant objects, or by pain arising in connection with unpleasant objects; he does not reach a state of mental perversion because of that happiness or pain. The phrase "sukhadukkhesu" is merely a teaching sequence; it means being unshaken by all worldly conditions (lokadhamma).

## The Commentary on the Second Sutta is Finished.
161:
Because it pierces beings, it is called the "thorn of sensual desire" (kāma-kaṇṭaka). All sensual desire (kilesa-kāma) and all distractions of sensual pleasure (kāma-visūka, the thorn of objective sensuality) have been struck and subdued by the staff of supreme knowledge, destroyed, and crushed without remainder. "Attained the destruction of delusion" means that, by destroying all delusion which is the domain of suffering and so forth, one has reached the destruction of delusion and subsequently attained the fruit of Arahantship and Nibbāna. "That monk who does not tremble in pleasure and pain" means that the monk who has destroyed the defilements does not tremble or shake when pleasure arises from union with pleasant objects or when pain arises from union with unpleasant objects; he does not undergo any mental alteration because of those causes. The phrase "in pleasure and pain" is merely a teaching method; it should be understood that he does not tremble in any of the worldly conditions (lokadhamma).

## The Commentary on the Second Sutta is finished.

## 3. Commentary on the Yasojā Sutta

In the third sutta, in the phrase "led by Yasojā" (Yasojappamukhāni), "Yasojā" is the name of that elder. Because those five hundred monks went forth making him their leader and moved about together, they are called "the monks led by Yasojā."

Their past practice was as follows: Long ago, during the dispensation of the Kassapa Buddha, a certain forest-dwelling monk lived in a leaf-hut built on a flat rock in the forest. At that time, five hundred robbers, who lived by plundering villages and so forth, were being pursued by the people of the countryside. Fleeing and entering the forest, they saw no refuge or shelter until they saw that monk sitting on the rock nearby. They paid homage to him, told him the situation, and pleaded, "Venerable sir, be our refuge." The elder said, "There is no refuge for you like virtue (sīla). All of you, undertake the five precepts." They accepted, saying "Very well," and undertook the precepts. The elder advised them with the Simile of the Saw: "Now you are established in virtue; do not harbor ill-will in your minds even toward those who take your lives." They accepted, saying "Very well." Then the country folk arrived at that place, searched here and there, found the robbers, and took all of their lives.
162:
Those robbers, without harboring even a slight ill-will toward the country folk, with minds that were not repulsed and with virtue that was unbroken and unblemished, passed away and were reborn in the heavens of the sense sphere (kāmāvacara-deva). Among them, the chief robber became the senior deva-son, and the others were his attendants. Wandering through saṃsāra, they spent the interval between two Buddhas in the deva world. In the time of our Blessed One, they passed away from the deva world. The senior deva-son was reborn as the son of a master fisherman in a fishing village of five hundred families near the gate of the city of Sāvatthī; they named him Yasojā. The others were also reborn as the sons of the remaining fishermen. Due to their past association, they all became friends. While playing together in the dust, they eventually reached maturity, and Yasojā became their leader. They all stayed together, taking nets and wandering about catching fish in rivers, lakes, and ponds. 

Then one day, when they cast a net into the Aciravatī River, a golden-colored fish entered the net. Seeing it, all the fishermen were delighted, thinking, "Our sons have caught a golden-colored fish while fishing." Then those five hundred friends placed the fish on a boat, lifted the boat, and showed it to the King. The King, seeing it, thought, "The Blessed One will know the reason for this fish's golden color," and had the fish taken to show the Blessed One. The Teacher said, "This fish became a monk when the dispensation of Kassapa Buddha was declining. By practicing wrongly and causing the dispensation to decline, he was reborn in hell. After being cooked in hell for the interval between two Buddhas, he passed away from there and was reborn as a fish in the Aciravatī River." He then had the fish itself speak about how its mother and sister were reborn in hell and how its elder brother had attained Parinibbāna. Based on this incident, he taught the Kapila Sutta. 

Hearing the Teacher's discourse, those five hundred sons of fishermen were struck with spiritual urgency (saṃvega). They went forth in the presence of the Blessed One, received full ordination, and lived in seclusion. Later, they came to see the Blessed One. Therefore, it is said: "At that time, about five hundred monks led by Yasojā..." and so forth. 

In that text, "tedhā" means "te idha" (they here). "Nevāsikehi" means "with those who live there permanently." "Paṭisammodamānā" means that when the resident monks performed the greeting by saying, "Friend, is it bearable? Is it tolerable?" and so forth, those visiting monks responded, "Yes, friend, it is bearable; it is tolerable," thus exchanging friendly greetings together. Arranging lodgings means that after inquiring about the places obtained for their teachers and preceptors as well as for themselves, and when the resident monks assigned the lodgings saying, "This place is for your teachers, this is for your preceptors, this is for you," they went to those places, opened the main doors and windows, took out the couches, benches, mats, and rugs, shook them out, arranged them appropriately, and put away their bowls and robes. Putting away bowls and robes means storing the monks' requisites while saying, "Venerable sirs, please place this bowl of mine here, place this robe here, place this stone bowl, this water bottle, and this walking staff here." "Mahāsaddā" (loud noise) refers to a high-pitched sound.
163:
With the words "khamanīya" and so forth, they again greeted the resident monks joyfully. "Arranging the lodgings" means they asked about the places allotted for their teachers, preceptors, and themselves. When the resident monks arranged the lodgings, saying, "This is for your teachers, this is for your preceptors, this is for you," they went there themselves, opened the doors, took out the couches, stools, mats, and rugs, dusted them, and arranged them in their proper places.

"Storing the bowls and robes" means they stored the requisites of the monks, saying, "Venerable sirs, please put away this bowl of mine, this robe, this stone bowl, this water pot, and this walking staff." "Having loud and great voices"—it is called "uccāsadda" (loud noise) because the sound rises upwards (changing the 'a' to 'ā'), and "mahāsadda" (great noise) because the sound spreads all around. "Like fishermen plundering fish" means just as fishermen—so called because they move about in the water to catch fish—cast their nets into the water and make loud and great noises, saying, "Has it entered? Has it not? Is it caught? Is it not?" Furthermore, when many people come to the place where the fishermen keep their fish baskets and scramble for them, saying, "Give me one fish, give me a slice of fish, the one given to that person is big, the one given to me is small," and so on, loud and great noises arise due to the fishermen's prohibitions and so forth. This is shown to illustrate that these monks acted in the same way.

"Te te" refers to those monks. "Kiṃ nu" means for what purpose. "Te me" refers to those monks. "Paṇāmemi" means I dismiss or expel. "Vo" means you. "You should not stay in my presence" means: "You who come to the dwelling place of a Buddha like me and make such a great noise, how can you behave appropriately when living according to your own nature? There is no need for people like you to stay in my presence." When the Blessed One dismissed them in this way, not even a single monk among them said, "Venerable Sir, do you dismiss us just for a loud noise?" or any other retort. Out of respect for the Buddha, they all accepted the Blessed One's words, saying, "Very well, Venerable Sir," and departed.

The monks thought: "We came to see the Teacher, to hear the Dhamma, and to stay in the Teacher's presence, but having come to such a Buddha's presence, we have made a great noise. It is only our fault. Therefore, because we are dismissed, we no longer have the opportunity to stay in the Teacher's presence, to behold his inspiring golden-hued body, or to listen to the Dhamma preached with his Brahma-voice." Thinking thus, the five hundred monks, led by the Elder Yasoja, were deeply distressed and departed.

"Saṃsedamettaṃ" refers to the princes living in the district called "Vo". A district that was the dwelling place of those Vajjī princes is also called "Vo". Therefore, it is said "among the Vajjīs". "Vā" is a river designated as a place for performing meritorious deeds by those people. There is also a Pali reading "Vaggumudā". "Atthakāmena" means desiring only welfare, without regard for any gain from offerings. "Hitesinā" means desiring the benefit: "How may my disciples be liberated from the suffering of saṃsāra?" Desiring the welfare of those... that which is called the Unconditioned...
164:
“We have come to the presence of the Teacher and made a great noise; this is our own fault, and because of it, we have been expelled. Having been expelled, we no longer have the opportunity to stay in the presence of the Blessed One, to behold his golden-hued body which inspires confidence from all sides, or to listen to the Dhamma taught with a sweet voice.” Thinking thus, those monks departed, filled with intense distress.

“Saṃsāmetvā” means having put away well. “Vajjī” is the name of such a district; it refers to the royal princes living in the Vajjī district. A single district that is the dwelling place of those princes is also traditionally called “Vajjī.” Therefore, it is said “among the Vajjīs” (Vajjīsu). “Vaggumudā” is a river regarded by the people as a place for merit. There is also a reading “Vaggamudā.” “Atthakāmena” means desiring the benefit without expecting any personal advantage. “Hitesinā” means seeking welfare, with the thought, “How may my disciples be liberated from the suffering of the round of rebirths?” It implies the habit of seeking that welfare, which is the benefit or the cause of that benefit. For that very reason, without considering his own physical exhaustion, he is a “compassionate one” (anukampaka) who travels even to distant places to reach those to be tamed out of compassion. It was out of that very compassion that we were expelled, not out of a desire for personal service and so forth.

Since the Blessed Buddhas, who honor the Dhamma, should be worshipped only through right practice, and since they expel those who merely make a loud noise, therefore, friends, let us now live by fulfilling the “unmistakable practice” (apaṇṇaka-paṭipadā), being endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension in all postures, bringing our chosen meditation subjects to the summit, and thus spend our time in the four postures. “Yathā no viharataṃ” means “so that while we are living thus, the Blessed One may be pleased, and he may be propitiated by the worship of right practice.”

“Teneva antaravassena” means within that very rainy season, without even passing the Great Pavāraṇā. “Sabbēva tisso vijjā sacchākaṃsu” means all those five hundred monks personally realized the three knowledges: the knowledge of recollecting past lives, the knowledge of the divine eye, and the knowledge of the destruction of taints. These are called “knowledges” (vijjā) because they pierce through the mass of delusion that covers the aggregates lived in the past, etc. Among the mundane superknowledges, only these two (the first two) are of great assistance to the knowledge of the destruction of taints; the knowledges of the divine ear, penetration of minds, and various psychic powers are not so. To show this, only the three knowledges are highlighted here in terms of the monks’ attainment. Indeed, in the Verañja Sutta, the Blessed One, when showing his own attainment to the Brahmin Verañja, taught only the three knowledges, not because of the absence of the divine ear, etc. Similarly, although they existed in those monks, the divine ear and so forth were not highlighted.
165:
Although the divine ear and other knowledges were not explicitly mentioned, those monks were indeed possessors of the six superknowledges (chalabhiññā). Because they were so endowed, the text will later describe their use of psychic power: “Having vanished from the banks of the Vaggumudā River, they appeared before the Blessed One in the Gabled Hall (Kūṭāgārasālā) in the Great Forest (Mahāvana).”

“Yathābhirantaṃ” means as long as one likes, according to one’s inclination. In truth, for the Buddhas residing in a certain place, there is no such thing as “discontent” (anabhirati) arising from the deficiency of shade or water, uncomfortable lodgings, or the lack of faith in people. Nor do they stay for a long time thinking “we live comfortably” because of the abundance of shade and so forth. However, the Teacher stays in a place where people, while the Blessed One is residing there, might establish themselves in the refuges, undertake the precepts, go forth into homelessness, or reach the Path of Stream-entry and so forth, for the purpose of establishing them in those achievements. In the absence of such benefits, he departs. At that time, there was no further Buddha-duty to be performed in Sāvatthī. Therefore, it is said: “Then the Blessed One, having stayed in Sāvatthī as long as he liked, set out on a wandering tour toward Vesālī.”

“Cārikaṃ caramāno” means traveling a long distance. This wandering of the Blessed One is of two kinds: “urgent wandering” (turita-cārikā) and “leisurely wandering” (aturita-cārikā). Among them, seeing a person capable of enlightenment (bodheneyya) even in a distant place and going there quickly for their enlightenment is called “urgent wandering”; this can be seen in instances such as going to meet the Venerable Mahā Kassapa. Traveling gradually through villages, market towns, and royal capitals, at the rate of one league or half a league per day, benefiting the world through alms-round and so forth, is called “leisurely wandering.” This latter one is intended here. “Tadavasarī” means he arrived at that [Vesālī] or entered it.

“Tatra” means in that Vesālī. “Sudaṃ” is merely a particle. “Vesāliyaṃ” refers to the city of the Licchavī kings, which received the name “Vesālī” because it was expanded (visālī-bhūta) three times. “Mahāvane” refers to the Great Forest. The Great Forest is a large, naturally grown forest, not planted by humans, and it has defined boundaries. The Great Forest near Kapilavatthu, however, is connected to the Himalayas and stands without boundaries, reaching as far as the Great Ocean. This [Vesālī forest] is not like that; it is a large forest with boundaries, hence called “Mahāvana.” “Kူဋာဂါရသာလာယံ” (Kūṭāgārasālā) refers to the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭi) of the Blessed Buddha, which was built within the monastery dedicated to the Blessed One in that Great Forest, featuring a gabled roof (kūṭāgāra) and covered in the shape of a swan’s wing, endowed with all excellent features.
166:
It occurred in that Kūṭāgārasālā monastery. "Vaggumudātīriyānaṃ" means those (monks) living on the banks of the Vaggumudā river. "Cetasa cetoparicca manasi karitvā" means encompassing the minds of those monks with his own mind and attending to it; or it means knowing the special attainment achieved by those monks through the knowledge of encompassing the minds of others (cetopariyañāṇa) or through the knowledge of omniscience (sabbaññutañāṇa).

"Ālokajātā viya" means as if light had arisen. The next phrase is a synonym for it, meaning as if illuminated by a thousand moons and a thousand suns. Because those five hundred monks, headed by the Elder Yasoja, lived as light and radiance by utterly destroying the darkness of ignorance (avijjā), the Blessed One praised those monks by way of a eulogy, referring to the direction where they were staying, saying: "Ānanda, this direction appears to me as if light had arisen." Therefore, he said: "In whichever direction the monks living on the banks of the Vaggumudā river dwell." "Appaṭikūlā" means not repulsive; "manāpā" means pleasing to the heart. Indeed, the place where the Great Sages (Arahants) endowed with virtues such as morality (sīla) dwell, even if it is a place of hills, valleys, uneven ground, and dangers, is certainly pleasant and delightful. For it has been said:

"Whether in a village or in a forest, in a valley or on a hill, wherever the Arahants dwell, that ground is delightful." (Dhammapada 98)

"Pahiṇeyyāsi" means you should send. This shows the manner of sending to those monks because the Teacher wished to see the venerable ones. The Blessed One, seeing that the purpose for which he had dismissed those monks had reached its pinnacle, with a satisfied mind, informed the Elder Ānanda of his desire to see them. It is said that he had this thought: "I will dismiss these monks for making a loud noise; then, like noble thoroughbred horses urged by the stroke of a whip, they will be urged by that dismissal and, reaching a sense of urgency (saṃvega), will enter the forest and strive to please me, and will quickly realize Arahantship." Now, seeing that they had reached the highest fruit, with a mind satisfied by their attainment of Arahantship, he commanded the Treasurer of the Dhamma, the Elder Ānanda, because he wished to see them.

"So bhikkhu" refers to a certain monk with the six higher powers (chaḷabhiñño) who was so commanded by the Elder Ānanda. "Pamukhe" means in the presence. "Āneñjasamādhinā" means by the concentration of the fruit of Arahantship based on the fourth jhāna; some also say "based on the immaterial jhānas." There is also a variant reading "āneñjena samādhinā".
167:
There is also a variant reading "samādhinā". Why did the Blessed One, knowing the arrival of those monks, not perform a greeting (paṭisanthāra) but instead enter only into a meditative attainment (samāpatti)? He entered it to let them know his own entry into attainment, to show those who were previously dismissed that they now possess an attainment similar to his own, to demonstrate his psychic power, and to show the declaration of their Arahantship without breaking into speech. Others, however, say: "It was to perform a unique greeting for those who were previously dismissed and have now come to his presence, by producing unsurpassed happiness." Those venerable ones also, knowing the Blessed One's intention, entered into that very same attainment. Therefore, it was said: "By what dwelling does the Blessed One now dwell?" and so forth.

In this context, the fourth fine-material jhāna is called "āneñja" (imperturbable) because it is very far from opposing states such as laziness, because it is endowed with the sixteen factors of purification (vodānadhamma) such as "unlowered mind" (anona-manas) which are the basis for psychic powers, and because it is itself unshakable. For it has been said:

The unlowered mind is imperturbable because it is not shaken by laziness.
The unelated mind is imperturbable because it is not shaken by restlessness (uddhacca).
The undissatisfied mind is imperturbable because it is not shaken by lust (rāga).
The unbent-away mind is imperturbable because it is not shaken by ill-will (byāpāda).
The independent mind is imperturbable because it is not shaken by wrong view (diṭṭhi).
The unfettered mind is imperturbable because it is not shaken by desire and lust (chandarāga).
The released mind is imperturbable because it is not shaken by sensual lust (kāmarāga).
The disassociated mind is imperturbable because it is not shaken by defilements (kilesa).
The boundless mind is imperturbable because it is not shaken by the boundaries of defilements.
The unified mind is imperturbable because it is not shaken by various defilements.
The mind grasped by faith is imperturbable because it is not shaken by lack of faith.
The mind grasped by energy is imperturbable because it is not shaken by laziness.
The mind grasped by mindfulness is imperturbable because it is not shaken by negligence (pamāda).
The mind grasped by concentration is imperturbable because it is not shaken by restlessness.
The mind grasped by wisdom is imperturbable because it is not shaken by ignorance (avijjā).
The mind that has reached illumination is imperturbable because it is not shaken by the darkness of ignorance.

The fourth fine-material jhāna itself, when developed by way of the meditation on the fading away of form, and the four immaterial jhānas by way of the division of objects—these five jhānas are termed "āneñja". The ancient teachers say that the fruition attainment of Arahantship (arahattaphala-samāpatti) entered into by making any of these five as a basis is "āneñjasamādhi".
168:
"Abhikkantāya" means passed (atītāya). "Nikkhante" means gone out, disappeared (niggata, apagata). "Tuṇhī ahosi" means the Blessed One remained silent with noble silence (ariyatuṇhībhāva). "Uddhaste aruṇe" means when dawn has risen. Dawn (aruṇa) is the light that appears in the eastern direction before sunrise. "Nandimukhiyā" means as the dawn rises in the night, the night becomes bright (vibhāyamānāya), like a face that gladdens beings who live by the light of the sun.

"Tamhā samādhimhā vuṭṭhahitvā" means emerging from that imperturbable concentration (āneñjasamādhi), which is the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphalasamāpatti), according to the predetermined time. "Sace kho tvaṃ, Ānanda, jāneyyāsi" means "Ānanda, if you had known that these monks spent this much time in the bliss of this attainment," then "ettakampi te nappaṭibhāseyyā" means that even this much would not have occurred to you to say, referring to the worldly greeting, "Venerable Sir, the night has passed," etc., which you intended to say three times. Ānanda, because you are a trainee (sekha) and do not know the dwelling in the attainment of non-trainees (asekkhasamāpattivihāra), you made an effort to have these monks greeted according to worldly custom. To show that "I and these five hundred monks have spent the three watches of the night only with supramundane joy," the Blessed One said, "Ānanda, I and all these five hundred monks sat in imperturbable concentration."

"Etamatthaṃ viditvā" means having known in every way the matter of their mastery (vasībhāva), which is the ability to enter imperturbable concentration along with himself. "Imaṃ udānaṃ" means he uttered this inspired utterance showing the nature of these monks' success in abandoning lust and so forth without remainder.

In that verse of inspired utterance, "yassa jito kāmakaṇḍako" means the thorn of defilement-based sensuality (kilesakāma), which is like a thorn because it pierces the side of merit, has been completely conquered (abandoned) by that noble person; by this victory, it shows the absence of attachment (anunaya) in that person. "Gāmakaṇṭako" is also a variant reading. Its meaning is: he by whom all objective sensuality (vatthukāma), which is like a thorn in the village, has been conquered. Victory should be understood only through the abandonment of desire and lust (chandarāga) bound to that objective sensuality. Therefore, this refers to the Path of Non-returning (anāgāmimagga) of those monks.
169:
"Conquered abuse" (akkoso ca jito) is connected to the preceding words. In the case of "killing and binding" (vadho ca bandhanañca), the same method should be understood. Among those victories, by conquering abuse, the absence of verbal misconduct is shown; by the others, the absence of bodily misconduct is shown. By showing this, the Path of Non-returning (tatiyamagga) is meant, due to the abandonment of ill-will (byāpāda) which is the cause of such misconduct, without remainder. Alternatively, by saying that abuse and so forth are conquered, the Third Path is spoken of; in that path, the absolute patience (khanti) towards abuse and so forth is manifested. In both ways, it shows the absence of conflict in them.

In "standing like a mountain, imperturbable" (pabbato viya so ṭhito anejo), the disturbance of defilements is called ejā. One is aneja (imperturbable) due to the absence of the remaining defilements which are the causes of ejā. Because of being imperturbable, one is unshakable by all defilements and by the winds of others' doctrines, thus standing like a solid rock mountain. "That monk does not tremble in pleasure or pain" means that the monk who has destroyed defilements is not shaken by the causes of pleasure and pain, as should be understood by the method mentioned below. Thus, the Blessed One, having unified the attainment of the state of tādi through the achievement of Arahantship by those five hundred monks, uttered this inspired utterance based on a single person.

## The Commentary on the Third Sutta is finished.

## 4. Commentary on the Sāriputta Sutta

In the fourth sutta, "setting up mindfulness in front" (parimukhaṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā) means setting up mindfulness directed towards the object, having placed it near the face (such as the tip of the nose). For it is said in the Vibhaṅga: "This mindfulness is present, well-established at the tip of the nose or at the sign of the face; therefore it is said, 'setting up mindfulness in front'."

Alternatively, pari has the sense of grasping, mukha has the sense of release (leading out), and sati has the sense of presence. Therefore, it is called parimukhaṃ satiṃ. The meaning here should also be understood according to the method stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga. The summary of the meaning in that text is: having made mindfulness of release grasped. Niyyāna (release) should be seen as the object to be plunged into by mindfulness. Here, the first and last meanings should be understood by way of encompassing everything, while the middle meaning should be understood by way of attention in the preliminary stage of the attainment. Sati refers to Jhāna with mindfulness as the head. It is just as in the Kāyagatāsati Sutta and others. If it is asked what that Jhāna is, it is the Jhāna of the fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphalajhāna) entered by taking the fourth form-sphere Jhāna as the object. If it is asked how this is known, the Blessed One uttered this verse of inspired utterance using the mountain simile to show the state of being completely imperturbable and the state of being indestructible by anyone, through the Venerable Sāriputta's imperturbable concentration. By this verse, this meaning should be understood. This sitting was not for the Venerable Sāriputta's realization of the Four Noble Truths, but rather for dwelling happily in the present life (diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra). That statement alone is appropriate. It should be understood that while the Blessed One was teaching the Dhamma to the wanderer Dīghanakha, the nephew of the Elder, in the Sukarakhata Cave, this Great Elder brought the task of realizing the Four Noble Truths to completion. That completion was due to the Elder's reaching the state of tādi through imperturbable concentration.
170:
As stated in the Aṅguttara Nikāya in such passages as "Those who enjoy mindfulness directed to the body..." and so forth, jhāna is intended here with mindfulness as its basis. What is that jhāna? It is the fruition of Arahantship jhāna attained by taking the fourth fine-material jhāna as a basis. How is this to be known? This meaning is to be understood from the verse itself, where the Blessed One uttered this inspired utterance (udāna) while illustrating, by means of the mountain simile, the Elder Sāriputta's particularly motionless state and his unshakeability by anyone through his engagement in imperturbable concentration (āneñja-samādhi). This sitting of the Elder was not for the penetration of the Four Noble Truths, but rather for dwelling in happiness in this very life (diṭṭhadhamma-sukhavihāra). For previously, while the Blessed One was teaching the Dhamma to his nephew, the wanderer Dīghanakha, in the Sūkarakhata cave, this Great Elder had already brought the task of penetrating the Truths to its culmination.

"Etam-atthaṃ": having known in every aspect that meaning, characterized as the state of being unshakeable by anyone due to the Elder's attainment of the state of "suchness" (tādibhāva) through his engagement in imperturbable concentration, he uttered this inspired utterance that clarifies that meaning.

In that verse, "yathāpi pabbato selo" means just like a mountain made of solid rock, being a single mass of rock, and not a mountain of earth or a mixed mountain. "Acalo suppatiṭṭhito" means being well-established at the base, it is motionless and unshakeable by natural winds. "Evaṃ mohakkhayā bhikkhu, pabbato va na vedhati": because of the total abandonment of delusion, and because delusion is the root of all unwholesome states, the monk who has abandoned all unwholesome states does not waver or shake due to the worldly conditions (lokadhamma), just as that mountain is not shaken by natural winds. Alternatively, since "destruction of delusion" (mohakkhaya) refers to Nibbāna and the fruition of Arahantship, because of the attainment of Nibbāna or the fruition of Arahantship—the cause for the destruction of delusion—he is well-established in the Four Noble Truths. Thus, even when not in meditative attainment, he is unshakeable by anyone like the aforementioned mountain, let alone when he is in attainment.

## The Commentary on the Fourth Sutta is finished.

## 5. Mahāmoggallāna Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the fifth sutta, "kāyagatāya satiyā" means by mindfulness directed to the body, which has the body as its object by way of the contemplation of the body (kāyānupassanā). In this sense, which has such a characteristic, this word is...
171:
...the instrumental case (karaṇa-vibhatti). "Ajjhattaṃ" (internally): here, "internal" means one's own internal [bases]; thus it means within one's own continuity. Or else, since the "body" (kāya) here is intended as the collection of the thirty-two parts such as hair of the head, etc., which are the objects of meditation, the meaning of the word "ajjhattaṃ" should be understood as "internal to the object" (gocarajjhattaṃ). "Supatiṭṭhitāya" (well-established): well-established in the body which is either one's own internal [bases] or the object.

What is this mindfulness that is said to be "well-established internally"? The body of thirty-two parts, such as internal hair of the head, etc., was spoken of by the Blessed One in such passages as "There are in this body hair of the head, hair of the body..." and so forth. For one who develops the attention to the repulsive (paṭikūlamanasikāra) therein, the mindfulness established in the body by way of access (upacāra) and absorption (appanā) is called "mindfulness directed to the body" (kāyagatāsati). Just as this is so, for one who develops attention by way of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna), the four postures (iriyāpatha), mindfulness and clear comprehension (satisampajañña), and by way of the foul (asubha) such as the bloated and the livid, the mindfulness established in the body by way of access and absorption as appropriate is called "mindfulness directed to the body".

But here, "ajjhattaṃ kāyagatā sati" is intended as the mindfulness associated with insight (vipassanā), established by way of contemplating the characteristics such as impermanence, after having defined the four elements such as earth by any one of the four methods such as the brief method of the constituent parts (sasambhāra-saṅkhepa). The Elder Mahāmoggallāna, having practiced insight in that way, sat down after entering his own fruition attainment (phalasamāpatti). In this sutta too, the meaning of the verse should be understood by applying the method already stated, such as "This sitting was not..." and so forth.

"Etam-atthaṃ": having known that matter, namely the entering into fruition attainment by plunging into insight through the mindfulness of the body by way of defining the four elements. "Imāṃ udānaṃ": he uttered this inspired utterance which illustrates the attainment of Nibbāna through the development of the foundations of mindfulness.

In that inspired verse, "sati kāyagatā upaṭṭhitā" means the mindfulness with the characteristics previously mentioned, having reached the state of being an associate of concentration, energy, and wisdom—which are preceded by faith—through the fulfillment of their respective functions, has abandoned the opposing states. For that very reason, it is sharp and clear, and it remains established, having approached and contemplated the non-perverted nature by way of the aforementioned restraint of the body and by way of converging on a single object. Thus, by way of contemplating the four elements called "body" and the derived materiality (upādārūpa) dependent on them, and by way of defining the causes and subsequently contemplating their characteristics such as impermanence...
172: He shows mindfulness that has come through the sequence of knowledge. Or, placing mindfulness at the head, He shows only the sequence of knowledge associated with that mindfulness, which is included within the three full understandings (pariññā). "Restrained in the six bases of contact" means that a bhikkhu endowed with mindfulness established in the body, as previously mentioned, does not allow unwholesome states like covetousness (abhijjhā) and so on to arise at the six doors—the eye and so on—which are the causes of contact. Because he has developed mindfulness of the body, he penetrates with the occurrence of knowledge and blocks those states; thus, he is called "restrained therein." By this, He shows restraint through knowledge (ñāṇa-saṃvara). "The bhikkhu is always concentrated" means that the bhikkhu, having such established mindfulness and being restrained in all respects, does not let his mind wander among various objects. Contemplating through the aspects of impermanence (anicca) and so on, he exerts effort in insight (vipassanā). When his knowledge flows sharply and heroically, he is first continuously concentrated through insight-concentration (vipassanā-samādhi). From the arising of change-of-lineage knowledge (gotrabhū-ñāṇa) immediately after conformity knowledge (anuloma-ñāṇa), [he is concentrated]. "He should know his own Nibbāna" means that Nibbāna is called "his own" because it is not an object even in dreams for other worldlings (puthujjana), but for the Noble Ones (ariya), it is their unique personal quality (āveṇika-guṇa). Because it is the supreme object of the knowledge of the path and fruit (magga-phala-ñāṇa), which is similar to themselves and thus designated as "self" (atta), Nibbāna, the unconditioned element (asaṅkhata-dhātu) that brings absolute happiness, is called "his own." He should know that Nibbāna; he should penetrate it and realize it through the knowledges of the path and fruit. By this, He shows the Noble Ones' resolution (adhimuttata) towards Nibbāna. Indeed, even during the occurrence of higher mind (adhicitta/samādhi), the Noble Ones dwell with a mind that is solely bent, inclined, and sloped towards Nibbāna. Here, the connection of the verse parts should be understood as follows: for whichever bhikkhu mindfulness directed to the body (kāyagatāsati) is established, that bhikkhu is restrained in the six bases of contact; because of that restraint, being always concentrated, he should know his own Nibbāna through personal realization. In this way, the King of Dhamma shows the path of deliverance for a bhikkhu up to Arahantship by way of mindfulness of the body (kāyānupassanā satipaṭṭhāna). Another method: By the phrase "Mindfulness directed to the body is established," He shows the mindfulness of the body (kāyānupassanā satipaṭṭhāna). "Restrained in the six bases of contact" means the bases of contact are so called because contact is the cause; [he is restrained] in those bases of contact. He is restrained by the non-occurrence of craving (taṇhā) and so on regarding the six types of feeling born of eye-contact and so on, which have contact as their cause and are produced by contact. By this method, He shows the mindfulness of feelings (vedanānupassanā satipaṭṭhāna). "The bhikkhu is always concentrated" means he is concentrated because of the constant absence of distraction. That absence of distraction is the reaching of the summit of the development of the foundations of mindfulness in every way. Indeed, when contemplating the five aggregates of clinging, divided into past and so on, without remainder...
173:
He shows the foundation of mindfulness of feeling (vedanānupassanā-satipaṭṭhāna). 'A monk who is always concentrated' (satataṃ bhikkhu samāhito) means a monk who is concentrated because of the constant and continuous absence of distraction. This lack of distraction occurs in every way when the development of the foundations of mindfulness reaches its peak. This is because he investigates the five aggregates of clinging (pañcupādānakkhandhā), which are divided into past and so forth, by grasping them without remainder. By this, he shows the remaining foundations of mindfulness. 'He would know Nibbāna for himself' (jaññā nibbānam-attano) means that a monk who has destroyed the defilements and stands having brought the development of the four foundations of mindfulness to completion, would himself know the Nibbāna that is the extinction of his own defilements through reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇā-ñāṇa).

Alternatively, by the words 'mindfulness directed to the body is established' (sati kāyagatā upaṭṭhitā), he shows the Elder Mahāmoggallāna's attainment of the fullness of mindfulness by illustrating the thorough knowledge of the nature of his own body and the bodies of others. By the words 'restrained in the six bases of contact' (chasu phassāyatanesu saṃvuto), he shows the attainment of the fullness of wisdom that manifests the Elder's clear comprehension (sampajañña) by way of constant abiding, illustrating absolute restraint in the six doors such as the eye. By the words 'a monk who is always concentrated' (satataṃ bhikkhu samāhito), he shows the nine successive attainments (anupubbavihāra-samāpatti) by showing the frequency of his meditative attainments. For a monk who has become thus, according to the words 'he would know Nibbāna for himself', since his task is done and there is nothing further to be done, he would only know or contemplate his own Nibbāna without residue remaining (anupādisesa-nibbāna); it means there is nothing else for him to contemplate.

## The Explanation of the Fifth Sutta is finished.

## 6. The Explanation of the Pilindavaccha Sutta

In the sixth sutta, 'Pilindavaccha': Pilinda is the name, and they know the Elder by his clan name, Vaccha. 'He addresses with the word "wretch"' (vasalavādena samudācarati) means he addresses and speaks to the monks using the term 'wretch' (vasala), saying 'Come, wretch; go, wretch,' and so forth. 'Many monks' (sambahulā bhikkhū) means a great number of monks. Seeing the Elder addressing them in that way, and not knowing that 'being an Arahant, he speaks thus because his habitual tendencies (vāsanā) have not been abandoned,' they thought, 'I suppose this Elder addresses us thus with a mind of anger,' and with the desire to complain, they reported it to the Blessed One to make him stop that behavior.

Therefore, it is said in the Pāḷi: 'Venerable Sir, the Venerable Pilindavaccha addresses the monks with the word "wretch".' Some teachers, however, say: 'The monks knew this Elder as "He"; they wondered if this monk was addressing them with harsh words without cause.' They say that because they did not know that he spoke thus by the power of habitual tendency despite possessing superhuman qualities (uttarimanussadhamma), and because they did not believe in the Elder's state of being an Ariya, they reported the matter to the Blessed One with the intention of complaining. The Blessed One, wishing to make clear that there was no fault of anger in the Elder, sent a monk to call the Elder Pilindavaccha and said in his presence that he spoke thus by the power of habitual tendencies practiced over many past lives, and not with the intention of speaking harsh words. Therefore, it is said: 'Then the Blessed One addressed a certain monk,' and so forth. In that Pāḷi, 'having reflected on the past lives' (pubbenivāsaṃ manasikatvā) means the Blessed One intended, 'You go, (call) that monk'.
174:
For this reason, it is said in the Pali: "Venerable Sir, the Venerable Pilindavaccha addresses the monks with the word 'wretch' (vasala)." Some teachers, however, say: "The monks recognized this Elder as an Arahant, yet this monk addresses them with such harsh words. Could it be that superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma) do not actually exist in this Elder?" Thus, not understanding that such speech was due to habitual tendencies (vāsanā), and not believing in his state as an Ariyan, they reported the matter to the Blessed One with a mind to complain.

The Blessed One, wishing to reveal the absence of the stain of anger in the Elder's mind, sent a monk to call him. In his presence, He said: "This Elder speaks in this way due to the power of habits (vāsanā) practiced over many past lives; it is not with the intention of speaking harsh words." Therefore, the words beginning with "Then the Blessed One addressed a certain monk" were spoken.

In that Pali, "reflecting on past lives" (pubbenivāsaṃ manasi karitvā) means: The Teacher asked the Elder, "Vaccha, is it true that you address the monks with the word 'wretch'?" When the Elder replied, "It is true, Blessed One," the Buddha reflected, "This Vaccha does not give up the word 'wretch' due to the imprint of defilements (kilesa-vāsanā). Could it be that he was born into the Brahmin caste in past lives?" Reflecting thus with the knowledge of past lives (pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa) or with omniscient knowledge (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa), He brought to mind the succession of aggregates lived in past births, making it clear to His mind like an emblic myrobalan (āmalaka) placed on the palm of the hand. "He addressed the monks" (bhikkhū āmantesi) means He spoke to them to make them understand. Therefore, the words beginning with "Monks, do not complain" were spoken.

In that Pali, the word "mā" is a particle of prohibition, and it should be connected with the word "ujjhāyittha". "Mā ujjhāyittha" means "Do not think lowly of him" or "Do not look upon him with disparagement." In the phrase "vacchassa bhikkhuno", the dative case (sampadāna) is used because complaining has the sense of envy. Now, wishing to show the reason why the Elder should not be complained about, He said: "Monks, the monk Vaccha does not address the monks with the word 'wretch' because of the stain of anger in his mind." The meaning is: Monks, this monk Vaccha does not have a mind of anger, nor a mind corrupted by ill-will (byāpāda), when he addresses the monks as 'wretch'; his ill-will has been utterly uprooted by the Path (magga). Although he is free from the stain of anger, wishing to show the cause established in previous lives for such speech, He said the words beginning with: "Monks, for the monk Vaccha..."

In that Pali, "unmixed" (abbokiṇṇāni) means not interspersed with other castes such as Khattiya, having no others in between. "Born five hundred times in a Brahmin family" (pañca jātisatāni brāhmaṇakule paccājātāni) means that all those five hundred lives of the monk Vaccha were born successively only in the Brahmin caste.
175:
"They were" is the meaning. That address of "wretch" (vasala) was practiced for a long time; although it occurs now even while he is one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), that address of "wretch" by the monk Vaccha was practiced for a long time, for a period of five hundred lives, because of being born as a Brahmin, counting upwards from this birth. Indeed, Brahmins are stubborn with pride born of their caste and are accustomed to addressing others with the word "wretch" (vasala). Some also read "ajjhāciṇṇo" (habitually practiced); the meaning is the same. "By that" (tena) means because of that state of being practiced for a long time. By this, He shows that the cause of such speech is habitual tendency (vāsanā).

What is this "habitual tendency" (vāsanā)? It is merely a capacity produced by defilements cultivated from beginningless time, which causes behavior similar to that of those whose defilements are not yet abandoned, even in the continuity of one who is free from defilements. They also call it a certain kind of disposition (adhimutti). This habitual tendency does not exist in the continuity of the Blessed One because of the perfection of His initial aspiration (abhinīhāra) and because of His abandoning of the obstacles to the known (ñeyyāvaraṇa) where defilements are abandoned. However, in the continuity of disciples (sāvakas) and Paccekabuddhas where defilements are not abandoned in that way, it may exist. Therefore, only the Tathāgata possesses the unobstructed knowledge and vision (anāvaraṇa-ñāṇadassana).

"Having known this matter" means having known the fact that although the Venerable Pilindavaccha addresses others as "wretch", there is an absence of the stain of anger. "This inspired utterance" (imaṃ udānaṃ) means He uttered this inspired utterance which clarifies the attainment of the highest fruit (arahantship) by that Elder.

In that verse, "In whom there dwells no deceit (māyā) nor conceit (māna)" means: in that Noble Person (ariya), there dwells no deceit, characterized by concealing one's own faults, nor conceit, characterized by haughtiness arising from self-exaltation such as "I am better". Because they have been uprooted by the Path, they do not occur and do not arise. "Who is free from greed (vītalobho), without selfishness (amamo), without longing (nirāso)" means: he is free from greed because greed, characterized by grasping at objects through various forms of lust (rāga), is entirely gone. Because of that very absence of greed, he is without selfishness (amamo), having no sense of "mine" or possession in any object such as visible forms; and he is without longing (nirāso) because he does not yearn for future existences and so forth. "Who has expelled anger" (panuṇṇakodho) means: he has expelled anger because anger, characterized by being incensed, has been entirely abandoned by the Path of Non-returning (anāgāmimagga), and his resentment (āghāta) is utterly cut off. "With a mind that is perfectly cooled" (abhinibbutatto) means: because all defilements have been well abandoned along with the uprooting of deceit, conceit, greed, and anger, his mind is perfectly cooled and tranquil through the total parinibbāna of defilements. He—
176:
"He is a Brāhmaṇa, he is a Samaṇa, he is a Bhikkhu" means that such an Arahant, whose taints are exhausted, is called a Brāhmaṇa because he has warded off all evil. He is called a Samaṇa because he has stilled evil and because of his even conduct. He is called a Bhikkhu because he has completely destroyed the defilements. O monks, how could such a person as Ven. Vaccha perform any bodily action, etc., out of a mind of anger? However, because he has not yet abandoned his habitual tendencies (vāsanā), he addresses others with the word "wretch" (vasala) merely out of habit.

## The Commentary on the Sixth Sutta is finished.

## 7. Commentary on the Sakkudāna Sutta

In the seventh sutta, regarding the passage "sitting for seven days in a single cross-legged posture, having attained a certain concentration," some teachers first say: "In this context, 'a certain concentration' should be understood as the Concentration of the Fruition of Arahantship (arahattaphala-samādhi)." This is true. That venerable one frequently enters that Concentration of the Fruition of Arahantship for the sake of a pleasant dwelling in this very life, and he is able to pass the time for seven days in the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti).

This is indeed true. The Blessed One placed the Venerable Mahākassapa on an equal footing with himself in terms of the superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma) such as the nine successive attainments and the six higher powers, saying: "Monks, for as long as I wish, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states... I dwell. Monks, Kassapa also, for as long as he wishes, secluded from sensual pleasures... dwells." Although he was placed on an equal footing with the Teacher, it should not be said that "the Elder Mahākassapa could also perform the Twin Miracle." This is because only the jhānas and other attainments common to disciples are intended here.

However, the ancient teachers (porāṇā) say: "Having attained a certain concentration" means having attained the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti). Why is the attainment of cessation called "concentration" (samādhi)? It is called concentration in the sense of "placing well" (samādhāna). What is this sense of "placing well"? It is the state of being placed perfectly. This attainment of cessation is unshakable by opposing states because of the two powers—the power of serenity (samatha-bala) and the power of insight (vipassanā-bala)—and it is associated with the contemplations of impermanence, suffering, non-self, revulsion, dispassion, cessation, relinquishment, and turning away (anicca-dukkha-anatta-nibbidā-virāga-nirodha-paṭinissagga-vivaṭṭānupassanā), as well as the four Path knowledges and the four Fruition knowledges...
177: ...by means of these sixteen knowledges and sixteen knowledge-modes (ñāṇacariya), and by means of the nine concentration-modes (samādhicariya) through the nine concentrations (the eight attainments starting with the first jhāna concentration taken together, and their access concentration), an Arahant or a Non-returner (Anāgāmī) who has attained mastery in the aforementioned states and wishes to dwell thus through the successive stilling of the three formations—bodily formation (kāyasaṅkhāra), verbal formation (vacīsaṅkhāra), and mental formation (cittasaṅkhāra)—brings about the perfect non-occurrence of the flow of mind and mental factors for the desired duration. This state of being thus well-placed is the meaning of 'well-placed' (samādhāna) here. Therefore, this dwelling is called concentration (samādhi), but not in the sense of non-distraction (avikkhepa). By this sense of 'well-placed', it should be understood that the meaning of 'attainment' (samāpatti) for that term 'concentration' is also stated. Regarding this Attainment of Cessation, it is asked in the Paṭisambhidāmagga: "How is it that there is knowledge of the attainment of the cessation of perception through mastery in the sixteen knowledge-modes and nine concentration-modes for the successive stilling of the three formations, due to being endowed with the two powers?" The explanation is given in detail: "By the two powers" means the power of serenity and the power of insight. The discussion on the Attainment of Cessation is already explained in the Visuddhimagga. Why does this Elder enter the Attainment of Cessation instead of the Fruition Attainment? He enters it out of compassion for beings. Indeed, this Great Elder makes use of all attainments, but he mostly enters the Attainment of Cessation out of a desire to favor beings. This is because even a small offering made to a person who has just emerged from the Attainment of Cessation is especially of great fruit and great benefit. "Wuṭṭhāsi" means he emerged through the arising of the Fruition-consciousness of Arahantship. When one who has entered the Attainment of Cessation is an Arahant, he is said to have emerged through the arising of the Fruition-consciousness of Arahantship; if he is a Non-returner, through the arising of the Fruition-consciousness of Non-returning. At that time, Sakka, the king of devas, desired to give alms-food to the Venerable Mahākassapa. Why did he have such a desire? Previously, Sakka had sent five hundred celestial maidens, his attendants who had feet as soft as a dove's (kakuṭapādiniyo), saying: "The noble Mahākassapa will enter the city of Rājagaha for alms; go and give an offering to the Elder." They went and stood there, desiring to offer divine food.
178:
Being rejected by the Elder, they returned only to the celestial realm. Now, reflecting on the previous rejection and thinking, "Perhaps he might accept this time," they wished to give alms to the Elder who had emerged from meditative attainment. Without informing Sakka, they came on their own and offered divine food. As before, the Elder rejected them, and they returned to the celestial realm. When Sakka asked, "Where did you go?" they reported the matter. When Sakka asked, "Did you give alms-food to the Elder?" they replied, "He did not wish to accept." "What did he say?" he asked. "Great King, he said, 'I will favor the poor,'" they replied. "In what form did you go?" he asked. "In this very (divine) form, Great King," they replied. Sakka said, "How could those like you give alms-food to the Elder?" Wishing to give alms himself, he turned into an old, decrepit weaver with broken teeth, grey hair, and a bent body. He made Sujātā, the Asura princess, into a similarly old woman. He created a weavers' street and sat there stretching out the web, while Sujātā filled the shuttle. Regarding this, it is said (in the Pāḷi): "At that time, Sakka, the king of devas... (pe)... was filling the shuttle."

In that passage, "tantaṃ vināti" means he was as if weaving the stretched-out web. "Tasaraṃ pūreti" means as if filling the shuttle-spool. "Yena sakko devānamindo nivesanaṃ tenupasaṅkami" means the Elder, having dressed and taken his bowl and robes, intending "I will favor the poor," headed toward the city. Reaching the weavers' street created by Sakka outside the city and looking around, he saw a dilapidated, ruined old hall. Seeing the couple there performing weaving work as described, he thought: "These people must work even in their old age. I think there are no people poorer than these in this city. I will favor them by accepting even just the boiled vegetables they offer." He headed toward their house. Seeing the Elder coming, Sakka said to Sujātā: "Lady, my Master is coming this way. Sit quietly as if you do not see him. We shall give alms by deceiving him in a moment." The Elder went and stood at the door of the house. They also waited a little, doing their work as if they did not see him. Then Sakka said: "It seems an Elder is standing at the door; go and investigate." "You go and investigate, lord," she said. He came out of the house, paid homage to the Elder with the fivefold prostration, and rising while groaning and clutching his knees with both hands, he stepped back a little and asked, "Which Elder is the Master?"...
179:
...saying, "My eyes are blurry," he placed his hand on his forehead, looked up, and said, "Oh, how sad! Our Master, the Elder Mahākassapa, has come to my door after a long time. Is there anything in the house?" Sujātā, acting a bit flustered, replied, "There is, lord." Sakka said, "Venerable Sir, please favor us without considering whether it is coarse or refined," and took the bowl. While giving the bowl, the Elder thought, "I should favor these poor, decrepit people." Sakka entered the house, took the rice called ghaṭiodana from the pot, filled the bowl, and placed it in the Elder's hand. Regarding this, it is said: "Sakka, the king of devas, saw... (pe)... and gave."

In that passage, "ghaṭiyā" means from the rice-pot. There is also a variant reading "ghaṭiodanaṃ"; they say that ghaṭiodana is a special kind of food for devas. "Uddharitvā" means having taken out from some vessel. That food, complete with various soups, appeared like the coarse food suitable for the poor when it was being put into the bowl and placed in the Elder's hand, but as soon as it was placed in the hand, it remained in its own divine nature. "Anekasūpo" means having many kinds of soups made from green gram, black gram, etc., and various kinds of snacks. "Anekabyañjano" means having various kinds of side dishes. "Anekarasabyañjano" means that which makes the primary tastes like sweetness and mixed tastes very distinct through many soups and side dishes; it means having various excellent soups and side dishes.

When that alms-food was placed in the Elder's hand, the entire city of Rājagaha was suffused with its divine fragrance. Then the Elder thought: "This man seems to have little merit, but the alms-food is extremely refined, like the food of Sakka. Who is this?" Knowing he was Sakka, he said: "Kosiya, you have done a serious deed by robbing the poor of their fortune. By giving alms to me today, some poor person could have obtained the position of a general or a treasurer." "Venerable Sir, is there anyone poorer than I?" he asked. "How can you be poor while enjoying the glory of the sovereignty of devas?" he asked. "Venerable Sir, it is indeed so; however, I performed good deeds before the Buddha appeared. But while the Buddha has appeared, these three devaputtas—Cūḷaratha, Mahāratha, and Anekavaṇṇa—having performed meritorious deeds..."
180:
"The young devas born in my vicinity are far more powerful and majestic than I. When those devas, saying 'We shall play at the star festival,' take their retinues and descend to the main street, I flee and enter my house. For the radiance from their bodies overwhelms my body, but the radiance from my body does not overwhelm theirs. Venerable sir, who could be more destitute than I?"

(The Elder) said, "Even so, from now on, do not deceive me in this way to give alms." "Venerable sir, is there merit for me when alms are given by deceiving you, or is there not?" (Sakka asked). "There is, friend," (the Elder) replied. "Venerable sir, if that is so, then performing merit is indeed my responsibility," he said. After paying homage to the Elder, taking the goddess Sujā with him, and circumambulating the Elder, he rose into the air and uttered this inspired utterance three times: "Oh, the gift! The supreme gift is well established in Kassapa!" Therefore, it is said (in the Pali), "Then this thought occurred to the Venerable Mahākassapa," and so forth.

In that passage, 'Kosiya' is an address to Sakka, the king of devas, by his clan name. 'Puññena attho' means having a need for merit. The word 'atthi' (there is) is the remaining part of the sentence. 'Vehāsaṃ abbhuggantvā' means rising from the ground into the sky. 'Ākāse antalikkhe' means that the sky is called 'antalikkhe' by way of a synonym. Or rather, it is said specifically to mean the sky known as the atmosphere, and not the space [arising from] the removal of a kasina and so forth. In the phrase 'Aho dānaṃ', 'aho' is an exclamation used in the sense of wonder. Indeed, Sakka, the king of devas, [thought:] "Since this gift of divine food was given by me with my own hands, respectfully, with honor, without discarding anything, at the proper time, without harming others, and preceded by right view, to the Venerable Mahākassapa who had just arisen from cessation (nirodha); therefore, because it is endowed with the three types of perfection—perfection of the field (khetta-sampatti), perfection of the gift (deyyadhamma-sampatti), and perfection of the mind (citta-sampatti)—I have indeed performed a gift complete in all its factors." Thus, with a heart full of great wonder and joy, expressing the rapture and happiness arising within his heart at that time, he said "Aho dānaṃ," and manifesting the supreme nature of that gift and its establishment in a noble recipient as previously described, he uttered the inspired utterance: "The supreme gift is well established in Kassapa!"

While Sakka was thus uttering this inspired utterance, the Blessed One, while staying in the monastery, heard that sound with his divine ear and said to the monks, "Look, monks, at Sakka, the king of devas, who is going through the sky uttering an inspired utterance." When asked by the monks, "But Venerable Sir, what has he done?" he said, "He gave alms to my son Kassapa by deception, and he is uttering an inspired utterance out of joy for that." Therefore, it is said, "The Blessed One heard with the divine ear-element," and so forth. In that passage, 'dibbāya sotadhātuyā' is called 'divine' (dibba) because it is like the ears of devas. In truth, devas possess a sensitive ear-element (pasāda-sota-dhātu) produced by meritorious kamma, which is not disturbed by bile, phlegm, blood, etc., and being free from impurities, can pick up even distant sounds. This ear-element of the Blessed One, which arose through the power of noble cultivation (ariya-bhāvanā), is also called 'divine' because it is similar to those ears of the devas. Alternatively, it is so called because it arises through the power of the divine abiding (dibba-vihāra).
181:
In that passage, "dibbayā sotadhātuyā" (by the divine ear-element) is called "divine" (dibba) because it is similar to that of the devas. Indeed, the devas possess a divine sensitive ear-element (pasāda-sotadhātu) that is born of their well-performed karma, is not obstructed by bile, phlegm, blood, etc., and is free from impurities, thus being capable of grasping an object even at a distance. This ear-element of the Blessed One, which consists of knowledge and is born of the power of his energy and meditation (vīriya-bhāvanā), is also like that of the devas; thus it is called "divine" because of its similarity to the divine. Furthermore, it is called "divine" because it is obtained by means of the divine abiding (dibba-vihāra) and because he himself dwells in that divine abiding. It is called "ear-element" (sotadhātu) because of the sense of hearing and because it bears its own nature. It is also called "ear-element" because it performs the function of an ear-element; by that divine ear-element (he heard).

"Visuddhāya" (purified) means completely pure and free from the defilements that cause impurity. "Atikkantamānusikāya" (surpassing that of humans) means standing beyond the human range and surpassing the human fleshly ear-element by hearing sounds.

"Etam-atthaṃ viditvā" (knowing this meaning) means knowing this meaning: "Gods and humans, filled with respect, greatly admire a superior man who is established in the special qualities of right practice," and thus he uttered this inspired utterance (udāna) that clarifies that meaning.

In that inspired verse, "piṇḍapātikassa" (for one who is an alms-food eater) is said because he undertakes and fulfills the ascetic practice (dhutaṅga) known as the alms-food eater's practice. Was this verse not spoken concerning the Venerable Mahākassapa? Since the Elder is the foremost of all those who profess the ascetic practices and is a bearer of all thirteen ascetic practices, why is he praised for only one ascetic practice? This description is made according to the specific occasion (aṭṭhuppatti). Or, this is merely the head of the teaching; by this head of the teaching, all his ascetic practices should be understood as mentioned. Alternatively, according to the method stated in the verse "Just as a bee [collects nectar from] a flower" (Dhp. 49), because of his extreme fewness of wishes and his compassion for families, he did not break any of the duties of an alms-food eater; thus "piṇḍapātikassa" is said to show his superior practice in that regard. The word "piṇḍapātikassa" is in the dative case in relation to the word "pihayanti" (they admire), but it should be understood in the sense of the accusative (the object). "Attabharassa" (for one who supports himself) means for one who supports only himself with the four requisites that are described as "few, easy to get, and blameless." "Ananyaposinno" (not supporting others) means one who is not anxious to support others, such as disciples, by providing material gifts (āmisa). By these two words, his light livelihood and ease of support are shown, as he wanders with robes to cover the body and alms-food to fill the stomach...
182:
...shows contentment. Alternatively, "attabharassa" in the singular means he supports only this one self, known as the individual existence (attabhāva), and no one else besides this; thus he is "self-supporting." Because he supports only himself, there is no other to be supported by him, thus he is "not supporting others." By these two words, the state of an Arahant (khīṇāsava) who has no future grasping is shown.

"Devā pihayanti... satīmato" (Devas admire... the mindful one) means that Sakka and other devas admire and long for that Arahant who is peaceful due to the subsiding of all distress and fever of defilements through the attainment of the highest fruit (arahatta-phala); who is mindful because he always acts with mindfulness due to reaching the fullness of mindfulness; and who, for that very reason, has reached the state of "suchness" (tādi) amidst the agreeable and disagreeable. They generate respect and great esteem for his special qualities such as virtue (sīla). If this is so for devas, what need is there to mention humans?

## The Commentary on the Seventh Sutta is finished.

## 8. Commentary on the Piṇḍapātika Sutta

In the eighth sutta, "pacchābhattaṃ" (after the meal) means that for those who have undertaken the practice of eating at one sitting (ekāsanika) or the practice of not eating after time (khalupacchābhattika) and have eaten in the morning, even the time within midday is "after the meal." However, in this sutta, "after the meal" should be understood as the time after the usual meal. "Piṇḍapātapaṭikkantānaṃ" (for those who have returned from the alms-round) means for the monks who have returned from seeking alms-food by way of finishing the meal-duty. In the phrase "karerimaṇḍalamāḷe" (in the Karerī circular pavilion), "Karerī" is the name of the Varuna tree. It is said that this tree stood between the Perfumed Chamber (Gandhakuṭī) and the pavilion or hall. Therefore, the Perfumed Chamber is also called the "Karerī hut" (karerikuṭikā), and both the pavilion and the hall are called the "Karerī circular pavilion." Thus, it refers to the circular pavilion, which is a sitting hall, built not far from the Karerī tree. Some say a "circular pavilion" (maṇḍalamāḷa) is a rain-proof place covered with grass and leaves. Others say it is a pavilion made of creepers such as the Atimuttaka.

"Kālena kālaṃ" (from time to time) means at various times or on certain occasions. "Manāpike" (pleasing) means mind-expanding, having a dear form, or "agreeable" (iṭṭha). The state of being agreeable (iṭṭha) or disagreeable (aniṭṭha) should be taken according to the person and according to the sense-door. For an object that is considered highly agreeable to one person may be disagreeable to another. An object that is considered highly disagreeable to one person may be [agreeable] to another.
183:
That Kareri tree stands between the Gandhakuti and the pavilion hall. Therefore, the Gandhakuti is also called the Kareri-kuṭikā. The pavilion and the hall are likewise called the Kareri-maṇḍalamāḷa. Thus, the Maṇḍalamāḷa is a rest house built not far from the Kareri tree; a place covered with grass and leaves that is not wet by rain is called a Maṇḍalamāḷa. Other teachers, however, say that a pavilion made of vines such as acacia (kin-pun) is a Maṇḍalamāḷa. 'Kālena kālaṃ' means at all times, or from time to time. 'Manāpike' means that which causes the mind to increase in joy, being of a lovely nature, or agreeable (iṭṭha). The state of being agreeable (iṭṭha) or disagreeable (aniṭṭha) is taken by the power of the individual or by the power of the sense-door. An object that is intensely reflected upon as agreeable by one person may be disagreeable to another. Similarly, an object reflected upon as disagreeable by one may be agreeable to another.

In the same way, an object that is agreeable to one sense-door may be disagreeable to another. However, in this context, the determination should be understood by the power of the resultant (vipāka). A wholesome resultant (kusala-vipāka) is strictly agreeable (iṭṭha), while an unwholesome resultant (akusala-vipāka) is strictly disagreeable (aniṭṭha).
